Detailed Findings (341)

CRITICAL P1 · 91 Gateway secinfo has overly permissive permit rules INTG-GW-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags gateway secinfo rules that permit all programs from all hosts (wildcard program and wildcard/blank host on a P/permit rule), effectively disabling the gateway's program-start authorization. The SAP Gateway's secinfo ACL controls which external programs may be started via the gateway (e.g. RFC server programs launched on demand); a permit-all rule means any host can instruct the gateway to start any program, which is a textbook remote code execution exposure on the application server host. This is precisely the class of misconfiguration weaponized by the 10KBLAZE exploit, which used permissive secinfo/reginfo (and message-server ACLs) to run arbitrary OS commands on SAP servers with the privileges of the <sid>adm user. Attack scenario: an attacker who can reach the gateway port (sapgwNN, typically 33NN) sends a start request for an OS command or a malicious program; with permit-all in place the gateway launches it under <sid>adm, giving the attacker command execution, then full compromise of the SAP system and its data. Because <sid>adm owns the SAP kernel and data files, this typically means total system takeover, credential theft (SAPSYS/DB), and lateral movement across the landscape. Business impact: full RCE, data breach, ransomware staging, and a critical audit failure - permissive gateway ACLs are one of the most severe SAP misconfigurations. A real incident looks like unexpected external programs started via the gateway (SMGW logs), new OS processes under <sid>adm, and subsequent data exfiltration or encryption. This is critical and should be remediated urgently.
Affected Items (1)
  • Rule: P TP=* HOST=* USER=*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the current secinfo file and confirm the permissive entries in SMGW (Goto → Expert Functions → External Security → Display/Reread) and via RZ11 for the gateway parameters. 2. Enforce ACL processing by setting gw/acl_mode = 1 (per SAP Note 1408081) and ensure gw/sec_info points to the maintained secinfo file (RZ10/RZ11). 3. Replace every wildcard permit with specific rules of the form 'P TP=<program> HOST=<source> USER-HOST=<host> USER=<user>' for each legitimate program/host combination. 4. Add an explicit deny-all default rule as the last line (see INTG-GW-002). 5. Use gateway logging/simulation (gw/logging, monitor mode) first to capture the legitimate program-start traffic so no required interface is lost. 6. Where external program start is not needed at all, disable it via gw/rem_start = DISABLED. 7. Reload the ACL (SMGW → Expert Functions → Reread) - most changes apply without restart, but plan a restart window if parameters changed. 8. Verify by attempting a disallowed program start (expect rejection in SMGW logs) and confirming legitimate RFC servers still start. 9. Apply consistently across every application server instance (each has its own gateway). 10. Feed SMGW security logs to the SIEM to detect future abuse. Caution: build the specific permit list from real captured traffic in non-prod/monitor mode before enforcing, or you will break legitimate registered-server and program-start interfaces.
References
  • SAP Note 1408081 — Gateway Security
  • SAP Note 2776748 — Gateway ACL Hardening
CRITICAL P1 · 91 Gateway reginfo permits unrestricted RFC server registration INTG-GW-004 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags gateway reginfo rules that permit any RFC server program (TP) to register from any host (wildcard TP and wildcard/blank host on a permit rule). The reginfo ACL governs which external RFC server programs may register with the gateway to receive RFC calls; a permit-all rule lets an attacker register a rogue RFC server under the name of a legitimate program and then intercept or inject RFC traffic. This is a powerful man-in-the-middle and impersonation primitive: registered servers receive the RFC requests routed to their program id, so a rogue registration can capture the data (including credentials and business payloads) that legitimate callers send, and can return manipulated responses. Attack scenario: an attacker on a reachable host registers an RFC server using the program id of a real integration (e.g. a tax or bank connector); the gateway, lacking restriction, accepts it; subsequent RFC calls intended for the real server are delivered to the attacker, who harvests sensitive data or feeds back forged results, corrupting downstream processing. Rogue registration can also be chained with program-start abuse for broader compromise, and it is a core technique in the 10KBLAZE attack class. Business impact: interception of RFC data (credentials, financial/HR content), data integrity corruption, and potential foothold for deeper compromise - a critical control failure against SAP Note 1408081. A real incident looks like unexpected RFC server registrations in SMGW (registered clients list) from unknown hosts, and integration data anomalies or leakage. This is critical because it undermines the trustworthiness of the entire RFC integration channel.
Affected Items (1)
  • Rule: P TP=* HOST=*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SMGW review registered servers and the reginfo file; confirm gw/reg_info points to the maintained file and gw/acl_mode = 1 (RZ10/RZ11, SAP Note 1408081). 2. Replace wildcard permits with specific rules naming each legitimate TP (program id), the exact registering HOST, and where applicable the access/cancel host restrictions. 3. Add an explicit deny-all default as the final line (see INTG-GW-005). 4. Consider setting gw/reg_no_conn_info appropriately and use CANCEL/ACCESS host controls to bind each program id to its known server host. 5. Use gateway monitor/simulation mode first to capture the legitimate set of program ids and source hosts so no integration server is locked out. 6. Reload the ACL (SMGW → Expert Functions → Reread). 7. Verify by attempting to register a test RFC server from a non-permitted host/program (expect rejection) and confirming the real integration servers still register. 8. Review SMGW registered-server list for any currently unexpected registrations and investigate them. 9. Apply consistently across all application-server instances. 10. Forward SMGW registration events to the SIEM to alert on new/unexpected registrations. Caution: build the permit list from real captured registrations in non-prod/monitor mode before enforcing - blocking a legitimate program id will silently break that RFC integration.
References
  • SAP Note 1408081 — Gateway Registration Security
  • SAP Note 2776748
CRITICAL P1 · 91 Missing HotNews (Priority 1) SAP Security Notes HOTNEWS-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding lists HotNews Security Notes (Priority 1, CVSS 9.0-10.0) from the curated catalog that are not recorded as implemented. HotNews notes fix the most severe SAP defects, and several here are pre-authentication, network-only remote-compromise flaws: RECON (CVE-2020-6287, note 2934135) in the AS Java LM Configuration Wizard, ICMAD (CVE-2022-22536, note 3123396) in the ICM/Web Dispatcher, the NetWeaver Visual Composer file-upload RCEs (CVE-2025-31324 note 3594142; CVE-2021-38163 note 3084487), the AS Java P4 missing-auth flaw (CVE-2023-23857 note 3252433), ABAP file-upload CVE-2024-33006 (note 3448171), ABA code injection CVE-2024-22131 (note 3420923) and the BTP @sap/xssec privilege escalation (CVE-2023-49583 note 3411067). The common thread is that an attacker needs only reachability to the HTTP(S)/ICM port or the Java stack — no valid SAP credentials. Concrete chain: with RECON the attacker POSTs to /CTCWebService/CTCWebServiceBean and creates a UME administrator, then pivots via trusted RFC/SSO into the connected S/4HANA ABAP system to create fictitious vendors, release payment runs (F110) or read mass HR/PII; with Visual Composer the attacker uploads a JSP webshell into servlet_jsp/irj/root/ and executes OS commands as <sid>adm, giving full read/write to the SAP database. Business and compliance impact is maximal: financial fraud, mass personal-data breach triggering GDPR Art. 32/33 notification within 72 hours, SOX ITGC failure, and ransomware staging. A real incident mirrors the April 2025 CVE-2025-31324 campaign in which threat actors and ransomware affiliates mass-scanned internet-facing NetWeaver and dropped webshells within hours of exposure. In RISE, these application-layer notes remain the customer's responsibility even though SAP runs the platform.
Affected Items (6)
  • Note 2934135 / CVE-2020-6287 / NetWeaver AS Java (LM Configuration Wizard) (CVSS 10.0, 2020-07) — RECON — unauthenticated account takeover / full compromise
  • Note 3123396 / CVE-2022-22536 / NetWeaver ABAP/Java, Web Dispatcher, Content Server (ICM) (CVSS 10.0, 2022-02) — ICMAD — HTTP request smuggling in ICM / Web Dispatcher
  • Note 3594142 / CVE-2025-31324 / NetWeaver Visual Composer (Metadata Uploader) (CVSS 10.0, 2025-04) — Unrestricted file upload → RCE in Visual Composer
  • Note 3252433 / CVE-2023-23857 / NetWeaver AS Java (P4 / open naming & directory API) (CVSS 9.9, 2023-03) — Improper access control (missing authentication check)
  • Note 3448171 / CVE-2024-33006 / NetWeaver AS ABAP (file upload) (CVSS 9.6, 2024-05) — Unrestricted file upload in SAP NetWeaver ABAP
  • Note 3411067 / CVE-2023-49583 / BTP Security Services (@sap/xssec) (CVSS 9.1, 2024-01) — Privilege escalation via SAP BTP security-services library
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Take the affected_items list and, for each note, confirm applicability to your exact product version and Support Package in System Recommendations (Solution Manager) or SAP Cloud ALM (RISE). 2. Download and implement each correcting note in transaction SNOTE; where SAP ships the fix only in a Support Package, plan it via Maintenance Planner and deploy with SPAM/SAINT. 3. For kernel-resident fixes such as ICMAD (note 3123396), replace the disp+work kernel to the patched patch level rather than using SNOTE, then restart the instance. 4. Execute every manual pre-/post-implementation step the note specifies — e.g. RECON additionally requires locking down the LM Configuration Wizard and disabling unused services in transaction SICF; do not mark the note done until these are complete. 5. For the BTP finding (@sap/xssec, note 3411067), update the library to the fixed version in your CAP/Node.js apps and redeploy through the Cloud Foundry/Kyma pipeline. 6. Route all changes through change control: implement in DEV, regression-test interfaces/IDocs/RFCs in QA, then PROD in a maintenance window. 7. For RISE landscapes, raise the change with SAP ECS via the agreed maintenance-planning process; coordinate kernel/DB actions they own with the ABAP notes you own. 8. Where an immediate patch is impossible, apply the note's documented compensating control (e.g. block the vulnerable ICF path, restrict the port at the Web Dispatcher/firewall) as an interim measure. 9. Verify each fix: SNOTE status must read 'Completely Implemented' (PRSTATUS = E), System Recommendations must drop the note after the SM:SYSTEM RECOMMENDATIONS collector re-runs, and kernel level must be confirmed via System > Status / SM51. 10. Institutionalise a monthly SAP Security Patch Day triage with a HotNews SLA. Caution: always test in non-prod first; kernel and Support Package changes require downtime and interface-owner coordination.

  • CISA — SAP exploitation advisories
CRITICAL P1 · 91 Armed background job runs under SAP*/DDIC or a SAP_ALL step user JOBCMD-JOB-001 ▶
Security Risk
Every background job step carries a step user in table TBTCP field AUTHCKNAM (header TBTCO-AUTHCKNAM), the identity whose authorizations are checked when the step runs. Here an armed job (TBTCO STATUS scheduled/released/ready/active) runs under SAP*, DDIC, or a holder of SAP_ALL / SAP_NEW. The step executes with that identity's full authorization - for SAP_ALL/DDIC/SAP* this is effectively unrestricted superuser access. Any report, SUBMIT, or external command in the job therefore runs with unlimited authority, bypassing SoD and every table/tcode restriction. This directly violates SAP's baseline rule that background/technical users must not hold SAP_ALL. It turns a routine scheduled job into a standing privilege-escalation vehicle. Attack scenario: a user who can create/edit a job step (S_BTCH_JOB / S_BTCH_ADM) points the step user at DDIC and submits RSBDCOS0 or a Z-report. The job then runs as DDIC with SAP_ALL and executes OS commands (as <sid>adm) or mass data changes with no further authorization checks. Business impact in S/4HANA: unrestricted read/write to FI/CO, MM and HR/PA, plus OS command execution on the app server. It is a full control-bypass and, in most jurisdictions, a reportable breach if abused. It also destroys accountability - activity is attributed to a shared technical account, not the real actor. Real incident: a legacy job left running as DDIC after a migration was abused by an attacker who compromised a mid-tier account, edited the step to run their own report as DDIC/SAP_ALL, exfiltrated payroll data, and left an audit trail pointing only at DDIC.
Affected Items (2)
  • JOB_FI_CLOSE — step user DDIC
  • JOB_MASS_UPD — step user JSMITH
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify: SM37 (Job Overview with the widest selection - all users, all statuses) and inspect each step's user; or SE16 on TBTCP/TBTCO where AUTHCKNAM in (SAP*, DDIC). 2. Cross-check SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW holders via SUIM (Users by Profile) or report RSUSR002 and treat those as critical step users too. 3. Create or reuse a dedicated least-privilege background user of type B (System) in SU01 for each job family. 4. Build its role in PFCG from the job's actual authorization objects (capture them with authorization trace STAUTHTRACE / ST01 during a QA run). 5. Re-plan each job onto the technical user: SM36/SM37 -> change the step's user (or delete and recreate the step) so AUTHCKNAM is the new account; save. 6. Remove SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW from any technical batch user still carrying it (SU01 -> profiles), and ensure SAP*/DDIC are locked/secured and not used for productive jobs. 7. Restrict who can set a foreign step user: authorization object S_BTCH_NAM (field BTCUSERNM) and S_BTCH_ADM - grant narrowly in PFCG; review holders with SUIM. 8. Verify: SE16 TBTCP shows no armed step under SAP*/DDIC/SAP_ALL. 9. Run each re-planned job in QA and confirm it completes; watch the SM37 job log and ST22 for missing-authorization dumps. 10. Add the new technical users to periodic critical-authorization scans (report RSUSR008_009_NEW) to prevent scope creep. 11. Rollout caution: an under-privileged new step user will fail the job - capture exact authorizations first, stage in DEV/QA, and cut over in a maintenance window since batch changes affect production processing.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — background users must not hold SAP_ALL
  • SAP Help — Background job step authorization user (SM36/SM37)
CRITICAL P1 · 90 Missing notes for actively-exploited SAP vulnerabilities HOTNEWS-003 ▶
Security Risk
This is the highest-urgency finding: it lists catalog vulnerabilities marked as actively exploited in the wild (public exploit code / CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) whose correcting notes are not recorded as implemented. The exploited set includes RECON (CVE-2020-6287, note 2934135), the Solution Manager missing-authentication flaw (CVE-2020-6207, note 2890213), ICMAD (CVE-2022-22536, note 3123396), and the two Visual Composer file-upload RCEs (CVE-2025-31324 note 3594142; CVE-2021-38163 note 3084487). Unlike theoretical CVSS ratings, 'exploited' means weaponised tooling already exists — Metasploit/PoC modules, mass-scanning botnets, and in the CVE-2025-31324 case confirmed ransomware-affiliate activity — so the window between exposure and compromise is measured in hours, not weeks. Attack chain for the Solution Manager flaw: an unauthenticated attacker abuses the missing auth check in the EEM/diagnostics agent to run OS commands on the SolMan host, which by design holds trusted RFC connections to every managed production system — turning one exposed SolMan into a landscape-wide compromise. For Visual Composer, attackers POST to /developmentserver/metadatauploader and drop a JSP webshell in servlet_jsp/irj/root/, then execute OS commands as <sid>adm. The business impact is worst-case: full system takeover, data exfiltration, fraudulent financial postings, and ransomware. Compliance consequences are severe — mandatory breach notification (GDPR Art. 33), SOX material-weakness reporting, and regulatory scrutiny for ignoring a CISA-catalogued KEV. A real incident looks exactly like the 2025 NetWeaver campaign: internet-facing SAP compromised, webshells and Brute Ratel/Cobalt Strike loaders deployed, and lateral movement into the corporate network. These items warrant out-of-band emergency patching and active compromise-hunting now.
Affected Items (3)
  • Note 2934135 / CVE-2020-6287 / NetWeaver AS Java (LM Configuration Wizard) (CVSS 10.0, 2020-07) — RECON — unauthenticated account takeover / full compromise
  • Note 3123396 / CVE-2022-22536 / NetWeaver ABAP/Java, Web Dispatcher, Content Server (ICM) (CVSS 10.0, 2022-02) — ICMAD — HTTP request smuggling in ICM / Web Dispatcher
  • Note 3594142 / CVE-2025-31324 / NetWeaver Visual Composer (Metadata Uploader) (CVSS 10.0, 2025-04) — Unrestricted file upload → RCE in Visual Composer
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Treat every listed note as an emergency change — invoke your out-of-band/emergency patch process immediately rather than waiting for the next cycle. 2. In parallel with patching, hunt for indicators of compromise: for Visual Composer inspect servlet_jsp/irj/root/ and the metadatauploader/developmentserver paths for unexpected .jsp/.war/.jar files; for RECON check USR02/SU01 and the AS Java UME for unrecognised admin users and review LM Configuration Wizard / CTCWebService access logs; for ICMAD review ICM access logs for anomalous/duplicated responses. 3. Implement the correcting notes via SNOTE, or apply the required kernel patch (ICMAD 3123396) and restart, or the AS Java patch (Visual Composer) — deploy the emergency patch SAP shipped for note 3594142. 4. If patching cannot be immediate, apply the note's interim mitigation now: disable the vulnerable service (e.g. remove/disable the Visual Composer VCFRAMEWORK and the metadatauploader endpoint, deactivate unused ICF services in SICF) and block external access at the Web Dispatcher/firewall. 5. For Solution Manager (note 2890213), because SolMan holds trusted RFC into production, also review and, if needed, rotate those trusted RFC connections and check for lateral movement. 6. If any IoC is found, do NOT just patch — invoke incident response, isolate the host, preserve forensics, and assume credential/data compromise. 7. For RISE, escalate to SAP ECS as a Priority 1 / security incident and coordinate emergency maintenance. 8. Verify each fix in SNOTE (PRSTATUS = E) and confirm kernel/AS Java patch level; confirm the vulnerable endpoint now returns 403/404. 9. After remediation, monitor for re-exploitation and add detections for these endpoints. Caution: emergency changes still need a documented back-out plan and interface-owner notification; balance speed against a restart/downtime window.

  • SAP Security Patch Day
CRITICAL P1 · 79 Default user SAP* is unlocked USR-001 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags well-known standard SAP accounts (SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM) whose lock flag USR02-UFLAG is 0 (unlocked). These accounts ship with documented default passwords and their names and credentials are public knowledge, so they are the first thing any attacker or automated scanner tries. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape the ABAP application layer, including standard-user hygiene, is the customer's responsibility under SAP's shared-responsibility model, so an unlocked SAP*/DDIC is customer exposure, not SAP's. SAP* is especially dangerous: if its user master record is deleted and profile parameter login/no_automatic_user_sapstar is 0, the kernel activates a hard-coded emergency SAP* with password PASS and implicit SAP_ALL, bypassing the user table entirely. DDIC owns the Data Dictionary and is used during upgrades/imports; SAPCPIC is a legacy CPIC/RFC user; TMSADM holds broad transport authorizations across the entire transport domain. Attack scenario: an intruder who reaches SAP GUI, the Fiori/Web GUI logon, or the message server tries the default credentials directly, or brute-forces them because these accounts are dialog-capable. On success they immediately grant themselves SAP_ALL, read HR/finance tables, post fraudulent documents, create backdoor users, run OS commands via SM49, or pivot across the transport domain into DEV/QA/PRD. A real incident looks like an off-hours SAP* or DDIC dialog logon from an unusual terminal followed by SU01 user creation and profile assignment. This is a textbook critical audit finding under SOX ITGC, and unauthorized access to financially-relevant and personal data also drives GDPR/data-breach exposure.
Affected Items (1)
  • SAP*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Run report RSUSR003 (via SA38 or SUIM) in every client (000, 001, 066 and all productive clients) to list SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM and see which still have default passwords or are unlocked. 2. For each client, in SU01 set a strong random password and apply an administrator lock to SAP* and DDIC (this sets USR02-UFLAG); only unlock DDIC temporarily for upgrades/imports, then re-lock it. 3. Secure the SAP* emergency logon: set profile parameter login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 1 in RZ10 (DEFAULT/instance profile), activate the profile, and restart the instance in a maintenance window; verify the runtime value with RZ11. 4. Ensure a real SAP* user master record exists in every client so the hard-coded fallback cannot activate; never delete SAP*. 5. For TMSADM, follow SAP Note 1414256 to change its password consistently across the whole transport domain, then restrict its authorizations to the minimum transport scope. 6. Lock SAPCPIC and EARLYWATCH if unused; if EarlyWatch is active, restrict it to minimal monitoring authorizations. 7. Use SU10 for mass lock/password changes when many clients/accounts are affected. 8. Verify by re-running RSUSR003 (no default passwords, standard users locked) and confirming USR02-UFLAG > 0 for SAP*/DDIC. 9. Enable the Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG / SM19) with a filter to alert on any dialog logon by these accounts. 10. Caution: locking DDIC can break scheduled imports/upgrades and the SAP* parameter change needs an instance restart, so test in DEV/QA and schedule a maintenance window with Basis.
References
  • SAP Note 1414256 — Secure default users
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 2.1
