A realistic incident is a post-breach investigation that finds no audit log at all: the team cannot scope which data was accessed or exfiltrated, cannot identify the actor, and must conservatively assume worst-case data loss, which magnifies breach-notification obligations and cost.
Affected Items (1)
  • SM19 — 0 active filters
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enable the log by setting the profile parameters: rsau/enable=1, rsau/selection_slots to at least 10, rsau/user_selection=1, rsau/integrity=1, and size the storage with rsau/max_diskspace/local (or log to the database); confirm which parameters are dynamic via RZ11 versus needing a restart per SAP Note 2191612. 2. Configure filters in RSAU_CONFIG (S/4HANA; SM19 on releases before BASIS 755) and activate a static profile. 3. Cover at minimum: dialog and RFC logon failures and successes for privileged users, transaction and report starts, RFC function-module calls, user-master record changes, role and authorization changes, debugging events, and changes to the audit configuration itself. 4. Ensure all events are captured for SAP*, DDIC, and any emergency/firefighter users, with critical events captured for all users. 5. Turn on integrity protection (rsau/integrity=1) so the log is tamper-evident, noting that logs must then be read via RSAU_READ_LOG/SM20 rather than at OS level (SAP Notes 2765858 and 2191612). 6. Forward the log to a SIEM for retention and alerting, and define a retention period meeting policy and regulatory minimums. 7. Verify by confirming RSAU_CONFIG shows an active profile, generating a deliberate failed logon, and confirming it appears in RSAU_READ_LOG/SM20. 8. Caution: broad filters can generate high volume, so size storage appropriately, test in non-production, and schedule any required restart in a maintenance window.
References
  • SAP Note 2191612
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 6.1
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Firefighter sessions not reviewed by controller IAM-FF-003 ▶
Security Risk
This flags emergency/firefighter sessions that were never reviewed by a controller — rated critical because controller review is the primary compensating control that makes broad emergency access acceptable in the first place. The model is: firefighter IDs may carry very high privileges, but every session is logged and an independent controller reviews the captured activity afterward to confirm it matched the stated emergency and contained no unauthorized actions. If sessions go unreviewed, that control has effectively not operated — powerful privileged activity occurred with no one checking what was done. The abuse scenario: a user (or someone who obtained the ID) performs unauthorized privileged actions during a session that is never examined, so fraud, data exfiltration or a planted back door passes silently. Impact is severe on two fronts: real risk of undetected superuser misuse, and a direct SOX Section 404 failure because the compensating control auditors rely on to accept emergency access is demonstrably not being performed. A real incident looks like a post-breach investigation revealing that the malicious change was made during a firefighter session weeks earlier that no controller ever reviewed, meaning the organization had the log evidence all along but never looked.
Affected Items (4)
  • JSMITH as FF_FIN_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-10 08:30:00)
  • JSMITH as FF_FIN_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-22 11:00:00)
  • LWANG as FF_BASIS_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-12 08:00:00)
  • TNGUYEN as FF_HR_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-14 09:00:00)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Immediately assign controllers to review every outstanding session in the list, comparing the logged activity to the stated justification and escalating anomalies. 2. Ensure each firefighter ID has a designated, independent controller in GRC EAM (Firefighter ID owner/controller assignment) and that the assignment is current. 3. Configure automated notification/escalation in EAM so controllers receive the log for review promptly and reminders fire if review is not completed. 4. Establish and enforce an SLA (e.g. review within 48 hours of session end) and track compliance. 5. Use the EAM Log Report / consolidated log review workflow as the standard mechanism rather than ad-hoc checks. 6. Verify by re-running the analysis and confirming the backlog is cleared and new sessions are reviewed within SLA. 7. Rollout caution: allocate sufficient controller capacity before tightening SLAs, and ensure controllers are independent of the firefighter users (see IAM-FF-004) so the review is meaningful.
References
  • SAP GRC SPM — Controller Review Configuration
  • SOX Section 404 — Compensating Controls
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Firefighter sessions reviewed by the same user who initiated them IAM-FF-004 ▶
Security Risk
This flags emergency/firefighter sessions that were reviewed or approved by the same person who used the firefighter ID — a self-review that voids the control entirely and is therefore critical. Controller review works only if the controller is independent of the requestor; when the user reviews their own session, there is no oversight at all, only the appearance of one. This is a segregation-of-duties failure inside the control process itself. The abuse scenario: a user checks out the firefighter ID, performs unauthorized privileged actions, then signs off their own session as 'reviewed — no exceptions', producing a clean audit trail that conceals the very misuse the review was meant to catch. It is especially dangerous because it can be entirely deliberate — the person committing the misuse is also the person certifying it was fine. Impact is undetected privileged fraud combined with fabricated assurance, and it is a direct SOX/ITGC control-design deficiency because the compensating control lacks independence. A real incident looks like an insider who both used a firefighter ID to make fraudulent postings and closed out the review themselves, so every periodic control test passed until an unrelated investigation exposed the self-approval pattern.
Affected Items (1)
  • LWANG as FF_BASIS_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-03 22:00:00) — reviewed by: LWANG
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Immediately re-review every self-approved session in the list using a genuinely independent controller, treating them as unreviewed. 2. Enforce controller ≠ requestor in GRC EAM: assign firefighter controllers who are organizationally independent of the firefighter users and never assign a user as their own controller. 3. Configure EAM so the workflow prevents the log reviewer from being the session's actual user (segregate owner/controller/firefighter roles). 4. Review the firefighter owner/controller matrix (GRC EAM master data) to eliminate any circular assignments across the team. 5. Add a periodic control that specifically tests for reviewer = requestor so any recurrence is caught quickly. 6. Verify by re-running the analysis and confirming no session shows the same person as user and reviewer. 7. Rollout caution: ensure enough independent controllers exist before enforcing the rule so emergencies are not left without any valid reviewer, and document the reassignment for audit.
References
  • SAP GRC SPM — Controller Assignment Best Practices
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Non-production systems without PII data masking DPP-MASK-001 ▶
Security Risk
Non-production S/4HANA systems (DEV, QA, TEST, SANDBOX, TRAINING) populated from production but with no PII masking/anonymization expose full, real personal data - names, addresses, phone numbers, bank/IBAN, tax IDs, salaries, national IDs - to a much larger and less-controlled population than production: developers, external consultants, testers, and in RISE potentially third-party implementation partners. Non-prod systems typically have weaker controls (shared/generic accounts, broad SE16/debug authorizations, relaxed password policy, no RAL, less monitoring), so the same PII is far easier to read and exfiltrate there than in production. Attack/abuse scenario: a contractor with a DEV login runs SE16N on PA0008/BUT000/KNA1 or debugs a program to dump live customer and employee data, or simply exports a test result set containing real bank details, with no logging and no business need. Because the data is production-real, this is a reportable personal-data breach even though it happened in a 'test' system - regulators explicitly reject the 'it is only non-prod' defense. Business impact: GDPR Art.5(1)(f)/Art.32 security-of-processing violations, insider fraud enabled by exposed bank/salary data, and a breach surface multiplied across every system copy. A real incident: a leaked QA database export or a departing consultant's local copy is found to contain unmasked production PII, triggering breach notification.
Affected Items (3)
  • DEV_S4H (type: DEVELOPMENT) — PII masking: not enabled
  • SANDBOX_S4H (type: SANDBOX) — PII masking: not enabled
  • TRAINING_S4H (type: TRAINING) — PII masking: not enabled
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory all non-production systems and identify which contain production-derived data (see DPP-MASK-002). 2. Implement masking during every system copy/refresh: for at-rest masking use SAP Test Data Migration Server (TDMS) data scrambling; for runtime field masking use SAP UI data protection masking for SAP S/4HANA. 3. Define masking scope to cover all PII: NAME1/NAME2, STRAS/PSTLZ, SMTP_ADDR/TEL_NUMBER, BANKN/BANKL/IBAN, STCD1/STCD2, and PA-infotype fields (salary BETRG, bank data), plus national IDs. 4. Integrate masking into the standardized system-copy procedure so no refresh completes without it (per SAP guidance on data scrambling in system copies). 5. For fields that cannot be scrambled at copy time, apply SAP UI Masking / field-level authorization and reveal-on-demand controls. 6. Restrict debug (S_DEVELOP with DEBUG), SE16/SE16N (S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM) and download authorizations in non-prod to reduce residual exposure. 7. Verify: sample key tables (PA0008, PA0009, BUT000, KNA1) in the refreshed non-prod system and confirm values are scrambled/unreadable. 8. Eliminate the unmasked window - with TDMS the target is unscrambled between refresh and finalization, so lock access until scrambling completes. 9. Document masking coverage in the ROPA and system inventory. 10. Caution: scrambling must preserve referential integrity (consistent mapping across tables) and be tested so it does not break test scenarios; coordinate with development/test owners.
References
  • GDPR Article 32 — Security of Processing
  • SAP TDMS — Test Data Migration Server
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Non-production systems identified as production copies without masking DPP-MASK-002 ▶
Security Risk
These non-production systems are explicitly identified as copies of production yet carry no masking, meaning they hold a complete, current replica of production personal data (every employee, customer, vendor, bank detail and financial document) inside an environment with development-grade controls. Unlike a partial or synthetic dataset, a production copy exposes the entire population at once, so a single compromised DEV/QA credential or an unscrupulous consultant yields the whole PII estate. In RISE/BTP engagements, system copies are often provisioned rapidly by the partner or SAP-managed operations, and if masking is not wired into that provisioning the copy sits fully exposed from the moment it is created. Attack scenario: immediately after a refresh, before anyone remembers to scrub it, a user with broad non-prod access exports BUT000/KNA1/PA0008 or takes a database snapshot; the copy may also be less monitored and retained long-term as a 'golden' test system, extending exposure for months. Impact: this is the highest-severity data-protection exposure because it combines certainty (confirmed prod data), scale (full copy), and weak controls - a textbook reportable breach. A real incident: an audit or leak reveals a long-lived QA 'prod copy' with unmasked live data accessible to dozens of non-production users, forcing breach notification and emergency scrubbing.
Affected Items (3)
  • DEV (env: DEVELOPMENT) — production copy without masking
  • SBX (env: SANDBOX) — production copy without masking
  • TRN (env: TRAINING) — production copy without masking
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Treat every flagged prod-copy as containing live PII and immediately restrict access (lock non-essential accounts / apply an interim authorization lockdown) until masked. 2. Schedule and run a masking/scrambling job now - SAP TDMS data scrambling or equivalent - over all PII tables in each flagged system. 3. Institute a mandatory policy: no production copy is released to users until masking completes, targeting masking within 48 hours of the copy (ideally an automated post-copy step). 4. Embed masking into the system-copy runbook/automation so it cannot be skipped; block manual copy requests lacking an approved masking plan. 5. For RISE, formalize with SAP-managed operations/the partner that system-copy requests trigger the masking step contractually and procedurally. 6. Apply SAP UI Masking for any residual sensitive fields not scrambled at copy time. 7. Tighten non-prod authorizations (debug, table display, data download) to limit any future unmasked window. 8. Verify: sample PA0008/PA0009/BUT000/KNA1 post-run to confirm scrambled values, and lift the interim access lock only afterwards. 9. Log and report each copy-and-mask cycle to the DPO for accountability. 10. Caution: preserve cross-table referential consistency during scrambling and coordinate the access lockdown with test/dev owners to minimize disruption while eliminating the exposure.
References
  • GDPR Article 25 — Data Protection by Design
  • SAP Note 2667054 — Data Scrambling in System Copies
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Cross-border data transfers without legal safeguards DPP-RES-001 ▶
Security Risk
A cross-border personal-data transfer with neither an adequacy decision nor an appropriate safeguard (SCCs, BCRs, consent, or a valid derogation) is an unlawful international transfer under GDPR Chapter V (Art.44-49) / DPDP Sec.16. In an S/4HANA RISE and BTP context this is a live risk because the platform is cloud-hosted and integrated: data may flow from an EU data center to support/operations, analytics, backup, or BTP services in third countries, and RFC/OData/replication interfaces routinely move personal data across regions. A transfer lacking any legal mechanism means personal data leaves the protected jurisdiction with no enforceable protection for the data subjects. Abuse/impact scenario: post-Schrems II, a regulator or data subject challenges the transfer; because there is no SCC/BCR/adequacy in place, the transfer must be suspended and may trigger fines and orders to repatriate or delete data. Concretely, a BTP integration or a support connection routes EU customer/employee PII to a third-country tenant with no SCCs, discovered during a transfer-mapping audit. Business impact: some of the largest GDPR fines relate to unlawful transfers; consequences include suspension of critical data flows (breaking integrations), mandatory Transfer Impact Assessments, and reputational harm. A real incident: an audit of data flows finds production PII replicated to a non-adequate region with no safeguard, forcing emergency suspension of the interface and regulatory notification.
Affected Items (2)
  • EU_to_US_Analytics: EU → US — no adequacy decision or transfer safeguard
  • EU_to_CN_Supplier: EU → CN — no adequacy decision or transfer safeguard
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, list each transfer lacking adequacy/safeguard with its source and destination region. 2. For each, determine whether the destination benefits from an adequacy decision; if so, document it. 3. Where no adequacy applies, implement an appropriate safeguard - the current EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) - and execute the contracts. 4. Complete a Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) per destination, considering local law, and add supplementary measures (encryption in transit/at rest, pseudonymization) where needed. 5. In RISE/BTP, confirm the data-center/region assignment and that the SAP data-processing agreement/SCCs cover the actual data flows; align with the subprocessor list. 6. For interfaces, identify the technical channel (RFC destination in SM59, OData/BTP integration) and restrict or re-route flows that lack a basis. 7. Update the ROPA and transfer register with the mechanism for every flow. 8. Verify: reconcile the transfer inventory so no flow remains without adequacy or safeguard. 9. Where no mechanism can be established, suspend the transfer and keep data in-region. 10. Caution: changing residency or suspending interfaces can break integrations - coordinate with interface owners, Legal, and (in RISE) SAP, and stage changes with testing.
References
  • GDPR Articles 44-49 — Transfer of Personal Data to Third Countries
  • DPDP Act 2023 Section 16 — Transfer Outside India
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Data subject requests overdue (>30 day SLA) DPP-DEL-001 ▶
Security Risk
GDPR Art.12(3) requires controllers to respond to data-subject requests (access, erasure, rectification, etc.) without undue delay and within one month. Requests open past the SLA (default 30 days) are direct, provable non-compliance - the clock is statutory and the breach is self-evident from the dates. This is dangerous because response deadlines are among the most consistently enforced GDPR provisions: a missed deadline is easy for a regulator to establish and hard to defend, and disgruntled data subjects who do not get a timely response frequently escalate to the supervisory authority. Abuse/impact scenario: an individual submits an erasure or access request, hears nothing for 45 days, and complains to the regulator; the organization is now defending both the underlying processing and a procedural failure. Overdue requests also tend to cluster when the fulfillment process is manual and un-tracked (see DPP-TOOLKIT-001), indicating a systemic capacity problem rather than a one-off. Business impact: regulatory enforcement, fines, and the reputational cost of visibly failing individuals who asserted their rights. A real incident: a backlog of overdue access/erasure requests surfaces during an audit or via multiple complaints, and the regulator issues an order plus penalty for chronic late responses.
Affected Items (5)
  • Request DSAR-2025-003 (DELETION, subject: vendor_9012) — open 571d (SLA: 30d), status: IN_PROGRESS
  • Request DSAR-2025-004 (DELETION, subject: employee_3456) — open 621d (SLA: 30d), status: IN_PROGRESS
  • Request DSAR-2025-006 (DELETION, subject: prospect_1111) — open 545d (SLA: 30d), status: OPEN
  • Request DSAR-2025-007 (ACCESS, subject: employee_2222) — open 540d (SLA: 30d), status: OPEN
  • Request DSAR-2025-008 (DELETION, subject: customer_3333) — open 637d (SLA: 30d), status: IN_PROGRESS
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, prioritize overdue requests by age and type (erasure/access first) and assign owners immediately. 2. Process each overdue request now: for access, generate the disclosure via the Information Retrieval Framework (IRF); for erasure, execute ILM blocking/deletion (BUPA_PRE_EOP / CVP_PRE_EOP and ILM destruction). 3. Where a request cannot be completed immediately, send the data subject a holding response with justification and expected timeline (Art.12(3) permits a limited extension with notice). 4. Verify identity before disclosure/erasure to avoid unlawful disclosure. 5. Implement automated SLA tracking with escalation alerts so requests are flagged well before the one-month deadline. 6. Establish a defined intake-to-fulfillment workflow with named responsibilities (DPO, Basis, process owners). 7. Address the root cause - if backlog stems from manual effort, configure the DPP toolkit features (DPP-TOOLKIT-001) to automate access/erasure. 8. Verify: confirm every flagged request is closed or has a documented, communicated extension, and that none exceeds the statutory limit going forward. 9. Log completion evidence for accountability (see DPP-DEL-003). 10. Caution: do not rush erasure without checking legal holds/retention obligations - balance timeliness against statutory retention and document any lawful refusal/exemption.
References
  • GDPR Article 12(3) — Response Time Limits
  • DPDP Act 2023 Section 12 — Right of Grievance Redressal
CRITICAL P2 · 65 SQL injection patterns detected in custom code CODE-INJ-001 ▶
Security Risk
Custom ABAP builds SQL predicates from unvalidated input: dynamic Open SQL WHERE clauses assembled by CONCATENATE/string templates, or native SQL via EXEC SQL, ADBC classes and CL_SQL_STATEMENT. In S/4HANA the ABAP application server connects to HANA with the schema owner (SAP<SID>/SAPHANADB) that has full DML on every business table, so a successful injection is not constrained by ABAP authorizations at all. Attack scenario: an attacker who can reach a vulnerable Z-report, Web Dynpro, or OData/Gateway service supplies input such as ' OR '1'='1, a UNION SELECT, or an appended sub-select. The manipulated statement bypasses the intended row filter and returns records for other company codes, plants, or business partners in a shared client. Because native SQL executes verbatim on HANA, ADBC/EXEC SQL injection can also read HANA system views (USERS, GRANTED_ROLES), invoke procedures, or write to financial tables (BKPF/BSEG), turning a data-read flaw into tampering. Business impact is severe: mass exfiltration of PII (GDPR Art. 32/33 breach), fraudulent or unauthorized changes to accounting data (SOX / ICFR failure), and integrity loss that may force a point-in-time restore. A real incident looks like an OData call or RFC returning far more rows than the Fiori UI should expose, or unexplained UPDATE/DELETE volume surfacing in the HANA audit trail. The code is transported, so one flawed object is exploitable in every client and is trivially scriptable for bulk scraping.
Affected Items (3)
  • Z_VENDOR_REPORT (PROG) line 145: Dynamic WHERE clause built via CONCATENATE without escaping
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI (FUGR) line 112: CL_SQL_STATEMENT used without parameterized query
  • Z_LEGACY_MIGRATION (PROG) line 89: EXEC SQL native SQL block without input validation
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open each flagged object in ADT/SE80 and confirm whether user input actually reaches a dynamic WHERE, EXEC SQL, or ADBC/CL_SQL_STATEMENT call (a true taint path, not a false positive). 2. Replace concatenated WHERE clauses with parameter-bound Open SQL: host variables (WHERE field = @lv_val), RANGES/SELECT-OPTIONS, or CDS views with input parameters. 3. For native SQL, migrate to Open SQL/CDS where feasible; where ADBC is unavoidable use CL_SQL_STATEMENT with '?' bind placeholders and SET_PARAM/EXECUTE_QUERY - never inline user data. 4. Allow-list any dynamic column/table name against a fixed DDIC whitelist before it enters a (dynamic) clause; reject anything else. 5. Activate SAP Code Vulnerability Analyzer: run report RSLIN_SEC_LICENSE_SETUP to enable security checks (CVA license per SAP Note 1921820), then run the CVA variant in transaction ATC / Code Inspector (SCI) over the Z*/Y* packages. 6. Remediate all injection findings, re-run ATC and confirm zero open findings; document any exemption with owner sign-off. 7. Configure ATC as a check step in the transport release (ATC-in-transport) so new injection findings block release in DEV. 8. Verify functionally in QA by driving the app/OData service with injection strings and confirming input is treated as a literal (no extra rows, no dumps). 9. Transport DEV->QA->PRD; regression-test with the app/interface owner before production import. 10. As a compensating control until fixes are live, monitor the HANA audit trail and table logs for anomalous query volume.
References
  • SAP Note 1520356 — Secure ABAP Programming
  • OWASP — SQL Injection Prevention
  • SAP ATC Check — CALL_INJECTION_DYNAMIC_SQL
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Hardcoded credentials detected in custom code CODE-INJ-003 ▶
Security Risk
Credentials are embedded directly in ABAP source: passwords, API keys, bearer tokens, client secrets or private keys as string literals. Because ABAP source is stored in the repository and moved through transports, a hardcoded secret is exposed to everyone with SE38/SE80/SE84 display, anyone reading the transport data files (E070/E071 / cofiles/data files on the transport directory), and anyone with version-history access. Rotating such a secret is slow and often forgotten, so it tends to live for years. Attack scenario: an insider with only display-level developer access, or an attacker who has compromised the transport filesystem or a QA/sandbox copy, greps the source (or the exported transport) for PASSWORD/SECRET/API_KEY and recovers a working credential. If it is an RFC/technical user password, a HANA/DB credential, or a BTP/cloud API key, the attacker pivots to the target system with that identity - potentially a high-privilege service account. Because the same code is copied to non-production systems (which are usually less protected and more widely accessible), the blast radius includes every landscape tier and every refresh copy. Business impact: credential theft leading to lateral movement, data breach, and non-repudiation loss (actions performed under a shared technical identity cannot be attributed). It also breaches PCI-DSS, GDPR and SAP Security Baseline requirements to never store secrets in clear text. A real incident looks like a technical/RFC account authenticating from an unexpected host, discovered only after the fact in the Security Audit Log.
Affected Items (2)
  • Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT (PROG) line 89: Literal PASSWORD value detected in RFC call parameters
  • Z_HR_SALARY_RPT (PROG) line 34: API_KEY literal string found in HTTP client setup
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Treat every flagged secret as already compromised: identify the target system/account and rotate the credential immediately, in parallel with code fixes. 2. Remove the literal from source; for RFC/system credentials store them in an SM59 destination (which holds the logon data encrypted) and have code call via the destination, not embedded logon. 3. For application secrets/keys, use the ABAP Secure Storage (SECSTORE / class-based secure store) or STRUST/SSF PSEs for certificates and private keys - never a source literal. 4. On SAP BTP, move secrets to the Credential Store service or the Destination service / XSUAA bindings and read them at runtime. 5. Purge the secret from history: because it persists in transport data files and prior versions, coordinate with Basis to ensure old transports containing it are not re-imported, and restrict the transport directory. 6. Enable CVA (report RSLIN_SEC_LICENSE_SETUP) and run the ATC hardcoded-credential/'password in source' checks across all Z*/Y* packages to catch remaining instances. 7. Tighten access: restrict S_DEVELOP and table/source display (S_TABU_*) in production and non-production copies to limit who can read source. 8. Verify by re-grepping source and re-running ATC to confirm no literal secrets remain, and confirm the app still authenticates using the externalized credential. 9. Transport DEV->QA->PRD; coordinate the credential rotation window with the interface owner to avoid outage. 10. Add a standing ATC/CVA gate so future transports with embedded secrets are blocked at release.
References
  • SAP Note 1520356
  • OWASP — Credential Management Cheat Sheet
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Unresolved critical ATC findings (4) CODE-ATC-001 ▶
Security Risk
The ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Inspector scan reports Critical (priority 1 / error) findings that remain in an unresolved state (not fixed, exempted, or marked false-positive). Critical ATC findings from the security variant typically map to genuinely exploitable defects - injection, missing authority checks, directory traversal, hardcoded secrets, insecure dynamic calls - present in code that is live in production. The danger is twofold. First, each unresolved critical finding is an individual, exploitable vulnerability (see the injection and auth-check risks). Second, a large backlog of unresolved criticals indicates the organization has no effective secure-SDLC gate: vulnerable code ships freely, and there is no evidence of remediation for auditors. Attack scenario: an attacker or red-team enumerates custom Z-objects (many are RFC- or OData-exposed), then targets the exact weaknesses ATC already documented internally - effectively a pre-written vulnerability catalog. Because custom code often runs with powerful technical/DB context, one exploited critical can yield data theft, unauthorized posting, or RCE. Business impact: elevated breach likelihood, failure of SOX ITGC change-management/secure-development controls, and GDPR exposure. A real incident is an exploited custom object whose flaw was already listed as an open critical ATC finding that no one actioned - a governance failure that materially worsens regulatory and legal consequences.
Affected Items (4)
  • Z_VENDOR_REPORT: SQL_INJECTION — Dynamic WHERE clause built via CONCATENATE without escaping
  • Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT: HARDCODED_CREDENTIAL — Literal PASSWORD value detected in RFC call parameters
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI: SQL_INJECTION — CL_SQL_STATEMENT used without parameterized query
  • Z_INTEGRATION_HUB: DYNAMIC_WHERE — String template used to build WHERE clause dynamically
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Export the current ATC result set (transaction ATC, or the central ATC quality-governance run) and confirm the count of open Priority 1 / error security findings. 2. Enable the full CVA security check set (report RSLIN_SEC_LICENSE_SETUP) if not already active, so criticals reflect the complete security ruleset. 3. Triage each critical: assign an owner (development team), and classify as fix / true false-positive / risk-accepted. 4. Remediate genuine findings at the source (see CODE-INJ-001/002/003 and CODE-STMT-001 procedures) with the highest-severity, most-exposed (RFC/OData) objects first. 5. Use the formal ATC exemption process (with approver and expiry) only for confirmed false positives - never to silence real issues. 6. Establish a remediation SLA (e.g., criticals within 30 days) tracked in the ATC quality governance dashboard. 7. Integrate ATC into the transport workflow (ATC check on transport release) so any new Priority 1 finding blocks release in DEV; configure the central check system and check variant accordingly. 8. Re-run the ATC mass run after fixes and confirm the open-critical count trends to zero. 9. Verify representative fixes functionally in QA (drive the affected app/service) before production import. 10. Report residual accepted risks to the security/GRC owner and transport fixes DEV->QA->PRD on the normal change path.
References
  • SAP ATC — Security Check Configuration
  • SAP Note 2364916 — ATC in Transport Workflow
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Transport routes allow direct dev-to-production delivery CODE-TMS-001 ▶
Security Risk
The Transport Management System (STMS) transport routes are configured so that a development system delivers directly to production, with no consolidation/delivery route through a QA/quality tier. This collapses the mandatory three-system (DEV->QA->PRD) landscape and removes the integration-test and quality gate between coding and production. The danger is both technical and governance. Technically, untested code and customizing reach production without regression, security (ATC), or performance validation - raising the chance of outages, data corruption, and shipping exploitable defects straight to the live system. From a control standpoint, a direct dev->prod route is the enabling condition for unreviewed and unapproved change: a developer can move objects to production without any independent step. Attack/abuse scenario: a developer (or an attacker who has compromised a developer account) creates a transport containing malicious or fraudulent logic - e.g., a backdoor FM, a payment-redirection change, or a weakened authority check - and releases it straight into production, bypassing QA review and four-eyes approval entirely. Business impact: loss of segregation between development and production, SOX ITGC change-management failure, elevated fraud and RCE risk, and inability to demonstrate a controlled promotion path to auditors. A real incident looks like an unauthorized production behavior change traced back to a transport that never passed through QA.
Affected Items (1)
  • DEV → PRD (direct, no QA)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In STMS (domain controller) -> Transport Routes -> graphical editor, document the current route topology and identify every consolidation/delivery route whose target is the production SID. 2. Redesign to a strict DEV -> QA(consolidation) -> PRD(delivery) path: define the standard transport layer with a consolidation route DEV->QA and a delivery route QA->PRD; remove any direct DEV->PRD route. 3. Distribute and activate the corrected route configuration to all systems in the transport domain. 4. Activate the 'Single transports' strategy and disable 'Import All' shortcuts so ad-hoc bulk imports cannot bypass the path. 5. Turn on the QA Approval Procedure on the QA system ('Delivery after confirmation') so transports must be confirmed before they can be delivered onward to PRD. 6. Restrict STMS/route administration authorizations (S_CTS_ADMI, S_TRANSPRT) to a small Basis group so routes cannot be re-opened. 7. Verify by inspecting the route graph (no DEV->PRD edge) and by test-transporting a dummy request end-to-end, confirming it must pass QA before PRD is offered. 8. Confirm import queues on PRD only accept requests that traversed QA (STMS_IMPORT). 9. Coordinate the change window with Basis and, under RISE, with SAP ECS since TMS domain changes affect the managed landscape. 10. Retain the before/after route configuration as audit evidence of the corrected promotion path.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Transport Route Configuration
  • SAP Note 18898 — TMS Configuration
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Transports imported into production directly from development CODE-TMS-005 ▶
Security Risk
Production import records show transports that were imported into production directly from a development or sandbox source, bypassing the QA/staging tier. This is the executed instance of the routing weakness in CODE-TMS-001: not merely that a direct route could exist, but that changes actually reached production without passing through integration testing, ATC security scanning, and the QA quality gate. The danger is that untested, unscanned code and customizing are already live. Skipping QA means no regression testing, no performance validation on production-like data, and no independent security review - so functional defects, data-integrity bugs, and exploitable vulnerabilities are shipped straight to the business-critical system. It also means the change likely skipped the approval and four-eyes steps that the consolidation path enforces. Abuse scenario: a developer or compromised developer account releases a transport from DEV/sandbox and it is imported into PRD without ever existing in QA, delivering a backdoor, a fraudulent logic change, or a weakened control directly to production while evading every intermediate checkpoint. Business impact: production instability, data corruption, and directly deployed vulnerabilities, plus a SOX change-management failure (no evidence of testing/promotion controls). A real incident is a production outage or fraud whose originating transport has a DEV/sandbox source SID and no corresponding QA import - proof the promotion path was circumvented.
Affected Items (2)
  • DEVK900101: DEV → PRD (type: WORKBENCH)
  • DEVK900103: DEV → PRD (type: WORKBENCH)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the transport history, list all production imports whose source SID is a DEV/sandbox system and confirm there is no prior QA import of the same request. 2. Investigate each: validate legitimacy, assess whether the change was tested elsewhere, and remediate/roll back anything unauthorized or defective. 3. Close the routing gap per CODE-TMS-001: enforce a DEV->QA->PRD route in STMS and remove any direct DEV/sandbox->PRD path. 4. Activate the QA Approval Procedure ('Delivery after confirmation') on QA and the 'Single transports' strategy so requests must be QA-confirmed before PRD is offered. 5. Restrict production import authorization (S_CTS_ADMI, STMS import) so operators cannot manually import an arbitrary request from a dev source into PRD. 6. Define a controlled hotfix/emergency process that still routes through QA (even if expedited) and requires post-deploy QA validation and approval. 7. Enable transport/import logging and the Security Audit Log to detect future direct-source imports. 8. Verify by attempting to import a DEV-sourced request that has not been through QA and confirming it is blocked. 9. Coordinate STMS domain changes with Basis and, under RISE, with SAP ECS; test the corrected path with a dummy transport. 10. Report the remediated historical cases and the enforced path to GRC/audit as evidence of a controlled landscape.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Transport Route Enforcement
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Production client allows changes (not locked) CODE-CLIENT-001 ▶
Security Risk
The production client is not locked in SCC4 (table T000): it permits direct client-specific customizing changes (CCCORACTIV), and/or cross-client customizing/repository changes (CCNOCLIIND), and/or is not protected against overwriting (CCCOPYLOCK). A production client must be closed so that the ONLY way to change it is a controlled transport import; leaving it open defeats the entire transport-based change-management model. The danger is that with the client open, a user holding the right customizing/development authorizations can change configuration, tables, or even repository objects directly in production - with no transport, no QA, and no approval. Cross-client settings are especially severe: a change made from an open production client can affect all clients on the system, including sensitive cross-client repository and system tables. Abuse scenario: an insider (or attacker on a privileged account) uses SM30/SE16N/SPRO in the open production client to alter a control table directly - e.g., change a tolerance group, a tax setting, an output/bank determination, or a security-relevant customizing entry - instantly and without any change record beyond table logging. Because it never went through a transport, there is no request, no approver, and no QA evidence. Business impact: complete breakdown of segregation and change control, high fraud and error risk against financial configuration, and a serious SOX ITGC deficiency. A real incident is an unexplained configuration change in production that maps to a direct table maintenance in an open client rather than to any transport.
Affected Items (1)
  • Client 100 (role: PRODUCTION) — changes_allowed=MODIFIABLE; cross_client_changes=allowed; repository_changes=allowed
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In transaction SCC4 for the production client, set 'Changes and Transports for Client-Specific Objects' to 'No changes allowed' (T000-CCCORACTIV) so only transport imports can change client-dependent customizing. 2. Set cross-client object protection to 'No changes to Repository and cross-client Customizing objects' (T000-CCNOCLIIND). 3. Enable client copy/comparison protection (CCCOPYLOCK) and set 'Protection: level 1/no overwriting' as appropriate to prevent accidental overwrite. 4. Confirm the client role (CCCATEGORY) is set to Production (P); production role interacts with these locks. 5. Set the system-wide change option (transaction SE06 / SE03 'Set System Change Option') for production to 'Not modifiable' so repository/global objects cannot be changed even if a client were opened. 6. Restrict authorizations to open the client (S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_CLI on the client-admin tables, and S_TABU_CLI CLIDMAINT) to a very small emergency group; opening the client must be an audited, time-boxed exception. 7. Ensure table logging is active (see CODE-CHG-001) so any change is recorded, and enable the Security Audit Log for client-open events. 8. Verify by inspecting T000 for the production client and by attempting a direct SM30 change - it must be rejected as 'client not modifiable'. 9. Coordinate the lock with functional teams to confirm no legitimate process relies on direct production maintenance (migrate any such config to transports); under RISE, align with SAP ECS. 10. Capture the SCC4/SE06 settings as audit evidence and re-check after any client copy, since a refresh can silently reset them (see SAP KBA on SCC4 changing after client copy).
References
  • SAP Note 135028 — Client Settings for Production
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Client Configuration
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Modifications to SAP security-critical standard programs CODE-MOD-002 ▶
Security Risk
SAP standard programs in security-critical areas have been modified - namespaces/programs related to authorization (SAPLAUTH), user management (SAPLSU*), transport/system administration (SAPLSTMS, SAPMSSY*, SAPLSMSY), and security services (SAPLSECUR). Modifying these standard components can directly weaken or bypass the platform's built-in security controls, and because it is a change to core code, its effects are global and largely invisible to normal application-level review. The danger is that a modification here can neutralize the very mechanisms that protect the system: an altered authorization routine can make AUTHORITY-CHECK always succeed, a modified user-management program can suppress logging or allow forbidden user changes, and a modified transport routine can bypass approval or route controls. Unlike custom Z-code, these changes hide inside trusted standard programs, so they are rarely suspected and hard to detect. Abuse scenario: an insider or attacker with modification capability patches the standard authorization check so a specific condition returns 'authorized' regardless of the user's roles, creating a universal backdoor that no PFCG role review would ever reveal; or patches user-maintenance code to silently create/elevate accounts without a change document. Business impact: catastrophic - a compromised security kernel means every other control (roles, SoD, logging, transport approval) can be silently defeated, enabling undetected fraud, data theft, and full system compromise. It is also a critical SOX/audit failure. A real incident is the discovery that the system's authorization or user-management logic was altered to grant hidden access, invalidating all prior access-control assurance.
Affected Items (4)
  • SAPLSU01 (type: PROG, by: LWANG) — modified security namespace: SAPLSU
  • SAPMSSY1 (type: PROG, by: ADMIN) — modified security namespace: SAPMSSY
  • SAPLAUTH (type: PROG, by: LWANG) — modified security namespace: SAPLAUTH
  • SAPLSTMS (type: PROG, by: ADMIN) — modified security namespace: SAPLSTMS
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Treat each security-critical modification as a potential backdoor: freeze and review it immediately with the security team, prioritizing SAPLAUTH/SAPLSU*/SAPLSECUR/SAPLSTMS changes. 2. Diff the modified code against SAP standard (SE95 Modification Browser / version management) to determine exactly what behavior was changed and whether any authorization/logging logic was weakened. 3. Validate whether the modification is authorized and documented; any undocumented change to security code should be handled as a suspected security incident and escalated to IR. 4. Reverse illegitimate or unnecessary modifications - reset the object to SAP standard - and where a genuine need exists, re-implement via a supported BAdI/enhancement rather than a core modification. 5. Request an SAP security review / open a support case for any modification that must remain in security-critical standard code. 6. Rotate credentials and re-review privileged access if a security-kernel modification is found, since prior controls may have been bypassed. 7. Enable the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG) and change logging to detect further tampering, and restrict S_DEVELOP so such modifications cannot recur in production. 8. Verify by re-running SE95 and confirming no unauthorized modifications remain in the security namespaces, and by testing that AUTHORITY-CHECK behaves correctly for a low-privileged user. 9. Test reverted logic thoroughly in QA (authorization/user-management flows) before transporting DEV->QA->PRD; coordinate with SAP ECS under RISE. 10. Report findings and remediation to security/GRC as a high-priority item and retain evidence of the review.
References
  • SAP — Modification Guidelines for Security Objects
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Potential brute-force attack patterns detected LOG-LOGON-001 ▶
Security Risk
This critical finding flags accounts whose failed-to-successful logon ratio is very high (greater than 5 with at least the failure threshold met), a pattern strongly consistent with an active credential attack - brute force or password spraying against SAP GUI, RFC, or the web/Fiori/BTP logon endpoints. If the password policy is weak or account lockout is not enforced (login/fails_to_user_lock unset or set high), the attacker eventually succeeds. In a RISE deployment the exposed HTTP surface (Fiori launchpad, OData services) makes internet-adjacent brute force realistic, and BTP identity via IAS/XSUAA is subject to credential stuffing. The blast radius depends on which account cracks: a standard dialog user is bad, an RFC/technical user with broad authorizations is worse, and a default or emergency account (SAP*, DDIC, a firefighter ID) is catastrophic. Step-by-step attack: the adversary enumerates usernames (commonly firstname.lastname), sprays common and seasonal passwords low-and-slow to stay under the lockout threshold, targets SAP GUI or /sap/bc endpoints, and on a hit logs in and immediately escalates - scheduling a malicious background job, reading BSEG/PA0008, or granting itself wide authorization. Business and compliance impact: a successful compromise leads to fraud, data exfiltration, or full system takeover; failure to detect and act breaches SAP Security Baseline expectations and GDPR breach-response duties. A real incident is a cracked batch/RFC user used to exfiltrate finance data, discovered only after the fact.
Affected Items (2)
  • UNKNOWN_USER1: 350 failures, 0 successes (ratio: 350.0)
  • ADMIN_TEST: 180 failures, 2 successes (ratio: 90.0)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Immediately investigate each flagged account in RSAU_READ_LOG (SM20) to obtain source IP/terminal, timing, and whether any success followed the failures. 2. Lock targeted or confirmed-compromised accounts in SU01 and reset their passwords. 3. Enforce lockout and policy in RZ10: login/fails_to_user_lock = 5, login/fails_to_session_end configured, and login/failed_user_auto_unlock = 0 so locks persist. 4. Strengthen authentication - enforce a strong password policy and, preferably, move interactive logon to SSO with MFA (SAML/IAS); for technical users disable password logon and use SNC/certificates. 5. Block hostile source IPs at the SAP Web Dispatcher or WAF and restrict RFC/GUI exposure to trusted networks. 6. Verify with report RSUSR200 (last logon / locked users) and re-run the SAL review to confirm the failure pattern has stopped. 7. Rollout caution: mass lockouts can deny service to legitimate users and can lock service accounts that break interfaces, so coordinate account actions and monitor interface health during response.
References
  • SAP — Brute-Force Attack Detection
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Expired certificates in system trust store CRYPTO-CERT-001 ▶
Security Risk
One or more certificates in the system trust store (STRUST/SMICM) have passed their validity date. An expired certificate causes the TLS/SNC handshake to fail, which immediately breaks whatever it secures - the Fiori/HTTPS front-end, OData and RFC-over-HTTPS interfaces, SNC-based SSO, and SAP BTP/Cloud Connector destinations. The primary consequence is an availability incident, but the security risk is the dangerous workaround it provokes: under outage pressure, administrators frequently disable certificate validation (accept-any-cert, TRUST_ALL, or removing the CA check on a destination) to restore service, which permanently opens the door to man-in-the-middle interception. An expired CA (root/intermediate) certificate in the trust list is worse - it invalidates the entire chain for every certificate issued under it, so many endpoints fail at once and the temptation to switch off validation is strong. In RISE the blast radius includes integration flows (IDoc/API to BTP, PI/PO, banks and third parties); a failed handshake can silently halt payment or master-data interfaces, causing missed SLAs and financial-process disruption. The attack angle: an adversary who anticipates or engineers the outage waits for the insecure workaround, then presents a forged/self-signed certificate to a client that is now accepting anything, and intercepts credentials and data. Business impact: service outage plus, if validation is disabled, credential/data interception and a breach; audit findings for expired production certificates are common SOX/ISO deficiencies. A real incident looks like a Monday-morning Fiori outage traced to an expired SSL server certificate, temporarily patched by disabling a validation check that then goes unremediated for months. This is rated Critical because it combines guaranteed service impact with a high likelihood of security-degrading workarounds.
Affected Items (6)
  • SSL_Server_Cert (purpose: HTTPS Server) — EXPIRED 457d ago (2025-05-15)
  • SNC_System_PSE (purpose: SNC) — EXPIRED 501d ago (2025-04-01)
  • SSO_Signing_Cert (purpose: SSO) — EXPIRED 623d ago (2024-11-30)
  • Legacy_Client_Cert (purpose: Client Auth) — EXPIRED 227d ago (2025-12-31)
  • Test_Cert (purpose: Testing) — EXPIRED 226d ago (2026-01-01)
  • BTP_Trust_Cert (purpose: BTP Trust) — EXPIRED 46d ago (2026-06-30)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In transaction STRUST open each PSE node (SSL server SAPSSLS, SSL client SAPSSLA/SAPSSLC, SNC SAPSNCS, and the SSO/SAML PSEs) and identify entries whose Valid To date has passed, including any expired CA certificates in the certificate list. 2. For an expired own certificate, generate a fresh CSR in STRUST (create/replace PSE, then Create Certificate Request), submit it to your CA, and import the signed response back into the same PSE node. 3. For an expired CA/intermediate, obtain the current CA certificate and import it via STRUST (Import Certificate, then Add to Certificate List) so the chain validates again. 4. Restart the ICM in SMICM so the renewed material is loaded; for Cloud Connector/BTP destinations, re-import the certificate on the connector side as well. 5. Verify in STRUST that the new Valid From/To dates are correct and test an actual handshake (browser to Fiori, and an interface test for RFC/OData). 6. Explicitly re-enable any certificate validation that was disabled as an emergency workaround and confirm no SM59 destination or profile has certificate checking switched off. 7. Stand up proactive expiry monitoring via SAP Solution Manager / Focused Run certificate monitoring (or a scheduled alert) so renewals happen ahead of expiry. 8. Rollout caution: in RISE the SSL server certificates may be co-managed by SAP ECS - raise the renewal through the provider and validate before the change window closes; never leave validation disabled.
References
  • SAP Note 510007 — Certificate Management
CRITICAL P2 · 65 HANA SYSTEM superuser is still active HANADB-USER-001 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that the built-in SYSTEM superuser is still active. SYSTEM is created at database provisioning and implicitly holds every system privilege; it is not subject to the role model, object ownership, or analytic-privilege filtering. An active SYSTEM account is effectively a single master key to the entire HANA database that underpins S/4HANA. It is dangerous because the credential is typically set during installation, is often shared among the project team, is weakly rotated, and frequently ends up embedded in install scripts, secure-store (hdbuserstore) keys, or interface connection strings. Attack scenario: an adversary who phishes or brute-forces the SYSTEM password, or finds it hard-coded in a script or backup, connects to the SQL port and gains unrestricted control - reading all business data (financials, HR, GDPR-relevant PII), minting hidden privileged users, changing ini parameters to disable auditing or TLS, and touching encryption/credential material. Because SYSTEM bypasses every compensating control, there is no secondary gate once it is used. In S/4HANA this equals total compromise of the ERP data layer beneath every Fiori/SAP GUI authorization. Compliance impact is severe: least-privilege and SoD violations (SOX ITGC), unattributable privileged access, and audit failure because actions cannot be tied to a named person. A real incident looks like anomalous SYSTEM logons from an app or jump host at odd hours, mass SELECTs against SAPHANADB tables, and new users suddenly holding DATA ADMIN.
Affected Items (1)
  • SYSTEM — status: active
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Ensure named administrator accounts already exist, each provisioned with only the roles they need; never keep using SYSTEM for daily work. 2. In RISE/PCE, confirm via the Roles and Responsibilities RACI whether SAP ECS owns SYSTEM; if the customer copy is active, raise a service ticket rather than acting unilaterally. 3. Verify status: SELECT USER_NAME, USER_DEACTIVATED FROM SYS.USERS WHERE USER_NAME='SYSTEM'; (or SAP HANA Cockpit -> User and Role Management, or transaction DBACOCKPIT from the ABAP stack). 4. Deactivate from a different admin user: ALTER USER SYSTEM DEACTIVATE USER NOW; 5. Store the SYSTEM password in a sealed break-glass vault, rotate it, and record custody. 6. Verify the change: re-query SYS.USERS and confirm USER_DEACTIVATED = TRUE. 7. Create an audit policy that fires on SYSTEM CONNECT so any future break-glass use is alerted to the SIEM. 8. Rollout caution: before deactivating, confirm no interfaces, hdbuserstore keys, or backup jobs authenticate as SYSTEM (inspect connection stores and DBACOCKPIT DB connections), or those connections will break; test in non-production first. 9. Reactivate only under change control (ALTER USER SYSTEM ACTIVATE USER NOW;) and re-deactivate immediately after the emergency. 10. Document the whole procedure in the break-glass runbook and review it quarterly.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Deactivate SYSTEM user
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — The SYSTEM User
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Sensitive privileges granted to PUBLIC HANADB-PRIV-001 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that sensitive privileges are granted to the PUBLIC role. PUBLIC is automatically and implicitly granted to every database user - present and future - so granting a system privilege, the _SYS_BI_CP_ALL analytic privilege, or any *ADMIN privilege to PUBLIC hands that capability to the entire user population, including low-privilege technical accounts, reporting users, and any account an attacker later compromises. This is a catastrophic least-privilege break: DATA ADMIN or CATALOG READ on PUBLIC means every user can administer data or read the full catalog/metadata; _SYS_BI_CP_ALL on PUBLIC means every user can read all modeled reporting data with no row filtering. Attack scenario: an adversary only has to compromise the single weakest DB credential - a dormant reporting user, an app technical account - and instantly inherits the admin or broad-data capability granted to PUBLIC, with no separate escalation step required. Business and compliance impact: mass data exposure (financial and GDPR-relevant), trivial privilege escalation, and audit failure - because the grant is systemic it defeats per-user access reviews entirely. A real incident looks like an auditor or attacker holding only a trivial read-only account discovering they can query all HANA metadata or every analytic view, because a privilege was granted to PUBLIC during a project and never revoked.
Affected Items (1)
  • PUBLIC ← CATALOG READ
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate: SELECT GRANTEE, PRIVILEGE, OBJECT_NAME, IS_GRANTABLE FROM GRANTED_PRIVILEGES WHERE GRANTEE='PUBLIC'; and also check GRANTED_ROLES for roles granted to PUBLIC. 2. Classify which privileges are legitimately public (a small set of harmless monitoring views) versus sensitive or administrative. 3. Revoke the sensitive system privileges: REVOKE <privilege> FROM PUBLIC; and for object privileges: REVOKE <priv> ON <object> FROM PUBLIC; 4. Re-provision the capability only to the specific users or, preferably, a named role that genuinely needs it. 5. For _SYS_BI_CP_ALL granted to PUBLIC, revoke it and replace with view-specific analytic privileges (see HANADB-PRIV-005). 6. Verify: re-run the GRANTED_PRIVILEGES query - the sensitive PUBLIC rows should be gone; then smoke-test that legitimate low-privilege users still function. 7. Rollout caution: revoking a privilege from PUBLIC that an application silently relied on breaks functionality for all users at once - identify dependent applications/interfaces first, test in non-production, involve the app owners, and stage the change under change control. 8. Add a recurring check for new PUBLIC grants so the condition does not reappear after future projects.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Restrict PUBLIC role
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — The PUBLIC Role
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Critical system privileges granted directly to users HANADB-PRIV-002 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that near-omnipotent system privileges - DATA ADMIN, USER ADMIN, ROLE ADMIN, INIFILE ADMIN, DEVELOPMENT, and the encryption/credential/trust admin privileges - are granted directly to individual named users rather than through a small number of reviewed roles. This both breaks least privilege and destroys reviewability: you cannot reason about who can perform a sensitive action when privileges are scattered across ad-hoc direct grants. The concrete danger of each: USER ADMIN plus ROLE ADMIN lets a holder mint themselves any privilege and create a stealth superuser; DATA ADMIN gives read and DDL over all catalog objects; INIFILE ADMIN lets a user change security parameters to disable auditing, TLS, or the password policy; DEVELOPMENT enables creation of executable server-side objects; ENCRYPTION ROOT KEY ADMIN and CREDENTIAL ADMIN touch cryptographic and secret material. Attack scenario: a compromised or malicious holder of USER ADMIN creates a hidden privileged account, or an INIFILE ADMIN holder turns auditing off and then exfiltrates data unlogged; because the grants are direct they are easy to miss in role-centric reviews. Business and compliance impact: privilege escalation to full DB compromise, tampering with security controls, and unlogged fraud - direct SOX and GDPR exposure. A real incident looks like a developer who was left DATA ADMIN 'temporarily' for a go-live using it months later to read payroll data, the direct grant never having surfaced in the periodic role review.
Affected Items (2)
  • J_SMITH ← DATA ADMIN
  • SVC_INTERFACE ← USER ADMIN
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List direct grants: SELECT GRANTEE, GRANTEE_TYPE, PRIVILEGE, IS_GRANTABLE FROM GRANTED_PRIVILEGES WHERE GRANTEE_TYPE='USER' AND PRIVILEGE IN ('DATA ADMIN','USER ADMIN','ROLE ADMIN','INIFILE ADMIN','DEVELOPMENT','AUDIT ADMIN','CERTIFICATE ADMIN','CREDENTIAL ADMIN','TRUST ADMIN','ENCRYPTION ROOT KEY ADMIN'); 2. For each, decide the legitimate owner and design a minimal set of named admin roles that enforce SoD (e.g. separate user-admin and config-admin roles). 3. Grant the role and remove the direct privilege: GRANT <admin_role> TO <user>; then REVOKE <privilege> FROM <user>; 4. Reserve DATA ADMIN and DEVELOPMENT for exceptional, time-boxed use and prefer object-specific privileges instead. 5. Ensure INIFILE, AUDIT, and encryption/credential admin are held by a tiny, named, four-eyes-reviewed group only. 6. Verify: re-query GRANTED_PRIVILEGES (no USER-type direct grants of the critical set remain) and confirm effective access via EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGES. 7. Enable an audit policy on grant/revoke of these privileges so future direct grants are detected. 8. Rollout caution: revoking a privilege an admin actively uses can break operational jobs - migrate to the role first, validate in non-production, and coordinate a change window; in RISE confirm ownership with SAP ECS.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — System privileges
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — System Privileges
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Analytic-privilege bypass (_SYS_BI_CP_ALL) granted HANADB-PRIV-005 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that the built-in structured (analytic) privilege _SYS_BI_CP_ALL is granted to a non-technical user or role. When held, _SYS_BI_CP_ALL switches off analytic-privilege row and column filtering for all classic (XML-based) modeled calculation and analytic views. Analytic privileges are HANA's mechanism for restricting which rows of a modeled view a user may see - for example only their own company code, region, or cost centre - so a holder of _SYS_BI_CP_ALL bypasses those restrictions entirely and sees the complete result set of every such view. In an S/4HANA embedded-analytics or BW-on-HANA landscape this typically means unrestricted access to the most sensitive reporting data - financials, HR, and customer data - regardless of the carefully designed row-level security. Attack scenario: an analyst, developer, or compromised account granted _SYS_BI_CP_ALL (often copied during modeling or testing and never removed) queries the modeled views and pulls every company's or region's data, defeating the intended data-segregation controls; because the bypass is 'by design' for that privilege, the queries look entirely legitimate. Business and compliance impact: a mass confidentiality breach and a segregation-of-duties failure, GDPR exposure for personal data, and financial-misstatement risk if restricted financial views become broadly readable. A real incident looks like a report developer retaining _SYS_BI_CP_ALL after go-live and exporting all subsidiaries' P&L data that they were only ever meant to see for a single entity.
Affected Items (1)
  • J_SMITH ← _SYS_BI_CP_ALL
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Find holders: SELECT GRANTEE, PRIVILEGE FROM GRANTED_PRIVILEGES WHERE PRIVILEGE='_SYS_BI_CP_ALL'; and check role-based grants via GRANTED_ROLES and EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES (MODELING and CONTENT_ADMIN can carry it). 2. For each grantee, identify which modeled views they legitimately need and the correct row/column restriction. 3. Revoke the master privilege: REVOKE STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE _SYS_BI_CP_ALL FROM <user_or_role>; 4. Replace it with specific analytic privileges - preferably SQL-based analytic privileges, or classic XML analytic privileges - that enforce the intended filters, and grant those instead. 5. For genuine admin/modeling needs, time-box the access and grant it only in non-production or under change control. 6. Verify: re-run the query (no non-technical grantees remain) and functionally test that affected users now see only their permitted rows in the modeled views. 7. Rollout caution: removing _SYS_BI_CP_ALL immediately restricts data for those users - build and validate the replacement analytic privileges in non-production first, and coordinate with the BI/reporting owners so production reports do not silently return empty or partial results.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — _SYS_BI_CP_ALL
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Analytic Privileges
CRITICAL P2 · 65 HANA database auditing is disabled HANADB-AUDIT-001 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that global.ini [auditing configuration] global_auditing_state is not 'true', so the HANA audit trail is globally switched off. With auditing disabled, none of the security-relevant events are recorded - privilege grants and revokes, user creation and alteration, configuration (ini) changes, failed and successful privileged logons, and any sensitive data access that policies would capture. There is therefore no forensic trail, no detection of misuse, and no ability to attribute actions to an actor. Attack scenario: an adversary or malicious insider who reaches the database can create users, escalate privileges, exfiltrate data, and change configuration with zero recorded evidence; even routine incident response becomes impossible because there is nothing to reconstruct. Auditing being off also makes the other audit controls (policy coverage and trail target) moot. Business and compliance impact: this is simultaneously a direct security-control failure and a compliance breach - SOX ITGC requires logging of privileged database activity, GDPR requires the ability to detect and investigate unauthorized access to personal data, and ISO 27001 (and PCI where in scope) mandate audit logging. A real incident looks like a data-exfiltration event discovered externally - data appearing for sale - after which the team finds the HANA audit trail was never enabled, so root cause, scope, and attribution simply cannot be established.
Affected Items (1)
  • global_auditing_state = false
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check current state: SELECT * FROM M_INIFILE_CONTENTS WHERE KEY='global_auditing_state'; (or SAP HANA Cockpit -> Security -> Auditing, or DBACOCKPIT). 2. Enable auditing: ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini','SYSTEM') SET ('auditing configuration','global_auditing_state')='true' WITH RECONFIGURE; 3. Set a production-grade trail target (see HANADB-AUDIT-002): default_audit_trail_type = SYSLOGPROTOCOL (forwarded to the SIEM) or CSTABLE. 4. Create and activate audit policies for critical actions - grants/revokes, user administration, configuration changes, and authentication (see HANADB-AUDIT-003/004). 5. Forward the trail to the enterprise SIEM and alert on privileged events. 6. Verify: re-query M_INIFILE_CONTENTS (value 'true'), then perform a test auditable action such as a dummy GRANT and confirm it appears in the trail (the AUDIT_LOG view for CSTABLE, or the OS syslog for SYSLOGPROTOCOL). 7. Rollout caution: in RISE/PCE, auditing configuration may be SAP ECS's responsibility - coordinate via the RACI or a ticket. WITH RECONFIGURE applies without a restart, but validate trail sizing and retention so the chosen target does not fill up.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Enable auditing
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Auditing Activity
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Role allows starting any transaction (S_TCODE = *) AUTH-005 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_TCODE with TCD='*', allowing the holder to start every transaction in the system. S_TCODE is the first gate the ABAP kernel checks when a transaction is launched; a wildcard removes that gate entirely, so the only remaining protection is whatever object-level authorizations happen to be present in the role. In practice roles built with S_TCODE='*' are almost always also broad at the object level, so this is effectively unrestricted interactive access and it completely defeats menu-based restriction. From an attacker's perspective, a wildcard S_TCODE is a launchpad: they can reach SE16/SE16N (table data), SM49/SM69 (OS commands), SU01/PFCG (user and role administration), SM59/SMT1 (RFC/trust), SCC4 (client control), and STMS/SE38 (transport and code) — every high-value transaction is one command away, limited only by object authorizations that in such roles are frequently also open. In an S/4HANA RISE production client this is a critical finding: it breaks least-privilege at the most fundamental level, makes SoD analysis meaningless (the user can reach conflicting transactions at will), and is a direct SOX/ITGC deficiency. A real incident looks like a business user navigating directly to administrative or data-browser transactions that their job never requires, then reading or changing data outside any documented process — with the audit trail showing transaction starts that make no sense for the user's role. Wildcard S_TCODE is explicitly called out as a critical authorization in the SAP Security Baseline and DSAG guidelines.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_BASIS_SUPER — 2 user(s) [ADMIN1, CONTRACTOR7] — S_TCODE TCD=*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_TCODE with TCD='*'; list the roles and their holders, and check RSUSR008_009_NEW. 2. In PFCG, remove the '*' from the S_TCODE authorization and rebuild the role's transaction set from the PFCG role menu, so S_TCODE values are generated from the menu (Authorizations tab -> regenerate). 3. Use an authorization trace (STAUTHTRACE, or ST01 short-term) on representative users to determine the transactions the role actually needs, and add only those to the menu. 4. Let SU24 provide the object-level proposals for the added transactions so the role is scoped at object level too, not just at S_TCODE. 5. Regenerate the profile and re-assign; for composite roles, regenerate them after the single roles are fixed. 6. Verify: re-run RSUSR002 for S_TCODE='*' and confirm zero assigned-role hits; have a test user attempt a transaction not in the role and confirm refusal (SU53). 7. Investigate why the role was built with a full wildcard (often a lift-and-shift shortcut) and correct the role-design standard so it cannot recur. 8. Rollout caution: users on a wildcard role may silently rely on transactions you don't yet know about — run the trace over a full business cycle, communicate, and provide a fast path to add missing legitimate transactions; test in QA before production cutover.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_TCODE
  • DSAG Audit Guideline
CRITICAL P2 · 65 Super-admin business role template assigned in production S4AUTHZ-001 ▶
Security Risk
SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR and SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR_MDG are broad SAP-delivered business-role TEMPLATES, not production roles. SAP ships them only for the very first configuration of a freshly provisioned S/4HANA (Cloud) tenant; per SAP KBA 3363028 the role is delivered, non-transportable, and intentionally carries an extremely wide job profile bundling nearly every administrative business catalog. Assigned to a named business user it grants near-complete control of the system: user and role administration, configuration/customizing, output and communication management, and access to most business apps and their data. In a RISE / S/4HANA Cloud context this single identity collapses segregation of duties, because one user can both change configuration and post/approve business transactions and can create or elevate other users. Concrete abuse: an attacker who phishes or brute-forces such an account (or an insider misusing it) can create a new privileged user, reset another user's credentials, weaken logging, alter vendor/bank master data and trigger a payment run, then export sensitive HR and finance data, all under one legitimate-looking account. Because the role is so broad, forensic attribution of which specific privilege was abused becomes nearly impossible. Business impact is severe: SOX/internal-control failure (no SoD), GDPR exposure through mass PII access, and material fraud risk such as a fictitious-vendor payment. Auditors treat any productive assignment of an administrator TEMPLATE as a reportable control deficiency, and a real incident typically surfaces as unexplained master-data changes or user creations traced back to this role.
Affected Items (2)
  • JDOE ← SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR
  • MSMITH ← SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR_MDG
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory all holders: S/4HANA Cloud use the Maintain Business Roles and Identity and Access Management apps plus the Display Authorization Trace; on-prem S/4HANA use SUIM > Roles by User, report RSUSR070/RSUSR002, or table AGR_USERS filtered on SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR*. 2. Also resolve indirect grants via composite/derived roles and any reference users so no hidden assignment is missed. 3. For every holder, confirm business justification with the role/data owner; assume no named production end user legitimately needs the template. 4. Build a purpose-specific admin role by copying the template into the customer namespace (Z*/Y*) via Maintain Business Roles (Cloud) or PFCG (on-prem), keeping only the business catalogs the job truly needs. 5. Apply scoped restrictions (see S4AUTHZ-002) for org values (company code, cost center, etc.) instead of Unrestricted. 6. Transport the customer role via the Export/Import Software Collection app (Cloud) or standard CTS transport (on-prem); never transport the SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR template itself. 7. Assign the new least-privilege role, then remove SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR* from the user. 8. For genuine emergency super-admin need, use a firefighter/emergency-access model (SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance or SAP Access Control EAM) with logging and time-boxed checkout. 9. Schedule a recurring SUIM/RSUSR070 check so the template does not reappear on users. 10. Verify: re-run the user-role report and confirm zero productive assignments; the authorization trace should show the template only on the initial-setup user. 11. Rollout caution: validate the replacement role in the Q/test tenant first and coordinate cutover with the affected admins so operations are not interrupted.
References
  • SAP KBA 3363028 — SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR is an initial-setup template (not transportable)
  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud — Identity & Access Management
CRITICAL P2 · 65 SoD conflict: Maintain Vendor Master and Process Vendor Payment ARA-P2P-01 ▶
Security Risk
This finding means one user account can both maintain the vendor master (FK01/FK02/XK01/XK02/MK01/MK02/BP with F_LFA1_APP and F_LFA1_BUK at ACTVT 01/02) and execute outgoing payments (F110 automatic payment run, or manual F-53/F-58/F-48 with F_REGU_BUK / F_BKPF_BUK at execute level). This is the canonical accounts-payable fraud path: a single person controls both the payee and the disbursement, so no independent party validates that a vendor is legitimate or that a payment is warranted. Attack scenario: a malicious or compromised AP clerk creates a ghost vendor (a shell they control, or a near-duplicate of a real supplier), sets bank details they own, lets or posts an invoice, then runs F110 or F-53 to disburse funds to that account, and afterwards flags the vendor for deletion to erase the trail. A variant redirects a genuine vendor's payment by editing the F110 payment proposal. The business impact is direct, often recurring cash loss kept below review thresholds, material misstatement of accounts payable, and a textbook SOX ITGC/entity-level control failure that auditors will raise as a significant deficiency or material weakness. In S/4HANA RISE the exposure is identical whether access is via SAP GUI, the Manage Supplier Master Data / Manage Automatic Payments Fiori apps, or an RFC/OData technical user; RISE does not shift SoD responsibility, which stays firmly on the customer side of the shared-responsibility model. A real incident usually surfaces only when a bank reconciliation exception or a whistle-blower flags an unknown payee, after several payment cycles have already run.
Affected Items (1)
  • ARAFRAUD1 (2 role(s))
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: SUIM -> RSUSR002 (Users by Complex Selection Criteria) for tcodes F110/F-53 AND FK01/XK01, or RSUSR008_009_NEW for the critical combination; in GRC Access Control run Access Risk Analysis for the standard Maintain Vendor & Process Payment risk. 2. For each user open SU01 (Roles tab) and PFCG; using table AGR_1251 determine which role grants the vendor-master side (F_LFA1_APP/F_LFA1_BUK) and which grants the payment side (F_REGU_BUK/F_BKPF_BUK). 3. Assign one side per job: keep vendor maintenance with the AP master-data team and F110 with a separate Treasury/disbursement team. In PFCG remove the conflicting transactions from the menu, strip the auth objects, then regenerate the profile (Generate / SUPC). 4. Where F110 must stay broad, restrict F_REGU_BUK by paying company code and split the proposal-edit vs payment-run steps across two users. 5. If separation is impossible, record a formal mitigating control (independent review of the F110 proposal/exception list, positive-pay bank file, periodic review of vendor bank changes via change documents on table LFBK) in mitigating_controls.csv or GRC with an owner and validity date. 6. Verify: re-run RSUSR002 / ARA and confirm zero residual users; confirm change-document logging is active. 7. Rollout caution: test in QA, coordinate with AP and Treasury interface owners (payment-run batch jobs, DME/host-to-host files), and regenerate profiles outside a payment-run window.
References
  • SAP GRC Access Control default ruleset (Maintain Vendor / Process Payment)
  • tcodesearch F_REGU_BUK / F_BKPF_BUK
  • authorizationexperts.com F_LFA1_APP
CRITICAL P2 · 65 SoD conflict: Maintain G/L Account Master Data and Post Journal Entries ARA-R2R-01 ▶
Security Risk
A single user can both maintain G/L account master data (FS00/FS01/FS02/FSS0/FSP0 with F_SKA1_BUK/F_SKA1_KTP/F_SKA1_AEN at ACTVT 01/02) and post accounting documents (FB01/FB50/F-02 with F_BKPF_BUK ACTVT 01 and F_BKPF_KOA KOART=S for G/L line items). Controlling both the chart of accounts and the postings to it is a classic financial-statement-fraud and concealment SoD: the same person can create a fictitious, suspense or clearing account and then post fraudulent or covering journal entries to it. Attack scenario: the perpetrator sets up a new G/L account (or unblocks/edits an existing one), posts manual journals that misappropriate funds or misstate results, and uses the account they control to park and later flush the offsetting entries, so the manipulation is buried in an account nobody else scrutinizes; they can also change account settings (e.g., open-item management, reconciliation flags) to make balances behave as needed. Business impact is direct financial-statement misstatement, concealment of fraud, and a top-tier SOX/close-process control failure — manual journal entries plus master-data control is one of the most scrutinized SoD combinations in any audit. In S/4HANA the Manage G/L Account Master Data and Post General Journal Entries Fiori apps reproduce it, and Universal Journal (ACDOCA) postings inherit the same authorization checks. A real incident looks like new/edited G/L accounts followed by manual journals from the same user, especially round-number or period-end entries to unusual accounts.
Affected Items (2)
  • ARAFRAUD2 (2 role(s))
  • ARAMULTI (6 role(s))
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: SUIM -> RSUSR002 for FS00/FS01/FS02 together with FB01/FB50/F-02, checking F_SKA1_* and F_BKPF_KOA KOART=S; confirm in GRC ARA (Maintain G/L Master vs Post JE). 2. Separate duties: G/L master maintenance belongs to a controlling/master-data function, manual posting to accountants; in PFCG remove FS00/FSS0/FSP0 and F_SKA1_BUK/F_SKA1_KTP from posting roles (or the posting tcodes from master-data roles) and regenerate. 3. Route manual journals through park + post (FV50 park, FBV0 post) so an independent approver posts what a preparer parks; combine with a workflow release if available. 4. Restrict posting by document type/account type and company code, and lock down high-risk accounts (suspense/clearing) with authorization groups. 5. Enable and monitor G/L master change documents and a manual-JE review report (preparer vs poster, new-account postings) as a detective control. 6.
