Where separation is impractical, register a mitigating control (independent JE review, account-reconciliation sign-off) in GRC/CSV with owner and expiry. 7. Verify: in QA attempt to create a G/L account and post a manual journal to it under split roles, confirming denial; re-run ARA for zero residual. 8. Caution: test in QA, coordinate with the record-to-report/close team, and time role changes to avoid disrupting period-end postings.
References
  • tcodesearch F_BKPF_BUK
  • authorizationexperts.com f_ska1_buk / f_ska1_ktp / f_bkpf_koa
CRITICAL P2 · 65 SoD conflict: Maintain HR Master Data and Execute Payroll Run ARA-H2R-01 ▶
Security Risk
A single user can both maintain pay-relevant HR master data (PA30/PA40 writing infotypes IT0008 Basic Pay, IT0014 Recurring Payments/Deductions, IT0015 Additional Payments, controlled by P_ORGIN with AUTHC W/E/S and INFTY 0008/0014/0015) and execute the payroll driver (PC00_M99_CALC / PC00_M10_CALC, controlled by P_PCLX AUTHC=U on the payroll cluster and P_ABAP). This is the flagship hire-to-retire SoD: whoever sets pay amounts must not be the one who runs payroll, or they can inflate their own or an accomplice's pay and immediately process it into a live payroll result with no review. Attack scenario: the perpetrator raises a salary, adds a recurring allowance, or posts a one-off additional payment to their own or a colluding employee's record, then runs the payroll calculation so the inflated amount is carried into the period's payroll results and, downstream, into net pay and posting; because they control both the input and the run, no independent payroll administrator ever validates the change against an authorized source. Business impact is direct payroll fraud/cash loss, understated payroll expense controls, GDPR-sensitive personal-data manipulation, and a high-severity SoD failure in a process with material, recurring monetary flow. In S/4HANA / SAP HCM (including where payroll runs on-prem alongside RISE S/4) and Employee Central Payroll the same input-vs-run separation applies. A real incident looks like pay-relevant infotype changes to a small set of employees immediately followed by a payroll run executed under the same user ID.
Affected Items (1)
  • ARAFRAUD4 (2 role(s))
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: SUIM -> RSUSR002 for PA30/PA40 (with P_ORGIN INFTY 0008/0014/0015, AUTHC W/E/S) together with PC00_M99_CALC/PC00_M10_CALC (P_PCLX AUTHC=U); confirm in GRC ARA (Maintain HR Master vs Execute Payroll). 2. Separate duties: pay-relevant master-data maintenance belongs to HR administrators, payroll execution to a distinct payroll team. In PFCG remove the payroll-run tcodes / P_PCLX AUTHC=U (or the infotype write access) from the conflicting roles and regenerate. 3. Use the HR structural/context authorization concept: restrict P_ORGIN by personnel area/subarea/employee group and, if context solution is active, P_ORGINCON with organizational-unit scoping so administrators cannot maintain the population they run payroll for. 4. Verify the HR main switches in OOAC (table T77S0, AUTSW/ORGIN, AUTSW/INCON) are set consistently with the authorization design. 5. Add detective monitoring: report of IT0008/0014/0015 changes vs payroll-run user (infotype change logs via report RPUAUD00 / logged changes T585A/B/C) reviewed independently. 6. Where separation is impractical, register a mitigating control (independent payroll-change audit before release, payroll-reconciliation review) in GRC/CSV with owner and expiry. 7. Verify: in QA attempt to change IT0008 and run payroll under split roles, confirming denial; re-run ARA for zero residual. 8. Caution: test in QA with sandbox personnel numbers, coordinate with the payroll calendar, and never test on live payroll results.
References
  • SAP Help P_ORGIN (INFTY/AUTHC)
  • SAP Help AUTHC values R/M/W/E/D/S
  • sap-tcodes PC00_M99_CALC
  • sapsecuritypages P_ABAP
CRITICAL P2 · 65 SoD conflict: User Administration vs Authorization/Profile Administration ARA-BASIS-01 ▶
Security Risk
A single user can both administer user master records (SU01/SU10/SU12 with S_USER_GRP ACTVT 01/02 to create/change users and reset passwords, and assign roles/profiles via S_USER_AGR/S_USER_PRO ACTVT 22) and define what those roles/profiles grant (PFCG/SU02/SU03/SU24 with S_USER_AGR/S_USER_AUT/S_USER_PRO ACTVT 01/02 to build role and authorization content). This is the foundational Basis privilege-escalation SoD: whoever can build authorizations must not also be able to assign them, or they can silently grant themselves (or a confederate/back-door account) unlimited access with no four-eyes control. Attack scenario: the perpetrator edits a role in PFCG to add a powerful authorization (e.g., a wildcard object, SAP_ALL-equivalent content, or S_TABU/S_DEVELOP), or builds a new role, and then assigns it to their own or a hidden user via SU01/SU10 — effectively self-service super-user, which they can also quietly reverse after abusing it; the same combination lets them reset any user's password and act as them. Business impact is total loss of authorization-control integrity: this access can defeat every other SoD and application control in the system, enabling large-scale fraud, data theft or sabotage, and it is a top audit finding (unrestricted or self-serviceable security administration). In S/4HANA RISE the customer still owns application user and role administration, so this conflict is a customer responsibility. A real incident looks like role-content changes followed by the same admin assigning that role to an account, then a burst of high-privilege activity and a reversal — visible only if the Security Audit Log and change documents were protected from the same admin.
Affected Items (2)
  • ARAFRAUD3 (2 role(s))
  • ARAMULTI (6 role(s))
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: SUIM -> RSUSR002 for SU01/SU10 (S_USER_GRP, S_USER_AGR ACTVT 22) together with PFCG/SU02/SU03 (S_USER_AGR/S_USER_AUT ACTVT 01/02); confirm in GRC ARA (User Admin vs Authorization Admin). 2. Split security administration into two roles: a User Administrator (create/change users, assign roles/profiles) and a Role/Authorization Builder (PFCG content, SU24), and never grant both to one person. In PFCG rebuild the roles and regenerate. 3. Restrict S_USER_GRP by user group (CLASS) so admins manage only their delegated population and cannot touch super-user IDs, and restrict S_USER_AGR by role namespace. 4. Remove SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW and any wildcard S_USER_* from all dialog users; grant powerful maintenance only via a controlled, logged firefighter (GRC EAM) process. 5. Ensure the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG) and change-document logging on users/roles are administered by yet another team (see BASIS-04) so admins cannot cover their tracks. 6. Where a very small team must retain both, register a mitigating control (independent daily review of role-content and role-assignment change logs via RSSCD100 / SUIM change documents) in GRC/CSV with owner and expiry. 7. Verify: in QA attempt to edit a role and assign it to yourself under split roles, confirming denial; re-run ARA for zero residual. 8. Caution: test in QA, coordinate with the security team's operating model, and ensure emergency-access (firefighter) coverage exists before tightening, to avoid lockout.
References
  • SAP Help S_USER_GRP (CLASS/ACTVT)
  • SAP KBA 2658656
  • SAP Help S_USER_AGR (ACTVT 01/02/22)
  • authorizationexperts.com s_user_agr
HIGH P2 · 68 Gateway secinfo missing deny-all default rule INTG-GW-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags a gateway secinfo configuration that lacks an explicit deny-all default rule. Gateway ACLs are evaluated as an ordered rule list; the safe design is default-deny - specific permits at the top, then a catch-all deny at the bottom - so that anything not explicitly allowed is refused. Without a terminating deny-all, the effective behavior depends on gateway version and the gw/acl_mode setting, and can fall back to implicitly allowing program starts that were never intended to be permitted, widening the attack surface unpredictably. In practice, a missing deny-all often coexists with, or silently re-enables, the permit-all exposure that 10KBLAZE-style attacks rely on, because the absence of a final deny means undefined requests are not reliably blocked. Attack scenario: an attacker submits a program-start request for a program/host combination that no rule explicitly covers; with no deny-all backstop and permissive defaults, the gateway allows it, leading to the same external-program RCE risk as INTG-GW-001. Business impact: potential remote program execution, inconsistent and non-auditable ACL behavior, and a hardening/audit gap against the SAP Security Baseline and SAP Note 1408081. A real incident looks like a program start succeeding that operators believed was disallowed, because no explicit rule denied it. This is high severity because it removes the safety net that makes the whole ACL trustworthy. A default-deny posture is fundamental to any ACL and cheap to add. Ensuring gw/acl_mode is active is equally important so the ACL is actually consulted.
Affected Items (1)
  • secinfo — no deny-all default found
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm gw/acl_mode = 1 so the gateway enforces the ACL (RZ11; set persistently in RZ10, per SAP Note 1408081). 2. Edit the secinfo file and add an explicit deny-all as the final rule: 'D TP=* HOST=* USER-HOST=* USER=*' (deny everything not previously permitted). 3. Ensure all required program-start permits are listed above the deny-all in the correct order (see INTG-GW-001). 4. Verify gw/sec_info points to the correct, shared secinfo file for every instance. 5. Reload the ACL via SMGW → Expert Functions → External Security → Reread. 6. Verify by attempting a program start not covered by any permit (expect it to be denied) and confirming legitimate program starts still work. 7. Cross-check the gateway logs (SMGW) to confirm denies are being logged. 8. Apply the same default-deny structure to reginfo (see INTG-GW-005) and prxyinfo if used. 9. Roll out identically across all application server instances. 10. Document the final rule set and place it under change control. Caution: adding deny-all only tightens behavior for requests not otherwise permitted, but confirm your permit list is complete first (capture real traffic in monitor mode) so no legitimate program start is caught by the new default deny.
References
  • SAP Note 1408081 — Gateway Security Configuration
HIGH P2 · 68 Gateway secinfo permits external program execution INTG-GW-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags secinfo permit rules that specifically allow starting external programs associated with OS-level execution - indicators such as SAPXPG, TP_*, /usr/, /bin/, CMD, or PROGRAM in the rule. SAPXPG is SAP's standard mechanism for launching external operating-system commands/programs from within the SAP system; permitting it broadly through the gateway hands remote callers a controlled path to run OS commands on the SAP host. This is the practical mechanism behind gateway RCE: an attacker does not need a memory-corruption bug when the ACL itself authorizes launching arbitrary OS programs. Attack scenario: an attacker who can reach the gateway invokes SAPXPG (or a permitted /bin path) to execute an OS command under the <sid>adm account - reading configuration and credential files, writing a web shell into the SAP web directory, or downloading and running additional tooling - achieving full host compromise. Combined with permissive host rules, this is exactly how the 10KBLAZE toolset achieved OS command execution on exposed SAP systems. Business impact: remote OS command execution, complete system and data compromise, ransomware/lateral movement, and a critical control failure against SAP Note 1408081 and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident looks like SAPXPG/external command invocations in the SMGW log from unexpected hosts, new files or processes on the server, and subsequent data theft. This is high severity because it is a direct, ACL-authorized route to code execution. External program start should be tightly constrained or disabled where not genuinely required.
Affected Items (2)
  • Rule: P TP=sapxpg HOST=* USER=*
  • Rule: P TP=SAPXPG HOST=internal.corp USER=ADMIN
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SMGW review the external-security configuration and identify each rule permitting SAPXPG / OS-program starts. 2. Determine whether external program start is genuinely required by any live interface (use gateway monitor/logging to see real usage). 3. If it is not required, disable external program start entirely by setting gw/rem_start = DISABLED (RZ10/RZ11). 4. If it is required, replace broad rules with tightly scoped permits naming the exact program (TP=), the specific source and user-host, and the specific user - never wildcards for SAPXPG. 5. Keep gw/acl_mode = 1 and ensure a deny-all default terminates the list (INTG-GW-001/002). 6. Where OS command execution is exposed to end users via SM49/SM69 external commands, review and restrict those command definitions and the S_LOG_COM authorization. 7. Reload the ACL (SMGW → Reread) and, if gw/rem_start changed, plan an instance restart window. 8. Verify by attempting a disallowed SAPXPG start (expect denial) and confirming any legitimate external command still runs. 9. Apply across all instances and feed SMGW logs to the SIEM to alert on external program starts. 10. Document the justification for any remaining SAPXPG permit under change control. Caution: disabling gw/rem_start or tightening SAPXPG can break legitimate operations (e.g. external backup/archiving jobs) - validate real usage in non-prod first and coordinate with the teams that own those jobs.
References
  • SAP Note 1408081
  • CVE-2020-6207 — SAP Gateway RCE
HIGH P2 · 68 Gateway reginfo missing deny-all default rule INTG-GW-005 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags a gateway reginfo configuration that lacks an explicit deny-all default rule. As with secinfo, reginfo is an ordered ACL and should follow default-deny: specific permits for known RFC server program ids and hosts, terminated by a catch-all deny so any unlisted registration is refused. Without the terminating deny-all, whether an unlisted RFC server can register depends on version behavior and gw/acl_mode, and can default to allowing registrations that were never intended - reopening the rogue-registration exposure described in INTG-GW-004. A missing deny-all makes the ACL non-deterministic and hard to audit, and in effect leaves the RFC registration channel partially open. Attack scenario: an attacker registers an RFC server whose program id/host matches no explicit rule; with no deny-all backstop and permissive defaults, the gateway accepts the registration, letting the attacker intercept or inject RFC traffic exactly as in the permit-all case. Business impact: potential RFC interception/impersonation, inconsistent and unauditable registration control, and a hardening gap against SAP Note 1408081 and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident looks like an unexpected RFC server registering successfully because no rule explicitly denied it, later found in the SMGW registered-clients list. This is high severity because it removes the safety net that makes reginfo enforcement reliable. Ensuring gw/acl_mode is active is essential so the reginfo file is actually evaluated. Default-deny is a fundamental ACL principle and trivial to add.
Affected Items (1)
  • reginfo — no deny-all default found
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm gw/acl_mode = 1 and gw/reg_info points to the correct reginfo file (RZ11 to check, RZ10 to set persistently; SAP Note 1408081). 2. Edit the reginfo file and add an explicit deny-all as the final line: 'D TP=* HOST=* ...' so any registration not previously permitted is denied. 3. Ensure all legitimate RFC server registrations are listed as specific permits above the deny-all (see INTG-GW-004). 4. Reload the ACL via SMGW → Expert Functions → External Security → Reread. 5. Verify by attempting a registration not covered by any permit (expect denial) and confirming all real integration servers still register. 6. Check the SMGW registered-clients list to ensure only expected servers are present. 7. Apply the same default-deny structure to secinfo (INTG-GW-002) and, if used, prxyinfo. 8. Roll out identically across every application-server instance. 9. Document the finalized reginfo under change control and forward registration events to the SIEM. 10. Re-run the audit to confirm the deny-all default is detected. Caution: confirm the permit list is complete from real captured registrations before adding deny-all, so the new default does not block a legitimate but infrequently-registering RFC server; validate in non-prod first.
References
  • SAP Note 1408081
HIGH P2 · 56 Missing High-priority SAP Security Notes HOTNEWS-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding lists High-priority Security Notes (Priority 2, CVSS 7.0-8.9) that are not recorded as implemented — in the shipped catalog this includes note 3123427 (CVE-2022-22532 / CVE-2022-22533), the AS Java Memory Pipe (MPI) / ICMAD-family HTTP-smuggling and memory-exhaustion issue. While rated below HotNews, High notes still describe directly exploitable weaknesses and are routinely chained by attackers who first land through a lower-severity foothold. The MPI/smuggling class is dangerous because a crafted request sequence can desynchronise the ICM/Web Dispatcher request queue, letting an attacker smuggle a second request past front-end controls (WAF, reverse proxy, SAP Web Dispatcher ACLs) — poisoning caches, hijacking another user's authenticated session, or bypassing URL-based authorization to reach protected ICF services. The memory-exhaustion variant enables denial of service against an internet-facing gateway, which for an S/4HANA order-to-cash or treasury system is a direct availability and revenue impact. In a RISE context these notes are still the customer's to schedule, and because they are not flagged HotNews they are frequently deferred indefinitely, quietly accumulating exposure. The abuse scenario: an attacker who has mapped a reachable NetWeaver front end scripts a smuggling probe, confirms desync, then reuses it to reach an admin ICF endpoint or to force a DoS during a business-critical run. Compliance impact includes ISO 27001 A.8.8 vulnerability-management findings and, for a session-hijack outcome, GDPR/data-confidentiality exposure. A real incident looks like intermittent, hard-to-diagnose session cross-talk or gateway crashes that are eventually root-caused to an unpatched smuggling note. Severity is High rather than Critical, but these must not be allowed to age past the next patch cycle.
Affected Items (1)
  • Note 3123427 / CVE-2022-22532 / CVE-2022-22533 / NetWeaver AS Java (Memory Pipe / MPI, ICMAD) (CVSS 8.1, 2022-02) — ICMAD HTTP smuggling / MPI exhaustion in AS Java
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the affected_items list and validate each note's relevance to your kernel/Support Package level in System Recommendations (Solution Manager) or SAP Cloud ALM. 2. Schedule the notes into the next scheduled patch cycle rather than as emergency changes, but with a firm target date and owner. 3. Implement correcting notes via transaction SNOTE; for MPI/ICM-class fixes (note 3123427) apply the corresponding kernel patch and restart the instance, as the fix is typically kernel-level. 4. If an SAP Web Dispatcher sits in front of the stack, patch it to the same corrected kernel level so front-end and back-end parsing stay consistent (a mismatch is what enables smuggling). 5. Review ICM logging/limits and any reverse-proxy/WAF normalisation rules as defence-in-depth against request-smuggling. 6. Run the change through DEV > QA > PROD with regression testing of HTTP interfaces, Fiori, and any proxied traffic. 7. For RISE, coordinate kernel/Web Dispatcher patching with SAP ECS and confirm ownership boundaries. 8. Verify: confirm SNOTE status 'Completely Implemented' (PRSTATUS = E), check the running kernel patch level via System > Status, and re-run System Recommendations to confirm the note clears. 9. Add these notes to the tracked backlog with a due date so they do not silently age. Caution: kernel replacement needs a maintenance window and instance restart; coordinate with interface owners and load-balancer/proxy teams before changing front-end parsing behaviour.
References
  • SAP Security Patch Day
HIGH P2 · 56 Critical SAP Notes only partially implemented HOTNEWS-004 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags catalog notes that appear in SNOTE with an incomplete / not-effective implementation status (e.g. 'Incompletely Implemented' or 'Partially Implemented'). This is more insidious than a plainly missing note because it creates a false sense of security: patch dashboards, auditors and the Basis team may see the note 'in progress' or listed, and assume the vulnerability is closed, when in fact the corrective code path is not fully active. SNOTE marks a note incomplete when automatic correction instructions were applied but required manual activities were skipped, when object adjustments (SPDD/SPAU) were left unresolved after a later Support Package overwrote the note's objects, or when a dependent note/prerequisite was never implemented. For a HotNews such as RECON or a Visual Composer RCE, a half-applied fix can leave the exact vulnerable endpoint reachable while the tracking system says otherwise — the worst of both worlds. The abuse scenario: an attacker exploits the still-open flaw exactly as if the note were missing, but the defenders waste critical response time because their records show the note as handled, delaying detection and patch verification. Business and compliance impact includes an inaccurate control evidence base (a SOX/ISO auditor relying on a status that misrepresents reality), plus the same breach exposure as an unpatched HotNews. System-consistency risk is also real: a partially implemented note can leave code/customising in an inconsistent state that causes runtime errors or dumps. A real incident looks like a post-breach review discovering that the 'implemented' note had unfinished manual steps or unresolved SPAU conflicts, so protection was never actually in place.
Affected Items (1)
  • Note 3420923 / CVE-2024-22131 / ABAP Platform (SAP ABA) (CVSS 9.1, 2024-02) — Code injection in SAP Application Basis (ABA) — status: incomplete
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open transaction SNOTE and, for each note in the affected_items list, display the implementation log and current status to see exactly which automatic/manual steps are outstanding. 2. Re-process the note to 'Completely Implemented' (target status PRSTATUS = E), executing every manual pre-/post-implementation activity described in the note text. 3. If the incompleteness stems from a Support Package overwriting note objects, resolve the modification adjustments in transaction SPAU (and SPDD for dictionary objects) and re-confirm the note. 4. Check and implement any prerequisite/dependent notes SNOTE reports as missing; HotNews fixes often chain several notes. 5. Where objects 'cannot be implemented', investigate whether a newer note version or the correcting Support Package (via Maintenance Planner + SPAM/SAINT) is the correct path instead of forcing SNOTE. 6. Do the rework in DEV first, then transport and re-confirm through QA to PROD under change control. 7. For RISE, coordinate with SAP ECS where the completion depends on a kernel/SP action they own. 8. Verify: SNOTE must show 'Completely Implemented', the implementation log must show no open manual tasks, and System Recommendations must drop the note after the collector job re-runs. 9. For actively-exploited notes in this list, additionally run the IoC checks from HOTNEWS-003, since a partial fix does not close the exploited flaw. Caution: re-processing notes can re-trigger object adjustments and regression risk — test thoroughly and schedule any activation/restart in a maintenance window.
References
  • SAP Note Implementation (SNOTE) — Best Practices
CRITICAL P3 · 47 SQL injection in custom ABAP — Z_LEGACY_MIGRATION ATC-SQLI ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. An attacker-controlled value is concatenated into an Open SQL statement — a dynamic WHERE, FROM, ORDER BY, GROUP BY or HAVING clause built from a variable. The database is asked to parse whatever arrives, so a crafted value changes which rows are read or written rather than merely which are selected. In SAP this rarely stops at data theft: the same clause frequently drives an update or a delete, so a read-only-looking report becomes a write path. The business impact is mass data exfiltration under any valid credential, and silent modification of records that the application's own authorization checks were meant to protect.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_LEGACY_MIGRATION (CLAS) line 89
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Replace the concatenated clause with a parameterised query: bind values through the SQL statement API, or express the filter as a range table / SELECT-OPTIONS so the kernel builds the WHERE. 2. Where a dynamic clause is genuinely required, validate the constructed string against an allowlist of column names before it reaches the statement — never against a denylist of characters. 3. Escape any remaining dynamic fragment with the SAP-supplied dynamic-programming utility class rather than with hand-written quoting. 4. Re-check the authorization: a statement that can now read arbitrary rows needs the AUTHORITY-CHECK that the narrowed query previously made unnecessary.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — secure custom code
  • CWE-89
HIGH P3 · 56 Unrestricted destination authorization (S_ICF ICF_FIELD=DEST, ICF_VALUE=*) AUTH-016 ▶
Security Risk
1 role(s) grant S_ICF with the DEST field and ICF_VALUE='*'. For ICF_FIELD=DEST, ICF_VALUE is NOT the destination name — it is the per-destination 'Authorization for Destination' authorization-group value maintained on the SM59 Logon & Security tab; S_ICF is only enforced for destinations that have such a value assigned. A value of '*' therefore grants use of every destination that is protected by ANY authorization group (and, combined with the fact that unprotected destinations are usable regardless, effectively removes destination scoping for the role). Destinations frequently store embedded logon credentials or are configured for trusted-RFC, so the ability to use an arbitrary protected destination is effectively the ability to authenticate to the connected target systems as whatever principal that destination carries — including high-privilege service accounts and connections to more sensitive systems (e.g. from a sandbox toward production). Combined with a generic RFC/OData caller this becomes a credential-reuse and lateral-movement path, and it is easy to overlook because S_ICF is often copied wholesale from a template role.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_BASIS_SUPER — 2 user(s) [ADMIN1, CONTRACTOR7] — S_ICF ICF_FIELD=DEST, ICF_VALUE=*
Remediation — Step by Step
Do not grant S_ICF ICF_VALUE='*' for the DEST field. Instead: (1) assign distinct 'Authorization for Destination' group values to sensitive destinations on the SM59 Logon & Security tab so they are actually protected by S_ICF, and (2) restrict S_ICF ICF_VALUE in each role to only those specific authorization-group values the role legitimately needs (not the destination names, and never '*'). Review which destinations store credentials or use trusted-RFC and treat authorization to those as privileged; prefer destinations without stored credentials (current-user / SSO propagation) so that destination use cannot escalate privilege, and reconcile S_ICF grants against the trusted-RFC findings (S_RFCACL, AUTH-002).
References
  • SAP Help — Authorization object S_ICF (ICF_FIELD DEST/SERVICE, ICF_VALUE)
  • SAP Note 1416085 — S_RFCACL trusted-RFC wildcard risk (cross-reference)
HIGH P3 · 56 Background-job impersonation (S_BTCH_NAM BTCUNAME = *) AUTH-012 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_BTCH_NAM with BTCUNAME='*'. S_BTCH_NAM controls under which user identity a background job STEP may run: when a job is scheduled, the step can be told to execute in the security context of a named 'step user', and S_BTCH_NAM is the authorization that permits choosing that user. With BTCUNAME='*', the holder can schedule job steps that run under ANY other user's identity — including technical batch users or accounts that carry SAP_ALL or other powerful roles. This is background-job impersonation: the attacker does not need to know the target user's password; they simply schedule a step to run as that user and let the SAP batch scheduler execute their chosen program (or a standard report) in the privileged context. The consequence is privileged code execution and data change performed under someone else's identity, which also muddies attribution — the job and its footprint appear to belong to the impersonated step user, not the attacker. In an S/4HANA production client this is a High-severity privilege-escalation and SoD risk: a user with a modest interactive role can reach SAP_ALL-level effect indirectly through a scheduled step, and can defeat GRC SoD analysis because the powerful action is executed by the batch identity. A real incident looks like a background job scheduled by one user but running under a privileged batch user, performing a mass change or data extract, discovered through job-log (SM37) review showing a mismatch between the scheduling user and the step user. Wildcard S_BTCH_NAM is a recognized critical authorization in SAP/DSAG guidance.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_SEC_ADMIN — 0 users (unassigned) — S_BTCH_NAM BTCUNAME=*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_BTCH_NAM with BTCUNAME='*'; list roles and holders. 2. In PFCG, restrict S_BTCH_NAM to the specific, legitimate step-user(s) each role needs; never '*'. 3. Make batch step-users dedicated service accounts of user type 'System' (SU01) with least-privilege roles, and never schedule steps under interactive or SAP_ALL-class users. 4. Review existing scheduled jobs (SM37) for steps running under privileged batch users and correct those that impersonate powerful accounts. 5. Separate batch duties across S_BTCH_JOB (schedule/manage jobs), S_BTCH_NAM (run as another user) and S_BTCH_ADM (batch administration) so no single role concentrates them. 6. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no assigned role keeps BTCUNAME='*'. 7. Verify: with a test user, attempt to schedule a step under an unauthorized step-user and confirm refusal (SU53); review SM37 to confirm no unexpected impersonation remains. 8. Rollout caution: legitimate interfaces sometimes run steps under a shared batch user — confirm the required step-users with job owners before locking down, test in QA, and stage the change so scheduled production jobs do not fail.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_BTCH_NAM
  • DSAG Audit — batch impersonation
HIGH P3 · 56 Standard users not locked STDUSR-003 ▶
Security Risk
Standard users are not locked. SAP, DSAG and the SAP Security Baseline require SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC and EARLYWATCH — and any standard user in clients 000/001/066 — to be locked and unlocked only for controlled maintenance, and SAP*/DDIC must never serve as everyday dialog users. An unlocked, dialog-capable SAP*/DDIC is a large attack surface: it is a standing target for password guessing, brute force and credential stuffing, and if the default password is also present (see STDUSR-002) it is a trivial takeover. Clients 000/001/066 are frequently forgotten: 066 is the historical EarlyWatch client, 001 is a template client, and both are low-traffic, weakly monitored places where an attacker prefers to operate. Even when passwords are strong, leaving these accounts open still increases brute-force exposure and is a direct baseline/audit deviation. Attack scenario: an attacker runs a slow credential-stuffing campaign against DDIC in client 000; because the account is unlocked and dialog-capable, a single success yields an interactive session that can run any transaction and grant further authorizations. Business impact: a privilege-escalation foothold, lateral movement across clients, and an audit/compliance finding. A real incident looks like repeated failed logons followed by a successful DDIC or SAP* logon in a rarely used client, off-hours.
Affected Items (4)
  • SAP* (client 000) — unlocked, dialog-capable
  • DDIC (client 001) — unlocked, dialog-capable
  • SAPCPIC (client 000) — unlocked
  • EARLYWATCH (client 066) — unlocked
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Run RSUSR003 to list the lock status of standard users per client, and RSUSR200 to review last-logon/inactivity. 2. In SU01 (or SU10 for mass action) set an administrator lock on SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC and EARLYWATCH in every client, prioritising 000/001/066. 3. Keep DDIC/SAP* out of daily use: do not operate them as Dialog users; unlock only inside an approved maintenance window and re-lock immediately afterwards. 4. If client 066 is unused, delete it following SAP Note 1749142, and lock/close unused client 001 via SCC4 (set it to not-modifiable, no client copies). 5. Assign the accounts to group SUPER so only authorized admins can unlock them. 6. Set login/fails_to_user_lock and login/failed_user_auto_unlock = 0 so brute-force attempts result in a persistent lock. 7. Verify by re-running RSUSR003 (all standard users show 'locked') and review SM19/SM20 security-audit logs for logon attempts. Caution: never delete SAP* (see STDUSR-001). Locking DDIC during an upgrade or transport import can break jobs — coordinate with Basis and test in non-production first.
References
  • SAP Note 2383
  • SAP Security Baseline — Standard users
HIGH P3 · 56 Inbound trusted-RFC relationships (verify no trust from a lower tier) TRUST-001 ▶
Security Risk
One or more systems are configured in RFCSYSACL as TRUSTED to log on to this system via trusted RFC. Trust must only ever flow from an equal-or-higher security tier down to a lower one — a production system must NEVER trust a development or QA system. When production trusts a lower tier, any user who holds a dialog logon plus the S_RFCACL authorization in that lower system can hop into production without knowing a production password, using SM59 trusted destinations or trusted RFC calls. Development and QA typically have relaxed controls, more developers, debug/replace access and weaker passwords, so they are the easy foothold. The module flags trusted SIDs beginning with D/Q/S/T as likely non-production and raises the severity accordingly. Attack scenario: an attacker who has compromised (or a developer who abuses) a dev account opens a trusted destination to production, or issues an RFC with trusted logon, and lands in production as their mapped user. If S_RFCACL in production is maintained with wildcards, this becomes arbitrary-user impersonation, up to and including super-users. Business impact: segregation-of-duties bypass, unauthorized production changes, financial fraud and mass data theft; this dev-to-prod pivot is a classic pattern in real SAP breaches. A real incident looks like a production logon via trusted RFC that originates from a development host and uses a user that only normally exists in dev.
Affected Items (3)
  • Trusted system DEV [likely NON-PRODUCTION tier]
  • Trusted system QAS [likely NON-PRODUCTION tier]
  • Trusted system PRD
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SMT1 (or by reviewing table RFCSYSACL) list every system that is allowed to log on to this system via trusted RFC. 2. Delete any trust entry that originates FROM a lower tier (dev/QA into prod). Trust must be one-directional from higher to lower security tier only. 3. For legitimate trust, tighten S_RFCACL in PFCG/SU24 to specific users, the specific calling SID, RFC_EQUSER = Y (same-user propagation) and specific transactions — never S_RFCACL with '*' (cross-reference AUTH-002). 4. Enforce SNC encryption on trusted connections (STRUST/SNC) so trust material cannot be sniffed. 5. Migrate all relationships to the 2020 trust security method (see TRUST-003). 6. Verify: SMT1 shows only approved higher-tier trusting systems, and use SUIM (users by authorization value) to enumerate who actually holds S_RFCACL in production. Caution: removing a trust relationship can break dependent interfaces, CUA (central user administration) and Solution Manager. Inventory the callers first, coordinate with interface owners, and test the removal in non-production before applying it to production.
References
  • SAP Note 128447 — Trusted/Trusting systems
  • SAP Security Baseline — RFC trust
HIGH P3 · 56 RFC self-trust enabled TRUST-002 ▶
Security Risk
The system trusts itself for trusted RFC — either rfc/selftrust = 1 or a self-referential RFCSYSACL entry naming the local SID. Self-trust means a trusted destination that loops back to the same system will accept trusted-RFC identity propagation locally. Combined with the S_RFCACL authorization, a lower-privileged local user can therefore log on as a different, higher-privileged user on the same box without a password. In effect, self-trust turns any user who holds S_RFCACL into a potential impersonator of privileged users on that system, which is a direct local privilege-escalation path. Attack scenario: a user with S_RFCACL and the ability to create or modify a self-pointing trusted destination in SM59 calls a function module as an administrative user — for example to grant themselves SAP_ALL, run external OS commands via SM49/SM69, or read sensitive tables. Because the hop is internal, it is easy to overlook in network monitoring. Business impact: privilege escalation and segregation-of-duties bypass, where a single compromised low-privilege account becomes full administrative control. A real incident looks like a user gaining privileges with no corresponding administrator action, and RFC traffic looping to the local host but authenticating as another, more powerful user.
Affected Items (1)
  • rfc/selftrust = 1
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check rfc/selftrust in RZ11. If it is 1, plan to set it to 0 in RZ10 (DEFAULT/instance profile) unless a documented, reviewed scenario genuinely requires it. 2. In SMT1 remove any self-referential trust entry (the local SID trusting itself) that is not required. 3. Schedule a restart to activate the parameter change (coordinate the window with SAP managed services on RISE). 4. Where self-trust is truly needed by an embedded scenario, scope S_RFCACL tightly: specific users only, RFC_EQUSER = Y so only same-user propagation is permitted, and no '*' values. 5. Migrate the relationship to the new trust method (TRUST-003) so even self-trust uses the unique-system-ID mechanism. 6. Verify: RZ11 shows rfc/selftrust = 0, SMT1 shows no self entry, and a SUIM review confirms the reduced population of S_RFCACL holders. Caution: some embedded/same-system applications rely on self-trust — confirm with the application owners before disabling, and test in non-production first to avoid breaking those flows.
References
  • SAP Note 128447
  • SAP Security Baseline — rfc/selftrust
HIGH P3 · 56 Trusted-RFC relationships not migrated to the current security method TRUST-003 ▶
Security Risk
Trusted RFC still relies on the legacy trust-ticket method rather than the 2020 security method: either rfc/allowoldticket4tt accepts old tickets, or RFCSYSACL entries have not been migrated (migration method 3). The legacy trusted/trusting mechanism (pre SAP Note 3089413) used a trust assertion that was not bound to a unique, unforgeable system identity. It is exposed to the capture-replay weakness (CVE-2023-0014) and to improper authentication in the RFC layer (CVE-2021-27610). An attacker who obtains logon material — by sniffing unencrypted RFC traffic or by reading table RFCSYSACL — can replay or forge a trust assertion and authenticate as a trusted system against any trusting system in the landscape. Researchers demonstrated this as a potentially wormable, landscape-wide chain (SEC Consult / Onapsis). Attack scenario: capture the trust assertion from one system, replay it against another trusting system, land as an arbitrary or privileged user, then chain onward across every trusting system and use further RFCs for code execution. Business impact: landscape-wide compromise, remote code execution via follow-on RFC, and mass data breach — all from actively-discussed, already-patched exploit chains, which makes an unpatched estate an audit red flag. A real incident looks like unexpected trusted logons, replayed tickets, and alerts from an SAP threat monitor about legacy-method trust usage.
Affected Items (1)
  • rfc/allowoldticket4tt = yes (legacy trust tickets accepted)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Implement SAP Notes 3089413 (kernel + Basis correction, on BOTH the trusted and the trusting systems) and 3157268 (migration how-to); confirm the minimum kernel/SP level. 2. In SMT1 migrate each trust relationship to the new security method (unique system ID), re-creating the relationship on both sides. 3. Once every relationship is migrated, set rfc/allowoldticket4tt = no in RZ10 so legacy tickets are rejected. 4. Enforce SNC encryption (STRUST) on trusted RFC so tickets cannot be sniffed, deny direct table access to RFCSYSACL, and enable table-change logging on RFCSYSACL. 5. Restart after kernel/parameter changes (coordinate with SAP managed services on RISE). 6. Verify with SAP's check report for the note (e.g. zcheck_note_3089413 from the SAP security-services-tools repository) or confirm SMT1 shows every relationship as migrated, and RZ11 shows rfc/allowoldticket4tt = no. Caution: setting allowoldticket4tt = no before all partners are migrated will break trust. Migrate every partner first in a staged, non-production-first rollout, and watch for certificate-path errors (KBA 3400529) after applying 3089413.
References
  • SAP Note 3089413 — Trusted-RFC security method (CVE-2021-27610)
  • SAP Note 3157268 — Trusted RFC migration how-to
HIGH P3 · 56 Trusted RFC destination configured with a fixed logon user TRUST-004 ▶
Security Risk
One or more trusted RFC destinations (SM59 type 3) are configured with a fixed stored logon user instead of 'current user' propagation. The entire purpose of trusted RFC is current-user identity propagation with no stored password. Storing a fixed user turns the destination into a stored-credential hop that always executes as that user — which in practice is often a highly privileged technical or dialog account. Anyone who can execute that destination, or invoke a report/function that uses it, inherits the fixed user's authorizations in the target system, which defeats the trusted-RFC identity model and destroys accountability because every action in the target is logged as the single technical user. Attack scenario: a low-privileged user invokes the trusted destination (or a program that fronts it) and executes in the target as the stored privileged user, performing actions far beyond their own rights; alternatively an attacker extracts the stored credentials from the destination and reuses them elsewhere. Business impact: privilege escalation, breakdown of segregation-of-duties and non-repudiation, and an audit failure because activity cannot be attributed to real individuals. A real incident looks like a stream of business actions in the target system all attributed to one technical user, but actually performed by many different people.
Affected Items (1)
  • S4_TRUSTED_ADMIN — trusted destination with fixed user 'TRUST_ADMIN'
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SM59 review every ABAP (type 3) destination flagged as Trusted System = Yes; use table RFCDES to build the full inventory. 2. For each trusted destination set the logon to 'Current User' and clear the stored user and password — do not store credentials on trusted destinations. 3. If a fixed user is genuinely unavoidable, use a dedicated Communication (type C) user with least privilege — never a dialog user and never SAP_ALL. 4. Restrict who can use the destination via the relevant S_RFCACL / authorization design in the target system. 5. Confirm SNC/TLS is active on the connection. 6. Verify: the SM59 connection/authorization test shows current-user propagation, an RFCDES review shows no stored users on trusted destinations, and a SUIM check confirms the technical users' authorizations are minimal. Caution: switching to current-user propagation can break batch/background jobs that relied on the technical user's broader rights — confirm each caller's own authorizations in the target first, and test in non-production before changing production destinations.
References
  • SAP Note 128447 — Trusted destinations
  • SAP Security Baseline — RFC destinations
HIGH P3 · 56 Armed background job runs under a standard/technical step user JOBCMD-JOB-001B ▶
Security Risk
This armed job step runs under a standard SAP account - SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, or TMSADM - rather than a purpose-built technical user. These accounts have well-known names and, in poorly maintained systems, default or widely-known passwords. They also carry broad or special-purpose authorizations: TMSADM for transport management, EARLYWATCH for monitoring, SAPCPIC for CPIC/RFC connectivity. Using one as a batch step user 'borrows' its privileges for whatever the job does. It also destroys accountability - the job's actions are attributed to a shared, well-known account instead of a named technical user. Any weakness in that account (default password, over-broad profile) immediately becomes the job's weakness. Attack scenario: TMSADM often holds transport-related and, in unhardened systems, broad authorizations; a job stepping as TMSADM can act across the TMS/transport layer. If TMSADM still has its default password, an attacker who knows it can log on and manipulate the same jobs. Business impact: privilege borrowing, weakened segregation of duties, and audit ambiguity across S/4HANA batch. TMSADM abuse specifically can affect transports - i.e., the promotion of code and configuration - a high-integrity concern. Real incident: jobs quietly scheduled under TMSADM/EARLYWATCH during setup and never corrected; a pentest later found TMSADM at its default password and used the existing jobs as a foothold into the landscape.
Affected Items (1)
  • JOB_TRANSPORT — step user TMSADM
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify: SM37 / SE16 TBTCP where AUTHCKNAM in (SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM). 2. Create a dedicated least-privilege type B (System) background user in SU01, with a PFCG role scoped to the job's real authorization needs. 3. Re-plan each affected job onto the new user (SM36/SM37 change step user); do not leave productive jobs on standard accounts. 4. Harden the standard accounts themselves: run report RSUSR003 to find standard users still on default passwords and change them. 5. Lock these accounts for interactive logon where they are not needed (SU01), and maintain TMSADM per current SAP hardening guidance. 6. Restrict S_BTCH_NAM (field BTCUSERNM) and S_BTCH_ADM so operators cannot set these accounts as step users (PFCG); review holders with SUIM. 7. Verify: RSUSR003 shows no default-password standard users. 8. Verify: SE16 TBTCP shows no armed step under SAPCPIC/EARLYWATCH/TMSADM. 9. QA-run each re-planned job and confirm success in the SM37 job log. 10. Rollout caution: TMSADM is used by the transport system and EARLYWATCH by Solution Manager/monitoring - do not lock or repurpose them blindly; coordinate with Basis and stage step-user changes in DEV/QA before PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — Background processing users (SM36/SM37)
HIGH P3 · 54 Parameter gw/acl_mode non-compliant PARAM-gw/acl_mode ▶
Security Risk
Decides how the RFC gateway behaves when no explicit ACL rule matches. A permissive default lets an external program register with the gateway and receive RFC traffic — the misconfiguration class behind the 10KBLAZE gateway attacks. Current value: '0'. The ECS standard value is '1'. SAP permits no exception to this value.
Affected Items (1)
  • gw/acl_mode = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
Set gw/acl_mode to the ECS standard value and maintain explicit secinfo and reginfo ACL files. In an ECS/RISE tenant profile parameters are maintained by SAP: raise a service request quoting SAP Note 3250501 rather than attempting the change in RZ10. Re-export the profile parameters (RSPARAM) afterwards and confirm the active value on every instance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 54 Parameter gw/prxy_info non-compliant PARAM-gw/prxy_info ▶
Security Risk
Names the prxyinfo ACL file that decides which systems may use this gateway as a proxy. Unset, the proxy path is governed by the default behaviour alone. Current value: ''. The ECS standard value is '$(DIR_GLOBAL)$(DIR_SEP)prxyinfo$(FT_DAT)'. SAP permits no exception to this value. Checked here: a configured proxy-info ACL file path. Verified: a path is configured. Not verified: that the file exists or what rules it contains — the ECS value is a $(DIR_GLOBAL) placeholder and the file is an OS artifact no profile export carries.
Affected Items (1)
  • gw/prxy_info =
Remediation — Step by Step
Point gw/prxy_info at a maintained prxyinfo ACL file and reload it in SMGW (Goto > Expert Functions > Reread). In an ECS/RISE tenant profile parameters are maintained by SAP: raise a service request quoting SAP Note 3250501 rather than attempting the change in RZ10. Re-export the profile parameters (RSPARAM) afterwards and confirm the active value on every instance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 54 Parameter service/protectedwebmethods non-compliant PARAM-service/protectedwebmethods ▶
Security Risk
Which sapstartsrv / SAP Host Agent SOAP methods require authentication. Left unprotected they expose instance start and stop, process listings and log and trace file retrieval to whoever can reach the port. Current value: 'NONE'. The ECS standard value is 'SDEFAULT'. SAP permits no exception to this value.
Affected Items (1)
  • service/protectedwebmethods = NONE
Remediation — Step by Step
Set service/protectedwebmethods to the ECS standard value. In an ECS/RISE tenant profile parameters are maintained by SAP: raise a service request quoting SAP Note 3250501 rather than attempting the change in RZ10. Re-export the profile parameters (RSPARAM) afterwards and confirm the active value on every instance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 54 RFC destinations with stored credentials NET-001 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags RFC destinations (maintained in SM59, persisted in table RFCDES) that store a fixed logon user and password. SAP encrypts the stored password with a system key, but it is decryptable at runtime and recoverable from a database/system copy, a table export, or by anyone able to read RFCDES. The core danger is credential inheritance: any user or process on the source system that can trigger a call through such a destination silently authenticates on the target as the stored user, with that user's full authorization set and no separate logon. This is the classic RFC-hopping lateral-movement path. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape there are many RFCs radiating from the central ABAP instance to satellite systems, Solution Manager, BW, and outward via the Cloud Connector to BTP, so a single destination carrying a powerful technical user (or worse SAP_ALL, DDIC, or a wide batch user) becomes a crown-jewel pivot. The attack is concrete: a low-privilege dialog user who can start a function module that uses the destination, or an attacker who has compromised the source host, hops to the target with the stored user's rights and then reads or posts data, dumps tables, or calls further RFCs. If the destination runs from a lower-trust tier (sandbox or development) into production, it collapses the segregation between environments. Business impact includes fraudulent financial postings, mass data exfiltration under GDPR, segregation-of-duties bypass, and failure of SOX IT general controls over access. A real incident typically looks like a forgotten dev-to-prod destination holding an FI power user that is abused to create unauthorized journal entries with no attributable dialog logon.
Affected Items (8)
  • SAP_ERP_PROD → user: RFC_ADMIN (auth type: STORED)
  • SAP_BW_SYSTEM → user: BW_RFC_USER (auth type: STORED)
  • ARIBA_CLOUD → user: ARIBA_INT (auth type: BASIC)
  • SF_EC_CONNECT → user: SF_API_USER (auth type: OAUTH)
  • VENDOR_PORTAL → user: VENDOR_RFC (auth type: STORED)
  • LEGACY_ECC → user: LEGACY_USER (auth type: STORED)
  • S4_TRUSTED_ADMIN → user: TRUST_ADMIN (auth type: TRUSTED)
  • BANK_INTERFACE → user: BANK_RFC_USR (auth type: STORED)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory the exposure: run report RSRFCCHK (or review SM59 and table RFCDES) to list every destination that carries stored logon data, and record the stored user and target system for each. 2. Prefer trust over stored passwords: where source and target are your own systems, replace the stored credential with a Trusted RFC relationship defined in SMT1 (trusted/trusting systems) so the caller identity flows and the target performs an S_RFCACL check rather than relying on a stored password. 3. Where trust is not possible, switch the SM59 destination to certificate/SNC single sign-on on the Logon and Security tab instead of user and password. 4. If a technical user must remain, create a dedicated account in SU01 of type System or Communication (never Dialog), and scope its role tightly, restricting authorization object S_RFC to only the required function groups; never assign SAP_ALL or use DDIC. 5. Set a long generated password, store it in a secrets vault, and rotate it on a schedule. 6. Lock down who can maintain destinations: restrict transaction SM59 and object S_RFC_ADM to the Basis team only. 7. Enforce inbound RFC authorization on targets by setting profile parameter auth/rfc_authority_check to 6 or 9 so the target validates S_RFC for the called function group. 8. Optionally deploy Unified Connectivity (transaction UCONCOCKPIT) to allow-list which function modules are callable externally. 9. Verify by re-running RSRFCCHK and confirming the count drops; test each interface in non-production first and coordinate with interface owners before removing stored credentials. SM59 changes take effect immediately, but SNC or parameter changes may require an instance restart.
References
  • SAP Note 1480644
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 4.2
HIGH P3 · 54 RFC destinations without SNC encryption NET-003 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags RFC destinations of connection type 3 (ABAP-to-ABAP over TCP/IP), T (external TCP/IP program), or W/HTTP that do not have SNC (Secure Network Communication) enabled, meaning the traffic is not cryptographically protected. The SAP DIAG and RFC protocols are only lightly obfuscated, not encrypted, so without SNC the logon credentials and all business payload traverse the network in effectively clear form. Any actor positioned on the network path can capture and decode this traffic. The attack is straightforward: an adversary with a foothold in the same network segment, or able to perform ARP spoofing, tap a switch span port, or observe traffic within a shared cloud tenancy, records the RFC session, recovers the technical user's password and the transported data, and then replays or reuses those credentials for lateral movement. In an S/4HANA RISE deployment the links between the customer-managed components and the SAP-managed application and HANA layers, and the links out to BTP, cross provider-controlled network fabric, so unencrypted RFC directly contradicts the SAP Security Baseline requirement for encrypted internal and external communication. The consequences are credential theft feeding onward compromise, disclosure of confidential business data in transit, and a documented control gap against the Security Baseline and DSAG audit guidance. A realistic incident is a packet capture of routine batch RFC traffic that yields a technical user's password, which turns out to be reused across several systems, giving the attacker a landscape-wide key.
Affected Items (7)
  • SAP_ERP_PROD (type: 3, SNC: disabled) — RFC via TCP/IP (Type 3) — verify SNC encryption
  • ARIBA_CLOUD (type: W, SNC: disabled) — WebRFC/HTTP — verify HTTPS and auth
  • SF_EC_CONNECT (type: W, SNC: disabled) — WebRFC/HTTP — verify HTTPS and auth
  • VENDOR_PORTAL (type: 3, SNC: disabled) — RFC via TCP/IP (Type 3) — verify SNC encryption
  • LEGACY_ECC (type: 3, SNC: disabled) — RFC via TCP/IP (Type 3) — verify SNC encryption
  • S4_TRUSTED_ADMIN (type: 3, SNC: disabled) — RFC via TCP/IP (Type 3) — verify SNC encryption
  • BANK_INTERFACE (type: T, SNC: disabled) — TCP/IP Connection — potentially unencrypted
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Install and configure the SNC cryptographic library (CommonCryptoLib / sapcryptolib) on all application servers and create the system SNC PSE via STRUST and transaction SNC0. 2. Set the enabling profile parameters: snc/enable=1, snc/data_protection/use=3, snc/data_protection/min=3, snc/data_protection/max=3, and snc/r3int_rfc_secure=1 to force internal system-to-system RFC over SNC. 3. During migration, temporarily allow legacy clients with snc/accept_insecure_rfc and related snc/accept_insecure_* parameters, then tighten them to 0 (or a named allow-list) once all partners are converted. 4. In SM59, for each type 3 and T destination, open the Logon and Security tab, activate SNC, and set the Quality of Protection to Privacy Protection (encryption; value 3, or 9 for maximum). 5. For type W/G/H destinations, change the target to HTTPS and import and trust the server certificate in STRUST, enforcing certificate validation. 6. Because the enabling parameters require an instance/kernel restart, schedule a maintenance window, validate in non-production first, and coordinate SNC name mapping (SNC0 / external identity mapping) with interface owners. 7. Verify using the SM59 Connection Test (it should report SNC active), a fresh scanner run, and a test-system packet capture confirming no cleartext credentials remain.
References
  • SAP Note 2416093
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 4.1
HIGH P3 · 54 High-risk ICF services are active NET-004 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags Internet Communication Framework (ICF) services that are active and known to be high-risk, such as /sap/public/info, /sap/public/icman/ping, /sap/bc/soap/rfc, /sap/bc/webrfc, /sap/bc/gui/sap/its/webgui, and various BSP/WebDynpro nodes. These endpoints are reachable over HTTP(S) and dramatically enlarge the attack surface. /sap/public/info and the ICM ping page leak kernel, patch, operating-system, and database details that let an attacker fingerprint the system and select matching CVEs. /sap/bc/soap/rfc and /sap/bc/webrfc are HTTP-to-RFC bridges that allow remote function-module invocation over the web, a path historically abused to reach dangerous modules and achieve remote code execution. WebGUI exposes a full SAP GUI inside a browser. The abuse chain, well documented by SAP security researchers, is to enumerate the ICF tree, hit the info page to fingerprint, then use the SOAP/Web RFC bridge with anonymous or captured credentials to call function modules that read data or execute code. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape the Fiori and gateway front-end sits close to the internet edge, so an exposed ICF node is directly reachable external attack surface rather than a purely internal concern. The impact spans information disclosure, remote code execution, full system compromise, and consequent data breach. A realistic incident resembles the ICF-driven exploitation classes that have led to complete SAP takeovers, where an exposed service was the initial entry point before privilege escalation and data theft.
Affected Items (10)
  • /sap/public/icman/ping — ICM ping — information disclosure
  • /sap/public/info — System info page — reveals version/kernel details
  • /sap/bc/soap/rfc — SOAP RFC gateway — remote function execution
  • /sap/bc/srt/rfc/sap — SRT RFC — web service RFC bridge
  • /sap/bc/gui/sap/its/webgui — WebGUI — full SAP GUI in browser (high risk if public)
  • /sap/bc/webrfc — WebRFC — HTTP-to-RFC bridge
  • /sap/bc/bsp/sap/it00 — ITS pages — legacy web interface
  • /sap/bc/soap/wsdl — WSDL exposure — service definition enumeration
  • /sap/bc/webdynpro — WebDynpro — may expose internal apps
  • /sap/public/icf_info/icr_groups — ICF group info — service enumeration
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In transaction SICF (or via table ICFSERVLOC) review the service tree and identify which high-risk nodes are active. 2. Deactivate services that are not required by right-clicking the node and choosing Deactivate Service; specifically evaluate /sap/public/info, /sap/public/icman/ping, /sap/bc/soap/rfc, /sap/bc/webrfc, /sap/bc/bsp/sap/it00, and webgui. 3. Align the deactivation list with SAP KBA 2661761 (ICF services: mandatory vs. deactivatable) and the SAP Security Baseline ICF recommendations, and use the standard SICF status/reporting tools to confirm state across clients. 4. For services that must stay active, enforce authentication on the SICF Logon Data tab (use Standard logon, not an alternative/anonymous logon) and protect the node with authorization object S_ICF. 5. Remove any stored anonymous service user, or replace it with a minimally-authorized technical user. 6. Add an edge control: configure the SAP Web Dispatcher or reverse proxy to URL-filter and block public diagnostic paths from external networks. 7. Verify by attempting to reach each path from an external client (it should return 403/404) and by re-running the scanner; document a business justification for anything left active. 8. Caution: deactivating ICF nodes can break Fiori apps and interfaces, so map dependencies and test thoroughly in non-production before changing production.
References
  • SAP KBA 2661761 (ICF services: mandatory vs. deactivatable)
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 5.1
HIGH P3 · 54 Sensitive APIs/OData services exposed RISE-005 ▶
Security Risk
Sensitive OData/REST services matching finance, HR/payroll, procurement, sales or master-data patterns (for example API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, API_JOURNAL_ENTRY, API_SALES_ORDER, /sap/opu/odata/sap/, PAYROLL, HCM_) are published and active. Every activated service is reachable attack surface: even with authentication in place, an exposed sensitive service can be abused by an over-entitled or compromised user/communication account, probed for authorization gaps and injection, or enumerated for bulk data. In S/4HANA these APIs expose highly regulated data and powerful write operations - posting journal entries, changing supplier bank details, reading personnel data. Services left active 'just in case', or activated during a project and never deactivated, are a recurring root cause: they widen the surface with no business owner and no monitoring. Attack scenario: an attacker with a foothold (a leaked communication credential, or a low-privilege dialog user holding an over-broad OData authorization) enumerates active services, finds API_BUSINESS_PARTNER exposed, and mass-exfiltrates supplier/customer PII and bank data via large $batch/$top reads, then attempts writes; because the service was unused and unmonitored the abnormal volume goes unnoticed. Business impact includes a GDPR-reportable data breach, financial fraud and IP loss; from an audit view it is a least-privilege and API-governance failure. A real incident looks like sustained bulk OData reads against a sensitive entity set from a single principal over a short window, only discovered later in gateway logs.
Affected Items (9)
  • API_BUSINESS_PARTNER (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER_SRV) — auth: oauth2
  • API_SALES_ORDER_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV) — auth: basic
  • API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV) — auth: oauth2
  • API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV) — auth: none
  • API_JOURNAL_ENTRY_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_JOURNAL_ENTRY_SRV) — auth: basic
  • API_MATERIAL_DOCUMENT_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_MATERIAL_DOCUMENT_SRV) — auth: oauth2
  • API_COST_CENTER_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_COST_CENTER_SRV) — auth: oauth2
  • API_PRODUCT_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_PRODUCT_SRV) — auth: oauth2
  • HCM_EMPLOYEE_MASTER (/sap/opu/odata/sap/HCM_EMPLOYEE_MASTER_SRV) — auth: none
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Produce an inventory of published/active sensitive services: in S/4HANA Cloud via the communication arrangements/scenarios that expose them; in Private Edition/on-prem via /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE (Activate and Maintain Services), /IWFND/V4_ADMIN for OData V4, and the ICF tree in transaction SICF. 2. For each sensitive service confirm a documented business owner and active consumer; deactivate services with no legitimate consumer (remove/deactivate the arrangement, or set the service inactive in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE or SICF). 3. Front externally reachable sensitive APIs with SAP API Management and apply OAuth scopes, rate limiting/quota, payload-size limits and IP-allowlist policies. 4. Tighten authorizations so only intended users/communication users can call each service - review SU24 defaults and the roles granting the service's authorization objects, and trace with SU53/ST01. 5. Restrict network exposure through the SAP Cloud Connector access-control allowlist, exposing specific resource paths rather than broad prefixes. 6. Enable gateway/API logging and alerting (/IWFND/ERROR_LOG and access logs) and alert on abnormal volume against sensitive entity sets. 7. Verify: attempt to reach a deactivated service and confirm HTTP 404/403; confirm remaining services enforce authentication and scopes. 8. Re-run the inventory after cleanup and record the approved exposed-service baseline for audit. 9. Rollout caution: validate each deactivation against live interfaces in a test tenant and coordinate with app/interface owners before turning services off in production.
References
  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud API Governance Guide
HIGH P3 · 54 API endpoints with weak or no authentication RISE-007 ▶
Security Risk
API/OData endpoints are configured with no authentication, anonymous access, or only Basic authentication. This is the endpoint-side view of the same weakness as RISE-004 but assessed at the individual service/ICF-node level, and in a RISE landscape every such endpoint is directly reachable attack surface. An anonymous or unauthenticated endpoint lets any party that can route to it invoke the service and read or manipulate data with no identity at all; a Basic-only endpoint protects potentially powerful operations with a single static, replayable secret susceptible to interception, brute force and credential spraying, and it provides no token scoping or expiry. Attackers routinely scan for active OData paths (for example under /sap/opu/odata/sap/) and probe their authentication; a weakly protected endpoint that reads or writes business data is a direct route to data exfiltration, fraudulent postings, or a pivot deeper into the system. Attack scenario: a scanner finds an OData service whose SICF node carries an anonymous logon alias; the attacker reads an entity set full of personal or financial data without credentials, then tests write operations; nothing in the logs shows a failed logon because none was required. Business impact spans GDPR-reportable breaches, financial fraud, and SOX interface-control failures, and it is a standard critical pen-test/audit finding. A real incident looks like data pulls or writes against an OData service from an unexpected source with no corresponding authenticated user session.
Affected Items (4)
  • API_SALES_ORDER_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV) — auth: basic
  • API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV) — auth: none
  • API_JOURNAL_ENTRY_SRV (/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_JOURNAL_ENTRY_SRV) — auth: basic
  • HCM_EMPLOYEE_MASTER (/sap/opu/odata/sap/HCM_EMPLOYEE_MASTER_SRV) — auth: none
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate endpoints and their authentication: in S/4HANA Cloud via the communication arrangements/systems; in Private Edition/on-prem via /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE (and /IWFND/V4_ADMIN) and the ICF service tree in transaction SICF. 2. Enforce OAuth 2.0 (client_credentials or authorization_code/SAML Bearer) or X.509 certificate authentication on every endpoint and disable Basic and anonymous access. 3. In SICF remove any anonymous or stored-logon alias from the service nodes so each call must authenticate, and set the correct logon procedure. 4. For gateway/OData services ensure the system alias and service require authentication and that no service is published without an auth method. 5. Place external-facing APIs behind SAP API Management and enforce OAuth scope, quota/rate-limit and IP-allowlist policies centrally. 6. Restrict reachability via the SAP Cloud Connector access-control allowlist to only the required resource paths. 7. Rotate any credentials previously protected only by Basic auth and remove the legacy Basic secrets after cutover. 8. Verify: send an unauthenticated request and a stale-Basic request and confirm HTTP 401/403; confirm the OAuth/certificate flow works for the legitimate client and review /IWFND/ERROR_LOG. 9. Rollout caution: coordinate with each API consumer to switch auth methods together and validate in a non-production tenant first to avoid breaking live integrations.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — API Authentication
HIGH P3 · 54 High-risk backend services exposed via Cloud Connector BTP-CC-002 ▶
Security Risk
A defined subset of Cloud Connector-exposed paths is inherently dangerous regardless of how narrowly the rest of the tunnel is scoped: /sap/bc/gui/sap/its/webgui (interactive SAP GUI for HTML, full transaction access), /sap/bc/soap/rfc and /sap/bc/srt/rfc (SOAP-to-RFC bridges that invoke RFC-enabled function modules), /sap/bc/webrfc (WebRFC), /sap/bc/adt (ABAP Development Tools - read/write source, execute classes and reports), /sap/bc/bsp (Business Server Pages) and broad /sap/opu/odata/sap or /sap/es5 gateways. Publishing these through the SCC turns it into a cloud-reachable interactive gateway to the ERP core. Attack scenario: an attacker who lands on a BTP app bound to a destination over this SCC can, via WebGUI, drive dialog transactions (SE38, SE16, SM59, SU01, PFCG) as far as the propagated or technical user's authorizations permit - enabling data theft, master-data manipulation, or creation of a privileged backdoor user; via the SOAP/WebRFC path they can call powerful function modules for effective remote code execution; via ADT they can inject ABAP that later runs with high privilege. Business impact is a straight cloud-to-core RCE and fraud path that bypasses the network isolation RISE is designed to provide, and is exactly the exposure that leads to ransomware staging, sabotage of financial data, or large-scale exfiltration of personal and financial records (GDPR/SOX exposure). A real incident manifests as GUI, ADT, or RFC calls entering the ABAP stack from the SCC service user outside the handful of OData services the business genuinely consumes, frequently at unusual times.
Affected Items (5)
  • S4H_Production: /sap/opu/odata/sap → 10.0.1.50:443
  • S4H_Production: /sap/bc/gui/sap/its/webgui → 10.0.1.50:443
  • S4H_Production: /sap/bc/adt → 10.0.1.50:443
  • ECC_Legacy: /sap/bc/soap/rfc → 10.0.2.100:443
  • ECC_Legacy: /sap/bc/webrfc → 10.0.2.100:443
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the SCC admin UI, open 'Cloud To On-Premise' > 'Access Control' and audit each backend's resource list against the high-risk paths above. 2. Remove /sap/bc/gui/sap/its/webgui, /sap/bc/adt, /sap/bc/webrfc, /sap/bc/soap/rfc, /sap/bc/srt/rfc and /sap/bc/bsp unless a documented cloud use case requires them. 3. Where an OData gateway is needed, expose only the specific service path /sap/opu/odata/sap/<SERVICE> with policy 'Path', never the whole /sap tree. 4. On the backend, deactivate the corresponding ICF nodes in transaction SICF for services that must not be reachable at all. 5. For RFC traffic that must legitimately flow, restrict callable function modules with UCON allowlists in transaction UCONCOCKPIT. 6. Enforce principal propagation so calls run as the real end user, and confirm those users lack SE38/SE16/S_DEVELOP/debug authorizations (analyse with SUIM and check S_TCODE, S_DEVELOP, S_RFC). 7. Save SCC changes (applied live) and re-test from the bound BTP destination. 8. Verify each removed path now returns HTTP 403 through the tunnel. 9. Rollout caution: confirm with integration and remote-support owners that WebGUI/ADT are not used by a legitimate Fiori or support scenario before removal, and stage in non-production. 10. Document any remaining exposed high-risk path with a named business owner, compensating controls, and a quarterly re-review date.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Recommendations — Cloud Connector
HIGH P3 · 54 Cloud Connector with unrestricted access control lists BTP-CC-004 ▶
Security Risk
The Cloud Connector access-control model is the primary gate that decides which internal hosts and resources the tunnel is permitted to reach; the module found ACL entries with no host restriction (empty allowlist or wildcards such as '*', '0.0.0.0/0', 'any'). Without an explicit, minimal host allowlist, a bound BTP service can be pointed at any internal host and port the SCC server can route to, turning the connector into an open reverse proxy into the corporate network. This is dangerous because the SCC by design sits between the untrusted cloud and the trusted on-premise zone: its allowlist is often the last enforceable boundary. Attack scenario: an attacker who obtains a valid BTP destination or service binding over this SCC (leaked service key, compromised app, insider) crafts requests to internal hosts that were never meant to be cloud-reachable - domain controllers, databases, management interfaces, other SAP systems - performing internal reconnaissance and SSRF-style pivoting from the cloud. Combined with weak backend authentication this yields lateral movement well beyond the intended integration. Business impact is loss of the cloud-to-on-prem trust boundary, expanded ransomware/exfiltration reach, and failure of network-segmentation controls demanded by SOX ITGC and ISO 27001. A real incident looks like the SCC service account initiating connections to internal IPs and ports that correspond to no documented integration.
Affected Items (2)
  • Subaccount: sa-prod-001 — hosts: ['*']
  • Subaccount: sa-dev-002 — hosts: ['*']
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the SCC admin UI, review 'Cloud To On-Premise' access control for each subaccount and confirm that only explicitly required internal host:port entries are mapped (the SCC does not support wildcard hosts by design - remove any over-broad virtual-to-internal mappings). 2. For each mapped backend, ensure the resource allowlist is minimal (align with BTP-CC-001/002) so the host is reachable only on the intended paths. 3. Restrict at the network layer: configure the firewall so the SCC host can egress only to the specific internal SAP backends it must serve, denying all other internal destinations. 4. Enforce principal propagation so end-user identity, not a shared technical user, governs backend access. 5. Validate that each connected subaccount is one you own and expect under the SCC 'Subaccounts' registration; remove unknown subaccount trusts. 6. Place the SCC in a hardened DMZ segment with OS hardening and restricted admin access. 7. Enable SCC audit logging and forward to the SIEM with alerts on connections to non-allowlisted internal hosts. 8. Save changes (applied immediately) and test that a bound destination can reach only the intended host/port and is refused elsewhere. 9. Verify via the SCC 'Monitoring' view and firewall logs that no unexpected internal destinations are reachable. 10. Rollout caution: coordinate firewall tightening with the network team and stage in non-production, as an overly aggressive egress rule can break legitimate interfaces.
References
  • SAP BTP Cloud Connector — Access Control Configuration
HIGH P3 · 54 Cloud Connector certificates expiring or expired BTP-CC-005 ▶
Security Risk
The Cloud Connector relies on X.509 certificates for two critical functions: the system certificate that authenticates and secures the tunnel to the SAP BTP region, and the CA/system certificate used for principal propagation (the short-lived user certificates the SCC issues and the backend trusts via STRUST/CERTRULE). The scan found certificates that are expired or expiring within the warning window. An expired tunnel or CA certificate has an immediate operational and security effect: the SCC tunnel drops or principal propagation stops working, breaking every integration that flows through it (Fiori extensions, iFlows, replication jobs). During the outage, teams under pressure frequently apply unsafe workarounds - disabling TLS validation, reissuing certificates without proper CA governance, or temporarily widening access - which introduce lasting weaknesses. From a pure security standpoint, an expired principal-propagation trust can also cause silent fallback to a shared technical user, collapsing user-level accountability and auditability on the backend. Business impact includes unplanned integration downtime affecting order-to-cash and other core processes, plus loss of end-user attribution for backend actions (a SOX and GDPR accountability gap). A real incident typically presents as a sudden mass integration failure at the exact certificate expiry timestamp, followed by a rushed, poorly documented certificate replacement.
Affected Items (3)
  • SCC_System_Cert — EXPIRED (2025-04-15, 487d ago)
  • Backend_CA — EXPIRED (2025-06-30, 411d ago)
  • Legacy_Cert — EXPIRED (2024-12-01, 622d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the SCC admin UI, open 'Configuration' and review the system/CA certificates and, under each subaccount, the tunnel and principal-propagation certificates and their validity dates. 2. Identify all certificates that are expired or within 90 days of expiry (align the warning window with your policy). 3. Generate a new key pair and CSR for the affected certificate using RSA 2048+ (or ECDSA P-256+) and obtain a certificate from your enterprise/managed CA. 4. Import the renewed certificate in the SCC and, for principal propagation, update the trusted CA in the backend via transaction STRUST and the certificate-to-user mapping rules in CERTRULE. 5. Renew at least 30 days before expiry to allow validation, and test a live tunnel connection and a principal-propagated backend call after replacement. 6. Implement automated certificate-expiry monitoring (SCC alerting plus an external monitor/SIEM alert) so expirations are caught weeks ahead. 7. Document the CA hierarchy and renewal runbook so replacements never require unsafe workarounds. 8. Verify by confirming the SCC tunnel status is 'Connected' and that backend calls arrive as the propagated end user (not a fallback technical user), checked in the backend security audit log (SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG). 9.
