Rollout caution: schedule renewals in a maintenance window, coordinate with interface owners, and keep the outgoing certificate trusted in STRUST until the new one is fully validated to enable rollback.
References
  • SAP BTP Cloud Connector — Certificate Management
HIGH P3 · 54 Cloud Connector certificates with weak cryptography BTP-CC-006 ▶
Security Risk
One or more Cloud Connector certificates use weak cryptography - key sizes below 2048 bits or deprecated signature algorithms such as SHA-1 or MD5. These certificates secure the tunnel between BTP and the on-premise landscape and, for principal propagation, vouch for the identity asserted to the backend. Weak keys and hashes are vulnerable to practical cryptographic attacks: SHA-1 has demonstrated collision attacks and RSA keys under 2048 bits are considered forgeable by well-resourced adversaries. If an attacker can forge or collide a certificate that the backend trusts, they can mount a man-in-the-middle attack on the tunnel or, worse, forge principal-propagation assertions that impersonate arbitrary end users on the ERP - authenticating as a privileged user without ever knowing a password. Attack scenario: a network-positioned adversary (or one who has compromised an intermediary) uses the weak trust anchor to intercept or inject traffic, or to present a fraudulent client certificate that the backend's STRUST/CERTRULE accepts, gaining authenticated access as a high-privilege identity. Business impact is compromise of the confidentiality and integrity of all cloud-to-core traffic and a total breakdown of identity assurance, enabling fraud and data theft while defeating audit trails. It is a direct violation of the SAP Security Baseline and modern TLS guidance (SAP Note 510007). A real incident may be nearly invisible, as forged-identity access blends into legitimate propagated traffic.
Affected Items (2)
  • Legacy_Cert — key size: 1024 bits (min: 2048)
  • Legacy_Cert — weak algorithm: SHA1withRSA
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the SCC admin UI, inventory all certificates (system, tunnel, principal-propagation CA) under 'Configuration' and each subaccount, noting key size and signature algorithm. 2. Replace every certificate below RSA 2048 bits (prefer RSA 3072/4096 or ECDSA P-256+) and any signed with SHA-1/MD5, reissuing with SHA-256 or stronger. 3. Generate fresh key pairs and CSRs in the SCC and obtain new certificates from a CA that enforces modern algorithms. 4. On the backend, update the trusted CA and system PSE in transaction STRUST and revalidate the certificate-mapping rules in CERTRULE (avoid wildcard mappings; map on a strong attribute such as email/UID). 5. Follow SAP Note 510007 for AS ABAP SSL/TLS configuration and ensure the backend enforces TLS 1.2+. 6. Remove the old weak certificates from all trust stores once the new ones are validated. 7. Verify the tunnel reconnects with the new certificate and that a principal-propagated call is accepted by the backend under the new CA. 8. Confirm via the backend security audit log (SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG) that propagated identities resolve correctly. 9. Rollout caution: perform in a maintenance window with interface owners informed; keep the previous CA trusted only until cutover is confirmed, then revoke it, to allow controlled rollback without leaving weak anchors in place.
References
  • SAP Note 510007 — SSL/TLS Configuration
HIGH P3 · 54 Service bindings not rotated in 180+ days BTP-SB-001 ▶
Security Risk
BTP service bindings and service keys embed long-lived credentials - typically an OAuth clientid/clientsecret or an X.509 key pair - that grant an application programmatic access to a bound service (XSUAA, Connectivity, Destination, HANA Cloud, Object Store, etc.). The scan found bindings older than the rotation policy. Credentials that are never rotated are dangerous because the probability that a secret has leaked grows with its lifetime: client secrets end up in source repositories, CI/CD variables, container images, application logs, developer laptops and support tickets. A leaked-but-unrotated secret gives an attacker persistent, silent access for as long as it remains valid - months or years. Attack scenario: an attacker harvests a clientsecret from a public or internal Git repository or a build log, then uses it to obtain OAuth tokens directly against the XSUAA/UAA token endpoint and calls the bound service's APIs as the application, from anywhere on the internet, without tripping user-based MFA or IP controls. Because the credential is long-lived, the access persists across the entire exposure window. Business impact includes data exfiltration through the bound service, abuse of connectivity into on-premise systems, and a compliance failure against the SAP Security Baseline and secret-lifecycle expectations of SOX and ISO 27001. A real incident often traces back to a secret committed to Git long ago and only rotated after the breach.
Affected Items (7)
  • xsuaa-prod-key (service: xsuaa) — age: 1156d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2023-06-15
  • dest-prod-binding (service: destination) — age: 947d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2024-01-10
  • hana-cloud-key (service: hana-cloud) — age: 1262d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2023-03-01
  • connectivity-key (service: connectivity) — age: 724d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2024-08-20
  • old-test-binding (service: xsuaa) — age: 1382d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2022-11-01
  • credstore-key (service: credstore) — age: 790d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2024-06-15
  • em-binding-01 (service: enterprise-messaging) — age: 1078d (max: 180d), last rotated: 2023-09-01
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate all service instances, bindings and service keys per subaccount using the BTP cockpit (Instances and Subscriptions) or the btp CLI (`btp list services/binding`) / Service Manager API. 2. Define and enforce a maximum credential lifetime (for example 180 days) as policy. 3. Rotate credentials by creating a new service key/binding, updating the consuming application/destination to the new secret, then deleting the old key - via the btp CLI, Service Manager API, or `cf create-service-key`/`delete-service-key` on Cloud Foundry. 4. Automate rotation in the CI/CD pipeline so secrets are regenerated on a schedule rather than manually. 5. Store application secrets in the SAP Credential Store service (or the platform secret store), never in code, and reference them at runtime. 6. Scan source repositories and pipelines for committed secrets and revoke any that are found. 7. Prefer X.509 certificate-based bindings over client secrets where the service supports it, as they are easier to manage and expire. 8. Verify by confirming old service keys are deleted and that only current, in-policy credentials remain, and that the application still authenticates with the new secret. 9. Rollout caution: perform rotation with a brief overlap (create-new-before-delete-old) and coordinate with app owners to avoid an outage; test in non-production first, especially for shared platform services.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — Credential Lifecycle Management
HIGH P3 · 54 Service bindings with admin-level scopes BTP-SB-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found service bindings whose granted scopes/authorities are administrative or overly broad (indicators such as ADMIN, MANAGE, WRITE_ALL, FULL_ACCESS, SUBACCOUNT_ADMIN, or a wildcard '*'). Service bindings authenticate as an application, not a person, and an admin-scoped binding gives that application - and anyone who obtains its credentials - the ability to manage the service or the subaccount itself: creating and deleting instances, changing role collections and trust, reading all data, or reconfiguring security. This violates least privilege at the machine-identity layer. Attack scenario: an attacker who compromises the app or harvests its clientsecret (see BTP-SB-001) exchanges it for an OAuth token carrying the admin scopes and then performs a full service or subaccount takeover - provisioning new instances, assigning themselves privileged role collections, disabling audit logging, or pivoting into connectivity/destination services that reach on-premise systems. Because the identity is a technical account with standing admin rights, the blast radius is the entire subaccount rather than a single business function. Business impact is catastrophic: complete loss of control over a BTP subaccount, tampering with security configuration, and destruction or theft of data, with weak user-level attribution to slow detection. It is a direct breach of least-privilege controls expected by the SAP Security Baseline, SOX segregation of duties, and ISO 27001. A real incident looks like an application token performing administrative API calls that no human operator initiated.
Affected Items (3)
  • xsuaa-prod-key (service: xsuaa) — scopes: admin, manage
  • hana-cloud-key (service: hana-cloud) — scopes: full_access
  • old-test-binding (service: xsuaa) — scopes: Subaccount_Admin, manage
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory all bindings/service keys and their granted scopes via the BTP cockpit, btp CLI, or Service Manager API, and for XSUAA-protected apps review the application's `xs-security.json` scope and role definitions. 2. Identify bindings carrying admin/manage/full-access/wildcard authorities that exceed the app's actual functional need. 3. Redefine scopes to the minimum required: split a single admin key into separate operational and administrative keys, granting the operational app only the read/write scopes it truly uses. 4. Recreate the binding/service key with the reduced scope and update the consumer, then delete the over-privileged key. 5. For platform/subaccount management scopes, restrict them to a small number of tightly controlled automation identities, not general application bindings. 6. Remove any wildcard ('*') authority and enumerate explicit scopes instead. 7. Rotate the credentials of any binding whose scope you reduced, in case the broad secret has already leaked. 8. Enable BTP Audit Log and alert on administrative API calls made with application tokens. 9. Verify by re-reading the effective scopes and confirming admin capabilities are gone while the app still functions. 10. Rollout caution: test scope reductions in a non-production subaccount, coordinate with the app team, and keep a rollback path since removing a needed scope will break the application at runtime.
References
  • SAP BTP — Service Key Scope Management
HIGH P3 · 54 BTP destinations with stored credentials BTP-DST-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found BTP Destination service configurations that store user credentials directly - Authentication set to BasicAuthentication (or OAuth2 Password grant) with an embedded user and password. The Destination service is a shared configuration store, and its contents, including stored secrets, are retrievable at runtime through the Destination service REST API by any application bound to that destination service instance with the appropriate read scope. That means the password is not a private secret of one app: it is readable by every workload bound to the destination service in that subaccount, and it appears in destination exports and backups. When the destination targets an on-premise S/4HANA/ECC system through the Cloud Connector, the stored credential is frequently a powerful technical or named user. Attack scenario: an attacker who compromises any bound BTP app, or a developer with legitimate binding access who exceeds their mandate, calls the Destination service to read back the clear credential, then reuses it to log directly into the target backend - bypassing the app entirely and often bypassing MFA. Because Basic Auth is a shared static secret, it also cannot be attributed to an individual, so backend actions lose user accountability. Business impact is credential theft leading to direct ERP access, fraud, and data exfiltration, plus a SOX/GDPR accountability failure. A real incident shows a shared technical account logging into the backend from unexpected locations after its password leaked via the destination store.
Affected Items (4)
  • S4H_Backend → https://10.0.1.50/sap/opu/odata (auth: BASIC_AUTHENTICATION, user: API_USER)
  • Legacy_ECC_SOAP → http://10.0.2.100/sap/bc/soap (auth: BASIC_AUTHENTICATION, user: RFC_LEGACY)
  • Bank_API → https://api.bank.com/payments (auth: OAUTH2_PASSWORD, user: bank_svc)
  • Test_System_Old → https://10.0.3.10/sap/opu (auth: BASIC_AUTHENTICATION, user: TEST_USER)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, open Connectivity > Destinations at the subaccount (and any service-instance) level and list destinations where Authentication is BasicAuthentication or OAuth2Password. 2. Migrate each to a token-based flow: OAuth2ClientCredentials, OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion, SAMLAssertion, or Principal Propagation for on-premise targets via the Cloud Connector. 3. For on-premise ABAP backends, prefer Principal Propagation so the real end-user identity is asserted (configure the trust and CERTRULE mapping on the backend) instead of a shared password. 4. Where a static secret is genuinely unavoidable, store it in the SAP Credential Store service and reference it, rather than embedding it in the destination. 5. Remove the stored User/Password fields from the destination once the new auth flow works. 6. Rotate the backend password of any account whose credential was previously stored, since it may already be exposed. 7. Restrict which apps are bound to the destination service instance and audit the bindings. 8. Verify by confirming the destination authenticates without stored user credentials and that a bound app can no longer read a password from the Destination API. 9. Confirm backend logons now carry individual identity (backend audit log SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG). 10. Rollout caution: test the new authentication in a non-production destination first and coordinate with interface owners, as switching auth type changes how the backend authorizes the call.
References
  • SAP BTP Destination Service — Authentication Types
HIGH P3 · 54 IAS applications without multi-factor authentication BTP-IAS-003 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found IAS applications that do not enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA). IAS is the front door for user access to SAP BTP and S/4HANA cloud applications, and without a second factor the only barrier to entry is a password. Passwords are routinely compromised through phishing, credential stuffing from breaches elsewhere, password spraying, and malware, so single-factor authentication on business-critical cloud applications is a leading cause of account takeover. The risk is acute for administrative and privileged applications, where a single stolen password can yield control of the subaccount, its configuration, and downstream ERP data. Attack scenario: an attacker sends a convincing phishing email that harvests a user's IAS password (or reuses a password exposed in an unrelated breach); with no MFA required, they log straight into the application, access or exfiltrate business and personal data, and, if the account is privileged, escalate by assigning role collections or reconfiguring trust and audit settings. Because the logon looks like a normal password success, detection is slow. Business impact includes data breach (GDPR), fraud, and privileged takeover, and the absence of MFA is a direct finding against the SAP Security Baseline, cyber-insurance requirements, and virtually every regulatory framework (SOX, PCI, NIS2) for remote and privileged access. A real incident is the classic 'valid account' intrusion - legitimate credentials used by an unauthorized party who faced no second factor.
Affected Items (5)
  • S4HANA_Fiori_Launchpad (MFA: not configured)
  • Integration_Suite (MFA: not configured)
  • Build_WorkZone (MFA: not configured)
  • Analytics_Cloud (MFA: not configured)
  • Custom_App_Portal (MFA: not configured)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the IAS admin console, open Applications & Resources > Applications and, in parallel, the tenant-level Authentication settings. 2. For each user-facing application, open Authentication and Access and enable two-factor/multi-factor authentication (TOTP authenticator app, WebAuthn/passkey, or SMS/email OTP as a fallback). 3. Use Conditional Authentication to require MFA at least for administrative and privileged user groups and for access from outside trusted networks; ideally enforce it for all users. 4. Prefer phishing-resistant factors (WebAuthn/passkeys, TOTP) over SMS where possible. 5. Configure risk-based authentication so unusual context triggers a step-up challenge. 6. Communicate to users and provide enrollment guidance and a supported recovery/reset process. 7. Save and test enrollment and a full MFA logon with a pilot group. 8. Verify via IAS login/audit logs that MFA challenges are occurring and single-factor logons to protected apps no longer succeed. 9. Extend enforcement progressively from privileged apps to all applications. 10. Rollout caution: pilot with a limited group, ensure a secure account-recovery and emergency-access administrator path exists before broad enforcement, and coordinate timing so a mass MFA rollout does not overwhelm the help desk or lock out shared/technical accounts (which should instead move to certificate-based auth).
References
  • SAP IAS — Multi-Factor Authentication Configuration
HIGH P3 · 54 IAS password policy for local users is weak BTP-IAS-004 ▶
Security Risk
The SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) tenant password policy that governs locally-stored user credentials falls below hardening expectations in the specific dimensions listed under affected items below. IAS local users are a frequent authentication fallback even in landscapes that federate to a corporate IdP, and each such weakness lowers the cost of password guessing and credential stuffing against the identity provider that fronts the entire BTP account and, via trust, the S/4HANA Fiori launchpad. Because IAS authenticates administrators of the BTP cockpit itself, a weak local-user policy is an account-wide exposure, not an application-local one. Note that IAS's built-in 'Standard' policy already enforces minimum length 8, 3-of-4 character complexity and lockout after 5 failed attempts; the main gap versus the 'Enterprise' policy is password expiry/history, so only the concretely-detected deviations below are reported (the policy tier name alone is not treated as a finding).
Affected Items (4)
  • minimum length = 6 (< 8)
  • account lockout threshold = 0
  • password complexity not enforced
  • password expiry = 0 (passwords never expire)
Remediation — Step by Step
In the IAS admin console (Applications & Resources → Tenant Settings → Password Policy) move the tenant to the 'Enterprise' password policy or a custom policy that enforces: minimum length ≥ 8 (12+ for privileged tenants), password complexity (mixed case, digits, special characters), account lockout after ≤ 5–10 failed attempts, a bounded maximum password age, and password-history reuse prevention. Where a corporate IdP is available, prefer delegating authentication to it and disabling local-user password logon entirely (see BTP-IAS-005) so this policy governs only unavoidable break-glass accounts. Re-export and re-scan to confirm the tightened values.
References
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services — Configure Password Policy
  • SAP BTP Security Recommendations — Identity Authentication
HIGH P3 · 54 Corporate IdP not enforced — local password fallback allowed BTP-IAS-005 ▶
Security Risk
A corporate identity provider is configured in IAS, but local IAS password authentication has not been disabled/enforced away. This leaves a parallel authentication path that bypasses the corporate IdP's controls — conditional access, MFA, session policies, joiner/mover/leaver deprovisioning and central logging. An attacker who obtains or guesses a local IAS password (or targets a former employee whose corporate account was disabled but whose IAS local user was not) can authenticate to BTP and the trusting S/4HANA applications without ever touching the corporate IdP, defeating the single-sign-on security model the organisation believes is in force. Enforcement gaps of this kind are a common root cause of 'we had MFA but the breach still happened' incidents in federated SAP landscapes.
Affected Items (2)
  • corporate IdP configured but not enforced (users may pick local logon)
  • local IAS password logon still permitted alongside corporate IdP
Remediation — Step by Step
Enforce the corporate IdP as the sole authenticating authority: in IAS, set the corporate identity provider as default and disable local password authentication for end users (Applications → Authentication & Access → Identity Providers / Logon Alternatives). Retain at most a small number of explicitly-documented break-glass local accounts, each with MFA and monitoring. Verify that conditional-authentication rules route every business application to the corporate IdP, and reconcile IAS local users against the corporate directory to remove orphaned accounts. Confirm no application still offers a 'log on with password' alternative after the change.
References
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services — Corporate Identity Providers
  • SAP BTP Security Recommendations — Enforce Single Sign-On
HIGH P3 · 54 Cloud Connector 2.15.2 is vulnerable to CVE-2024-25642 BTP-CC-008 ▶
Security Risk
The SAP Cloud Connector reports software version 2.15.2, which falls in the 2.15.0–2.16.1 range affected by CVE-2024-25642 (CWE-295, improper certificate validation, CVSS 7.4). In these versions the Cloud Connector does not properly validate the server certificate on its outbound cloud connections and will trust a self-signed / untrusted certificate, so an attacker positioned on the network path can impersonate the genuine endpoint and perform a man-in-the-middle attack, breaking the mutual authentication and confidentiality/integrity of the tunnel (no privileges or user interaction required; no availability impact). Because the Cloud Connector sits at the trust boundary between the BTP tenant and the on-premise/private network — it holds the system certificates and the backend allow-list that reach into S/4HANA — a compromised tunnel is a direct exposure of the internal landscape. The Cloud Connector is customer-managed even in RISE, so patching it is the customer's responsibility, and this flaw was introduced by a regression, so systems that were patched to 2.15.x/2.16.0/2.16.1 are affected.
Affected Items (1)
  • Cloud Connector version: 2.15.2 (affected 2.15.0–2.16.1; fix: 2.16.2+)
Remediation — Step by Step
Upgrade the Cloud Connector to at least 2.16.2 (ideally the latest patch of the current line) to remediate CVE-2024-25642. Plan the upgrade using the master/shadow high-availability pair so the tunnel is not interrupted: upgrade the shadow, fail over, then upgrade the former master. Subscribe to the SAP Cloud Connector release notes and treat SCC patching as part of monthly SAP Security Patch Day handling. After upgrade, confirm the reported version, re-establish the subaccount tunnels, and re-validate the backend allow-list and certificates.
References
  • CVE-2024-25642 — SAP Cloud Connector improper certificate validation (CWE-295)
  • SAP Security Note 3424610
  • SAP BTP Cloud Connector — Release Notes and Upgrade
HIGH P3 · 54 Event Mesh queues with wildcard topic subscriptions BTP-EM-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found SAP Event Mesh queues that subscribe to wildcard topic patterns (containing '*', '>', or '#'). Event Mesh distributes business events across BTP and to/from S/4HANA, and topic subscriptions are the authorization boundary that determines which events a consumer receives. A wildcard subscription captures far more than the specific events a consumer needs - potentially every event in a topic space or namespace, including events from unrelated and more sensitive business processes. Because business events frequently carry meaningful payloads or keys (sales orders, HR changes, financial documents, master-data updates), an over-broad subscription can silently leak sensitive event data to a consumer that should never see it. Attack scenario: a low-privileged or compromised application binds a queue with a wildcard subscription and passively harvests events across business domains - for example capturing all financial or personnel events to build a picture of transactions, or to detect and time fraudulent activity - without ever needing to breach the source systems. Even absent a malicious actor, wildcard subscriptions violate least privilege and create data-flow paths that are undocumented and untested for confidentiality. Business impact is unintended disclosure of business and personal data across domains (a GDPR and data-segregation concern) and a weakened event-authorization model. A real incident looks like a consumer application accumulating events well outside its business scope because a convenience wildcard was used instead of explicit topic paths.
Affected Items (4)
  • Queue: integration/events/all — topic: sap/s4/beh/*/created/*
  • Queue: integration/events/all — topic: sap/s4/beh/*/changed/*
  • Queue: hr/employee/all — topic: sap/successfactors/employee/*
  • Queue: hr/employee/all — topic: sap/s4/beh/employee/#
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the Event Mesh dashboard (or via the Messaging/Management API), review each queue and its queue-subscription topic patterns. 2. Identify subscriptions containing wildcards ('*' single-level, '>' multi-level, or '#') that are broader than the consumer's actual need. 3. Replace each wildcard with explicit, namespace-qualified topic paths for only the specific events the consumer must receive. 4. Where several specific topics are required, enumerate them individually rather than using a broad wildcard. 5. Align subscriptions with least privilege and document the intended event flows per consumer. 6. Combine with queue access control (see BTP-EM-002) so only authorized client IDs can create these subscriptions. 7. Save and test that the consumer still receives the intended events and no longer receives out-of-scope events. 8. Verify via the Event Mesh monitoring/message counters that unexpected topics are no longer delivered to the queue. 9. Establish a periodic review of queue subscriptions. 10. Rollout caution: adjust in a non-production Event Mesh instance first and coordinate with the consuming application team, since narrowing a subscription can drop events the app legitimately (if implicitly) depended on - validate end-to-end before production.
References
  • SAP Event Mesh — Topic Authorization Best Practices
HIGH P3 · 54 Event Mesh queues without access control policies BTP-EM-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found SAP Event Mesh queues with no access-control policy defined (access policy none/open/public). Event Mesh queues are the channels through which business events are published and consumed, and the queue access policy is what restricts which client identities may publish to or consume from a given queue. With no policy, any application holding an Event Mesh service binding in the instance can both read events from the queue and inject events into it. This breaks the integrity and confidentiality of the eventing layer. On the consume side, an unauthorized or compromised app can drain sensitive business events (as in BTP-EM-001). On the publish side, an attacker can inject forged events that downstream consumers trust and act upon - triggering business processes, creating or altering documents, or driving integration flows in S/4HANA. Attack scenario: an attacker who compromises any app bound to the Event Mesh instance publishes crafted events to an unprotected queue (for example a spurious 'order approved' or 'payment released' event) that a consuming iFlow or backend handler processes as legitimate, or subscribes to a queue and exfiltrates a stream of financial/HR events. Business impact spans event-driven fraud, data leakage, and process disruption, with weak attribution because the eventing layer did not authorize the client. It is a least-privilege and integrity failure under the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident manifests as unexpected downstream actions triggered by events no legitimate producer sent, or as sensitive events appearing in a consumer that was never authorized.
Affected Items (2)
  • integration/events/all — access policy: none
  • cross_domain/ariba — access policy: none
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the Event Mesh dashboard / Management API, inventory all queues and their access policies, flagging those with none/open/public. 2. Define explicit access policies per queue specifying which client IDs (applications) may publish and which may consume. 3. Grant each producing and consuming application only the specific queue permissions it requires (publish vs subscribe), following least privilege. 4. Remove any 'open'/'public' permission and replace it with a named-client allowlist. 5. Ensure the underlying service bindings/scopes (xs-security) for Event Mesh consumers are also scoped minimally (see BTP-SB-002). 6. Combine with specific (non-wildcard) topic subscriptions (see BTP-EM-001). 7. Save and test that authorized clients can still publish/consume and that an unauthorized client is denied. 8. Verify via Event Mesh monitoring and, if available, audit logs that only intended clients interact with the queue. 9. Establish a recurring review of queue access policies. 10. Rollout caution: apply and validate in a non-production Event Mesh instance first and coordinate with all producer/consumer app owners, since adding an access policy will immediately block any client not on the allowlist and could break an undocumented integration.
References
  • SAP Event Mesh — Queue Access Control
HIGH P3 · 54 CPI credentials not rotated in 180+ days BTP-CPI-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found SAP Cloud Integration (CPI / Integration Suite) security material - deployed credentials - not rotated within the policy window. CPI iFlows authenticate to a wide range of endpoints (SFTP, SOAP, OData, HTTP, JDBC, RFC, Mail, SuccessFactors, AS2, IDoc) using security material stored in the tenant: user credentials, OAuth2 credentials, keystore entries, and secure parameters. These credentials are frequently high-value: an SFTP or JDBC credential may reach a partner or database directly, and an RFC/OData credential may reach the S/4HANA backend. Credentials that are never rotated accumulate exposure risk over time - they leak through exports, backups, transported artifacts, developer access, and support interactions - and a leaked-but-unrotated integration credential grants persistent access for as long as it remains valid. Attack scenario: an attacker (or a departing integration developer) who obtained an old deployed credential uses it to connect directly to the partner system, database, or backend that the iFlow targets, bypassing CPI entirely and operating with the integration user's often-broad authorizations, exfiltrating or manipulating data across the B2B/EAI landscape. Because integration users tend to be technical accounts with elevated backend rights, the blast radius is large and the activity attributes only to a shared account. Business impact is data breach across integration partners and backends, supply-chain/B2B fraud, and a compliance failure against the SAP Security Baseline credential-lifecycle guidance. A real incident traces to an integration credential that had not been rotated in years being reused outside CPI.
Affected Items (5)
  • SF_EC_Credential (type: USER_CREDENTIAL) — age: 1095d (deployed: 2023-08-15)
  • S4H_OAuth_Client (type: OAUTH2_CLIENT) — age: 651d (deployed: 2024-11-01)
  • Ariba_API_Key (type: PLAIN_TEXT) — age: 1243d (deployed: 2023-03-20)
  • Bank_SFTP_Key (type: KEYPAIR) — age: 804d (deployed: 2024-06-01)
  • Legacy_ECC_Basic (type: BASIC) — age: 1352d (deployed: 2022-12-01)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the Integration Suite / Cloud Integration tenant, open Monitor > Manage Security > Security Material and review the deployment date of each artifact (User Credentials, OAuth2 Credentials, Secure Parameters, and Keystore entries under Manage Keystore). 2. Establish and enforce a maximum credential age (for example 180 days). 3. Rotate each stale credential: change the secret at the target system, then redeploy the updated Security Material under the same alias so referencing iFlows pick it up without change. 4. Use the Cloud Integration OData/Operations API to automate rotation and deployment where possible, and integrate it into CI/CD. 5. Prefer OAuth2 client credentials or X.509 certificate-based material over static passwords where the target supports it (see BTP-CPI-002). 6. Track credential ownership and rotation schedule in a register. 7. Verify by redeploying and running the affected iFlow, confirming successful authentication with the new secret, and re-check the Security Material deployment date. 8. Rotate keystore certificates before expiry and update partner trust as needed. 9. Rollout caution: rotate the secret at the target and redeploy the alias in a coordinated window (change-target-then-redeploy) and test in a non-production tenant or a low-volume iFlow first, coordinating with partner/interface owners so a mismatched credential does not halt production message processing.
References
  • SAP CPI — Security Material Management
HIGH P3 · 54 CPI iFlows with no sender authentication BTP-CPI-004 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found CPI iFlows that accept inbound messages with no sender authentication (sender auth none/anonymous/open). An iFlow's inbound (sender) channel is an internet- or platform-reachable endpoint that, when unauthenticated, allows any caller to submit messages into the integration flow. Since iFlows commonly transform and forward messages into core systems - posting IDocs, calling OData/RFC into S/4HANA, writing to databases, or dispatching events - an unauthenticated sender endpoint is an unauthenticated path to trigger business processing. Attack scenario: an attacker who discovers or guesses the iFlow's endpoint URL sends crafted payloads directly to it; with no authentication, CPI accepts and processes them, potentially creating or altering business documents, injecting fraudulent transactions, causing message floods/denial of service, or exploiting weaknesses in downstream handlers. Even without deep backend impact, the attacker can probe the integration surface and abuse it for spam or resource exhaustion. Because there is no authenticated identity, the malicious traffic is hard to attribute and may look like legitimate integration input. Business impact includes fraudulent or spurious postings into the ERP, process disruption, denial of service, and a control failure against the SAP Security Baseline and CPI sender-authentication guidance. A real incident manifests as unexpected messages processed by an iFlow - and their downstream effects in the backend - originating from an unauthenticated external caller.
Affected Items (2)
  • Ariba_PO_Sync — sender auth: NONE
  • Legacy_IDOC_Bridge — sender auth: ANONYMOUS
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, review each iFlow's sender (inbound) channel authentication setting and flag those set to None/Anonymous/Open. 2. Configure sender authentication on every inbound channel: 'User Role' (client credentials mapped to a role such as ESBMessaging.send or a custom role), 'Client Certificate', or 'OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials'. 3. Prefer certificate- or OAuth-based authentication for external/partner senders; use role-based (client ID/secret) for internal callers. 4. Restrict authorization with dedicated roles so only intended senders can invoke each iFlow, rather than a single shared role for all flows. 5. For internet-facing endpoints, front them with API Management for additional authentication, throttling, and IP allowlisting. 6. Ensure the endpoint is only reachable over HTTPS (see BTP-CPI-005). 7. Redeploy and test that authenticated calls succeed and unauthenticated calls are rejected (HTTP 401). 8. Verify via Monitor Message Processing and access logs that only authenticated senders reach the flow. 9. Establish a review to prevent new iFlows from being deployed with open sender authentication. 10. Rollout caution: coordinate with every sending system/partner to provision their credentials or certificates before enforcing authentication, and test in a non-production tenant, since enabling auth will immediately block any sender not yet configured.
References
  • SAP CPI — Sender Authentication Configuration
HIGH P3 · 54 CPI iFlows using unencrypted HTTP endpoints BTP-CPI-005 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found CPI iFlows referencing plain HTTP (non-HTTPS) endpoints for non-local targets. HTTP transmits data - including any credentials, tokens, business payloads and personal data - in cleartext over the network. In an integration context this is dangerous because iFlow traffic frequently carries sensitive content (orders, invoices, employee data, payment details) and sometimes authentication headers. Any party able to observe or intercept the network path between CPI and the target can read and modify this traffic. Attack scenario: an attacker positioned on the path (a compromised intermediary, a rogue network device, DNS/BGP manipulation, or a malicious actor within a shared network segment) captures cleartext payloads to exfiltrate business and personal data, harvests any credentials or tokens sent in the clear, and can tamper with message content in transit - for example altering bank account or quantity fields on a document before it reaches the backend - because HTTP provides neither confidentiality nor integrity. Cleartext endpoints also make replay and injection easier. Business impact spans confidentiality breach of regulated data (GDPR, PCI), integrity compromise of business transactions leading to fraud, and credential theft, all in violation of the SAP Security Baseline and CPI transport-security guidance which require TLS. A real incident presents as intercepted or manipulated integration data whose exposure is invisible to the application because the transport itself was never encrypted.
Affected Items (1)
  • Bank_Statement_Import — endpoint: http://cpi.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/http/bank/statement
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, review iFlow receiver/sender channel addresses and identify any using http:// (non-local) endpoints. 2. Migrate each to https:// and confirm the target endpoint supports TLS. 3. Import the target's server/CA certificate into the tenant keystore (Manage Security > Manage Keystore) so the TLS chain validates properly, and enable certificate validation. 4. Remove any HTTP fallback configuration. 5. For endpoints that cannot yet support TLS, route them through the Cloud Connector or a TLS-terminating reverse proxy rather than sending cleartext over untrusted networks, and prioritize upgrading the target. 6. Ensure TLS 1.2+ is used and weak ciphers are not negotiated. 7. Redeploy and test the iFlow, confirming successful HTTPS connectivity with a validated certificate. 8. Verify via Monitor Message Processing that the flow runs over HTTPS and no http:// address remains in the artifact. 9. Add a design-time check to prevent new HTTP endpoints from being introduced. 10. Rollout caution: import and validate certificates in a non-production tenant first and coordinate with the target-system owner, since switching to HTTPS with strict validation will fail if the correct certificate/hostname is not trusted - remediate the trust root cause before cutover.
References
  • SAP CPI — Transport Layer Security
HIGH P3 · 54 BTP subaccounts without audit logging BTP-GOV-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found BTP subaccounts without the Audit Log service enabled (or with audit logging disabled). The subaccount audit log is the authoritative record of security-relevant events and configuration changes in BTP - role-collection and trust changes, service provisioning, credential and destination changes, and administrative actions. A subaccount without audit logging is effectively operating without a security camera: there is no reliable record of who did what, which cripples both detection and post-incident forensics and breaks the accountability chain regulators require. This is especially dangerous in a multi-subaccount RISE landscape where administrative and integration activity concentrates in BTP. Attack scenario: an attacker who gains access to an unaudited subaccount (via a compromised admin credential, a leaked service key, or an insider) can assign themselves privileged role collections, alter trust configuration, provision outbound-capable services to exfiltrate data, and modify destinations to redirect or capture traffic - all without leaving a durable, reviewable trail. When the incident is later suspected, responders find no logs to reconstruct the timeline or scope, and the organization cannot prove what was and was not accessed. Business impact is an inability to detect, investigate, or attribute security incidents, plus direct non-compliance with SOX (change logging), GDPR (accountability for data access), ISO 27001, and the SAP Security Baseline, which mandate audit logging and monitoring. A real incident is one where the breach is real but effectively invisible and unprovable because the subaccount never recorded it.
Affected Items (4)
  • Quality (sa-qa-002, region: eu10)
  • Development (sa-dev-003, region: eu10)
  • Sandbox (sa-sbx-004, region: us10)
  • Integration_Test (sa-int-005, region: eu10)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, review each subaccount and confirm whether the Audit Log service/Audit Log Viewer is enabled and retention is configured. 2. Enable the Audit Log service in every subaccount that lacks it (it is available by default; ensure the Audit Log Viewer subscription and, where needed, the Audit Log Management service are provisioned). 3. Configure retention to meet compliance requirements using the Audit Log Retention API / Audit Log Management service (the default retention is limited - extend it to your policy). 4. Set up audit-log forwarding/streaming to the enterprise SIEM (for example via Cloud Logging or an audit-log retrieval integration) so events are centrally retained and monitored. 5. Define alerts in the SIEM for high-risk events (role-collection changes, trust changes, service-key creation, destination changes). 6. Add audit-log enablement to the standard subaccount provisioning blueprint so new subaccounts inherit it. 7. Assign ownership for periodic audit-log review. 8. Verify by generating a test administrative change and confirming it appears in the Audit Log Viewer and in the SIEM. 9. Confirm retention settings match policy. 10. Rollout caution: validate SIEM ingestion capacity before enabling forwarding across many subaccounts, and roll out enablement systematically so all environments (including non-production) are covered without overwhelming downstream logging.
References
  • SAP BTP — Audit Log Service Configuration
HIGH P3 · 54 API proxies missing required security policies INTG-APIM-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags active API proxies in SAP API Management (SAP Integration Suite on BTP) that are missing one or more baseline security policies: Spike Arrest, Quota, Verify API Key, OAuthV2, JSON/XML threat protection, or CORS. An API proxy is the internet-facing front door that fronts S/4HANA OData/SOAP services reached through the Cloud Connector, so a gap here is directly exposed to external consumers. Without Spike Arrest and Quota, a single misbehaving or malicious client can flood the proxy and exhaust backend dialog work processes and the ICM, causing a denial of service on order, invoice, and posting APIs. Without JSON/XML threat protection, oversized payloads, deeply nested JSON, or XML documents with external entities (XXE) reach the backend parser, enabling injection, XXE-based file disclosure, or memory exhaustion. Without a restrictive CORS policy, a browser-based attacker can drive cross-origin calls that ride a victim's authenticated session. Attack scenario: an attacker enumerates the published base path, sends crafted high-rate requests and malformed payloads; with no quota the load and cloud cost are uncapped and the backend eventually dumps (ST22) or leaks data. Business impact: loss of availability for revenue-critical integration flows, potential data leakage, uncontrolled BTP consumption cost, and failure of the API-governance controls expected under the SAP Security Baseline and SOX ITGC. A real incident looks like ICM overload, repeated backend short dumps, and unexplained data egress that is later traced to an unthrottled, unfiltered proxy. Because the proxy is the enforcement point, missing policies mean the backend's own authorization checks are the only remaining line of defence. This is a systemic governance weakness whenever multiple proxies share the gap.
Affected Items (6)
  • BusinessPartner_API (/api/v1/bp) — missing: quota, verify_api_key, threat_protection
  • SalesOrder_API (/api/v1/sales) — missing: spike_arrest, quota, oauth_v2, threat_protection, cors
  • Payment_API (/api/v1/payments) — missing: spike_arrest, quota, verify_api_key, oauth_v2, threat_protection, cors
  • Legacy_Vendor_Proxy (/api/legacy/vendor) — missing: spike_arrest, oauth_v2, threat_protection, cors
  • Internal_Test_API (/api/test) — missing: spike_arrest, quota, verify_api_key, oauth_v2, threat_protection, cors
  • HR_Employee_API (/api/v1/hr/employee) — missing: verify_api_key
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SAP Integration Suite open the API Management → API Portal, then API Proxies, and open each flagged proxy in the Policy Editor. 2. Attach a SpikeArrest policy in the ProxyEndpoint PreFlow, sized to measured peak throughput (e.g. per-second limit). 3. Attach a Quota policy bound to the consumer's contracted daily/monthly volume via the API product/rate plan. 4. Add JSONThreatProtection and XMLThreatProtection policies limiting container depth, element/attribute counts, and string length; add RegularExpressionProtection for common injection patterns. 5. Add a CORS policy restricting Access-Control-Allow-Origin to known front-end origins; never combine wildcard origin with credentials. 6. Ensure an authentication policy (OAuthV2 or VerifyAPIKey) is present (see INTG-APIM-002). 7. Save and redeploy the proxy to the API runtime. 8. Standardise by creating reusable policy templates / a shared FlowHook so every new proxy inherits the baseline automatically. 9. Verify by sending a call that exceeds the spike/quota limit (expect HTTP 429) and an oversized/deeply-nested JSON payload (expect rejection). 10. Roll the change out in the non-productive API Management tenant first, validate with interface owners, then promote the API content via the transport/CTS+ pipeline. Caution: size Spike Arrest/Quota against real batch peaks so legitimate high-volume integrations are not throttled.
References
  • SAP API Management — Security Policy Best Practices
  • OWASP API Security Top 10
HIGH P3 · 54 API proxies allowing unencrypted HTTP traffic INTG-APIM-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags API proxies that do not enforce HTTPS, allowing plain-text HTTP requests to the API Management runtime. API traffic to S/4HANA via BTP carries OAuth bearer tokens, API keys, basic-auth headers, and business payloads; over HTTP all of these traverse the network in clear text. Any party positioned on the path - a compromised proxy, rogue Wi-Fi, a malicious ISP hop, or an attacker performing ARP/DNS spoofing - can passively capture credentials and data or actively tamper with requests and responses. The most damaging outcome is bearer-token or API-key theft: a captured token is immediately replayable by the attacker against the same proxy until it expires, granting the attacker the consumer's full access. Attack scenario: an attacker on a shared network sniffs an HTTP call, extracts the Authorization header, and replays it within the token lifetime to read or post business data; the victim sees nothing unusual. HTTP also permits transparent man-in-the-middle downgrade and response injection, so returned business data cannot be trusted for integrity either. Business impact: credential and data breach (GDPR Art. 32 requires encryption in transit), integrity loss on financial data, and non-compliance with the SAP Security Baseline and NIST TLS guidance. A real incident looks like credential reuse from an unexpected IP shortly after a legitimate call, or manipulated payloads reaching the backend. Even if the backend link (Cloud Connector) is TLS-protected, the consumer-facing HTTP leg remains fully exposed. This undermines every other API control because the credentials protecting them are exposed on the wire.
Affected Items (3)
  • Payment_API (/api/v1/payments) — HTTPS not enforced
  • Legacy_Vendor_Proxy (/api/legacy/vendor) — HTTPS not enforced
  • Internal_Test_API (/api/test) — HTTPS not enforced
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In API Management, enable HTTPS-only for each flagged proxy by removing/rejecting the HTTP virtual host binding and keeping only the HTTPS virtual host. 2. Where an HTTP listener must remain temporarily, add a policy or virtual-host rule that returns a redirect to the HTTPS URL as a transitional step only. 3. Confirm the HTTPS virtual host presents a valid, non-expired certificate from a trusted CA and that the SNI/hostname matches. 4. Set the minimum TLS version to 1.2 (see INTG-APIM-004) and disable weak ciphers at the platform level. 5. Ensure the target/backend destination to S/4HANA also uses HTTPS/SNC through the Cloud Connector, so no leg is clear-text. 6. Update all consumer configurations and published catalog URLs to the HTTPS endpoint. 7. Redeploy the proxy. 8. Verify by attempting an HTTP call (expect refusal or redirect) and confirming the HTTPS call succeeds with a valid certificate chain. 9. Review access logs for prior HTTP calls to gauge historical token exposure and rotate any credentials that were used over HTTP. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and notify all consumer owners of the endpoint change to prevent outages. Caution: legacy clients pinned to HTTP will break at cutover - inventory and migrate them before disabling HTTP.
References
  • SAP API Management — TLS Configuration
HIGH P3 · 54 API proxies allowing deprecated TLS versions INTG-APIM-004 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags API proxies that still permit TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 as the minimum protocol version. TLS 1.0/1.1 are formally deprecated (IETF RFC 8996) and are vulnerable to well-known attacks such as BEAST and POODLE, and they rely on weak MACs and cipher constructions no longer considered safe. Allowing these versions means a network attacker can force a protocol downgrade during the handshake and then exploit the older protocol's weaknesses to decrypt or tamper with API traffic that is nominally encrypted. In the S/4HANA / BTP integration context, that traffic includes OAuth tokens, API keys, and business payloads, so a successful downgrade attack yields the same credential and data exposure as running plain HTTP. Attack scenario: an on-path attacker interferes with the ClientHello to negotiate TLS 1.0, then applies a chosen-plaintext or padding-oracle technique to recover session data or a bearer token, which is then replayed. Even without full decryption, advertising legacy TLS signals a weak security posture and typically fails external attack-surface scans and penetration tests. Business impact: interception risk to sensitive data, non-compliance with PCI DSS (which prohibits early TLS), the SAP Security Baseline, and NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, and audit findings on cryptographic hygiene. A real incident looks like a downgrade-then-decrypt attack surfaced during a red-team engagement or, worse, silent token theft in production. The risk compounds when weak TLS coexists with clients that do not pin a minimum version. Modern clients almost universally support TLS 1.2/1.3, so legacy support is rarely a genuine business need.
Affected Items (1)
  • Payment_API (/api/v1/payments) — min TLS: 1.0 (should be 1.2+)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Set the minimum TLS version to 1.2 (preferably 1.3 where clients allow) for each flagged proxy's HTTPS virtual host in API Management. 2. Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 at the API Management platform / virtual-host level so no proxy can negotiate them. 3. Restrict the cipher suite list to strong AEAD suites (e.g. ECDHE + AES-GCM / CHACHA20) and disable RC4, 3DES, CBC-legacy, and export ciphers. 4. Confirm the certificate uses a modern key (RSA 2048+ or ECDSA P-256) and SHA-256 signature. 5. Align the backend/Cloud Connector TLS configuration to the same minimum so both legs are consistent. 6. Redeploy the proxy / apply the platform TLS policy. 7. Verify externally with a TLS scanner (e.g. testssl or an SSL Labs-style test) that TLS 1.0/1.1 are refused and only strong ciphers are offered. 8. Verify a normal consumer call still succeeds over TLS 1.2/1.3. 9. Inventory consumers before enforcement to identify any client still incapable of TLS 1.2 and upgrade or isolate it. 10. Stage in non-prod, communicate the cutover window, then enforce in production. Caution: a small number of legacy middleware/JVM clients may need a JCE/library update to speak TLS 1.2 - fix those first to avoid interface outages.
References
  • NIST SP 800-52 Rev 2 — TLS Guidelines
HIGH P3 · 54 IDOC ports without encryption (no TLS/SNC) INTG-IDOC-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags IDOC ports (WE21) that transmit without encryption: HTTP/XML-HTTP ports without TLS, and tRFC/RFC ports without SNC. IDOC payloads routinely carry highly sensitive business documents - purchase and sales orders, invoices, payment orders, bank statements, HR master data - so an unencrypted port exposes core financial and personal data in transit. For RFC-based ports without SNC, the traffic is not merely readable; the legacy DIAG/RFC protocol offers weak protection, so credentials and payloads can be captured and the channel can be manipulated by an on-path attacker. For HTTP/XML ports without TLS, the entire message and any transport credentials cross the network in clear text. Attack scenario: an attacker with network visibility between the S/4HANA system and a partner/middleware (e.g. SAP PI/PO, a subsidiary, or a bank connector) sniffs the tRFC or HTTP stream, reconstructs the IDOC, and reads or alters order and payment data before it is posted. Manipulation is especially dangerous for financial IDOCs (e.g. changing a payee bank account on a PEXR2002 payment order) - a classic payment-redirection fraud. Business impact: confidentiality breach of financial/HR data (GDPR, SOX), payment fraud, and non-compliance with the SAP Security Baseline requirement for secure communications. A real incident looks like altered or leaked IDOC content, reconciliation breaks between sender and receiver, and fraudulent payments traced to a clear-text interface leg. Because IDOC volumes are high and automated, exposure is continuous rather than occasional. This is a high-severity gap wherever the port carries data leaving a trusted network segment.
Affected Items (3)
  • TRFC_ARIBA (type: TRFC) — RFC without SNC, host: ariba.cloud.sap.com
  • TRFC_ECC (type: TRFC) — RFC without SNC, host: 10.0.2.100
  • XML_VENDOR (type: XML_HTTP) — HTTP without TLS, host: vendor-portal.example.com
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In WE21, identify each flagged port and its type (tRFC, HTTP, XML-HTTP) and the associated RFC destination (SM59) or HTTP connection. 2. For tRFC/RFC ports, enable SNC on the underlying SM59 destination: set SNC active, the partner's SNC name, and a strong quality of protection. 3. At the system level ensure SNC is enabled and enforced via the profile parameters snc/enable=1 and snc/data_protection/min and /max set to 3 (privacy), managed in RZ10/RZ11, with SAP CommonCryptoLib and PSEs configured (STRUST/SNCWIZARD). 4. For HTTP/XML-HTTP ports, change the endpoint to HTTPS and configure the SSL client PSE in STRUST; verify the partner certificate chain. 5. Restrict acceptance of insecure connections using snc/accept_insecure_rfc and related parameters once all partners are migrated. 6. Coordinate the SNC/TLS name and certificate exchange with each interface partner before switching. 7. Verify by sending a test IDOC (WE19) and confirming in SM58/gateway logs that the connection is SNC/TLS protected end to end. 8. Confirm certificate validity and expiry on both ends (STRUST) and add them to certificate-expiry monitoring. 9. Roll out per interface in non-prod first, then production during an agreed maintenance window, as SNC/TLS misconfiguration will stop the interface. Caution: a kernel/CommonCryptoLib update and coordinated partner cutover are usually required - never enforce snc/accept_insecure_* before every partner is confirmed working.
References
  • SAP Note 2416093 — Secure RFC/IDOC Communication
HIGH P3 · 54 IDOC partner profiles with wildcard message types INTG-IDOC-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags IDOC partner profiles (WE20) whose message type is a wildcard (*, blank, or ALL), meaning the partner is authorized to send or receive any IDOC message type. Partner profiles are the primary message-type-level access control for ALE/EDI; a wildcard entry removes that control, so the partner is no longer constrained to the specific documents its business relationship requires. This breaks least privilege at the interface layer: a partner that should only exchange, say, ORDERS can now push HRMD_A (HR master), PEXR2002 (payments), or ACC_DOCUMENT (accounting postings) into the system. Attack scenario: an attacker who controls or spoofs an inbound partner (or compromises the middleware feeding it) submits high-impact IDOC types that the partner was never meant to send; because the profile accepts all types, the IDOC is accepted and processed by the corresponding function module under the partner's technical user. This enables unauthorized master-data changes, fraudulent financial postings, and injection of payment orders - all without any additional authorization check at the message-type level. Wildcard profiles also make monitoring and auditing meaningless, since no expected-type baseline exists to alert on anomalies. Business impact: fraud, unauthorized data modification, segregation-of-duties bypass, and a clear SOX/audit finding on interface access control. A real incident looks like unexpected IDOC types appearing in WE05/WE02 for a partner, followed by anomalous master-data or financial changes. Because inbound IDOC processing is automated, a single accepted malicious IDOC can post immediately. This is high severity because it directly enables unauthorized business transactions.
Affected Items (2)
  • Partner: SF_EC (LS) — message type: * (direction: INBOUND)
  • Partner: ECC_LEGACY (LS) — message type: ALL (direction: BOTH)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In WE20, open each flagged partner profile and review its inbound and outbound parameter lists. 2. Replace the wildcard/blank message-type entry with explicit entries for only the message types (and process codes) that the business relationship actually requires. 3. For each entry, set the correct process code, port, and (inbound) the appropriate processing settings; document a business justification per message type. 4. Cross-check the underlying partner-profile tables (EDP13 outbound, EDP21 inbound, EDPP1 general) to confirm no residual catch-all rows remain. 5. Ensure the partner's technical user has correspondingly scoped authorizations (auth objects B_ALE_RECV, S_IDOCDEFT and related) so the application layer also enforces least privilege. 6. For sensitive types, pair with encrypted transport (see INTG-IDOC-001/004) and additional monitoring. 7. Verify by sending an out-of-scope test IDOC (WE19) and confirming it is now rejected rather than processed. 8. Verify legitimate in-scope IDOCs still process correctly (WE05/BD87). 9. Enable/adjust IDOC monitoring so any unexpected message type for the partner raises an alert. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate with the partner/interface owner, as tightening the profile can block previously-accepted traffic. Caution: capture the current live message-type mix from WE05 before restricting, so no legitimate document type is accidentally excluded.
References
  • SAP IDOC — Partner Profile Authorization
HIGH P3 · 54 High-risk BAPIs/RFCs exposed as web services INTG-WS-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags active SOAP web service endpoints (SOAMANAGER) that expose high-risk function modules - user management BAPIs (BAPI_USER_*), company-code access (BAPI_COMPANYCODE), arbitrary table read (RFC_READ_TABLE), system information disclosure (RFC_SYSTEM_INFO), XI/PI handlers (SXMB_*), and financial/payment BAPIs (BAPI_ACC_*, BAPI_PAY*). Exposing these as web services turns powerful internal function modules into remotely callable endpoints; if authentication or authorization is weak, they become a direct remote attack surface. RFC_READ_TABLE is especially dangerous: it allows an authorized-but-scoped caller to read arbitrary database tables (including USR02 password hashes, financial tables, or PII) subject only to S_TABU authorization, effectively a generic data-exfiltration primitive. BAPI_USER_* exposure can allow remote user creation, password reset, or profile assignment - a direct path to privilege escalation and persistence. BAPI_ACC_* / BAPI_PAY* exposure can allow remote financial postings or payment manipulation - direct fraud. Attack scenario: an attacker who obtains or brute-forces a weak service credential calls the RFC_READ_TABLE endpoint to dump sensitive tables, then calls BAPI_USER_CREATE1 to plant a privileged user, then pivots deeper - all over the web service channel. Business impact: remote code/data compromise, privilege escalation, financial fraud, and severe GDPR/SOX exposure. A real incident looks like large table reads and unexpected user-master changes originating from a web service consumer, visible in SOAP runtime and security audit logs. The combination of powerful function module plus internet-adjacent exposure is why this is high severity. Each such endpoint should be justified, hardened, or removed.
Affected Items (6)
  • BAPI_USER_GET_DETAIL (binding: UserGet_WS) — auth: BASIC, transport: HTTPS
  • BAPI_COMPANYCODE_GETLIST (binding: CompanyCode_WS) — auth: NONE, transport: HTTPS
  • RFC_READ_TABLE (binding: ReadTable_WS) — auth: BASIC, transport: HTTP
  • BAPI_ACC_DOCUMENT_POST (binding: AccDoc_WS) — auth: X509, transport: HTTPS
  • RFC_SYSTEM_INFO (binding: SysInfo_WS) — auth: TRANSPORT, transport: HTTP
  • SXMB_MESSAGE_SEND (binding: XIMsg_WS) — auth: ANONYMOUS, transport: HTTPS
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SOAMANAGER, review the Web Service Configuration / service and endpoint list and identify each flagged high-risk service and its binding. 2. Deactivate any endpoint that has no clear, documented business consumer; remove the corresponding service binding. 3. For endpoints that must remain, enforce strong authentication on the logical port - X.509 client certificates or SAML/OAuth via WS-Security, not basic auth alone (see INTG-WS-003). 4. Lock down authorization: ensure the calling user is a least-privileged communication user and constrain S_SERVICE to only the specific service, and for RFC_READ_TABLE constrain S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM to the minimum table set (ideally block this service entirely). 5. Restrict network reach: expose only through the Web Dispatcher / reverse proxy with source-IP allowlisting to known consumers. 6. Prefer purpose-built OData/REST services with proper scopes over raw generic BAPI/RFC web services. 7. Confirm transport is HTTPS end to end (STRUST SSL PSE). 8. Verify by attempting an unauthorized call (expect rejection) and confirming the authorized call is scoped correctly; consult SAP Note 2321968 for SOAP security troubleshooting. 9. Review the SOAP runtime and Security Audit Log (SM20/RSAU) for prior calls to these endpoints to assess exposure. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate deactivation with consumers. Caution: deactivating a live endpoint breaks its consumer - inventory usage (ICF/SICF logs) before removal and stage the change.
References
  • SAP Note 1503579 — SOAMANAGER Security
  • OWASP — Web Service Security Cheat Sheet
HIGH P3 · 54 Webhook callbacks using unencrypted HTTP INTG-WH-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags registered webhook/callback endpoints whose URL uses plain HTTP instead of HTTPS. Webhooks push event payloads (and frequently a shared secret, signing token, or bearer token in headers) from the SAP/BTP side to a consumer endpoint; over HTTP all of this crosses the network in clear text. An on-path attacker can passively capture the event data and any embedded credential, and can actively tamper with or forge the payload since HTTP provides neither confidentiality nor integrity. Webhook payloads often describe business events - a created sales order, a completed payment, an approval - so interception leaks business intelligence and potentially PII, and tampering can drive the consumer to act on false events. Attack scenario: an attacker on the path sniffs an HTTP webhook, extracts the signing secret or auth header, then forges arbitrary events to the consumer (or replays captured ones), causing the consumer to process fraudulent or duplicate transactions; alternatively they simply harvest the event stream for reconnaissance. Because webhooks are automated and frequent, the exposure is continuous. Business impact: confidentiality breach of business events/PII (GDPR), integrity/fraud risk on the consuming side, and non-compliance with encryption-in-transit requirements. A real incident looks like a consumer acting on events that SAP never actually sent, or leaked event data appearing outside the trust boundary, later traced to an HTTP callback. This is high severity because it exposes both data and the very secret meant to protect the webhook. HTTP callbacks should never exist for business events.
Affected Items (2)
  • Vendor_Updated → http://middleware.company.com/hooks/vendor — unencrypted HTTP
  • Legacy_ERP_Sync → http://10.0.2.100:8080/callback/erp — unencrypted HTTP
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory all webhook/callback registrations from the source system (BTP Event Mesh subscriptions, Alert Notification actions, or the application-specific webhook registry) and identify those with http:// URLs. 2. Obtain the consumer's HTTPS endpoint and update each registration to the https:// URL. 3. Confirm the consumer's TLS certificate is valid and trusted; import the CA into the relevant BTP destination/keystore if needed. 4. Configure the platform to reject registration of non-HTTPS callback URLs going forward. 5. Ensure a signing secret/HMAC is configured on the now-encrypted channel (see INTG-WH-002). 6. Rotate any signing secret or token that was previously transmitted over HTTP, since it must be assumed compromised. 7. Verify by triggering a test event and confirming delivery over HTTPS with a valid certificate. 8. Verify the consumer validates the certificate (no insecure/skip-TLS-verify setting on their side). 9. Review delivery logs for prior HTTP deliveries to gauge historical exposure. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate the URL change with each consumer owner. Caution: some consumers may have self-signed or internal-CA certificates - arrange trust configuration before switching, or the interface will fail on TLS validation.
References
  • OWASP — Webhook Security Best Practices
HIGH P3 · 54 Webhooks without signature/HMAC verification INTG-WH-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags webhook registrations that have no HMAC/signature verification configured. A signature (typically HMAC-SHA256 over the payload using a shared secret) is what lets the receiving endpoint prove that a delivered event genuinely originated from the sender and was not altered in transit; without it, the receiver has no way to distinguish an authentic event from a forged or replayed one. This matters even over HTTPS, because TLS authenticates the transport hop, not the message, and does not protect against a compromised intermediary, an SSRF-style forged request from within the network, or replay of a captured legitimate payload. Attack scenario: an attacker who can reach the consumer's callback URL (discovered via config leakage, referer, or enumeration) sends fabricated event payloads; with no signature to check, the consumer processes them as real - creating spurious orders, approvals, status changes, or payments. Replay is equally damaging: a captured 'payment completed' event resent multiple times can drive duplicate downstream actions. Business impact: event spoofing and replay leading to fraud, data corruption, and unauthorized automated actions on the consumer side; it also undermines non-repudiation for audit. A real incident looks like the consumer acting on events that the source system has no record of sending, or repeated processing of a single real event. This is high severity because it removes authenticity/integrity assurance from an automated, trusted channel. Signature verification is the core defence for webhook trust and is cheap to implement.
Affected Items (4)
  • Vendor_Updated → http://middleware.company.com/hooks/vendor — no HMAC/signature validation
  • Invoice_Approved → https://ariba.procurement.com/callback/invoice — no HMAC/signature validation
  • Legacy_ERP_Sync → http://10.0.2.100:8080/callback/erp — no HMAC/signature validation
  • Test_Hook_Old → https://test.company.com/hooks/test — no HMAC/signature validation
Remediation — Step by Step
1. For each flagged webhook, generate a strong, unique per-registration secret and configure HMAC-SHA256 signing on the sender side. 2. Ensure the sender includes the signature and a timestamp/nonce in a header on every delivery. 3. Implement verification on the consumer endpoint: recompute the HMAC over the raw body with the shared secret and compare in constant time before processing. 4. Add replay protection on the consumer: reject deliveries whose timestamp is outside a short tolerance window and de-duplicate on the event/nonce id. 5. Store the secret securely on both sides (BTP Credential Store / destination properties on the sender; a secrets manager on the consumer), never in code or plain config. 6. Enforce HTTPS as well (see INTG-WH-001) so the secret and payload are also confidential in transit. 7. Establish a secret-rotation schedule and rotate immediately if exposure is suspected. 8. Verify by sending a valid signed event (accepted) and a tampered or unsigned event (rejected), plus a replayed event (rejected). 9. Log signature-verification failures and forward them to the SIEM as a tamper indicator. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate the secret exchange with each consumer. Caution: enabling verification requires the consumer to implement the check with the exact same canonicalization/algorithm - agree the scheme jointly before enforcing to avoid dropping legitimate events.
References
  • OWASP — Webhook Signature Verification
HIGH P3 · 54 Missing integration monitoring alert rules INTG-MON-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags that one or more required integration monitoring alert categories are not configured: iFlow runtime errors, IDOC processing failures, API authentication/authorization failures, certificate expiry, RFC communication failures, or API quota/rate-limit breaches. Monitoring and alerting are detective controls; their absence does not create a vulnerability directly, but it means that failures and active attacks against the integration layer go unnoticed, dramatically increasing dwell time and blast radius. Missing auth-failure alerting is the most security-relevant gap: credential-stuffing, brute force, or token abuse against APIs and RFC destinations produces exactly the failure signal that should trigger investigation, and without it an attacker can probe freely. Missing certificate-expiry alerting causes sudden interface outages (expired SNC/TLS/OAuth certs) that are both an availability incident and a scramble that often tempts operators into insecure quick fixes. Missing iFlow/IDOC/RFC error alerting means data that should have flowed is silently stuck or lost, causing financial mis-statement, missed payments, and reconciliation breaks. Attack scenario: an attacker slowly enumerates and abuses an API; because no auth-failure or quota alert exists, the activity never surfaces, and the first sign of compromise is the eventual data breach itself. Business impact: undetected breaches, prolonged outages, financial/SOX errors from silently failed postings, and an audit finding on inadequate monitoring. A real incident looks like an intrusion or a multi-day interface outage discovered by a downstream business complaint rather than by an alert. This is high severity because visibility is foundational to every other control's effectiveness.
Affected Items (4)
  • idoc_failure: IDOC processing failures
  • auth_failure: Authentication/authorization failures on APIs
  • rfc_error: RFC communication failures
  • quota_exceeded: API quota/rate limit exceeded
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SAP BTP, configure the SAP Alert Notification service (or the Integration Suite monitoring alerting) to cover each missing category. 2. Create conditions/subscriptions for: iFlow runtime errors (from Cloud Integration message monitoring), IDOC failures, API auth/authorization failures, RFC errors, quota/rate-limit breaches, and certificate expiry. 3. For the on-premise S/4HANA side, complement with CCMS/Solution Manager or Focused Run monitoring for IDOC (BD87/WE05 error status), RFC (SM58) and tRFC/qRFC queue failures (SMQ1/SMQ2). 4. Configure certificate-expiry monitoring for STRUST PSEs, SNC certificates, and BTP/OAuth keystores with sufficient lead time (e.g. 30/14/7 days). 5. Route alerts to actionable channels (email, ticketing, on-call) with clear ownership per category. 6. Set severities and thresholds so that security-relevant categories (auth failures, quota breaches) page appropriately. 7. Verify each alert by injecting a controlled test failure (e.g. a deliberately failing test iFlow/IDOC) and confirming the alert fires and routes correctly. 8. Forward the same events to the SIEM (see INTG-MON-002) for correlation. 9. Document the alert catalogue and review it periodically. 10. Assign runbooks so each alert has a defined response. Caution: tune thresholds in non-prod first to avoid alert fatigue, and ensure notification actions do not themselves leak sensitive payload data in alert bodies.
References
  • SAP BTP Alert Notification Service — Configuration Guide
HIGH P3 · 54 CPI data stores with sensitive data names but no encryption INTG-CPI-DS-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags SAP Cloud Integration (CPI) Data Stores whose names suggest sensitive content (password, token, secret, key, credential, ssn, bank, salary, payment, PII, etc.) but which are not marked as encrypted. CPI Data Stores persist message payloads and state between integration steps and are accessible via the CPI/OData management API and the monitoring UI; storing sensitive data there unencrypted exposes it to anyone with tenant management access and enlarges the data-at-rest footprint. Sensitive data in a data store is retained beyond the transient life of a message, so a credential or PII record written once can linger and be read repeatedly, long after the business process completed. Attack scenario: an operator or attacker with CPI monitoring/management authorization (or a leaked API credential) browses the data store via the OData API and harvests stored secrets or personal data in bulk; because it is not encrypted, no additional barrier stands in the way. Storing credentials/tokens in a data store is also an anti-pattern - secrets belong in the Security Material store, not in general-purpose persistence. Business impact: credential and PII exposure (GDPR), potential onward compromise if stored tokens are still valid, and audit findings against SAP CPI security guidance. A real incident looks like sensitive fields recovered from a CPI data store during a review or after a tenant-credential compromise, and valid tokens found reusable. This is high severity because it combines sensitive content, broad API accessibility, and lack of encryption. Secrets and PII should either move to proper stores or be encrypted and minimized.
Affected Items (2)
  • payment_token_cache — entries: 250, encrypted: False
  • bank_credentials_staging — entries: 12, encrypted: False
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, open Monitor → Manage Stores → Data Stores and identify each flagged store and its content type. 2. For any store that actually holds credentials, tokens, or keys, remove that usage and relocate the secret to Monitor → Manage Security → Security Material (Secure Parameter, User Credentials, OAuth2 Credentials, or Keystore). 3. For stores that must hold sensitive business data (e.g. PII), enable the encrypted option on the Data Store (Write step 'Encrypt Store' / global data store encryption) so entries are stored encrypted. 4. Update the relevant iFlows' Data Store Write steps to set encryption and to write only the minimum necessary fields. 5. Set a short retention/expiry (TTL) on entries so sensitive data does not persist longer than needed (see INTG-CPI-DS-003). 6. Purge existing plaintext sensitive entries after migration. 7. Restrict who holds CPI monitoring/management roles so data-store access is limited to authorized staff. 8. Verify by inspecting the store via the OData API/monitor and confirming entries are encrypted and secrets are gone. 9. Rotate any credential/token that was previously stored in plaintext. 10. Roll out via the transport/CI pipeline to the productive tenant after testing in non-prod. Caution: enabling encryption changes how iFlows read/write entries - retest the affected flows end to end before promoting, and coordinate the secret relocation so running interfaces are not interrupted.
References
  • SAP CPI — Data Store Security
HIGH P3 · 54 OAuth clients with admin-level or wildcard scopes INTG-OAUTH-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags OAuth clients whose scopes are admin-level or wildcard (*, ADMIN, MANAGE_ALL, FULL_ACCESS, uaa.admin, $XSAPPNAME.admin). OAuth clients (typically XSUAA/IAS client registrations on BTP) authenticate service-to-service integrations; an admin/wildcard scope grants that client sweeping authority, so the client credential becomes a master key to the platform or application. This violates least privilege at the machine-identity layer: a single leaked client secret then equals administrative control, not a narrow, purpose-scoped capability. The scope uaa.admin is especially dangerous - it allows management of the authorization server itself (creating clients, granting scopes), so a holder can escalate arbitrarily and establish persistence. Attack scenario: an attacker obtains an over-scoped client secret (from a leaked config file, a compromised CI pipeline, a hard-coded secret in a repo, or an over-privileged developer), requests a token via client_credentials, and with admin scope reads all data, reconfigures services, creates new privileged clients, or pivots into connected S/4HANA backends - full platform takeover from one credential.
