HIGH P3 · 42 Critical security parameters not found in export PARAM-MISSING ▶
Security Risk
This finding lists CRITICAL/HIGH baseline parameters that were entirely absent from the export. Missing does not mean safe: when a parameter is not set in any profile the system silently uses the kernel default, and for many security parameters that default is weak or off. Concretely, if login/no_automatic_user_sapstar, rsau/enable, gw/sec_info or gw/reg_info are absent, the system may be exposed to the SAP* hard-coded backdoor, may have no security audit trail, and may have an unrestricted RFC gateway that permits remote registration and start of external programs - each of which is independently exploitable. The danger is compounded because operators frequently assume 'we didn't change it, so it's fine', when in fact the SAP-delivered default is the insecure state. In a RISE/ECS context these are precisely the application-layer controls the customer still owns, so leaving them at default is a customer-side gap that SAP's infrastructure controls do not cover. Attack scenario: an adversary who reaches the gateway port (3300/33NN) of a system with no reg_info/sec_info can register a malicious RFC server or start OS-level programs, achieving remote code execution as the <sid>adm user; separately, if no_automatic_user_sapstar is unset on an older release, deleting the SAP* master record re-activates SAP* with the default password PASS. Business impact spans full system compromise, undetectable fraud (no audit log), and audit findings for missing ITGC. A real incident would look like unexplained external program starts in SMGW logs, or an SAP* logon from an unexpected terminal, with no Security Audit Log to reconstruct events.
Affected Items (8)
  • gw/reg_no_conn_info (Gateway Security)
  • gw/logging (Gateway Security)
  • gw/rem_start (Gateway Security)
  • ixml/dtd_restriction (Network & Service Exposure)
  • login/create_virtual_user_sapstar (Login Security)
  • ms/acl_info (System Trust & Standard Users)
  • ssl/client_ciphersuites (Transport Security)
  • system/secure_communication (Transport Security)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Take the affected-items list from this finding as the work list of parameters to explicitly set. 2. In RZ10 open the DEFAULT profile (system-wide) or the relevant instance profile in extended maintenance. 3. For each missing parameter, add it with the secure target value: login/no_automatic_user_sapstar=1, rsau/enable=1 (or configure via RSAU_CONFIG on 7.50+), gw/sec_info and gw/reg_info pointing to hardened ACL files, gw/reg_no_conn_info per SAP Note 1444282, and the password/lockout minimums from the other findings. 4. Confirm each parameter's exact meaning and allowed values first in RZ11 (it shows official documentation and whether the parameter is dynamically switchable). 5. Save and activate the profile; schedule the required instance restart during a maintenance window for static parameters (RZ11 flags which are dynamic). 6. For gateway ACL parameters, after placing the files reload them via SMGW -> Goto -> Expert Functions -> Reread (no restart needed). 7. Verify with report RSPARAM after restart that every previously-missing parameter now shows an explicit, compliant value rather than 'default'. 8. Roll out in DEV/QA first and coordinate with interface owners, because gateway and RFC hardening can break registered external programs if ACLs are wrong. 9. In RISE/ECS raise a change request to the SAP operations team for any parameter you cannot maintain directly. 10. Re-export parameters and re-run the scanner to confirm PARAM-MISSING is cleared.
HIGH P3 · 42 Firefighter sessions exceeding 4h duration IAM-FF-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags emergency/firefighter sessions that ran longer than the configured maximum (default 4 hours). Firefighter access grants far-reaching privileges for a specific, time-boxed emergency; a session that stays open for many hours (or overnight) is a control failure because the window during which someone can perform unrelated, unmonitored privileged actions expands dramatically. Long sessions often indicate the ID was checked out and then left logged on, shared, or used for routine work it was never intended for. The abuse scenario: a user checks out a firefighter ID for a genuine incident, then keeps the session alive to perform additional, unlogged-in-context activities — configuration changes, data extracts, transaction postings — well beyond the original justification, blending legitimate and illegitimate actions in one hard-to-review session. Impact is increased exposure to privileged misuse and a weakened compensating control; extended sessions also make the controller's after-the-fact review far harder because there is more activity to sift and less correlation to a single incident. For SOX this undermines the 'time-boxed, reviewed emergency access' assertion. A real incident looks like a firefighter session spanning a full day during which an unauthorized master-data or authorization change was made, buried among legitimate incident-response steps.
Affected Items (2)
  • JSMITH as FF_FIN_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-01 09:15:00) — duration: 6.5h (max: 4h)
  • LWANG as FF_BASIS_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-03 22:00:00) — duration: 8.5h (max: 4h)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review each long session in the GRC EAM log against its incident/change ticket to confirm whether the extended duration was justified or indicates misuse. 2. Enforce a session time-limit: in GRC EAM configuration (SPRO > Governance, Risk and Compliance > Access Control > Emergency Access Management) set the firefighter validity/timeout so IDs auto-expire after the approved window (align to the 4-hour target or your policy). 3. Configure SAP profile parameter rdisp/gui_auto_logout (and comparable idle-timeout controls) so idle privileged sessions are terminated. 4. Require re-checkout for continued work rather than keeping one session open, so each interval carries its own justification and log. 5. Investigate any session that materially exceeded the limit for unauthorized activity, using the EAM transaction log and Security Audit Log (SM20). 6. Verify by re-running the analysis after the next review cycle and confirming sessions now fall within the threshold. 7. Rollout caution: test the timeout in a non-production GRC/EAM setting first and communicate to firefighter users so an auto-logout does not interrupt a genuine critical fix mid-step.
References
  • SAP GRC SPM — Session Duration Controls
HIGH P3 · 42 Firefighter sessions without documented justification IAM-FF-002 ▶
Security Risk
This flags emergency/firefighter sessions that have no documented reason or justification. A defining requirement of controlled emergency access is that every check-out carries a traceable business reason — typically an incident or change ticket — so the privileged activity can be explained and defended in audit. Sessions with a blank reason break the accountability chain: nobody can later establish why superuser access was used, whether it was authorized, or whether the actions taken matched a legitimate need. The abuse scenario is straightforward — a user checks out the firefighter ID without stating a reason and performs privileged actions that are effectively unexplained, giving cover to unauthorized changes because there is no stated purpose to compare the actual activity against. Impact is a failed compensating control and an audit exception: SOX/J-SOX and internal control frameworks require documented justification for privileged access, and undocumented emergency use is routinely cited as a deficiency. A real incident looks like an auditor sampling firefighter logs, finding sessions with empty justification, and being unable to obtain any after-the-fact explanation — turning a procedural gap into a reportable control weakness and prompting a wider look for actual misuse.
Affected Items (2)
  • JSMITH as FF_FIN_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-10 08:30:00)
  • LWANG as FF_BASIS_ADMIN (login: 2025-02-12 08:00:00)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the listed sessions and retroactively obtain and document the business reason/ticket for each, recording it in the EAM log so the audit trail is complete. 2. Make justification mandatory: in GRC EAM configuration enable the reason-code requirement and maintain a controlled list of reason codes (EAM 'Maintain Reason Codes') so no session can start without one. 3. Require an incident/change ticket reference in the reason field via workflow, linking each firefighter use to ITSM. 4. Configure the firefighter log-on screen/workflow to reject blank justifications. 5. Train firefighter users and controllers on the documentation standard and the audit consequences of blank reasons. 6. Verify by re-running the analysis for the next period and confirming all new sessions carry a justification. 7. Rollout caution: test the mandatory-reason enforcement in non-production EAM first so it does not block a genuine emergency, and grandfather/annotate historical sessions rather than leaving them blank.
References

HIGH P3 · 42 BTP subaccount users with administrative role collections IAM-XID-003 ▶
Security Risk
This flags BTP subaccount users holding administrative role collections (e.g. Subaccount Administrator, Global Account Administrator, Space Developer, Security Administrator, Connectivity/Destination Administrator). BTP administrative access is highly powerful in a RISE landscape: these role collections can change trust configuration and identity-provider settings, create and edit destinations and the Cloud Connector configuration that bridge BTP to the S/4 backend, provision services, and manage other users' access. Excessive or unjustified admin assignments concentrate control over the entire extension and integration layer in too many hands, and each admin is a high-value target. The abuse scenario: an over-privileged BTP admin (or an attacker who phishes one) reconfigures a destination or trust to point at an attacker-controlled endpoint, creates a destination that exposes S/4 data, weakens authentication, or grants themselves further access — effectively compromising the bridge between cloud and core ERP. Impact spans data breach, integration tampering, and potential lateral movement into S/4, plus a least-privilege and SoD failure (e.g. one person holding both Subaccount Admin and Security Admin). A real incident looks like a BTP admin account being used to add a rogue destination or modify trust so that data or tokens flow to an external system, discovered during a BTP security configuration review.
Affected Items (5)
  • mwilson@company.com — Subaccount_Admin, Security_Admin, Destination_Admin, Connectivity_Admin
  • lwang@company.com — Global_Account_Admin, Subaccount_Admin, Security_Admin, Subaccount_Service_Admin
  • ext_consultant1@partner.com — Subaccount_Admin, Space_Developer
  • ext_devops@vendor.io — Space_Developer, Connectivity_Admin
  • old_admin@company.com — Subaccount_Admin
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Export the list of admin role-collection holders (BTP cockpit > Security > Role Collections / Users) and review each against least privilege and documented business need. 2. Remove admin role collections from users who do not require them; assign the minimal collection needed (e.g. developer vs administrator) rather than blanket admin. 3. Separate duties within BTP administration — do not combine Subaccount Administrator with Security Administrator on one person; split platform, security and connectivity administration. 4. Restrict and monitor Connectivity/Destination Administrator, since those roles control the S/4 bridge (destinations, Cloud Connector, trust). 5. Bring BTP admin access under privileged-access governance and periodic review, and document a business justification for each remaining admin. 6. Verify by re-exporting role collections and confirming the admin population is reduced to the approved, segregated set. 7. Rollout caution: retain at least one break-glass global-account/subaccount admin (monitored) so you are not locked out, coordinate with the BTP platform team, and test role-collection changes in a non-production subaccount first.

HIGH P3 · 42 Overdue access review campaigns IAM-REV-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags access-review (user access recertification) campaigns that are past their due date and not completed. Periodic access review is a foundational detective control: at defined intervals, managers or role owners re-attest that each user's access is still appropriate, catching privilege creep, orphaned access, SoD drift and leaver residue. When campaigns run overdue, that control is not operating on schedule — inappropriate access that a timely review would have removed stays live, and the organization loses its recurring checkpoint on the access model. The abuse angle is indirect but real: access that should have been revoked (a mover's old financial role, a dormant admin grant) persists because no one re-examined it, extending the window for misuse and SoD conflict. For SOX Section 404 and ITGC, timely periodic recertification is an explicitly tested control, and overdue campaigns are a common audit exception that can escalate if pervasive. Impact is both elevated standing risk and a documented control deficiency. A real incident looks like an auditor finding a quarter's recertification campaign months overdue, then discovering during their own sample that several users retained access they should have lost — turning a scheduling lapse into a finding about the effectiveness of the entire access-governance program.
Affected Items (5)
  • Q1 2025 Finance Access Review — due: 20250228, 532d overdue
  • Q1 2025 Procurement Access Review — due: 20250228, 532d overdue
  • Q1 2025 Basis Admin Review — due: 20250301, 531d overdue
  • Q4 2024 Security Review — due: 20241231, 591d overdue
  • Q1 2025 BTP Access Review — due: 20250315, 517d overdue
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Escalate the overdue campaigns to the responsible managers and control owners immediately and set a firm completion deadline (e.g. within two weeks). 2. Complete the outstanding reviews — in GRC Access Control run/resume the User Access Review (UAR) or SoD Review campaign and ensure each item is actioned (keep/remove) by the reviewer. 3. Configure automated reminders and escalation in GRC ARM so approaching and missed deadlines notify reviewers and their managers. 4. Enforce the defined review cycle (e.g. 90 days) with scheduled campaign generation so a new cycle starts automatically. 5. Track completion metrics and report overdue campaigns to governance so accountability is visible. 6. Verify by re-extracting the campaign status and confirming the flagged campaigns are now completed and the next cycle is scheduled. 7. Rollout caution: ensure reviewers have adequate time and guidance so 'rubber-stamp' approvals do not replace genuine review; stagger campaigns to avoid overloading reviewers and undermining quality.

HIGH P3 · 42 Read Access Logging missing coverage for key channels DPP-RAL-002 ▶
Security Risk
RAL configuration is per-channel; enabling it for SAP GUI (Dynpro) alone leaves the modern access paths uninstrumented. This finding shows one or more of Dynpro, Web Dynpro/Fiori, OData, RFC, and ALV list output are unlogged. In S/4HANA RISE the OData/Gateway channel is the most important gap: every Fiori app, the launchpad, mobile clients and external API consumers read personal data through OData services, so an unlogged OData channel means the bulk of legitimate and illegitimate reads are invisible. The RFC channel is equally dangerous because BAPIs and RFC-enabled function modules (e.g. BAPI_BUPA_* and HR read BAPIs) let a trusted-RFC or interface user pull personal data programmatically, bypassing dialog screens entirely; without RFC RAL these bulk reads leave no trace. ALV/list-output gaps matter because users routinely export displayed lists to spreadsheets. Attack scenario: an attacker or over-privileged integration account calls a Business Partner OData service or an HR BAPI in a loop, harvesting PII at scale; because only Dynpro is logged, monitoring shows nothing. Impact: partial RAL creates a false sense of compliance. Auditors and regulators treat incomplete access logging as effectively no logging for the uncovered channels, undermining Art.15/Art.30 evidence and breach forensics.
Affected Items (3)
  • ODATA: OData API access (Fiori apps, external APIs)
  • RFC: Remote Function Call access
  • ALV: ALV report output / list displays
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SRALMANAGER -> Configuration, list existing configurations per channel and identify which of Dynpro, Web Dynpro, RFC, Web Services, Gateway (OData) and ALV are missing. 2. For OData: create RAL configurations for the relevant Gateway services (leveraging SAP Note 2347271 and Gateway RAL content) covering BP/customer/vendor/HR services. 3. For RFC: configure RAL for the RFC-enabled function modules/BAPIs that expose personal fields. 4. For Web Dynpro/classic Fiori: add Web Dynpro channel configurations for the personal-data applications. 5. For Dynpro: cover the key HR/BP display transactions (PA20/PA30, BP, FD03/FK03, XD03/XK03). 6. Map every configuration to a Log Purpose so evaluation is meaningful. 7. Activate each configuration and enable logging in the client. 8. Verify: exercise each channel (open a Fiori app, call the BAPI via SE37, display and export a list) and confirm entries appear per channel in SRALMANAGER -> Monitor. 9. Prioritise OData and RFC first given their exfiltration potential. 10. Caution: test in QA to gauge log volume - high-traffic OData services generate large volumes, so tune conditions/fields to log only sensitive attributes.

HIGH P3 · 42 ILM policies without end-of-purpose definitions DPP-ILM-003 ▶
Security Risk
The 'end of purpose' (EoP) is the trigger that tells SAP when a business object's processing purpose has been fulfilled and the data may move into blocking and, later, destruction. An ILM policy with no EoP/legal-basis defined has a retention period but no start signal for the retention clock - SAP cannot determine when to block or delete the data, so it effectively never ages out. This is a foundational GDPR Art.17 (right to erasure) and purpose-limitation gap: without an EoP, data that has served its purpose (contract closed, employee left, customer relationship ended) stays fully accessible indefinitely. Abuse/impact scenario: a former customer requests erasure; because no EoP is defined, the standard blocking/deletion logic (BUPA_PRE_EOP / CVP_PRE_EOP for business partners) returns 'end of purpose not reached' and refuses to block, so staff cannot even demonstrate the data is eligible for deletion, while the un-aged data remains readable by support and integration users. Business impact: systemic inability to honor erasure requests, purpose-limitation violations, and audit findings that the data-lifecycle has no defined trigger. A real incident is a regulator asking to see the erasure workflow and finding data can never leave the 'in-purpose' state.
Affected Items (2)
  • HR_Payroll_Retention (object: PA0008)
  • Customer_Master (object: KNA1)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. For every ILM policy in IRMPOL, define the end-of-purpose condition tied to the business event (contract completion, employment end, last business transaction, consent withdrawal). 2. Configure the application-side EoP / Start-of-Retention (SoR) checks so the retention clock starts at the correct event. 3. For Business Partner/customer/vendor data, set up and test the standard EoP checks using transactions BUPA_PRE_EOP and CVP_PRE_EOP and the Data Controller Rule Framework (DCRF). 4. Activate the relevant business functions (e.g. ILM_BLOCKING, BUPA_ILM_BF) enabling blocking/deletion. 5. Map each EoP to the documented GDPR Art.6 legal basis/processing purpose so blocking aligns with lawful basis. 6. Implement application-specific EoP adaptations for applications consuming Business Partner (per SAP EoP adaptation guidance). 7. Transport and test the configuration end-to-end in QA with representative records. 8. Verify: run the EoP check on a sample record that should be blockable and confirm it transitions to blocked; run one still in purpose and confirm it is protected. 9. Reconcile EoP definitions to the ROPA so every processing purpose has a corresponding trigger. 10. Caution: incorrect EoP timing can block live business data prematurely or fail to block eligible data - validate with process owners and the DPO before production activation.
References
  • GDPR Article 17 — Right to Erasure
  • SAP ILM — End of Purpose Configuration
HIGH P3 · 42 Personal data tables without ILM retention policies DPP-ILM-004 ▶
Security Risk
The scanner cross-references tables known to hold personal data (HR infotypes PA0000-PA0185, HRP1000/1001, Business Partner BUT000/BUT020/BUT050, address ADRC/ADR*, customer/vendor KNA1/KNB1/LFA1/LFB1, financial BSEG/BKPF, user master USR02/USR21) against objects covered by ILM policies, and flags tables with no retention rule. Uncovered tables retain their personal data indefinitely because nothing schedules them for blocking or destruction. This is dangerous because these exact tables are the crown jewels for an attacker or malicious insider: USR02 holds user/credential metadata, PA0008 holds salary, PA0009 holds bank details, BUT000/ADRC/KNA1 hold names, addresses and contact PII, and BSEG/BKPF hold financial line items. With no ILM policy, a SE16/SE16N or database-level read returns the full historical population, not just current in-purpose records. Impact: erasure and retention obligations cannot be met for these tables, audits flag uncontrolled PII stores, and a breach touching them is maximally severe because it exposes decades of records. A real incident: a subject-access/erasure request for an ex-employee cannot be fulfilled because PA* infotypes have no lifecycle policy and the historical records were never eligible for deletion.
Affected Items (24)
  • PA0000
  • PA0002
  • PA0003
  • PA0006
  • PA0009
  • PA0021
  • PA0077
  • PA0105
  • PA0185
  • HRP1000
  • HRP1001
  • BUT000
  • BUT020
  • BUT021
  • BUT050
  • BUT100
  • ADR2
  • ADR3
  • ADR6
  • KNB1
  • LFB1
  • BSEG
  • USR02
  • USR21
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In IRMPOL, review coverage and, for each listed table/object, confirm whether a standard SAP ILM object already exists (many HR, FI and BP objects ship with SAP-delivered ILM objects). 2. Assign/activate the standard ILM retention objects for HR (PA infotypes), FI (BSEG/BKPF via financial archiving objects), and Business Partner/customer/vendor data. 3. Create ILM policies in IRMPOL for each object with residence, retention and destruction rules plus an EoP trigger (DPP-ILM-003). 4. For custom tables without a standard object, define a custom ILM/archiving object and its policy. 5. Where data must remain live, apply ILM blocking (authorization-group based) so out-of-purpose records are access-restricted even before destruction. 6. Complement with table-level access control: restrict S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM and SE16/SE16N so these tables are not broadly readable. 7. Transport policies through the landscape under change management. 8. Verify: list ILM-covered objects and confirm every flagged table maps to an active policy; simulate retention for sample records. 9. Coordinate financial-document retention (BSEG/BKPF) with Finance/Tax to respect statutory minimums before setting destruction. 10. Caution: FI and HR archiving have strong business/legal dependencies - validate residence periods with process owners and never destroy financial data inside its statutory retention window.
References
  • SAP ILM — Standard Retention Objects
  • GDPR Article 5(1)(c) — Data Minimisation
HIGH P3 · 42 DPP toolkit features not configured DPP-TOOLKIT-001 ▶
Security Risk
SAP S/4HANA's data-protection & privacy capabilities operationalize data-subject rights: the Information Retrieval Framework (right of access, Art.15), ILM blocking/deletion (right to erasure, Art.17), change-of-purpose handling (Art.6), end-of-purpose blocking, consent recording (Art.7), and breach-notification support (Art.33/34). When these are not configured, the organization has no systematic, repeatable way to fulfill legal obligations - each request becomes a manual, error-prone scramble across tables, archives and BTP services. This is dangerous operationally and legally: missing an Information Report capability means a subject-access request cannot be answered completely or on time; missing deletion/blocking means erasure cannot be performed or proven; missing change-of-purpose and consent management means data is processed without a maintained lawful basis. Abuse/impact scenario: a data subject exercises rights and the organization cannot respond within the statutory window, or responds incompletely, exposing it to complaints and fines; separately, without breach-notification support the team cannot rapidly scope and report an incident within the 72-hour GDPR deadline. In a regulated, auditable RISE environment, unconfigured DPP tooling is a systemic controls gap, not an isolated misconfiguration. A real incident: a regulator audits the rights-fulfillment process and finds it undocumented and manual, treating the whole privacy program as non-compliant.
Affected Items (3)
  • deletionReport: GDPR Art.17 — Right to Erasure / Deletion Report
  • consentManagement: GDPR Art.7 — Consent Recording & Withdrawal
  • dataBreachNotification: GDPR Art.33/34 — Breach Notification Support
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify which DPP capabilities are unconfigured from the finding and map each to its SAP function. 2. Configure the Information Retrieval Framework (IRF) to generate data-subject information/disclosure reports for Art.15 requests. 3. Configure ILM-based blocking and deletion (IRMPOL policies, SARA, ILM_BLOCKING business function) to fulfill Art.17 erasure - see DPP-ILM-002/003. 4. Set up end-of-purpose blocking for Business Partner/customer/vendor via BUPA_PRE_EOP / CVP_PRE_EOP and the Data Controller Rule Framework (DCRF). 5. Implement change-of-purpose handling so re-use of data is governed by a maintained legal basis. 6. Integrate consent management with an appropriate platform (e.g. SAP Enterprise Consent and Preference Management / SAP Customer Data Cloud) and record consent/withdrawal. 7. Establish breach-notification support: combine RAL and Security Audit Log (RSAU_CONFIG/SM20) evidence with an incident runbook to meet the 72-hour deadline. 8. Assign clear ownership (DPO + Basis + process owners) and document each procedure in the ROPA. 9. Verify: execute an end-to-end test of each right (access, erasure, blocking) against a test data subject and confirm complete, timely output. 10. Caution: sequence ILM/blocking configuration before enabling deletion in production, test in QA, and coordinate with application teams whose objects consume Business Partner.
References
  • SAP S/4HANA — Data Protection & Privacy Toolkit
  • GDPR Articles 6, 7, 15, 17, 33, 34
  • DPDP Act 2023 Sections 6, 8, 11, 12, 13
HIGH P3 · 42 Purposes of processing without documented legal basis DPP-POP-001 ▶
Security Risk
Under GDPR Art.6 (and DPDP Sec.4) every processing activity on personal data must rest on a documented lawful basis - consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public task, or legitimate interest. A purpose-of-processing entry with no legal basis recorded means personal data is being processed with no demonstrable justification, which is unlawful processing per se, independent of any breach. This is dangerous because it is a foundational compliance failure that undermines everything downstream: without a legal basis you cannot correctly set retention/end-of-purpose, cannot answer a subject's 'why do you hold my data', and cannot defend the processing to a regulator. Abuse/impact scenario: a data subject or regulator asks on what basis their data is processed and the organization has no answer on record; or an internal audit of the ROPA finds processing purposes with blank legal grounds, forcing suspension of those activities. It often cascades - a purpose without a basis frequently coincides with data being retained and shared with no controls. Business impact: unlawful-processing findings, orders to cease processing, fines (explicitly tied to Art.6 breaches), and reputational damage. A real incident: during a regulatory inquiry the ROPA is produced and multiple high-volume activities (marketing use of customer data, HR analytics) show no lawful basis, converting a routine audit into enforcement.
Affected Items (3)
  • Purpose: Customer Relationship Management — legal basis: not documented
  • Purpose: Analytics and Reporting — legal basis: not documented
  • Purpose: Legacy CRM Migration — legal basis: not documented
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the list of purposes lacking a legal basis from the finding and the source purpose-of-processing register. 2. For each purpose, work with the DPO/Legal to determine and document the correct GDPR Art.6(1)(a-f) basis (or DPDP Sec.4 ground). 3. Record the legal basis in the S/4HANA DPP purpose configuration / Data Controller Rule Framework and in the corporate ROPA (Art.30 record). 4. Where the basis is consent, ensure a consent record exists and is linked (see consent management under DPP-TOOLKIT-001). 5. Where the basis is legitimate interest, document a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA). 6. Tie each documented purpose to its retention/end-of-purpose trigger so lawful basis drives lifecycle (DPP-ILM-003). 7. For any purpose that genuinely has no lawful basis, stop the processing and block/delete the affected data. 8. Verify: reconcile the purpose register against the ROPA and confirm zero purposes with blank legal basis. 9. Establish a control that new processing purposes cannot be activated without a recorded legal basis. 10. Caution: this is a legal determination, not a technical one - do not self-assign a basis without DPO/Legal sign-off, and treat marketing/profiling and special-category data with extra scrutiny.
References
  • GDPR Article 6 — Lawfulness of Processing
  • DPDP Act 2023 Section 4 — Grounds for Processing
HIGH P3 · 42 Special category personal data in cross-border transfers DPP-RES-002 ▶
Security Risk
Cross-border transfers that carry special-category data (health, biometric, genetic, racial/ethnic, political, religious, trade-union, sexual, or criminal-offence data) demand a higher bar than ordinary PII: an Art.9 condition (typically explicit consent or another specific legal ground) in addition to a Chapter V transfer mechanism, and usually a DPIA. This finding flags transfers where such categories are present. It is dangerous because special-category data carries the greatest harm potential to individuals (discrimination, safety, profiling) and the strictest legal treatment; moving it across borders multiplies both the legal exposure and the real-world risk if intercepted or misused. Abuse/impact scenario: employee health or ethnicity data, or biometric identifiers, are transferred to a third-country service or analytics tenant without explicit consent/Art.9 basis and without supplementary safeguards; a breach or regulator inquiry then exposes both an unlawful-transfer and an unlawful special-category-processing violation simultaneously. Because these categories often appear in HR (RACKY ethnicity, CONFG religion, health-related absence data) and are frequently overlooked, they can flow through routine HR integrations unnoticed. Business impact: compounded violations (Art.9 + Chapter V), a higher fine tier, mandatory DPIA, and severe reputational damage. A real incident: an HR analytics or occupational-health integration is found to export special-category employee data to a non-adequate region with neither explicit consent nor a DPIA.
Affected Items (1)
  • EU_to_CN_Supplier: EU → CN — special categories: Health and Safety Records
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, identify each transfer and the specific special categories involved. 2. Confirm and document an Art.9(2) condition for processing each category (commonly explicit consent, employment-law obligation, or another listed ground). 3. Conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA, Art.35) for each such transfer given its high-risk nature. 4. Ensure a Chapter V transfer mechanism is in place (adequacy/SCCs/BCRs) - see DPP-RES-001 - layered on top of the Art.9 basis. 5. Apply supplementary technical measures: strong encryption in transit and at rest, and pseudonymization/anonymization before transfer where feasible. 6. Minimize the special-category payload - transfer only the strictly necessary attributes; strip or tokenize the rest. 7. In HR/BTP integrations, verify field mappings so special-category fields (RACKY, CONFG, health data) are not transferred unless required and lawful. 8. Update the ROPA, transfer register, and DPIA records accordingly. 9. Verify: review interface payloads/field lists to confirm only lawful, minimized, safeguarded special-category data crosses the border. 10. Caution: if a lawful Art.9 basis cannot be established, halt the special-category transfer; escalate to the DPO and Legal before any change and coordinate with interface owners.
References
  • GDPR Article 9 — Special Categories of Personal Data
  • GDPR Article 35 — Data Protection Impact Assessment
HIGH P3 · 42 Data subject requests marked complete but incomplete DPP-DEL-002 ▶
Security Risk
A data-subject request (typically erasure) marked 'completed' while its completion percentage is below 100% means the organization closed the ticket but left residual personal data in the system - a partial deletion masquerading as done. This is dangerous precisely because it is hidden: the record says the individual's data was erased, but copies remain in some tables, archives, BTP services, or backups, so the organization is both non-compliant and unaware. In SAP landscapes, personal data is spread across many objects (HR infotypes, Business Partner, customer/vendor, FI documents, addresses) plus archives and connected BTP/analytics systems, so a deletion that only touched the primary object commonly leaves residuals. Abuse/impact scenario: an individual whose data was 'erased' later finds the organization still holds and even processes their data (still receives marketing, or their record surfaces in a report); they complain, and the false 'completed' status aggravates the violation because it shows a control that reports success without achieving it. Business impact: unfulfilled Art.17 erasure, misleading records that undermine the accountability principle, and audit findings that the deletion process is not verifiable. A real incident: a re-test of 'completed' erasures finds residual PII in secondary tables or archives, exposing that the erasure workflow does not span the full data map.
Affected Items (1)
  • Request DSAR-2025-005 (RECTIFICATION, subject: customer_7890) — status: COMPLETED, completion: 85%
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, reopen every request marked complete with less than 100% completion. 2. Determine residual locations using the personal-data map/inventory - check all objects: HR infotypes, Business Partner/customer/vendor, FI documents, addresses, plus archives and connected BTP systems. 3. Complete the deletion/blocking across all locations using ILM destruction and blocking (SARA / ILM, BUPA_PRE_EOP / CVP_PRE_EOP). 4. Include archived data (ILM-managed archives) and coordinate backup handling per policy for data that cannot be selectively deleted from backups. 5. Use the DPP disclosure/deletion reporting (Information Retrieval Framework) to confirm no residual personal data remains for the subject. 6. Only then set the request to genuinely complete (100%) with evidence attached. 7. Fix the workflow so 'complete' cannot be set unless completion is verified at 100% across the data map. 8. Verify: run an information/disclosure report on the data subject post-erasure and confirm an empty/blocked result. 9. Periodically sample 'completed' erasures to confirm the control is effective. 10. Caution: some data legitimately cannot be deleted (statutory retention, legal hold) - in those cases block rather than delete and document the exemption instead of marking a false 100%.
References
  • GDPR Article 17 — Right to Erasure
HIGH P3 · 42 Custom code missing authority checks CODE-INJ-002 ▶
Security Risk
Custom function modules, RFC-enabled FMs, and OData/Gateway service implementations execute business logic without an AUTHORITY-CHECK. In SAP the transaction-start check (S_TCODE) only guards the entry point; once code runs it must re-verify object-level authorizations itself. Missing checks mean any authenticated user - or any caller that reaches the object over RFC or the /sap/opu/odata Gateway - executes the logic regardless of their PFCG roles. Attack scenario: a low-privileged user (or an integration/service account with broad S_RFC) calls the FM directly via SE37, an RFC destination, or the OData entity set. Because GET_ENTITYSET/GET_ENTITY or the FM body never calls AUTHORITY-CHECK on the relevant object (e.g., F_BKPF_BUK for company code, or a business object authorization), the user reads or posts data they are not authorized for. This is a classic horizontal/vertical privilege escalation: display roles become effectively write roles, and company-code / plant segregation is bypassed. RFC-enabled FMs are especially dangerous because they are reachable from other systems and from external callers holding an RFC user. Business impact: broken segregation of duties, unauthorized access to HR/finance/PII data, and audit findings against SOX access controls and GDPR least-privilege. A real incident manifests as a user performing actions their role review says are impossible - detectable only if the object is later instrumented, since no failed-auth trace (SU53/ST01) is ever generated when the check is simply absent.
Affected Items (4)
  • Z_VENDOR_REPORT (PROG) line 12: No AUTHORITY-CHECK for S_TCODE in function entry
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI (FUGR) line 45: Missing authority check in BAPI wrapper function module
  • Z_MM_PO_UPLOAD (PROG) line 22: No AUTHORITY-CHECK before BAPI_PO_CREATE1 call
  • Z_DATA_EXPORT (PROG) line 15: Function module callable via RFC without authorization check
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review each flagged object in SE37/SE80/ADT and identify the sensitive operation (data read, posting, config change) that must be gated. 2. Add AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT '...' for the correct authorization object(s) at method/FM entry - e.g., S_TCODE plus business objects like F_BKPF_BUK, and check ACTVT for the actual operation; SY-SUBRC <> 0 must abort. 3. Use SU22/SU24 to maintain authorization default values so the objects flow into PFCG roles via SU25/SU24 proposals. 4. For SEGW/OData services, implement the check in the DPC_EXT GET_ENTITYSET/GET_ENTITY (and CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE) methods; for RAP business objects, define authorization control in the Behavior Definition. 5. For RFC-enabled FMs, also confirm S_RFC and S_RFCACL are appropriately restricted so external callers cannot reach the FM broadly. 6. Run SAP Code Vulnerability Analyzer 'missing authorization check' variant in transaction ATC over the affected packages to find all instances. 7. Rebuild affected PFCG roles (transaction PFCG), regenerate profiles, and re-run SU25 step 2 where SU24 defaults changed. 8. Verify with a low-privileged test user: attempt the operation and confirm it is now denied, and inspect SU53/ST01 to see the expected failed AUTHORITY-CHECK trace. 9. Confirm authorized users still succeed (no over-restriction) via QA regression with the app owner. 10. Transport DEV->QA->PRD and coordinate role changes with the authorization team; monitor the Security Audit Log (SM20/RSAU) for auth failures post go-live.
References
  • SAP Note 1520356 — Secure ABAP Programming
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Custom Code Authorization Checks
HIGH P3 · 42 Dangerous ABAP statement: CALL 'SYSTEM' CODE-STMT-001 ▶
Security Risk
Custom code uses dangerous or obsolete ABAP statements. This family covers: CALL 'SYSTEM' / CALL 'C_SAPGPARAM' (direct kernel calls that run OS commands or read system parameters), GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL / GENERATE REPORT (runtime code generation), INSERT/DELETE/READ REPORT (reading or modifying ABAP source at runtime), EDITOR-CALL (opening the ABAP editor at runtime), EXPORT ... TO MEMORY (cross-session data leakage), and CALL TRANSACTION / SUBMIT ... VIA JOB used without a preceding authority check. The kernel and code-generation statements are the most dangerous: CALL 'SYSTEM' executes operating-system commands under the SAP service account (typically <sid>adm), and GENERATE/INSERT REPORT let an attacker construct and run arbitrary ABAP at runtime. If any of these consume user-controlled input, the result is remote code execution on the application server - the highest-impact SAP compromise. Attack scenario: an attacker who can influence a parameter that flows into CALL 'SYSTEM' or a generated program injects an OS command or ABAP snippet, gaining a shell as <sid>adm or executing privileged ABAP, then reads/writes the HANA database, secure store, or transport directory. CALL TRANSACTION/SUBMIT without AUTHORITY-CHECK/WITH AUTHORITY-CHECK allows starting transactions the user is not entitled to. Business impact: full system takeover, data destruction, planting of backdoors, and complete audit-trail bypass (an OS-level attacker can alter logs). Even without user input, these statements defeat static review and upgrade safety. A real incident looks like unexpected OS processes or files owned by <sid>adm, or unexplained new/modified programs in TRDIR.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT (PROG) line 203
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory each occurrence via ATC/Code Inspector (transaction ATC/SCI) 'critical statements'/security variant and the SLIN extended program check; rank CALL 'SYSTEM', GENERATE*, INSERT/DELETE REPORT, EDITOR-CALL first. 2. Eliminate CALL 'SYSTEM': replace ad-hoc OS calls with defined external commands in SM69, executed via SM49/SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE, which enforce authorization object S_LOG_COM and an allow-list of commands/parameters. 3. Remove GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL/GENERATE REPORT/INSERT REPORT patterns; refactor to BAdI/enhancement-framework implementations, predefined method dispatch, or configuration tables instead of runtime code generation. 4. Remove READ/DELETE REPORT and EDITOR-CALL from productive code; these have no legitimate place in business logic. 5. For every retained CALL TRANSACTION add ... WITH AUTHORITY-CHECK, and precede SUBMIT/CALL TRANSACTION with an explicit AUTHORITY-CHECK on the target transaction (S_TCODE) and business objects. 6. Replace EXPORT ... TO MEMORY with session-scoped, keyed shared memory or explicit parameter passing to prevent cross-session leakage. 7. Harden the platform: restrict S_LOG_COM, S_DATASET (file access), S_DEVELOP; and constrain runtime debugging via profile parameter rdisp/wpdbug_max_no (coordinate the value/restart with SAP ECS under RISE). 8. Re-run ATC/SLIN to confirm the critical statements are gone or exempted with documented justification. 9. Verify functionally in QA that refactored logic behaves identically and that the SM69 command path enforces S_LOG_COM. 10. Transport DEV->QA->PRD; add an ATC gate at release so these statements cannot re-enter productive code.
References
  • SAP Note 1520356 — Secure ABAP Coding Guidelines

This family covers: CALL 'SYSTEM' / CALL 'C_SAPGPARAM' (direct kernel calls that run OS commands or read system parameters), GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL / GENERATE REPORT (runtime code generation), INSERT/DELETE/READ REPORT (reading or modifying ABAP source at runtime), EDITOR-CALL (opening the ABAP editor at runtime), EXPORT ... TO MEMORY (cross-session data leakage), and CALL TRANSACTION / SUBMIT ... VIA JOB used without a preceding authority check. The kernel and code-generation statements are the most dangerous: CALL 'SYSTEM' executes operating-system commands under the SAP service account (typically <sid>adm), and GENERATE/INSERT REPORT let an attacker construct and run arbitrary ABAP at runtime. If any of these consume user-controlled input, the result is remote code execution on the application server - the highest-impact SAP compromise. Attack scenario: an attacker who can influence a parameter that flows into CALL 'SYSTEM' or a generated program injects an OS command or ABAP snippet, gaining a shell as <sid>adm or executing privileged ABAP, then reads/writes the HANA database, secure store, or transport directory. CALL TRANSACTION/SUBMIT without AUTHORITY-CHECK/WITH AUTHORITY-CHECK allows starting transactions the user is not entitled to. Business impact: full system takeover, data destruction, planting of backdoors, and complete audit-trail bypass (an OS-level attacker can alter logs). Even without user input, these statements defeat static review and upgrade safety. A real incident looks like unexpected OS processes or files owned by <sid>adm, or unexplained new/modified programs in TRDIR.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_UTILS_COMMON (PROG) line 234
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory each occurrence via ATC/Code Inspector (transaction ATC/SCI) 'critical statements'/security variant and the SLIN extended program check; rank CALL 'SYSTEM', GENERATE*, INSERT/DELETE REPORT, EDITOR-CALL first. 2. Eliminate CALL 'SYSTEM': replace ad-hoc OS calls with defined external commands in SM69, executed via SM49/SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE, which enforce authorization object S_LOG_COM and an allow-list of commands/parameters. 3. Remove GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL/GENERATE REPORT/INSERT REPORT patterns; refactor to BAdI/enhancement-framework implementations, predefined method dispatch, or configuration tables instead of runtime code generation. 4. Remove READ/DELETE REPORT and EDITOR-CALL from productive code; these have no legitimate place in business logic. 5. For every retained CALL TRANSACTION add ... WITH AUTHORITY-CHECK, and precede SUBMIT/CALL TRANSACTION with an explicit AUTHORITY-CHECK on the target transaction (S_TCODE) and business objects. 6. Replace EXPORT ... TO MEMORY with session-scoped, keyed shared memory or explicit parameter passing to prevent cross-session leakage. 7. Harden the platform: restrict S_LOG_COM, S_DATASET (file access), S_DEVELOP; and constrain runtime debugging via profile parameter rdisp/wpdbug_max_no (coordinate the value/restart with SAP ECS under RISE). 8. Re-run ATC/SLIN to confirm the critical statements are gone or exempted with documented justification. 9. Verify functionally in QA that refactored logic behaves identically and that the SM69 command path enforces S_LOG_COM. 10. Transport DEV->QA->PRD; add an ATC gate at release so these statements cannot re-enter productive code.
References
  • SAP Note 1520356 — Secure ABAP Coding Guidelines
HIGH P3 · 42 Unresolved high-severity ATC findings (9) CODE-ATC-002 ▶
Security Risk
The ATC/Code Inspector scan shows High-severity (priority 2 / warning) findings that are unresolved. While individually lower-impact than criticals, High findings still represent real security and robustness weaknesses - for example incomplete authority checks, unsafe dynamic constructs, weak input handling, or performance/robustness issues that can be chained into a larger exploit or lead to denial of service. A persistent High backlog signals that secure-coding standards are not enforced and that technical debt is accumulating in code that runs with business-critical data access. Attackers frequently chain a High-severity weakness (e.g., partial authorization coverage or an information-disclosure defect) with another flaw to reach a critical outcome; defenders who ignore Highs leave those chains intact. Attack scenario: an authenticated user leverages a High-rated missing/partial check in a custom OData service to enumerate data they should not see, or triggers an unhandled dynamic call to cause a short dump / resource exhaustion affecting availability of a productive Fiori app. Business impact: gradual erosion of the control environment, audit findings on secure development lifecycle maturity, and increased likelihood that a future change introduces a critical. A real incident is rarely a single High alone, but Highs are the raw material for the incidents that do occur, and their neglect is itself an ITGC deficiency.
Affected Items (9)
  • Z_VENDOR_REPORT: MISSING_AUTHORIZATION — No AUTHORITY-CHECK for S_TCODE in function entry
  • Z_CUSTOMER_EXTRACT: CALL_SYSTEM — CALL 'SYSTEM' — OS command execution in custom code
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI: MISSING_AUTHORIZATION — Missing authority check in BAPI wrapper function module
  • Z_HR_SALARY_RPT: GENERATE_SUBROUTINE — GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL — dynamic code generation
  • Z_MM_PO_UPLOAD: MISSING_AUTHORIZATION — No AUTHORITY-CHECK before BAPI_PO_CREATE1 call
  • Z_SD_PRICING_EXIT: READ_REPORT — READ REPORT used to access ABAP source at runtime
  • Z_UTILS_COMMON: INSERT_REPORT — INSERT REPORT — can modify ABAP source at runtime
  • Z_LEGACY_MIGRATION: EXEC_SQL — EXEC SQL native SQL block without input validation
  • Z_BATCH_SCHEDULER: SUBMIT_VIA_JOB — SUBMIT via JOB without preceding authorization check
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the open Priority 2 / warning findings from transaction ATC and group them by object, package, and finding type. 2. Assign each group to the responsible development owner and set a remediation target (SAP practice: resolve within ~90 days of detection). 3. Prioritize High findings on RFC/OData-exposed and finance/HR-relevant objects, since these are the most reachable and sensitive. 4. Remediate at source following secure-ABAP guidance; convert repeated patterns into reusable secure helper methods to prevent recurrence. 5. Use the ATC exemption workflow (with justification and expiry) only for validated false positives. 6. Track progress in the ATC quality-governance dashboard and review the trend in security/change-advisory meetings. 7. Add ATC to the transport release check so new High findings are surfaced (warn or block per policy) before code leaves DEV. 8. Re-run the ATC mass scan after each remediation sprint and confirm the open-High count is decreasing. 9. Verify fixes in QA by exercising the affected functionality; ensure no regression for authorized users. 10. Transport fixes DEV->QA->PRD on the standard change path and report residual accepted Highs to the GRC owner.
References
  • SAP ATC — Finding Management
HIGH P3 · 42 Production transport imports without approval CODE-TMS-002 ▶
Security Risk
Transports were imported into the production system with no recorded approval. Change management requires that every production change be explicitly authorized before import; an unapproved import means code/customizing entered production outside the control framework, with no evidence that a change owner, CAB, or QA confirmation ever sanctioned it. The danger is that unapproved imports are the mechanism by which fraudulent, malicious, or simply untested changes reach production undetected. Without an approval gate, a developer or Basis operator can push arbitrary objects live, and there is no independent checkpoint to catch a payment-redirection change, a backdoor, a weakened role, or a risky config toggle. Attack/abuse scenario: an insider prepares a transport containing a self-benefiting change (e.g., altering a tolerance/approval limit, adding themselves to a role via a role transport, or inserting a backdoor RFC), then imports it into production during an unmonitored window. Because no approval was required, the change looks like routine activity in the STMS import history. Business impact: direct SOX ITGC change-approval control failure (a reportable deficiency), heightened fraud and sabotage risk, and inability to prove change legitimacy during audit or incident response. A real incident is a production defect or fraud whose root-cause transport shows a blank approver field - demonstrating the control never operated.
Affected Items (3)
  • DEVK900101 → PRD (imported by: JSMITH)
  • DEVK900103 → PRD (imported by: MWILSON)
  • DEVK900105 → PRD (imported by: LWANG)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the production import history (STMS_IMPORT import history / table records) and reconcile every prod import against an approval record. 2. Implement an enforced approval gate: activate the STMS QA Approval Procedure on the pre-prod system, or adopt SAP Change Request Management (ChaRM) in Solution Manager / SAP Cloud ALM so imports require a released, approved change document. 3. Define the approval RACI: change owner + technical approver (four-eyes) must sign off before any production import. 4. Restrict production import authorization (S_CTS_ADMI import functions, STMS import) to a named Basis group that operates only against approved changes. 5. For the existing unapproved imports, perform retroactive review: validate each change is legitimate, and document a formal after-the-fact approval or raise an exception. 6. Enable/verify the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG) and transport logging so future imports are traceable to a user and time. 7. Verify the control by test: attempt a production import of a request that has no approval and confirm it is blocked/queued pending approval. 8. Establish an emergency-change (break-glass) process that still captures a post-hoc approval and review, so 'urgent' is not a bypass. 9. Roll out with Basis and, under RISE, coordinate with SAP ECS for any TMS domain configuration change. 10. Report residual unapproved imports and the remediation to the GRC/audit owner as evidence the gap is closed.
References
  • ITIL Change Management — Approval Process
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Transport Approval Controls
HIGH P3 · 42 Transports released and imported by the same user CODE-TMS-003 ▶
Security Risk
One or more transports were both released (in the source system) and imported (into the target/production system) by the same user. This violates the maker-checker / four-eyes principle and segregation of duties: the person who authors and releases a change must not also be the person who promotes it to production. When one identity controls both ends, there is no independent verification between development and go-live. The danger is that a single actor can unilaterally push their own change into production. Combined with any authoring capability, this lets a developer bypass review entirely - the exact condition that enables insider fraud and sabotage, because the same person defines the change, releases it, and lands it live. Attack/abuse scenario: a developer with both release authorization and production-import authorization crafts a transport that, for example, raises their own approval limit, adds a critical authorization to their role, or plants a backdoor, then releases and imports it themselves within minutes - no other human ever sees it. Business impact: a textbook SOX segregation-of-duties deficiency, high fraud/insider-threat exposure, and failure of the change-management control that auditors specifically test. A real incident looks like a production change where the STMS release user and import user are identical and no third party reviewed it, undermining non-repudiation and control assurance.
Affected Items (3)
  • DEVK900101 → PRD — released and imported by: JSMITH
  • DEVK900103 → PRD — released and imported by: MWILSON
  • DEVK900105 → PRD — released and imported by: LWANG
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the transport history, list all requests where the release user equals the import user for production targets and treat them as SoD exceptions to review. 2. Separate the roles: developers hold release authorization in DEV (S_TRANSPRT) but must NOT hold production import authorization; Basis operators hold import authorization (S_CTS_ADMI import functions) but do not develop/release. 3. Review PFCG roles (transaction PFCG) and remove the combination of transport-release and production-import authorizations from any single role/user; use SUIM/RSUSR008_009_NEW to detect the toxic combination. 4. Enforce technically via the STMS QA Approval Procedure and/or ChaRM so the importer/approver must differ from the releaser. 5. For the flagged historical transports, validate each change was legitimate and document compensating review; escalate anything suspicious. 6. Restrict who can perform STMS imports to a named operations team, and log imports via the Security Audit Log. 7. Verify by testing that a user who released a transport cannot also import it into production (import is blocked or requires a different approver). 8. Re-run the SoD/critical-combination report to confirm no user retains both capabilities. 9. Coordinate role changes with the authorization team and communicate the new release/import responsibilities to developers and Basis. 10. Report the closed exceptions and the enforced control to GRC/audit as evidence.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Transport SoD Controls
HIGH P3 · 42 Security Audit Log is not enabled (rsau/enable = 0) LOG-AUD-010 ▶
Security Risk
Profile parameter rsau/enable = 0, so the Security Audit Log (SM20/RSAU) records NOTHING regardless of how the audit filters (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG) are configured. A system can therefore look 'audited' — filters defined for logons, RFC calls, transaction starts — while capturing zero events, leaving no forensic trail for incident response and no evidence for SOX/ISO logging controls.
Affected Items (1)
  • rsau/enable = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
Set rsau/enable = 1 (activate on the next restart) or activate dynamically via RSAU_CONFIG 'Kernel Parameters', and confirm the audit filters are active. Verify events appear in SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG.
References
  • SAP Note 2191612 — Audit log parameters (rsau/*)
  • SAP Security Baseline — Security Audit Log activation
  • SOX ITGC / ISO 27001 A.12.4 — event logging
HIGH P3 · 42 Critical tables without change logging enabled LOG-TBL-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding means one or more critical tables lack change logging. The module's list covers the crown jewels: user master and authorization (USR02, USR04, USR21, AGR_USERS, AGR_DEFINE, AGR_1251), RFC destinations (RFCDES), authorization customizing (PRGN_CUST), client control (T000 - which holds the production client change-protection flags), transport configuration (TMSPCONF, TADIR, E070, E071), HR/payroll master including bank data (PA0000, PA0001, PA0002, PA0008), customer and vendor master with bank details (KNA1, LFA1), and financial documents (BKPF, BSEG). Table change logging requires two things: the profile parameter rec/client set to log the relevant client(s), and the 'Log Data Changes' flag on each table in SE13. If either is missing, direct changes - via SE16N, debugger replace, an RFC/BAPI, or backend SQL - leave no change-document trail in DBTABLOG. Classic fraud scenario: an attacker or malicious insider with S_TABU_DIS edits vendor bank details in LFA1 via SE16N, triggers an F110 payment run to their own account, then reverts the field - completely invisible without table logging. Equally severe: flipping T000 to open the production client for changes, or editing RFCDES to repoint a trusted RFC destination at an attacker-controlled system for lateral movement. Business and compliance impact: SOX IT general controls over master-data and security changes fail without this trail; GDPR integrity/accountability is undermined; auditors will raise a finding. A real incident is a payment-fraud loss that cannot be traced because the master-data change was never logged.
Affected Items (16)
  • USR04
  • USR21
  • AGR_DEFINE
  • AGR_1251
  • PRGN_CUST
  • TMSPCONF
  • PA0000
  • PA0001
  • PA0002
  • PA0008
  • KNA1
  • LFA1
  • BSEG
  • TADIR
  • E070
  • E071
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Set the profile parameter rec/client in RZ10 to log the production client(s) - for example rec/client = <prod client> (or ALL to log every client). This activates client-dependent table logging and requires a restart. 2. For each critical table, open SE13 (Maintain Technical Settings) and enable the 'Log Data Changes' checkbox; many SAP standard tables ship with this on, so verify rather than assume. 3. Use SAP Note 112388 as the reference list of recommended tables to log and align your scope to it. 4. Reduce the underlying exposure by tightening direct table maintenance: restrict S_TABU_DIS / S_TABU_NAM and remove SE16N change access in production. 5. Verify which tables are logged with report RSTBHIST, and review actual changes via transaction SCU3 or report RSVTPROT (data stored in DBTABLOG). 6. Rollout caution: logging adds database writes, so enable it selectively on the critical tables rather than universally, test performance impact in a non-production system, and coordinate the restart required for rec/client with SAP RISE operations. Reference CIS SAP table-logging guidance and SAP Note 112388.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark 6.2 — Table Logging
  • SAP Note 2098872
HIGH P3 · 42 Table change logging master switch off (rec/client not set) LOG-TBL-010 ▶
Security Risk
Profile parameter rec/client is empty/OFF, so table change logging is disabled at the system level. Even for tables flagged 'log data changes' in DD09L (technical settings), NO change records are written to DBTABLOG. Customizing/config changes to sensitive tables therefore leave no audit trail — a SOX change-management gap and a blind spot the per-table logging check (LOG-TBL-001) cannot detect on its own.
Affected Items (1)
  • rec/client = (empty)
Remediation — Step by Step
Set rec/client to ALL (or the explicit list of productive/relevant clients, e.g. '100,200') in the instance profile and restart, so DD09L-flagged tables are logged to DBTABLOG. Confirm logging via SCU3 / RSTBHIST.
References

  • SOX ITGC — change logging of critical configuration tables

HIGH P3 · 42 Audit filter 'Report_Exec' is defined but switched off LREV-FLT-001 ▶
Security Risk
Audit filter 'Report_Exec' exists in the Security Audit Log configuration for event class 'report_start' but is not active, so no event of that class is being written. Somebody defined this filter deliberately and it is now off — which is a different situation from a class that was never configured, and a materially worse one: the configuration reads as though the class is covered. Any retrospective review of a window in which this filter was inactive cannot report on that class at all.
Affected Items (1)
  • Report_Exec: class=report_start, type=DYNAMIC, client=100, active=no
Remediation — Step by Step
Activate the filter in SM19 / RSAU_CONFIG, or delete it if the class is genuinely not required — an inactive filter left in place misrepresents the coverage of the whole configuration. Confirm events appear afterwards via SM20 / RSAU_READ_LOG.
References
  • SAP Note 2191612 — Security Audit Log
  • SAP Security Baseline — Security Audit Log configuration

Somebody defined this filter deliberately and it is now off — which is a different situation from a class that was never configured, and a materially worse one: the configuration reads as though the class is covered. Affected Items (1)
  • Table_Access_Filter: class=table_access, type=STATIC, client=100, active=no

Security Risk
3 of the 4 client(s) in this system are not covered by any active audit filter: 000, 200, 300. Nothing that happens in those clients is written to the Security Audit Log, so a retrospective review of any window can say nothing about them — including about the SAP-delivered default accounts, which reside in the technical clients rather than the production one. The active filters cover client(s) 100.
Affected Items (3)
  • Client 000: no active audit filter
  • Client 200: no active audit filter
  • Client 300: no active audit filter
Remediation — Step by Step
Set the client field of the audit filters to '*' so every client is recorded, or add an explicit active filter per client. Client 000 and any other technical client must be included — the SAP-delivered default accounts sign on there.

HIGH P3 · 42 TLS endpoints allowing deprecated protocol versions CRYPTO-TLS-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding means one or more ICM/Web Dispatcher HTTPS listeners still negotiate deprecated transport protocols (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSLv3 or SSLv2). In an S/4HANA RISE landscape these same ports carry the Fiori Launchpad, OData/REST APIs, SAP GUI for HTML (WebGUI), Web Dynpro, and RFC-over-HTTPS traffic, so the exposure is broad and Internet- or corporate-LAN-facing through the Web Dispatcher. The protocols themselves are cryptographically broken: TLS 1.0/1.1 CBC modes are exploitable via BEAST, SSLv3 via POODLE, and all of them rely on weak PRF/MAC constructions (MD5/SHA-1) that permit downgrade. The concrete attack: an on-path adversary (a compromised proxy, rogue Wi-Fi, malicious egress device, or an attacker who gained a foothold in the hyperscaler VPC or a jump host) forces the client-server handshake to downgrade to TLS 1.0, then runs a CBC padding-oracle/BEAST-style attack to recover bytes of the session. The prize is the SAP session material carried in cookies - the MYSAPSSO2 logon ticket, SAP_SESSIONID and CSRF token. Recovering these lets the attacker replay the victim's authenticated Fiori/WebGUI session and act as that user without ever knowing the password. Business impact is direct fraud and data breach: an impersonated finance user can approve a payment run or maintain bank details, and any personal data rendered in the session is exposed. Compliance impact is severe - PCI-DSS explicitly prohibits early TLS, and GDPR Art. 32 / SOX ITGC expect state-of-the-art transport encryption; an auditor who runs a TLS scan will flag this immediately. A real incident looks like a red-teamer on the internal network capturing the Fiori login, downgrading it, lifting the SSO ticket, and posting a fraudulent vendor payment that is only discovered at bank reconciliation.
Affected Items (1)
  • HTTPS_Default (port: 443) — protocol: TLSv1.0 TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In transaction RZ11 display the current values of ssl/ciphersuites (server side) and ssl/client_ciphersuites (client side) on every application server and the Web Dispatcher. 2. Per SAP Note 510007, the leading number encodes the enabled protocol versions - set it so only TLS 1.2 (and 1.3 where CommonCryptoLib supports it) is offered, e.g. ssl/ciphersuites = 135:PFS:HIGH::EC_P256:EC_HIGH and ssl/client_ciphersuites = 150:PFS:HIGH::EC_P256:EC_HIGH. 3. First confirm CommonCryptoLib is at least 8.5.x (TLS 1.2 needs 8.4.38+, TLS 1.3 needs newer) via SAP Note 1848999, upgrading it before you tighten protocols. 4. Persist the parameters in the instance profile using RZ10 (not just RZ11, which is runtime-only), for every instance including the Web Dispatcher (wdisp/ssl_... and the icm/server_port_ entries with SSL). 5. Activate by restarting the ICM in SMICM (Administration menu, hard/soft restart) or restarting the instance during a change window. 6. Verify with the SAP tool 'sapgenpse tlsinfo', and independently from a non-prod jump host with 'openssl s_client -connect host:44300 -tls1' (must fail) or testssl.sh. 7. Rollout caution: legacy Java clients, old middleware and outdated browsers may break - inventory interface partners and test in the sandbox/QA tiers first; coordinate with RFC and API interface owners before enforcing in production.
References
  • SAP Note 510007 — SSL/TLS Configuration
  • NIST SP 800-52 Rev 2
HIGH P3 · 42 TLS cipher suites include weak algorithms CRYPTO-TLS-002 ▶
Security Risk
Here the TLS listeners advertise cipher suites containing algorithms that are known-broken: RC4, DES, 3DES/CBC3, NULL, EXPORT-grade, and MD5/SHA-1-based suites. Even if the protocol version is TLS 1.2, the negotiated cipher determines the actual confidentiality, so a strong protocol with a weak cipher is still weak. Each algorithm carries a specific weakness: RC4 has keystream biases that leak plaintext over many captures; DES and 3DES are 64-bit-block ciphers vulnerable to the SWEET32 birthday attack; NULL provides no encryption at all (cleartext behind an https:// URL); EXPORT suites enable FREAK/Logjam downgrades to 512-bit keys; MD5 is collision-broken. The attack scenario: an on-path adversary either forces negotiation of the weakest mutually supported cipher or captures a long-lived TLS session (RFC-over-HTTPS or a bulk OData extract). Against 3DES they run SWEET32 - after roughly 2^32 blocks of a repeated secret (such as an auth cookie) the birthday collision recovers it. Against a NULL cipher they simply read the traffic. In RISE this matters because high-volume integration flows (IDoc/OData/API to SAP BTP, PI/PO, or third parties) create exactly the long, high-throughput sessions SWEET32 needs. Business impact: interception of credentials, SSO tokens and business/personal data, leading to session hijack, fraud and a reportable data breach. Compliance impact: PCI-DSS, NIST SP 800-52r2 and the SAP Security Baseline all forbid these ciphers; an external scan will flag the endpoint and jeopardise attestations. A realistic incident is a penetration test that decrypts a captured RFC/OData session over a weekend batch window and extracts HR or payment records from the plaintext.
Affected Items (1)
  • HTTPS_Default (port: 443) — weak cipher: RC4 in suite
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In RZ11 review ssl/ciphersuites and ssl/client_ciphersuites on all application servers and the Web Dispatcher/SAProuter. 2. Set the cipher profile to a hardened value that resolves to PFS + AES-GCM only and excludes weak suites, e.g. ssl/ciphersuites = 135:PFS:HIGH::EC_P256:EC_HIGH; the HIGH keyword already drops RC4, DES, NULL and EXPORT, and PFS enforces ECDHE/DHE key exchange (SAP Note 510007). 3. Explicitly ensure 3DES/CBC3 is not negotiable - prefer GCM suites; if backwards compatibility previously required 3DES, retire those legacy clients. 4. Upgrade CommonCryptoLib to the current 8.x first (SAP Note 1848999) so the strong suites are actually available. 5. Persist changes in RZ10 (instance/default profile) and restart the ICM via SMICM. 6. Verify the effective, negotiable list with 'sapgenpse tlsinfo', and confirm externally with 'nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 44300 host' or testssl.sh from a non-prod host - no weak cipher should appear. 7. Apply the identical hardening to the SAP Web Dispatcher and SAProuter, which terminate/forward the same traffic. 8. Rollout caution: validate in QA that all partner interfaces still negotiate an allowed suite before enforcing in production.
References
  • SAP Note 510007
  • Mozilla TLS Configuration Guide
HIGH P3 · 42 Certificates with weak key sizes or algorithms CRYPTO-CERT-003 ▶
Security Risk
Certificates in the trust store use cryptographically weak parameters - an RSA key smaller than 2048 bits, or a signature made with SHA-1 or MD5. These no longer meet NIST SP 800-131A or SAP Security Baseline requirements. The weaknesses are exploitable, not merely theoretical: RSA-1024 is within reach of well-resourced factoring; SHA-1 is broken by chosen-prefix collisions (the SHAttered/Chosen-Prefix attacks), which allow an attacker to craft two certificates with the same signature; and MD5 collisions were weaponised in the wild by the Flame malware to forge a Microsoft-signed certificate. The attack scenario: an adversary uses a collision to forge a certificate that the SAP trust store or an SNC/SSO partner will accept as valid, then presents it during a handshake to impersonate a legitimate server (or CA) and mount a man-in-the-middle - decrypting or silently altering RFC/OData/TLS traffic and harvesting credentials and SSO tickets. A weak own-key (small RSA) can also be brute-forced/factored offline from captured traffic to recover the private key and decrypt past sessions if forward secrecy was not used. There is an operational dimension too: modern browsers, Java runtimes and CommonCryptoLib increasingly reject SHA-1/weak-key certificates, so these will start breaking interfaces and Fiori access as clients are updated. Business impact: server impersonation, interception of business and personal data, forged trust, plus interoperability outages; NIST/PCI non-compliance and audit findings. A real incident: an interface partner tightens its TLS policy, the SAP-presented SHA-1 certificate is rejected, and during the scramble a forged-certificate MITM against the still-trusting SAP side goes undetected. Rated High.
Affected Items (4)
  • SSO_Signing_Cert (purpose: SSO) — key: 1024 bits
  • SSO_Signing_Cert (purpose: SSO) — algorithm: SHA1withRSA
  • Test_Cert (purpose: Testing) — key: 512 bits
  • Test_Cert (purpose: Testing) — algorithm: MD5withRSA
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In STRUST review each PSE and note the key length and signature algorithm columns to pinpoint sub-2048-bit keys and SHA-1/MD5-signed certificates. 2. Re-key rather than just re-sign: in STRUST create a new PSE/CSR with an RSA key of at least 2048 bits (or ECDSA P-256/P-384) and request the CA to issue with a SHA-256 (or stronger) signature. 3. Import the new signed certificate, replace the weak one in the PSE, and update the certificate list/CA chain accordingly. 4. Confirm CommonCryptoLib is a current 8.x version (SAP Note 1848999) so SHA-256 and modern key types are fully supported before rollout. 5. Restart the ICM via SMICM and verify in STRUST that the algorithm now shows SHA-256 and the key length is 2048+ (or the ECC curve). 6. Notify and update any partner systems that pinned the old certificate so trust is re-established on both sides. 7. Audit SNC and SSO/SAML signing certificates for the same weakness, not just the SSL server certificate. 8. Rollout caution: re-keying changes the certificate fingerprint - coordinate with interface owners and test in QA to avoid breaking pinned connections; schedule the ICM restart in a change window.
References
  • NIST SP 800-131A — Cryptographic Standards
HIGH P3 · 42 HANA data volume encryption is disabled CRYPTO-HANA-001 ▶
Security Risk
SAP HANA data volume encryption (encryption at rest for the persistence/data volumes) is disabled. That means the database's data pages - the entire S/4HANA business dataset including customer PII, HR/payroll data, financial records and pricing - are written to disk in cleartext, and by extension any data backup taken from those volumes is unencrypted unless separately protected. In a RISE deployment HANA runs on hyperscaler storage managed by SAP ECS; the realistic threat is not someone walking off with a server but a mis-scoped or over-shared storage snapshot, an exfiltrated backup file, a decommissioned/replaced disk that is not securely wiped, or an OS-level administrator or compromised infrastructure account reading the data files directly. In every one of these cases, disabled encryption turns a storage-layer exposure into a full database breach. Attack scenario: an adversary (or a negligent process) obtains a copy of the data volume or a backup - via a cloud storage misconfiguration, a leaked snapshot, or filesystem access on the HANA host - and simply opens the files or restores the backup to read the entire schema with no key required. Business impact is a mass data breach: GDPR Art. 32 mandates encryption of personal data at rest, and unencrypted HANA volumes fail SOX ITGC, ISO 27001 and customer contractual security clauses; the financial and reputational consequences of a full-database disclosure are severe. A real incident looks like a HANA backup copied to a shared bucket for a support case, later found to be world-readable, exposing the complete production dataset. Rated High because it exposes the crown-jewel data store and is a foundational at-rest control.
Affected Items (1)
  • Data volume encryption: disabled
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Connect to the HANA system database/tenant via hdbsql, HANA Cockpit or DBA Cockpit as a user holding the required system privilege (e.g. RESOURCE ADMIN / appropriate encryption privilege). 2. FIRST secure the root keys: HANA protects data/log root keys in the instance SSFS - ensure you have a current backup of the SSFS (and the system PKI SSFS) taken before and after any key change; back up the encryption root keys before enabling encryption. 3. Enable data volume encryption with: ALTER SYSTEM PERSISTENCE ENCRYPTION ON; (HANA uses AES-256 for the volumes). 4. Enable backup encryption as well so future backups are protected: ALTER SYSTEM BACKUP ENCRYPTION ON; and take fresh encrypted backups afterwards. 5. Verify with: SELECT * FROM M_ENCRYPTION_OVERVIEW WHERE NAME = 'DATA_VOLUME'; (and check M_PERSISTENCE_ENCRYPTION_STATUS) to confirm encryption is active and pages are converting. 6. Store the SSFS/root-key backups separately from the data backups so a single storage compromise cannot yield both ciphertext and keys. 7. Rollout caution: enabling encryption triggers a background re-encryption of existing pages with additional I/O - schedule during a low-load window and monitor performance. 8. In RISE, HANA is operated by SAP ECS - raise the encryption enablement and key-backup handling as a formal request and obtain confirmation of the resulting M_ENCRYPTION_OVERVIEW status.
References
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Data Volume Encryption
HIGH P3 · 42 HANA backup encryption is disabled CRYPTO-HANA-004 ▶
Security Risk
HANA backup (data backup) encryption is not enabled. Backup encryption is configured and keyed independently of data-volume encryption at rest, so enabling volume encryption does NOT imply backups are encrypted. In a RISE/hyperscaler deployment, complete data and log backups are written to object storage; if those backups are unencrypted, anyone who obtains a copy — via mis-scoped storage permissions, a snapshot, a support dump, or the hosting provider's operational staff — can restore the full database on an attacker- controlled system and read every record offline, entirely outside the source system's authorization and audit controls. This is one of the highest-impact and most frequently overlooked HANA data-at-rest gaps.
Affected Items (1)
  • Backup encryption: disabled
Remediation — Step by Step
Enable backup encryption: ALTER SYSTEM BACKUP ENCRYPTION ON; (or via the cockpit Data Encryption page). This requires that a backup encryption root key already exists — if not, first run ALTER SYSTEM SET ENCRYPTION ROOT KEYS BACKUP PASSWORD "<passphrase>" (privilege ENCRYPTION KEY ADMIN). Confirm the backup encryption root key has been created and backed up to a secure location separate from the backups themselves — losing the key makes encrypted backups unrecoverable. Re-run a full data backup after enabling so a usable encrypted baseline exists, and verify that both data and log backups report as encrypted. Reconcile this with the data-volume and log-volume encryption settings so all three at-rest scopes are protected consistently.
References
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Backup Encryption
  • SAP HANA Administration Guide — Data and Log Backup Encryption
HIGH P3 · 42 HANA system replication is not TLS-encrypted CRYPTO-HANA-005 ▶
Security Risk
global.ini [system_replication_communication] enable_ssl = false while system replication is configured.
