HANA system replication continuously streams the primary's redo log — i.e. the complete change data of the database, including every inserted and updated business record — to the secondary site. With TLS disabled this replication stream crosses the network in clear text, so an attacker positioned between the primary and secondary (a particular concern for cross-datacentre or cross-zone replication in a hosted RISE landscape) can passively reconstruct the entire dataset or tamper with the stream, without ever authenticating to either database.
Affected Items (1)
  • [system_replication_communication] enable_ssl = false
Remediation — Step by Step
Enable TLS for system replication: set [system_replication_communication] enable_ssl = true on both primary and secondary, provision the system-PKI (or enterprise) certificates used for internal communication, and restart replication. Verify the replication status returns to ACTIVE and that the hand-shake uses TLS. Enforce this together with sslenforce for SQL and the ICM HTTPS configuration so no HANA-facing channel remains in clear text.
References
  • SAP HANA Administration Guide — Secure System Replication (TLS)
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Secure Internal Communication
HIGH P3 · 42 Outdated SAP Crypto Library: sapcryptolib 5.5.5c CRYPTO-LIB-001 ▶
Security Risk
The SAP Crypto Library in use appears to be a pre-8.x version (the check flags a major version below 8), i.e. the legacy SAP Cryptographic Library (SAPCRYPTOLIB, e.g. the old 5.5.5 line) rather than the current CommonCryptoLib 8.x. This library is the single crypto engine underpinning TLS, SNC, Secure Store and Forward (SSF) and X.509 handling across the ABAP stack, so its version gates the security of everything above it. Older versions lack support for current TLS standards and strong cipher suites - TLS 1.2 interoperability requires at least CommonCryptoLib 8.4.38 (8.4.49+ recommended), and TLS 1.3 needs newer still - so a pre-8.x library forces the system to fall back to deprecated protocols and weak ciphers regardless of profile settings, directly enabling the downgrade/interception attacks described in the TLS findings. Beyond missing features, superseded crypto libraries accumulate known vulnerabilities and stop receiving security fixes; a flaw in the library (in certificate parsing, cipher handling, or key management) can lead to memory corruption, authentication bypass or crypto downgrade that an attacker triggers via a crafted TLS/SNC handshake. Practical impact in RISE: the SAP support backbone and many BTP/partner endpoints now mandate TLS 1.2+, so an outdated library breaks connectivity and support tooling while simultaneously leaving external-facing services on weak crypto. Attack scenario: an on-path attacker negotiates a downgraded, weak session that the outdated library still accepts, then exploits the weak cipher/protocol (or a library CVE) to intercept credentials and business data. Business impact: broad exposure of TLS/SNC/SSF, interface and support outages, and audit findings for running unsupported cryptographic software. Rated High because the library is a landscape-wide crypto dependency and its weakness undermines multiple other controls.
Affected Items (1)
  • sapcryptolib 5.5.5c at /usr/sap/PRD/SYS/exe/run/
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Determine the current version on every application server: run 'sapgenpse -v' (or check disp+work output / STRUST environment) and compare against SAP Note 1848999, the central note for CommonCryptoLib 8. 2. Download the latest CommonCryptoLib 8.x (component SAPCRYPTOLIBP) from the SAP Software Center / Support Portal for the correct OS and platform. 3. Deploy it per SAP Note 1848999 - replace the library in the kernel directory (DIR_EXECUTABLE / the instance's exe path) on all application servers, or update it as part of a kernel update via SUM; ensure the kernel patch level is compatible. 4. Update the library on adjacent components too where present: SAP Web Dispatcher, SAProuter, and the host agent. 5. Restart the instances and verify the new version with 'sapgenpse -v' and by confirming crypto functions load without errors in the work process/dev traces. 6. Only after the library is current, tighten ssl/ciphersuites/ssl/client_ciphersuites to enforce TLS 1.2/1.3 and strong ciphers (SAP Note 510007), which the new library now supports. 7. Verify TLS behaviour with 'sapgenpse tlsinfo' and an external scan to confirm strong protocols/ciphers are now negotiable. 8. Rollout caution: apply in a non-production system first and confirm SNC, SSL and SSF interfaces still function, since the library affects many services; schedule the kernel/library swap and restart in a coordinated change window.
References
  • SAP Note 1848999 — CommonCryptoLib Updates
HIGH P3 · 42 PSE files with errors or expired certificates CRYPTO-PSE-001 ▶
Security Risk
One or more Personal Security Environment (PSE) files are in an error/invalid/corrupted state or contain an expired certificate. A PSE is the SAP container that stores a private key together with its certificate and trust list; distinct PSEs underpin the SSL server (SAPSSLS), SSL client (SAPSSLA/SAPSSLC), SNC (SAPSNCS), and the SSO/SAML and system-PKI functions. A broken PSE therefore directly disables whatever secure channel it serves. The immediate effect is failure of encrypted communication - HTTPS/Fiori, RFC/OData over TLS, SNC-based single sign-on, or internal PKI trust - producing outages very similar to expired certificates, along with the same temptation to apply insecure workarounds (accept-any-cert, disabling SNC/validation) to restore service. A particularly common and dangerous cause is a system copy or migration: the target inherits the source system's PSE (and thus its private keys and identity). This is both an integrity problem (the system presents the wrong identity) and a key-management problem (the private key now exists in two systems), and administrators under pressure may keep using it rather than regenerating. Threat scenario: because a corrupted/expired PSE breaks trust, clients get conditioned to bypass warnings, and an attacker in an on-path position presents a substitute certificate that the now-permissive clients accept, enabling man-in-the-middle interception of credentials and data. If a source-system PSE/private key is reused across environments, compromise of one system's key compromises the others. Business impact: outage of secured services, MITM exposure via insecure workarounds, and potential cross-environment key compromise; auditors flag invalid PSEs and shared keys as PKI hygiene failures. A real incident: after a production-to-QA copy, the SNC PSE from production is left active, so QA presents production's identity and shares its private key. Rated High.
Affected Items (5)
  • SAPSSLS.pse (SSL Server) — PSE certificate expired: 2025-05-15
  • SAPSNCSSLS.pse (SNC) — PSE certificate expired: 2025-04-01
  • SAPSSOC.pse (SSO) — status: EXPIRED
  • SAPSSOC.pse (SSO) — PSE certificate expired: 2024-11-30
  • SAPSPSE.pse (System) — PSE certificate expired: 2026-01-01
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In STRUST inspect each PSE node (SSL server, SSL client, SNC, SSO/SAML, system PKI) and note any showing an error/invalid/corrupted status or an expired embedded certificate. 2. For a repairable PSE, renew the certificate within it: create a fresh CSR in STRUST, obtain the CA-signed certificate, and import it into that PSE node. 3. For a corrupted or wrong-identity PSE, recreate it: replace/create the PSE with a new key pair and the correct Distinguished Name, then request and import a new certificate. 4. After any system copy/migration, regenerate the SSL and SNC PSEs on the target so source-system private keys and identities are never reused - do not carry PSEs across environments. 5. Restart the ICM via SMICM (and reconfigure SNC as needed) so the repaired PSEs are loaded. 6. Verify in STRUST that each PSE now shows a valid status and correct certificate, and validate a live handshake for each affected service (Fiori HTTPS, an RFC/OData interface, and SNC GUI logon). 7. Take secure, access-controlled backups of the repaired PSEs and use sapgenpse to confirm PSE integrity. 8. Rollout caution: schedule the ICM restart in a change window, and remove any accept-any-cert / disabled-validation workarounds that were introduced while the PSE was broken; test in QA first.
References
  • SAP STRUST — PSE Management
HIGH P3 · 42 DB users with password lifetime check disabled HANADB-USER-002 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that one or more non-technical HANA users have IS_PASSWORD_LIFETIME_CHECK_ENABLED set to FALSE, so their password never expires. This flag is set with ALTER USER ... DISABLE PASSWORD LIFETIME and is legitimately used for a narrow set of technical/interface users, but it is frequently applied to human accounts too, or copied when cloning users. A never-expiring password removes the natural forcing function to rotate credentials: a password leaked years ago in a breach dump, a screenshot, a decommissioned laptop, or a script remains valid indefinitely. Attack scenario: an adversary who obtained the credential from an old backup, a phished helpdesk interaction, or a compromised admin workstation can reuse it long after the fact; the absence of expiry also defeats the common incident-response assumption that a stale password would have changed by now. Combined with a weak password policy, static long-lived passwords are highly susceptible to offline cracking and credential stuffing against the SQL port. Business and compliance impact: it violates password-rotation requirements in SOX ITGC and ISO 27001 A.9 and most internal standards, and it enables persistent unauthorized access to the S/4HANA data layer. A real incident looks like a former contractor's DB login still working months after departure because the password never expired and dormancy monitoring missed the account.
Affected Items (1)
  • SVC_INTERFACE — password lifetime check: disabled
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List offenders: SELECT USER_NAME, IS_PASSWORD_LIFETIME_CHECK_ENABLED FROM SYS.USERS WHERE IS_PASSWORD_LIFETIME_CHECK_ENABLED='FALSE'; (or SAP HANA Cockpit -> User Management). 2. Classify each account: genuine technical/interface user (SSO, X.509, or hdbuserstore based) versus interactive human. 3. For interactive/human users, enable expiry: ALTER USER <user> ENABLE PASSWORD LIFETIME; 4. Ensure a bounded maximum_password_lifetime is set in the [password policy] section (see HANADB-PARAM-001) so that 'enabled' actually forces rotation. 5. For true technical users that must not expire, migrate authentication to X.509 certificate, SAML, Kerberos, or Secure User Store (hdbuserstore) keys, and record the exception in a risk register instead of leaving a password-based login immortal. 6. Verify: re-run the SYS.USERS query; the flag should read TRUE for every human user. 7. Rollout caution: enabling lifetime on an account whose password is already older than the maximum lifetime forces an immediate change - schedule this for interface users, coordinate with the interface owner to avoid a lockout during batch windows, and test in non-production. 8. Add this control to a recurring least-privilege/user review so it does not regress.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Password lifetime
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Password Policy
HIGH P3 · 42 Broad system privileges granted directly to users HANADB-PRIV-003 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that powerful, though not 'keys to the kingdom', system privileges are granted directly to users rather than via roles: CATALOG READ, BACKUP ADMIN, TRACE ADMIN, IMPORT, EXPORT, and the RESOURCE/SERVICE/SESSION/MONITOR/TABLE/LOG/SAVEPOINT ADMIN family. Each still enables meaningful abuse. CATALOG READ exposes all metadata - schemas, table and column names, user and role structures - which is precisely the reconnaissance an attacker needs to plan a targeted attack. EXPORT and IMPORT can move whole tables out of or into the database, a direct data-exfiltration and data-tampering vector. BACKUP ADMIN can trigger or redirect backups. TRACE ADMIN can enable verbose traces that may capture sensitive data in trace files and can fill disks to cause a denial of service. As with the critical set, direct grants undermine reviewability and least privilege. Attack scenario: a compromised account holding EXPORT dumps sensitive tables to a filesystem location and exfiltrates them, or CATALOG READ is used to map the schema before a focused attack on the highest-value tables. Business and compliance impact: data exposure, reconnaissance enablement, potential DoS via traces, and SoD/audit findings. A real incident looks like an interface account that accumulated EXPORT and CATALOG READ across successive projects being used to bulk-export a customer master table.
Affected Items (2)
  • DBADMIN ← BACKUP ADMIN
  • CONTRACTOR1 ← TRACE ADMIN
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate: SELECT GRANTEE, PRIVILEGE FROM GRANTED_PRIVILEGES WHERE GRANTEE_TYPE='USER' AND PRIVILEGE IN ('CATALOG READ','BACKUP ADMIN','TRACE ADMIN','IMPORT','EXPORT','RESOURCE ADMIN','SERVICE ADMIN','SESSION ADMIN','MONITOR ADMIN','TABLE ADMIN','LOG ADMIN','SAVEPOINT ADMIN'); 2. Justify each grant against the user's actual role and remove any that cannot be justified. 3. Consolidate the genuinely needed privileges into purpose-built roles (e.g. a monitoring role, a backup-operator role) and grant the role: GRANT <role> TO <user>; then REVOKE <priv> FROM <user>; 4. Restrict EXPORT and IMPORT especially tightly and enable an audit policy so their use is logged and alerted. 5. Verify: re-run the query - direct grants should be replaced by role-based access - and confirm via EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGES that required tasks still work. 6. Periodically re-review these roles as part of the access-recertification cycle. 7. Rollout caution: monitoring and backup tooling often depends on these privileges - identify the tool service accounts, migrate them to roles first, test in non-production, and coordinate with the operations team before revoking.
References
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — System Privileges
HIGH P3 · 42 Powerful predefined roles granted to users HANADB-ROLE-001 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that broadly powerful predefined or repository roles are granted to end users: CONTENT_ADMIN, MODELING, MONITORING, SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT, and any role ending in ADMIN or containing SUPPORT. Each over-provisions the user well beyond normal needs. CONTENT_ADMIN carries wide privileges over activated repository content and historically includes the ability to grant and revoke activated analytic privileges; MODELING typically brings _SYS_BI_CP_ALL and full modeling rights (and therefore the analytic-privilege bypass); SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT exposes internal, largely undocumented system views intended only for SAP support staff during an active incident and must never be a standing grant. Attack scenario: a user with CONTENT_ADMIN or MODELING manipulates modeled content or effectively grants themselves broad data access, while a standing SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT grant on a compromised account hands an attacker rich internal reconnaissance and capabilities beyond any normal role. Business and compliance impact: privilege escalation, data exposure, and audit findings - SAP explicitly documents SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT as temporary-only, so a standing grant is a clear control failure. A real incident looks like SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT being granted during a support case and never revoked, so months later that account is used to browse internal system state and pivot deeper into the platform.
Affected Items (3)
  • J_SMITH ← role CONTENT_ADMIN
  • CONTRACTOR1 ← role SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT
  • DBADMIN ← role MONITORING
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List grants: SELECT GRANTEE, ROLE_NAME FROM GRANTED_ROLES WHERE ROLE_NAME IN ('CONTENT_ADMIN','MODELING','MONITORING','SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT') OR ROLE_NAME LIKE '%ADMIN' OR ROLE_NAME LIKE '%SUPPORT'; 2. Treat SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT first - it should have zero standing grantees; revoke: REVOKE SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT FROM <user>; 3. For CONTENT_ADMIN and MODELING, confirm the user genuinely performs modeling/content activation; move day-to-day users onto narrower, task-specific custom roles. 4. Where a broad role is truly needed, grant it to the minimum set of users and time-box it (revoke after the task or support case closes). 5. Prefer building custom least-privilege roles over granting the powerful predefined ones. 6. Verify: re-run the GRANTED_ROLES query (SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT shows no grantees, the others only justified ones) and check EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGES for residual _SYS_BI_CP_ALL inherited via MODELING. 7. Enable an audit policy that logs grants of these roles so future standing grants are detected. 8. Rollout caution: revoking MODELING or CONTENT_ADMIN can break a developer's activation workflow - coordinate with the modeling team and test in non-production before removing.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — SAP_INTERNAL_HANA_SUPPORT
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Predefined Roles
HIGH P3 · 42 Audit trail written to CSV text file (tamperable) HANADB-AUDIT-002 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that the audit trail target (default_audit_trail_type or emergency_audit_trail_type) is set to CSVTEXTFILE. A CSV file audit trail is written to the operating-system filesystem and is not protected by the database, so anyone with OS or file access - a Basis admin, a compromised OS account, a backup operator - can read it (exposing the sensitive data captured in audit records) or modify and delete it to erase evidence of malicious activity. SAP explicitly documents CSVTEXTFILE (and KERNELTRACE) as unsuitable for production; only SYSLOGPROTOCOL and CSTABLE provide adequate protection and reliability. Attack scenario: an adversary who gains OS-level access after compromising the database simply edits or truncates the CSV audit files to cover their tracks, defeating the entire purpose of auditing; alternatively they read the audit CSV to harvest information such as statements containing literal values. Business and compliance impact: audit integrity is broken - the logs are neither tamper-evident nor access-controlled - which fails the log-integrity requirements of SOX and ISO 27001 and undermines any forensic investigation. A real incident looks like an investigation after a breach discovering that the CSV audit files were altered or that the relevant rows are missing, so the logs cannot be trusted or used as evidence.
Affected Items (1)
  • default_audit_trail_type = CSVTEXTFILE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the target: SELECT * FROM M_INIFILE_CONTENTS WHERE KEY IN ('default_audit_trail_type','emergency_audit_trail_type','critical_audit_trail_type'); 2. Choose a protected target: SYSLOGPROTOCOL (forwarded to a write-once/SIEM-protected syslog) is preferred; CSTABLE (an internal DB table queryable via the AUDIT_LOG view) is acceptable for local storage. 3. Set it: ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini','SYSTEM') SET ('auditing configuration','default_audit_trail_type')='SYSLOGPROTOCOL' WITH RECONFIGURE; and repeat for emergency_audit_trail_type. 4. If using SYSLOGPROTOCOL, harden the OS syslog and forward it off-box so a DB or OS compromise cannot erase it; if using CSTABLE, restrict access to the audit table. 5. Retain any existing CSV audit content per the retention policy, then stop writing CSVTEXTFILE. 6. Verify: re-query M_INIFILE_CONTENTS for the new value, then generate a test audit event and confirm it lands in syslog or CSTABLE. 7. Rollout caution: ensure the syslog pipeline (rsyslog/SIEM collector) is in place before switching, or events could be dropped; coordinate with the SIEM/OS team and, in RISE, with SAP ECS, and test in non-production.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Audit trail target
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Audit Trail Targets
HIGH P3 · 42 Weak HANA password-policy parameters HANADB-PARAM-001 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that one or more [password policy] parameters are weaker than recommended. minimal_password_length below 8 makes passwords far easier to brute-force or crack offline. force_first_password_change = false means initial or admin-set passwords stay in use, so provisioning-time or default passwords persist and may be widely known. maximum_invalid_connect_attempts above 6 weakens lockout, giving brute-force and password-spraying attackers more attempts before an account locks. maximum_password_lifetime above 365 days (or unset) lets passwords live too long, extending the window during which a leaked credential remains valid. Together these make DB-authenticated accounts materially easier to compromise. Attack scenario: an adversary sprays common passwords against the HANA SQL port or a reporting user; with a high lockout threshold and a short minimum length the odds of success rise sharply, and if force_first_password_change is off an account still using its provisioning password is trivially guessed. Business and compliance impact: unauthorized DB access to S/4HANA data and failure to meet SOX, ISO 27001 A.9, and enterprise password standards. A real incident looks like a service or reporting account with a 6-character, never-forced-change, never-expiring password being cracked and used to reach the database.
Affected Items (4)
  • minimal_password_length = 6 (recommend ≥ 8)
  • force_first_password_change = false (initial passwords not forced to change)
  • maximum_invalid_connect_attempts = 10 (recommend ≤ 6)
  • maximum_password_lifetime = 730d (recommend ≤ 365)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review current values: SELECT KEY, VALUE FROM M_INIFILE_CONTENTS WHERE FILE_NAME='indexserver.ini' AND SECTION='password policy'; (use nameserver.ini for the system DB), or SAP HANA Cockpit -> Security -> Password Policy. 2. Set minimal_password_length >= 8 (align with the enterprise standard, e.g. 10-12): ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('indexserver.ini','SYSTEM') SET ('password policy','minimal_password_length')='10' WITH RECONFIGURE; 3. Set force_first_password_change = true using the same statement pattern. 4. Set maximum_invalid_connect_attempts to a value <= 6 (e.g. 5) and confirm password_lock_time is set (default 1440 minutes / 24h). 5. Set a bounded maximum_password_lifetime (<= 365, commonly 90-180) and consider last_used_passwords and minimum_password_lifetime to prevent immediate reuse. 6. Also review password_layout and complexity requirements per your standard. 7. Verify: re-query M_INIFILE_CONTENTS for the new values, then create a throwaway user to confirm the policy is enforced and drop it. 8. Rollout caution: tightening lifetime or length can force mass password changes and affect technical accounts on next login - communicate to users, schedule around batch windows, migrate technical users to certificate/SSO, test in non-production, and in RISE coordinate with SAP ECS.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Password policy
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Password Policy Parameters
HIGH P3 · 42 TLS not enforced for HANA SQL connections HANADB-PARAM-003 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that global.ini [communication] sslenforce is set to false, meaning the HANA SQL port (JDBC/ODBC, and the connection from the S/4HANA application server, SDI/DP agents, and analytics clients) will accept plaintext, non-TLS connections. Credentials and all query and result data - which for S/4HANA is effectively the entire business dataset, including financial and personal data - can then traverse the network unencrypted, exposing them to passive sniffing and active man-in-the-middle attacks by anyone positioned on the network path: a compromised host, a rogue admin, a hypervisor or network tap, or an attacker who has gained a foothold in the datacentre or VPC. This is separate from HTTPS/ICM TLS - it specifically governs the SQL layer. Attack scenario: an adversary on the same segment as the app server or a DB client captures the login handshake and subsequent SQL traffic, harvesting credentials and reading or altering data in transit; a MitM can even inject or modify statements. Business and compliance impact: a confidentiality and integrity breach of all SQL traffic, credential theft, and non-compliance with encryption-in-transit requirements (GDPR, PCI where in scope, and internal cryptography standards). A real incident looks like a network capture during an internal penetration test revealing HANA logon credentials and sensitive query results in cleartext because SQL TLS was not enforced.
Affected Items (1)
  • sslenforce = false
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value: SELECT * FROM M_INIFILE_CONTENTS WHERE FILE_NAME='global.ini' AND SECTION='communication' AND KEY='sslenforce'; 2. Ensure valid server certificates and the SSL key/trust stores are in place for the index/SQL server (in-database certificate collection or PSE) before enforcing. 3. Enforce TLS: ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini','SYSTEM') SET ('communication','sslenforce')='true' WITH RECONFIGURE; 4. Configure all SQL clients to use encryption - the S/4HANA secondary DB connection, JDBC (encrypt=true and validateCertificate as appropriate), ODBC, SDI/DP agents, and analytics tools. 5. Verify: re-query M_INIFILE_CONTENTS (value 'true'), attempt a non-TLS connection (should be refused) and a TLS connection (should succeed), and check M_CONNECTIONS for encrypted sessions. 6. Rollout caution: this is a breaking change - any client not configured for TLS will lose connectivity, including the app server and interfaces. Inventory every SQL client, roll out client-side TLS first, test end-to-end in non-production, and schedule a change window. 7. In RISE/PCE, SQL-layer TLS is typically SAP ECS-managed - coordinate via the RACI or a ticket rather than changing sslenforce unilaterally.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Enforce SSL for SQL
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Secure Client Communication
HIGH P3 · 42 HANA log_mode = overwrite (no point-in-time recovery) HANADB-PARAM-004 ▶
Security Risk
global.ini [persistence] log_mode = overwrite. In this mode HANA reuses redo-log segments after each savepoint instead of retaining them, so no log backups are produced and the database cannot be recovered to a point in time after the last complete data backup. Any corruption, ransomware event, or erroneous mass change that occurs after that backup is therefore unrecoverable, and the recovery-point objective collapses to the age of the last full/delta data backup. 'overwrite' is intended only for sandbox or bulk-loading systems and must never be used on production or any system whose data is subject to SOX/audit retention obligations.
Affected Items (1)
  • [persistence] log_mode = overwrite
Remediation — Step by Step
Set [persistence] log_mode = normal and restart the database. Take a full data backup immediately afterwards — log backups only begin once a data backup exists. Schedule automatic log backups (bound log_backup_timeout_s) to a secure, encrypted target, verify that log backups are actually being written, and perform a test recovery to confirm the point-in-time recovery chain is intact. Ensure backup encryption is enabled so the retained logs are protected at rest.
References
  • SAP HANA Administration Guide — Log Modes
  • SAP HANA Administration Guide — Backup and Recovery
HIGH P3 · 42 Debug privileges (DEBUG / ATTACH DEBUGGER) granted to users HANADB-PRIV-006 ▶
Security Risk
2 grant(s) of the DEBUG or ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege were found. These privileges let a user attach the SQLScript debugger to procedures or to another user's sessions, single-step through server-side logic and inspect the live values of every variable and intermediate result — including data the debugged code reads from protected tables. ATTACH DEBUGGER in particular can expose the runtime data of another user's session, bypassing analytic-privilege and authorization filtering that would normally restrict what that data consumer can see. On a production database these privileges are almost never legitimate and are a strong candidate for both data exfiltration and logic tampering.
Affected Items (2)
  • CONTRACTOR1 ← DEBUG ON ZFI_PAYMENT_RUN
  • J_SMITH ← ATTACH DEBUGGER ON DBADMIN
Remediation — Step by Step
Revoke DEBUG and ATTACH DEBUGGER from all users on production: REVOKE DEBUG ON <object> FROM <user>; and revoke ATTACH DEBUGGER accordingly. Perform SQLScript debugging only in non-productive systems that do not contain real business data. If a break-glass debugging need arises in production, grant the privilege through a firefighter/EAM session that is time-boxed, logged and reviewed, and revoke it immediately afterwards.
References
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Debugging Privileges
  • SAP HANA SQLScript Reference — Debugging
HIGH P3 · 42 Generic table write via S_TABU_NAM (TABLE = *) AUTH-007 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_TABU_NAM with TABLE='*' and ACTVT=02 (change). S_TABU_NAM authorizes table maintenance by explicit table/view name and was introduced by SAP Note 1481950 as the finer-grained companion to S_TABU_DIS; it is evaluated when the classic S_TABU_DIS (authorization-group) check does not already grant access. With TABLE='*' and change activity, the role grants direct write access to virtually every table in the system through generic maintenance tools such as SE16N, SM30/SM31 and table-view maintenance — completely bypassing the table authorization-group concept that is supposed to compartmentalize sensitive data. This means a holder can directly edit configuration and master/transactional tables without going through the application transactions that enforce business validation, workflow and change documents. Concrete abuse in S/4HANA production: change the contents of finance/customizing tables, alter a user's data, tamper with control tables that govern postings or number ranges, or modify security-relevant tables — all with no business-level audit trail and no four-eyes. This is a severe SoD and data-integrity risk and a direct ITGC/SOX finding because it lets someone circumvent every application control by writing straight to the persistence layer. A real incident looks like altered table rows with no corresponding change document or transaction log, discovered during reconciliation or a table-logging review, where the entry point was a generic table-maintenance transaction rather than the owning business transaction. Broad direct table write is a classic auditor red flag.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_TABLE_ADMIN — 1 user(s) [BATCH1] — S_TABU_NAM TABLE=*, ACTVT=02
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_TABU_NAM with TABLE='*' and ACTVT=02; list roles and holders. 2. Determine which tables the role legitimately maintains (trace with STAUTHTRACE over a business cycle) and, in PFCG, replace TABLE='*' with those specific table/view names. 3. Prefer display (ACTVT 03) over change (ACTVT 02); grant change only where a documented business need exists and no owning application transaction is available. 4. Ensure sensitive tables carry a proper table authorization group (maintain via SE54 -> Assign authorization group; the mapping lives in table TDDAT) so that both S_TABU_DIS and S_TABU_NAM checks are meaningful. 5. Use report SU24_S_TABU_NAM / SU24 to align default values when introducing name-based table authorizations. 6. Enable table change logging (rec/client parameter and the 'log data changes' flag in SE13/technical settings) for critical tables so any direct edits are recorded (review via SCU3). 7. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm the wildcard is gone from assigned roles. 8. Verify: with a test user, attempt SE16N change on an unauthorized table and confirm refusal (SU53). 9. Rollout caution: some teams genuinely maintain config via SM30 — inventory those needs first, test in QA, and provide the scoped table list before removing the wildcard.
References
  • SAP Note 1481950 — S_TABU_NAM
  • SAP Help — Table authorizations
HIGH P3 · 42 Generic table maintenance via S_TABU_DIS (all / no auth group) AUTH-008 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_TABU_DIS with change activity (ACTVT=02) for authorization group '*' or '&NC&'. S_TABU_DIS is the classic table-maintenance authorization that works at the level of table authorization GROUPS: each table is assigned a group and the object grants access to all tables in the granted group(s). Granting group '*' means change access to tables of every authorization group; granting '&NC&' means change access to all tables that have NO authorization group assigned — and in practice a very large number of standard and custom tables carry no group, so '&NC&' with change is nearly as broad as '*'. Either way this is sweeping direct table-maintenance access to most sensitive customizing and master-data tables via SM30/SM31/SE16N, bypassing the business transactions and their controls. In an S/4HANA production client this lets a holder edit configuration and master data directly at the persistence layer without application validation, workflow or reliable change documents — the same integrity and SoD exposure as AUTH-007 but reached through the group mechanism. The '&NC&' case is especially insidious because it is easy to grant 'by accident' (it looks narrow) yet effectively covers the long tail of ungrouped tables, including many custom Z-tables that hold sensitive data. A real incident looks like unauthorized changes to control or master tables with no matching application audit trail, surfaced only through table logging or reconciliation, where the offender used a generic maintenance transaction and their access rode on a broad or ungrouped S_TABU_DIS. Auditors treat '*'/'&NC&' with change as a critical table-authorization finding.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_TABLE_ADMIN — 1 user(s) [BATCH1] — S_TABU_DIS DICBERCLS=&NC&, ACTVT=02
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_TABU_DIS with DICBERCLS='*' or '&NC&' and ACTVT=02; list roles and holders. 2. Assign proper authorization groups to sensitive tables that currently have none: use SE54 -> Assign authorization group (mapping stored in table TDDAT); this removes tables from the '&NC&' catch-all. 3. In PFCG, replace DICBERCLS='*'/'&NC&' with the specific, narrow authorization group(s) the role must maintain, and prefer display (03) over change (02). 4. Where finer control is needed than groups allow, complement with name-based S_TABU_NAM for individual tables rather than widening the group. 5. Use STAUTHTRACE to confirm which groups/tables the role really needs before narrowing. 6. Enable change logging for critical tables (rec/client + SE13 log flag) and review via SCU3. 7. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no assigned role keeps '*'/'&NC&' with change. 8. Verify: with a test user, attempt to maintain a table outside the granted group and confirm refusal (SU53). 9. Rollout caution: reassigning authorization groups affects everyone who relied on the old grouping — inventory current maintenance, do the SE54 changes in a transport, test in QA across a full cycle, and communicate to config owners.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_TABU_DIS
  • SAP Help — Table authorization groups
HIGH P3 · 42 Cross-client table maintenance (S_TABU_CLI) AUTH-009 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_TABU_CLI with CLIIDMAINT=X, which authorizes maintenance of client-INDEPENDENT (cross-client) tables. Normal table maintenance is client-specific, so changes affect only the current client; S_TABU_CLI is the additional gate required to change tables whose data is shared across all clients of the system — for example T000 (client table and its protection settings), and many technical/customizing tables that are cross-client by design. Because a single change to a cross-client table takes effect in every client on that system simultaneously, this authorization has system-wide blast radius. The most dangerous combination is S_TABU_CLI together with SCC4 (or S_TABU_* on T000): a holder can alter the client role and, critically, the client-change and cross-client customizing protection flags — turning a 'not modifiable / no changes allowed' production client into one that accepts customizing and repository changes, or opening cross-client customizing that was meant to be locked. That single move disables a fundamental production safeguard for the whole system, enabling further unauthorized changes that would otherwise be blocked. In an S/4HANA RISE production system this is a High-severity change-control and integrity risk and a clear ITGC finding, because production immutability depends on exactly these flags. A real incident looks like the production client's protection settings being flipped, followed by unexpected customizing/repository changes appearing directly in production — with the T000/SCC4 change being the enabling event. Cross-client maintenance must be confined to a very small, controlled administrator population.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_TABLE_ADMIN — 1 user(s) [BATCH1] — S_TABU_CLI CLIIDMAINT=X
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_TABU_CLI with CLIIDMAINT=X; correlate with who also holds SCC4 and broad S_TABU_DIS/NAM (see AUTH-007/008). 2. Remove S_TABU_CLI from any role that is not a core system-administration role; grant it only to a small, named group of Basis administrators. 3. Confirm production client protection in SCC4: the production client should be 'Not modifiable', with 'No changes to cross-client customizing objects' and 'No changes to repository' set; changes to these settings must be tightly controlled. 4. Enforce four-eyes / change control on any cross-client table maintenance and log it. 5. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm S_TABU_CLI is limited to the intended administrators. 6. Ensure table logging is active for T000 and other critical cross-client tables (rec/client, SE13 log flag) and review via SCU3. 7. Verify: with a non-admin test user, attempt to maintain a cross-client table and confirm refusal (SU53); confirm SCC4 protection flags are unchanged. 8. Rollout caution: some legitimate cross-client customizing (e.g. transport routes, currencies) requires this object during projects — grant it temporarily and controlled rather than permanently; test in QA and keep an approval trail.
References
  • SAP Help — S_TABU_CLI
  • SAP Security Baseline
HIGH P3 · 42 Arbitrary OS file access from ABAP (S_DATASET) AUTH-010 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_DATASET with FILENAME='*' and PROGRAM='*'. S_DATASET is the authorization checked when ABAP performs OPEN DATASET operations against the application-server file system; its fields scope which physical files (FILENAME) and which programs (PROGRAM) may read/write, together with the activity (33 read, 34 write/delete). With both fields wildcarded, any ABAP program the user can run may read or overwrite ARBITRARY files on the application-server host under the <sid>adm identity. This turns file access into a powerful primitive: read the SecStore/SSFS files and profile parameters, harvest transport data files, tamper with or truncate logs to cover tracks, or write attacker-controlled content into a path that another process will execute or ingest. Combined with the ability to run reports (AUTH-011) or custom Z-programs that call OPEN DATASET, wildcard S_DATASET is a route to disclosing secrets and undermining the integrity of the SAP file layer without ever touching the OS shell directly. In an S/4HANA RISE managed environment this still exposes application-owned secrets and files within the customer's responsibility boundary and can be chained with other weaknesses for escalation. A real incident looks like sensitive files being read or modified by an SAP work process outside any documented interface — for example configuration or credential files being copied to an output directory, or log files being altered — with the enabling factor being a program with unrestricted S_DATASET. It is a High-severity confidentiality/integrity exposure and a common finding in SAP file-handling reviews.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_DEV_UNRESTRICTED — 1 user(s) [DEV1] — S_DATASET FILENAME=*, PROGRAM=*
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_DATASET with FILENAME='*' and PROGRAM='*'; list roles and holders. 2. In PFCG, scope S_DATASET to the specific logical/physical file paths and the specific programs each role needs; never leave FILENAME='*' with write access (ACTVT 34). 3. Constrain the file system itself: define allowed paths via logical file names (transaction FILE) and the physical-path allowlist in table SPTH, so even authorized programs cannot stray outside approved directories. 4. Review custom programs that use OPEN DATASET (search via SE38/Code Inspector) and ensure they use logical file names and validate paths, preventing directory traversal. 5. Prefer read-only (ACTVT 33) where write is not strictly required. 6. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no assigned role retains the FILENAME='*'/PROGRAM='*' combination. 7. Verify: run an authorization trace (STAUTHTRACE) while executing the legitimate file interface to confirm it still works with the scoped values; attempt an out-of-scope file access with a test user and confirm refusal (SU53). 8. Rollout caution: batch/interface jobs frequently read and write server files — inventory those paths with the interface owners first, test in QA over a full cycle, and stage the SPTH/FILE tightening carefully to avoid breaking legitimate file transfers.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_DATASET
  • SAP Help — S_DATASET
HIGH P3 · 42 Run-any-report authorization (S_PROGRAM) AUTH-011 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_PROGRAM with SUBMIT/BTCSUBMIT activity and P_GROUP='*' or blank, allowing execution of any ABAP report regardless of its program authorization group. S_PROGRAM is checked when a report is started via SA38/SE38 or submitted in background; the P_GROUP field is meant to limit a user to reports of specific program authorization groups. A wildcard or blank P_GROUP defeats that, so the holder can run any executable report — including powerful standard utilities such as the RSUSR* user/authorization reports, mass-maintenance and data-extraction programs, and any custom Z-report — bypassing the transaction-menu restrictions that would normally keep those reports out of reach. This matters because a great deal of sensitive functionality in SAP lives in reports rather than dialog transactions; being able to SUBMIT anything is close to being able to start anything, but through a channel (SA38) that role designers often overlook. Concrete abuse in production: run a report that reads or exports sensitive data (payroll, finance, personal data) outside the owning application, execute a mass-update report that changes data without the usual controls, or run a diagnostic/authorization report to enumerate the landscape for further attack. In an S/4HANA production client this is a High-severity least-privilege and data-protection gap and a frequent SoD bypass, because a user constrained at the transaction level can still reach conflicting or sensitive functionality via SUBMIT. A real incident looks like execution of a report that the user's role has no business reason to run, producing a data extract or mass change with no corresponding transaction footprint.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_DEV_UNRESTRICTED — 1 user(s) [DEV1] — S_PROGRAM P_ACTION=SUBMIT, P_GROUP=*/blank
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_PROGRAM where P_ACTION includes SUBMIT/BTCSUBMIT and P_GROUP is '*' or blank; list roles and holders. 2. Assign program authorization groups to sensitive reports: set the group in the report attributes (SE38 -> Goto -> Attributes) or use report RSCSAUTH to assign authorization groups en masse (the group is stored in the SECU field of table TRDIR). 3. In PFCG, replace P_GROUP='*'/blank with the specific program groups the role needs, and scope P_ACTION to what is required (e.g. SUBMIT only). 4. Prefer driving report execution through defined transactions in the role menu rather than open SA38 access. 5. Use STAUTHTRACE to confirm which report groups the role genuinely uses before narrowing. 6. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no assigned role retains a wildcard/blank P_GROUP with SUBMIT. 7. Verify: with a test user, attempt to run a sensitive report (e.g. an RSUSR* report) via SA38 and confirm refusal (SU53). 8. Rollout caution: many operational jobs SUBMIT reports in background — inventory those with the job owners, ensure the relevant reports carry the correct groups, test in QA, and communicate before removing the wildcard so scheduled jobs do not fail.
References
  • SAP Help — S_PROGRAM
  • DSAG Audit — report execution
HIGH P3 · 42 Sensitive Basis / administration transactions in roles AUTH-013 ▶
Security Risk
The role contains one or more sensitive Basis/administration transactions delivered in S_TCODE — the module flags the presence of high-risk codes such as SE16/SE16N/SM30 (direct table display/maintenance), SE38/SA38/SE80 (ABAP and report execution), SM49/SM69 (external OS commands), SU01/SU10/PFCG/SU02/SU03 (user and role administration), SM59/SMT1/SMGW (RFC, trust and gateway), SCC4/SCC5/RZ10/RZ11 (client and profile-parameter administration), SICF/SMICM (ICF services / ICM), STMS/SE09/SE10 (transport management), SM19/RSAU_CONFIG/SM20/ST01 (audit and trace), SUIM, and DBACOCKPIT/DB02/SM12/SM13 (database, lock and update administration). Each of these grants capability that, in a productive role assigned to non-Basis users, is high-risk on its own and frequently violates segregation of duties. The danger is twofold. First, individually powerful transactions in a business role give ordinary users administrative reach they should never have — e.g. a finance user who also holds SE16N can read data outside their applications, or one holding SM59 can inspect and abuse RFC destinations. Second, and worse, is toxic combination: a role that mixes, say, user administration (SU01/PFCG) with transport control (STMS) or with table maintenance (SM30) enables self-service privilege escalation, change smuggling, or control circumvention, all within one role. In an S/4HANA production client this is a High-severity SoD and ITGC exposure and a recurring SOX audit finding. A real incident looks like a business user reaching an administrative transaction unrelated to their job — browsing tables, editing an RFC destination, or touching a security-audit setting — with the enabling factor being an over-broad role that accreted Basis transactions over time. Even where object-level authorizations are partly restrictive, mere reachability of these transactions is a governance and audit problem.
Affected Items (3)
  • Role Z_ARA_ROLEADMIN — 2 user(s) [ARAFRAUD3, ARAMULTI] — sensitive tcodes: PFCG
  • Role Z_ARA_USERADMIN — 2 user(s) [ARAFRAUD3, ARAMULTI] — sensitive tcodes: SU01
  • Role Z_TABLE_ADMIN — 1 user(s) [BATCH1] — sensitive tcodes: SE16, SM30
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate exposure: run SUIM / RSUSR002 for S_TCODE against the sensitive transaction list (SE16, SE16N, SM30, SE38, SA38, SM49, SM69, SU01, PFCG, SM59, SMT1, SCC4, RZ10, SICF, STMS, RSAU_CONFIG, SM20, DBACOCKPIT, SM12, SM13, etc.) and list which roles and users hold each. 2. For every hit, assess it against the role's documented business purpose; a business role should contain no Basis/administration transaction without written justification. 3. In PFCG, remove the unjustified transactions from business roles (rebuild S_TCODE from the role menu) and relocate genuine administrative tasks into dedicated, least-privilege administrator roles. 4. Design those admin roles by duty (user admin, transport admin, RFC/interface admin, DB/monitoring) so no single role concentrates conflicting Basis powers, and gate emergency use through GRC firefighter (EAM). 5. Run SoD analysis (GRC Access Control ruleset, or manual conflict matrix) to catch toxic combinations before and after remediation. 6. Regenerate profiles; where transactions must remain, tighten the underlying object authorizations via SU24 so reachability does not equal full capability. 7. Verify: re-run RSUSR002/SUIM and confirm the sensitive transactions no longer sit in business roles; spot-check with a test user (SU53 on a removed transaction). 8. Rollout caution: some 'Basis' transactions have limited legitimate business use (e.g. SM37 job monitoring) — confirm real needs with process owners, remove in a change window with QA testing, and provide a controlled path for genuine exceptions.
References
  • DSAG Audit Guideline — critical transactions
  • SAP Security Baseline
HIGH P3 · 42 ABAP development change access (S_DEVELOP create/change) AUTH-014 ▶
Security Risk
The role grants S_DEVELOP with create/change activity (ACTVT 01/02) on development object types other than pure debugging — i.e. developer access to create or modify ABAP repository objects such as programs, classes, function modules and dictionary objects. In a properly governed landscape all code and repository changes are made in the development system and moved to production only through the transport management system, so the production and often the QA client are set 'not modifiable' and no one holds developer change access there. Where a role grants S_DEVELOP create/change in a productive system, it breaks that model: a holder can create or alter ABAP directly, introducing untested or malicious code without the review, four-eyes and audit trail that the transport process provides. This is a serious code-integrity and backdoor risk. Concrete abuse: implant a small report or an enhancement/implicit-enhancement that reads or exfiltrates data, weakens an authorization check, or creates a hidden privileged user, then optionally delete it — leaving little trace beyond version history. Even without malice, ad-hoc production code changes cause outages and defeat change control. In an S/4HANA RISE production client this is a High-severity finding and a direct SOX/ITGC change-management deficiency, because the whole point of the transport-based process is that production code cannot be altered outside a controlled pipeline. A real incident looks like an object with a recent local change in production that never came through a transport, or an unexplained enhancement to a standard program, discovered via version management (SE80/SE38 versions) or a repository comparison — the enabling factor being developer change access that should not exist in production at all.
Affected Items (1)
  • Role Z_DEV_UNRESTRICTED — 1 user(s) [DEV1] — S_DEVELOP ACTVT=01/02 (create/change ABAP objects)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: run RSUSR002 for S_DEVELOP with ACTVT 01/02 on non-DEBUG object types in the production (and QA) systems; list roles and holders. 2. Remove development create/change authorizations from all productive-system roles; developer S_DEVELOP change access belongs only in the development system and only for developers. 3. Enforce system-level immutability: confirm the client change option in SCC4 and the global/system change option (SE06 / SE03 -> System Change Option) set production to 'Not modifiable', so repository/customizing changes are blocked regardless of role. 4. Ensure all changes flow through STMS transports from DEV; there should be no local objects created directly in production. 5. Where a rare, controlled production fix is unavoidable, gate it through GRC firefighter (EAM) with logging and a follow-up transport, not a standing role. 6. Regenerate profiles and re-run RSUSR002 to confirm no assigned production role retains S_DEVELOP create/change. 7. Verify: with a test user in production, attempt to change an object in SE38/SE80 and confirm it is refused by both the authorization and the system-change setting (SU53). 8. Rollout caution: some support processes lean on production 'quick fixes' — communicate the transport-only policy, ensure the firefighter/transport path is ready first, and test the SCC4/SE06 lockdown in QA to avoid blocking legitimate customizing where it is still allowed.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — S_DEVELOP
  • DSAG Audit — developer access in production
HIGH P3 · 42 UCON RFC allowlist is not active TRUST-007 ▶
Security Risk
The UCON (Unified Connectivity) RFC allowlist is not active (ucon/rfc/active is not 1). By default every RFC-enabled function module (RFM) in an ABAP system is externally callable, and a typical S/4HANA system exposes thousands of RFMs. Many are powerful — RFC_READ_TABLE reads arbitrary tables, RFC_ABAP_INSTALL_AND_RUN and similar modules can execute code or OS commands. Without UCON enforcing a Communication Assembly allowlist, an attacker or an over-privileged interface user who holds S_RFC can call ANY RFM, not just the handful the business genuinely needs. Attack scenario: an attacker with valid RFC credentials (or arriving via trusted RFC) calls RFC_READ_TABLE to dump the USR02 password-hash table for offline cracking, or invokes a code-execution RFM for remote command execution. The enormous default surface makes both exfiltration and exploitation easy and hard to spot. Business impact: mass data breach through unrestricted table reads, remote code execution, and a large unmonitored attack surface that is a direct SAP Security Baseline deviation. A real incident looks like RFC calls to sensitive RFMs the business never uses, and bulk table reads of HR/finance/credential tables from an interface account.
Affected Items (1)
  • ucon/rfc/active = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open transaction UCONCOCKPIT and start the UCON RFC scenario in the Logging phase to record which RFMs are actually called from outside. 2. Let Logging run across a full business cycle, including period-end, so no legitimate interface is missed. 3. Move the recorded RFMs into the Evaluation phase, review them, then promote the vetted set into the Final/active allowlist (Communication Assembly) so only needed RFMs stay externally callable. 4. Set ucon/rfc/active = 1 in RZ10 to enforce the allowlist, and restart to activate. 5. Combine this with tight S_RFC authorizations (per user and function group) and keep UCON logging on to catch new requirements. 6. Verify: RZ11 shows ucon/rfc/active = 1, UCONCOCKPIT shows the active allowlist, and blocked calls appear in the UCON log without breaking business functions. Caution: activating with an incomplete allowlist will break interfaces — gather enough logging first, involve interface owners, roll out non-production to production in stages, and monitor the UCON block log immediately after go-live.
References
  • SAP Help — Unified Connectivity (UCON)
  • SAP Security Baseline — UCON RFC allowlist
HIGH P3 · 42 RFC authorization check disabled (auth/rfc_authority_check) BASELINE-001 ▶
Security Risk
The profile parameter auth/rfc_authority_check governs whether the ABAP kernel enforces the S_RFC authorization object when a remote-enabled function module is invoked over RFC. With value 0 the AUTHORITY-CHECK against S_RFC (fields RFC_TYPE=FUGR, RFC_NAME=function group, ACTVT=16) is skipped for EVERY RFC call. The direct consequence is that any authenticated dialog, communication or system user, and critically any caller arriving over a trusted-RFC relationship, can execute ANY RFC-enabled function module irrespective of the roles assigned to them. In S/4HANA RISE landscapes this is severe because systems are densely interconnected: Fiori front-end ABAP servers, SAP PI/PO, SLT, BTP connectivity via the Cloud Connector, SAP GUI and Central User Administration all rely on RFC. A single low-privileged account or one compromised trusted-RFC hop can then call powerful modules such as RFC_READ_TABLE (mass extraction of any table including USR02 password hashes, PA0008 payroll, BSEG finance), BAPI_USER_CREATE1 or SUSR_USER_CHANGE_PASSWORD_RFC (create/reset users), or RFC_ABAP_INSTALL_AND_RUN (arbitrary code). Attack path: attacker obtains any valid credential (phished dialog user, service account in a config file), opens a JCo/RFC session, dumps USR02 and financial tables, then grants itself SAP_ALL and escalates to remote code execution. Business impact is total loss of confidentiality and integrity, collapse of Segregation of Duties, fraudulent postings, exfiltration of GDPR-relevant personal data and a clear SOX ITGC failure. A real incident surfaces as anomalous RFC traffic and unexpected table reads that generate no authorization-failure records because the check itself is disabled.
Affected Items (1)
  • auth/rfc_authority_check = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current value with report RSPARAM (SE38/SA38) or transaction RZ11 for parameter auth/rfc_authority_check. 2. Set the parameter to 9 (check enforced for all function modules) in the DEFAULT/instance profile via RZ10; value 6 is the modern kernel default and acceptable, but 9 is strictest (SAP Note 93254). 3. Because moving from 0 activates checks previously bypassed, first run an authorization trace with STAUTHTRACE/ST01 and the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU) over a representative period to learn which S_RFC values interface/service users actually need. 4. Maintain least-privilege S_RFC authorizations (RFC_TYPE=FUGR, RFC_NAME=<needed function groups>, ACTVT=16) on the affected technical users through PFCG roles; never grant S_RFC=*. 5. Update SU24 proposals so future roles inherit correct S_RFC defaults. 6. Although the parameter is dynamic, schedule an instance restart so enforcement is consistent across all work processes. 7. Roll out in DEV/QAS first, run a full interface regression (batch jobs, PI/PO, CUA, BTP Cloud Connector RFCs) and watch ST22 for RFC_NO_AUTHORITY dumps. 8. Verify by re-running RSPARAM on every app server (SM51) and confirming no new RFC_NO_AUTHORITY dumps for legitimate interfaces. Caution: coordinate with all interface owners; missing S_RFC grants break integrations. Never revert to 0 as a workaround.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — auth/rfc_authority_check
  • SAP Note 93254
HIGH P3 · 42 Profile-generator authorization checks not active (auth/no_check_in_some_cases) BASELINE-002 ▶
Security Risk
auth/no_check_in_some_cases is the master switch that activates the Profile Generator (PFCG) and the evaluation of the SU24 check indicators. With value N, the check-indicator logic PFCG uses to derive authorization defaults (which authorization objects are proposed for a transaction/service and whether their fields are pre-filled) is not honoured; the system behaves as if the customer check indicators do not exist. As a result, roles built in PFCG do not receive correct authorization proposals, and administrators compensate with broad manual authorizations or SU53 trial-and-error, which drifts steadily toward over-entitlement. In S/4HANA the authorization model is complex (Fiori catalogs, OData services, CDS-based analytics), so a mis-driven Profile Generator undermines the whole role-design methodology and the ongoing SU24 maintenance during Support Packages and upgrades (SU25 steps 2A-2D). This is not a single technical exploit but a systemic weakness: over-broad roles created because defaults were never enforced produce Segregation-of-Duties conflicts, for example a user who can both create a vendor and post a payment. A malicious insider then exploits that standing privilege for fraud, or an attacker who compromises one such account gains far more than intended. Business and compliance impact includes SoD violations, failed access-control audits (SOX 404 ITGC, ISO 27001 A.9), and an inability to demonstrate least privilege; auditors frequently flag this parameter directly as a Security Baseline deviation. A real incident looks like fraud or a data leak enabled by excessive standing authorizations that trace back to poorly generated roles rather than one dramatic breach.
Affected Items (1)
  • auth/no_check_in_some_cases = N
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value with RSPARAM/RZ11 for auth/no_check_in_some_cases. 2. Set it to Y in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10). This is a static parameter, so schedule an instance restart to activate it. 3. Ensure Profile Generator setup is complete: run transaction SU25 step 1 (initial fill of customer tables USOBT_C/USOBX_C from SAP defaults) if never done, and steps 2A-2D after every Support Package/upgrade to reconcile SU24 check indicators. 4. Maintain SU24 check indicators for custom transactions/services so authorization defaults are proposed correctly. 5. Adjust affected roles in PFCG using Expert mode (read old status and merge with new data) to pull in the corrected proposals, then regenerate profiles. 6. Verify with RSPARAM that value Y is active on all servers (SM51), and confirm in PFCG that authorization proposals now appear for transactions. 7. Run SUIM / report RSUSR008_009_NEW to review critical authorizations and SoD after the change. Caution: test role generation in DEV/QAS; regenerating production profiles must pass through change control and user regression so that needed authorizations are not inadvertently removed.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — auth/no_check_in_some_cases
HIGH P3 · 42 SNC accepts insecure (unencrypted) connections BASELINE-003 ▶
Security Risk
SNC (Secure Network Communications) provides authentication, integrity protection and encryption for SAP GUI (DIAG), RFC, CPIC and internal RFC traffic. The parameters snc/accept_insecure_gui, snc/accept_insecure_rfc, snc/accept_insecure_cpic and snc/accept_insecure_r3int_rfc govern whether the server still accepts UNprotected plaintext connections while SNC is enabled. A value of 1 (accept insecure) or U (accept insecure where individually allowed) makes SNC effectively optional: even with snc/enable=1, a client can simply omit SNC and connect in clear text, silently. This defeats the purpose of SNC because the landscape believes DIAG/RFC traffic is encrypted while an attacker can force a downgrade to plaintext. Attack scenario: an adversary with network access (a foothold on a jump host, a compromised admin workstation, or a man-in-the-middle position inside the RISE/hyperscaler VPC or on the VPN path to the SAP-managed environment) sniffs a GUI or RFC session that connected without SNC. DIAG carries the user's credentials and every screen field; RFC carries the function payload and, for trusted RFC, the propagated logon identity. The attacker harvests credentials and business content and replays them to log on. Because acceptance is silent, one non-SNC-capable or deliberately downgraded client is enough to expose traffic. Business and compliance impact includes interception of logon credentials and PII/financial data in transit and violation of encryption-in-transit obligations (GDPR Art. 32, PCI-DSS, and the SAP Security Baseline requirement to encrypt). A breach manifests as credential theft with no failed logons, followed by lateral movement using sniffed sessions.
Affected Items (1)
  • snc/accept_insecure_rfc = 1
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory the offending parameters via RSPARAM: snc/accept_insecure_gui, snc/accept_insecure_rfc, snc/accept_insecure_cpic, snc/accept_insecure_r3int_rfc. 2. Ensure SNC is fully deployed first: CommonCryptoLib installed, server PSE created and trust set up in STRUST, snc/enable=1, snc/identity/as set, and snc/data_protection_min at least 2 (integrity), ideally 3 (privacy/encryption). Transaction SNCWIZARD gives a guided setup. 3. Confirm all SAP GUI clients, SM59 RFC destinations and CPIC/interface partners are SNC-enabled (e.g. Secure Login Client, Kerberos or X.509). 4. Set each snc/accept_insecure_* parameter to 0 in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10) so only SNC-protected connections are accepted; optionally add the stricter snc/only_encrypted_gui=1 and snc/only_encrypted_rfc=1 to enforce encryption (SAP Note 1690662). 5. These are static parameters, so schedule an instance restart. 6. Verify by attempting a non-SNC GUI/RFC logon and confirming it is rejected, testing SM59 connections over SNC, and reviewing dev_w traces for the SNC handshake. Caution: do this ONLY after every client and interface supports SNC, otherwise legitimate connections break. Roll out per instance in a maintenance window and coordinate PSE distribution with interface owners and the RISE provider.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — SNC insecure connections
  • SAP Note 1690662
HIGH P3 · 42 SAP GUI Scripting enabled server-side (sapgui/user_scripting) BASELINE-004 ▶
Security Risk
SAP GUI Scripting is a client-automation API. When the server-side switch sapgui/user_scripting is TRUE, any SAP GUI connected to the system can be driven programmatically (VBScript or other languages) to read every field, table and value shown on screen and to replay keystrokes and transactions as the logged-on user. The API runs with the full authorizations of the interactive user and, by default, without leaving a distinct application-log trail, which makes it an ideal data-exfiltration and unattended-automation vector. Attack scenario: a user is phished into running a malicious script, or malware on the endpoint attaches to the running SAP GUI session (the client WarnOnAttach popup can be suppressed), then the script iterates through transactions such as SE16, PA30 (HR), or FB03 (finance) to scrape master and transactional data and write it out, or performs unauthorized postings, all as legitimate authorized user actions. Because the activity looks like normal GUI use, it evades many detections; combined with a privileged user it enables mass data theft or fraud at machine speed. In RISE/S4 landscapes with remote or BYOD access the endpoint is often outside the customer's full control, increasing the attach/inject risk. Business and compliance impact includes bulk exfiltration of GDPR personal data and trade secrets, fraudulent financial transactions, and an integrity/repudiation gap because the scripted actions are indistinguishable from the user's own. A real incident surfaces as anomalous high-volume transaction sequences from a single session, or business data appearing outside SAP with no corresponding download record.
Affected Items (1)
  • sapgui/user_scripting = TRUE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value with RSPARAM/RZ11 for sapgui/user_scripting. 2. Set sapgui/user_scripting = FALSE in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10) unless a specific, approved automation use case exists. It is dynamic, so you can switch it immediately in RZ11 and persist it in the profile for the next restart. 3. Where scripting is genuinely required (e.g. an RPA or test tool), do not enable it globally: set sapgui/user_scripting_per_user = TRUE so only explicitly authorized users can script (SAP Note 692245), and restrict it to the specific service accounts. 4. Harden the remaining exposure: set sapgui/user_scripting_disable_recording = TRUE where only pre-built scripts run, and consider sapgui/user_scripting_set_readonly = TRUE to block scripted input where only read automation is needed. 5. Do not suppress the client notifications; keep WarnOnAttach/WarnOnConnection enabled so users see attach attempts. 6. Reference SAP Notes 480149 (introduces the parameter) and 692245 (fine-grained server-side options). 7. Verify with RSPARAM that the value is FALSE on all app servers (SM51) and attempt to start a GUI script to confirm it is refused. Caution: coordinate with any RPA/test-automation owners before disabling globally, and pilot in non-prod so sanctioned automation is not broken.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — SAP GUI Scripting
  • SAP Note 480149 (introduces sapgui/user_scripting)
  • SAP Note 692245 (server-side scripting security options)
HIGH P3 · 42 Weak legacy password hashes retained (login/password_downwards_compatibility) BASELINE-005 ▶
Security Risk
login/password_downwards_compatibility controls whether the ABAP system, in addition to the strong current hash (CODVN H, salted iSSHA-1 stored in USR02-PWDSALTEDHASH), also generates and stores the old, weak downward-compatible hashes (CODVN B, an unsalted MD5 stored in USR02-BCODE, and related values in PASSCODE). Any value greater than 0 keeps producing these legacy hashes for backward compatibility with old systems and tools. The weak hashes are unsalted and truncate/upper-case the password, so they are trivially recovered offline with rainbow tables or GPU cracking in minutes. The strong hash then becomes irrelevant: if BCODE exists, an attacker cracks that instead, so the system is only as strong as its weakest stored hash. Attack scenario: an adversary who can read USR02 (via RFC_READ_TABLE, a database dump, an over-broad S_TABU_DIS grant, or an unprotected backup) extracts the BCODE column, cracks it offline to recover cleartext passwords, then logs on as those users, including administrators, with valid credentials and no exploit. This is precisely the technique in the public 'All your SAP passwords belong to us' research. Business and compliance impact includes mass credential compromise, privilege escalation, undetectable account takeover, and failure of GDPR/PCI/SOX obligations to protect stored credentials. A real breach looks like legitimate logons from stolen-but-valid passwords, often long after the table was exfiltrated, with no failed-logon trail.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/password_downwards_compatibility = 1
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the value via RSPARAM/RZ11 for login/password_downwards_compatibility (target value 0). 2. First ensure no connected system still requires old hashes: upgrade or retire any older-release systems that perform password-based logon against this system's hashes, and check CUA/central-system links (SAP Note 1023437). 3. Set login/password_downwards_compatibility = 0 in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10); it is dynamic, so set it in RZ11 and persist it in the profile. 4. Purge the already-stored weak hashes by running report CLEANUP_PASSWORD_HASH_VALUES (SE38) to remove obsolete BCODE/PASSCODE values from USR02 and the password-history tables (e.g. USH02/USRPWDHISTORY). 5. Optionally verify hash strength: report RSUSR003 shows the code version, and USR02 confirms CODVN H is in use. 6. Verify: after cleanup, inspect USR02 (SE16) to confirm BCODE/PASSCODE are blank for user records, and re-run RSPARAM to confirm the parameter is 0. Caution: run CLEANUP_PASSWORD_HASH_VALUES in non-prod first and take a backup; once old hashes are removed, downward-compatible logon from legacy systems fails by design, so coordinate with interface owners beforehand.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — Password hashes
  • SAP Note 1023437
HIGH P3 · 42 sapstartsrv / Host Agent web methods not protected (service/protectedwebmethods) BASELINE-006 ▶
Security Risk
sapstartsrv (the SAP Start Service) and the SAP Host Agent expose a SOAP/HTTP management interface (SAPControl) offering web methods such as Start, Stop, RestartInstance, ReadLogFile, ABAPReadSyslog, GetProcessList, ABAPGetTraceFile, ReadDeveloperTrace, GetEnvironment and ListLogFiles. service/protectedwebmethods defines which of these require administrative authentication. If it is not SDEFAULT (the recommended set) or ALL, the sensitive methods are reachable unauthenticated on the sapstartsrv ports (5xx13/5xx14). Unauthenticated read methods leak developer traces, syslogs, log files, environment variables and process lists, a rich source of hostnames, user names, file paths and even secrets that supports further attack; unauthenticated control methods allow Stop/Restart, i.e. denial of service against the SAP instance. Attack scenario: an attacker who can reach the instance-agent port (a flat network segment, an exposed management interface, or a pivot inside the RISE VPC) calls GetProcessList/ReadLogFile to map the system and read traces, then calls Stop to take the instance down, or uses leaked information to attack the database and OS layer. These open interfaces have long been a documented SAP attack surface (ERPScan/Onapsis research). Business and compliance impact includes information disclosure, denial of service against production SAP, and a foothold for deeper compromise, and it violates the Security Baseline hardening of the instance agent. A real incident looks like unexplained instance shutdowns or exfiltrated trace/log files with no ABAP logon record.
Affected Items (1)
  • service/protectedwebmethods = NONE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value via RSPARAM/RZ11 for service/protectedwebmethods, and also review the SAP Host Agent host_profile. 2. Set service/protectedwebmethods = SDEFAULT in the instance profile (RZ10); SDEFAULT protects the full sensitive method set. You may extend it (SDEFAULT plus specific methods) but do not reduce it to NONE or a short custom list (SAP Notes 1439348 and 927637). 3. Apply the same setting in the SAP Host Agent host_profile so its sapstartsrv is equally protected. 4. Confirm kernel/Host Agent patch levels support SDEFAULT (per SAP Note 1439348) and update if older. 5. Restart sapstartsrv to activate (sapcontrol -nr <nr> -function RestartService, or restart the instance agent); a full ABAP instance restart is not required for the agent alone. 6. As defense in depth, restrict network access to the sapstartsrv/Host-Agent ports via OS firewall/security groups so only admin jump hosts can reach them. 7. Verify: from an unauthenticated client run sapcontrol -function GetProcessList/ReadLogFile against the port and confirm it now requires credentials or is refused; re-check RSPARAM. Caution: monitoring tools (SAP Host Agent, Landscape Management, Focused Run) call these methods, so provision proper credentials before locking down and test in non-prod.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — service/protectedwebmethods
  • SAP Note 1439348
HIGH P3 · 42 Weak password hash algorithm (login/password_hash_algorithm) BASELINE-011 ▶
Security Risk
login/password_hash_algorithm configures the one-way function used to store the current (CODVN H) password hash in USR02: encoding=RFC2307, algorithm=iSSHA-1, iterations=1024, saltsize=96. The exported value uses a weak or obsolete algorithm and/or a low iteration/work-factor. SAP password hashes are a routine offline-cracking target once an attacker reads USR02 (for example via broad S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM access, a table download, or a stolen backup): a SHA-1-based (iSSHA-1) or MD5-based hash and a low iteration count collapse the cost of recovering plaintext passwords, and any recovered password is then usable for lateral movement, especially where the same credentials are reused across the landscape. Because this parameter governs how EVERY dialog user's password is protected at rest, a weak setting is a systemic exposure that undermines the entire password policy no matter how strong the complexity rules are. This is independent of, and should be fixed alongside, login/password_downwards_compatibility (BASELINE-005).
Affected Items (2)
  • weak/obsolete hash algorithm in: encoding=RFC2307, algorithm=iSSHA-1, iterations=1024, saltsize=96
  • iterations = 1024 (< 10000 work factor)
Remediation — Step by Step
Set login/password_hash_algorithm to a current, salted, iterated SHA-2 configuration, e.g. encoding=RFC2307, algorithm=iSSHA-512, iterations=15000, saltsize=256. After changing the parameter, force affected users to set a new password so the strong hash is generated, ensure login/password_downwards_compatibility = 0, and run CLEANUP_PASSWORD_HASH_VALUES to purge any residual weak BCODE/PASSCODE hashes. Validate against the SAP Security Baseline recommended value and re-export security_params to confirm.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — Password hash algorithm
  • SAP Help Portal — Profile parameter login/password_hash_algorithm
HIGH P3 · 42 RFC callback protection not enforced (rfc/callback_security_method) BASELINE-012 ▶
Security Risk
rfc/callback_security_method = 1 means simulation only — violations are logged, not blocked. When this system makes an outbound RFC call to a less-protected system, an attacker controlling that system can call back into this one using the predefined destination BACK. The callback runs in the user context of whoever initiated the outbound call, so no credentials are required — the trust flows in the opposite direction to the data.
Affected Items (1)
  • rfc/callback_security_method = 1
Remediation — Step by Step
Set rfc/callback_security_method = 3 to reject callbacks that are not on the calling destination's allowlist, and maintain the per-destination callback allowlist in SM59 (called function module / callback function module pairs). Activating UCON to restrict which function modules are remotely callable at all is the broader control.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — RFC callback protection
HIGH P3 · 42 Business-role restriction left 'Unrestricted' S4AUTHZ-002 ▶
Security Risk
In S/4HANA Cloud business roles, data access is scoped through RESTRICTIONS on restriction fields, the modern equivalent of organizational authorization fields (company code, cost center, controlling area, sales organization, profit center, plant, purchasing organization) plus a Read/Write/Value-Help access level. Setting a restriction to 'Unrestricted' is the cloud analogue of placing '*' on an org field in classic PFCG: the user can operate across every organizational unit, not just their own. When the Write access level is Unrestricted, the role can create, change, and delete across the entire enterprise. This silently defeats the data-scoping and SoD controls that business owners and auditors assume are in place. Abuse scenario: a clerk whose role should be limited to company code 1000 but is left Unrestricted can post documents, change master data, or approve transactions in every company code, enabling cross-entity fraud (for example booking to a low-scrutiny entity) or unauthorized access to another region's financial and HR data. An attacker who compromises such an account immediately inherits enterprise-wide write reach with no org boundary to contain them. Impact includes SOX segregation-of-duties and completeness/accuracy control failures, GDPR over-exposure of PII beyond the user's remit, and an inability to demonstrate least privilege at audit. A real incident typically appears as anomalous postings or master-data changes in company codes the user has no business reason to touch, discovered only after the money or data has moved.
Affected Items (2)
  • Z_FINANCE_MANAGER — COMPANY CODE: Unrestricted
  • Z_SALES_ADMIN — WRITE: Unrestricted
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract current restriction settings: Maintain Business Roles app > select role > Restrictions tab (S/4HANA Cloud); review every field flagged Unrestricted, prioritizing Write and Value Help. 2. For each org restriction (Company Code, Cost Center, Controlling Area, Sales Organization, Profit Center, Plant, Purchasing Organization) replace Unrestricted with explicit values or ranges matching the actual job scope. 3. Set the Write access level to Restricted with specific values; reserve Unrestricted Write only for genuinely cross-organization roles. 4. Where a role must legitimately span all org units, document the exception and route it through formal risk acceptance / role-owner sign-off. 5. On-prem S/4HANA equivalent: in PFCG maintain Organizational Levels and field values instead of leaving '*', tightening objects such as S_TABU_DIS/S_TABU_NAM, F_BKPF_BUK and K_CCA. 6.
