Regenerate the role/profile and re-derive any derived roles. 7. Run an SoD analysis (SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance or Access Control ARA) to confirm scoping did not leave a toxic combination. 8. Verify: use the restriction view (Cloud) or SUIM/RSUSR070 (on-prem) to confirm no sensitive restriction remains Unrestricted, and test with a representative user that access outside scope is now denied. 9. Document the target values as the role design baseline for future recertification. 10. Rollout caution: apply changes in the Q system first and run a business regression test, since over-tightening org values can block legitimate postings; coordinate go-live with process owners and stage via transport.
References
  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud — Business Role Restrictions
HIGH P3 · 42 OData V4 service group published without authorization S4AUTHZ-005 ▶
Security Risk
In S/4HANA, OData V4 services are grouped into service groups and published to a productive system alias via transaction /IWFND/V4_ADMIN. Access to a Gateway/OData service is protected by the authorization object S_SERVICE (external service access). A service group that is published against a productive alias but has no matching S_SERVICE authorization means the entity sets it exposes can be called by any authenticated user, because the service-start check is effectively open. OData V4 is a common audit blind spot: reviews historically concentrate on V2 (/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE) and on transaction/Fiori-catalog checks, so a published V4 group can slip through unexamined. Attack scenario: an attacker holding any valid dialog or technical account enumerates published V4 groups, calls an unprotected group's entity sets, and reads or (where the underlying CDS/BOPF permits) writes business data without holding any business role for it, a direct authorization bypass and a ready data-exfiltration channel. If this is combined with a CDS view whose authorization is disabled (S4AUTHZ-004), there is effectively no check at any layer. Impact includes disclosure of confidential, financial, or PII data (GDPR, SOX), possible unauthorized data changes, and a control gap where teams wrongly assume that a user without a Fiori tile cannot reach the data. A real incident appears as API traffic to a service group that no assigned role should grant.
Affected Items (2)
  • ZSG_BUSINESS_PARTNER_V4 (alias S4H_PROD) — published, no S_SERVICE authorization
  • ZSG_SALES_ORDER_V4 (alias S4H_PROD) — published, no S_SERVICE authorization
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate published V4 service groups: transaction /IWFND/V4_ADMIN > Publish Service Groups, noting each group's system alias and publication status. 2. For each published group, confirm an S_SERVICE authorization gates it and that this authorization is granted only through the specific business/PFCG roles that genuinely need the service. 3. Unpublish groups that are published but unused (remove them from the productive alias) to shrink the attack surface. 4. Ensure the ICF nodes behind the services (transaction SICF) are active only where required and are protected. 5. Add or adjust S_SERVICE in the relevant roles (PFCG) with the correct service type/name values and regenerate the profiles. 6. Verify: as a least-privileged test user, call the group's metadata and an entity set and confirm HTTP 403 without the authorization and success only with it. 7. Confirm S_SERVICE is actually being checked using transaction STAUTHTRACE or the /IWFND error log. 8. Cross-check the result against SAP Security Baseline and DSAG Gateway-service protection guidance and align. 9. Document the intended service-to-role mapping for recertification. 10. Rollout caution: tightening S_SERVICE can break legitimate Fiori apps and interfaces that consume the group, so identify all consumers first, test in Q, coordinate with interface owners, and stage the change via transport.
References
  • SAP Help — OData V4 Service Groups (/IWFND/V4_ADMIN)
HIGH P3 · 42 Cloud Connector system mapping without principal propagation S4AUTHZ-006 ▶
Security Risk
SAP Cloud Connector (SCC) links BTP/Cloud Foundry apps to on-premise or RISE private-landscape backends. Each Cloud-To-On-Premise system mapping defines a Principal Type controlling how the caller's identity reaches the backend. Setting Principal Type to 'None' on an HTTPS mapping means no end-user identity is forwarded; the BTP app connects to the S/4 backend as a single shared technical/service user (via the destination's basic-auth or a fixed credential). The consequence is that end-user attribution is lost: every action in the backend appears as that one technical user, so backend authorization checks and the security audit log cannot distinguish individual users, and any BTP app user effectively inherits the technical user's (often broad) backend authorizations. This breaks least privilege and accountability across the RISE landscape boundary. Attack scenario: a low-privileged BTP app user invokes a function that, through the shared technical user, reads or posts data far beyond their own entitlement; an attacker who compromises the BTP app or its destination credentials gains the technical user's full backend reach, and the security log shows only the technical account, hampering detection and forensics. Impact includes loss of segregation of duties and traceability, SOX/GDPR accountability failure (no way to attribute who accessed PII or financial data), and a wider blast radius from a single credential. A real incident looks like backend changes attributed to a generic service account with no way to identify the human actor behind them.
Affected Items (1)
  • S4H_Production — principalType: None (no principal propagation)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review each mapping in the Cloud Connector admin UI > Cloud To On-Premise > system mappings, identifying HTTPS backends with Principal Type = None. 2. Switch Principal Type to X.509 Certificate (principal propagation) for user-facing HTTPS mappings so the end user's identity flows to the backend. 3. Establish the trust chain: configure the SCC CA for principal propagation and import that CA into the backend's trust store via transaction STRUST (SSL server / trusted CA). 4. Map the propagated certificate subject (DN) to the real SAP backend user via transaction EXTID_DN (or CERTRULE) so the certificate resolves to an actual user. 5. Configure the BTP destination to use Authentication = PrincipalPropagation instead of a fixed technical user. 6. Remove or tightly restrict any shared technical-user fallback and pare back its backend authorizations. 7. Verify: run the app end-to-end and confirm the backend security audit log (transaction SM20 / report RSAU_READ_LOG) records the real end user, not the technical user. 8. Confirm in the Cloud Connector monitor that principal propagation is in effect for the mapping. 9. Document the propagation configuration and certificate validity/renewal dates. 10. Rollout caution: certificate and trust setup is delicate, so pilot on one backend in a non-prod SCC, coordinate with the Basis team owning STRUST and system clock/CA validity, and retain a rollback because a misconfigured trust chain breaks the connection entirely.
References
  • SAP Help — Cloud Connector Principal Propagation
HIGH P3 · 42 Cloud Foundry privileged platform role over-assigned S4AUTHZ-007 ▶
Security Risk
On SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, platform roles (Org Manager, Space Manager, Space Developer) govern the runtime environment itself, separate from the application role collections that govern app functionality. Space Developer is especially sensitive: it permits deploying/pushing applications and therefore executing arbitrary code within the space, binding services, reading environment variables that frequently contain service credentials and secrets, and restarting apps. Org Manager can manage spaces, users, and org-level settings. Over-assigning these roles to many human users (here more than the configured threshold, default 5) dramatically widens who can alter the productive runtime. These platform roles are routinely missed in access reviews because reviewers focus on business/application authorizations rather than the platform layer. Attack scenario: a user with Space Developer, or an attacker who compromises one, pushes a malicious app or modifies an existing one to exfiltrate bound-service credentials (HANA Cloud, XSUAA, destinations), pivots into connected systems, or tampers with productive services, a supply-chain-style compromise of the BTP subaccount; Org Manager abuse can add attacker-controlled users or spaces. Impact includes potential remote code execution in the productive environment, secret theft, lateral movement into S/4 backends, and loss of change control when deployments occur outside CI/CD, all carrying SOX segregation-of-duties and audit implications. A real incident looks like an unexpected app deployment or a credential-harvesting app running in a productive space.
Affected Items (1)
  • SPACE DEVELOPER: 6 assignments (> 5)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate assignments per role and space: BTP cockpit > subaccount > Cloud Foundry > Org/Space Members, or CLI cf org-users ORG and cf space-users ORG SPACE. 2. For each Space Developer / Space Manager / Org Manager holder, confirm a current operational justification; treat routine developers in productive spaces as exceptions. 3. Remove excess grants with cf unset-space-role USER ORG SPACE SpaceDeveloper (and cf unset-org-role ... OrgManager) or via the cockpit. 4. Replace human deployment access with dedicated CI/CD technical users (service accounts / mTLS) so people do not need standing Space Developer in production. 5. Reserve Org Manager for a small named platform-operations team. 6. Separate productive from non-productive spaces so broad developer access lives only in Dev/Test. 7. Adjust the scanner threshold max_cf_privileged_users only with documented approval. 8. Verify: re-run cf space-users / cf org-users and confirm counts are at or below the agreed limit. 9. Confirm CI/CD pipelines still deploy successfully using the technical user before human roles are withdrawn. 10. Rollout caution: coordinate with DevOps so removing Space Developer does not block pipelines, cut over the CI/CD technical user first, then withdraw human roles, and validate the change in a non-prod subaccount before touching production.
References
  • SAP BTP — Cloud Foundry Org & Space roles
HIGH P3 · 42 SoD conflict: Maintain Role vs Assign Role to User ARA-BASIS-02 ▶
Security Risk
A single user can both build role content (PFCG with S_USER_AGR ACTVT 01/02 and S_USER_TCD to define the role menu and authorizations) and assign that role to users (SU01/SU10/PFCG/PFUD with S_USER_AGR ACTVT 22 and S_USER_GRP ACTVT 22). This is the build-vs-assign split at role granularity: the person who defines what a role grants must not be the person who assigns it, or they can insert powerful transactions/authorizations into a role and then assign it to their own account, bypassing role-owner review and approval. Attack scenario: the perpetrator adds a sensitive transaction or a broad authorization value to a role in PFCG (S_USER_TCD lets them widen the transaction scope), regenerates it, then assigns it via SU01/SU10 (or a mass PFUD user-master comparison) to themselves or a confederate — gaining escalated access without anyone approving the role change or the assignment. It is a narrower but very common variant of BASIS-01: even without full user-administration rights, the ability to both modify a role and push it to users is enough to self-escalate. Business impact is uncontrolled privilege escalation, defeat of role-owner/approval governance, and an audit finding on change control over roles. In S/4HANA the same PFCG/user-assignment separation applies, and it is often violated in lean security teams. A real incident looks like a role modified and, shortly after, assigned to the modifier or a related account, followed by activity the role newly enables — detectable through role change documents and user-assignment logs if held by an independent team.
Affected Items (2)
  • ARAFRAUD3 (2 role(s))
  • ARAMULTI (6 role(s))
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify offenders: SUIM -> RSUSR002 for PFCG (S_USER_AGR ACTVT 01/02, S_USER_TCD) together with SU01/SU10/PFUD (S_USER_AGR ACTVT 22); confirm in GRC ARA (Maintain Role vs Assign Role). 2. Split roles: a Role Builder maintains PFCG content only; a User Administrator assigns roles only. In PFCG remove S_USER_AGR ACTVT 22 (assignment) from builder roles and ACTVT 01/02/S_USER_TCD from assignment roles; regenerate. 3. Restrict S_USER_AGR by role name/namespace and S_USER_GRP by user group so neither party operates outside its delegated scope. 4. Route role changes and assignments through a request/approval workflow (GRC Business Role Management + Access Request Management) so a role owner approves content changes and assignments independently. 5. Enable and independently monitor role change documents (SUIM change documents for roles/authorizations, table AGR_* change logs) and user-role assignment logs. 6. Where a small team must retain both, register a mitigating control (independent review of role-change-then-assignment events) in GRC/CSV with owner and expiry. 7. Verify: in QA modify a role and attempt to assign it to yourself under split roles, confirming denial; re-run ARA for zero residual. 8. Caution: test in QA and ensure the approval workflow or a firefighter path covers urgent role changes before removing combined access.
References
  • SAP Help / authorizationexperts.com S_USER_AGR (01/02 vs 22)
  • SAP Help S_USER_TCD (TCD)
  • SAP Help S_USER_SAS
HIGH P3 · 42 Users concentrating multiple access risks (SoD risk profile) ARA-SCORE-001 ▶
Security Risk
This aggregate finding flags individual users who each concentrate multiple unmitigated access risks — meeting or exceeding the configured threshold (default 2) of Segregation-of-Duties conflicts and critical accesses — with the list ranked by a weighted score (CRITICAL=10, HIGH=5, MEDIUM=2, LOW=1). It is not a new technical weakness but a prioritization signal: users who carry many SoD conflicts and critical accesses are the highest-probability single points of internal-control failure, because one compromised or malicious account can execute several end-to-end fraud or abuse paths at once. Attack scenario: an attacker who phishes or otherwise takes over one of these high-score IDs (or the insider who owns it) inherits, for example, both the create-vendor/pay path and the maintain-customer/apply-cash path simultaneously, so a single credential yields multiple independent avenues to divert funds, manipulate the ledger, or escalate privilege — dramatically increasing blast radius and lowering the effort to commit material fraud. These accounts are also the ones whose over-entitlement most often results from role creep, emergency access left standing, or copy-a-colleague provisioning. Business impact is concentrated fraud exposure, an outsized share of the organization's total SoD risk resting on a few identities, and an audit finding on access governance and least privilege; regulators and external auditors specifically look for the small population of users who accumulate conflicting access. A real incident traces back to one of these IDs being the common denominator across several control breaches. Remediating the top of this list delivers the largest risk reduction per unit of effort.
Affected Items (2)
  • ARAMULTI — 3 risk(s), 2 critical, score 25
  • ARAFRAUD3 — 2 risk(s), 1 critical, score 15
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Work the ranked list top-down: start with the highest-score users and those with the most CRITICAL conflicts, since they carry the greatest concentrated exposure. 2. For each user run a full entitlement review: SU01 -> Roles, and SUIM -> RSUSR002 / RSUSR070 to see which roles deliver each conflicting function; in GRC run user-level Access Risk Analysis to enumerate every risk on the account. 3. Apply least privilege: remove roles/transactions the user does not need for their current job (validate against actual usage via the statistics in ST03N / STAD or an authorization trace STAUTHTRACE over a representative period), and resolve each SoD pair by removing one side. 4. Redesign the underlying roles where the conflict is built into a single wide role — split into task-based roles so future users do not inherit the same combination (GRC Business Role Management if available). 5. Retire standing emergency access: move break-glass needs to a controlled firefighter (GRC EAM) model rather than permanent grants. 6. For any residual risk that cannot be removed, attach a documented mitigating control (independent review/monitoring) in mitigating_controls.csv or GRC with owner and validity date, driving each user's unmitigated count toward zero. 7. Verify: re-run this analysis / GRC ARA and confirm the user's residual risk count and score have dropped below threshold; track over time. 8. Caution: stage removals in QA and communicate with the affected users' managers, since these are often senior/power users whose access changes can disrupt operations if not coordinated; remove access incrementally and monitor for access-denied (SU53) issues.
References
  • SAP GRC Access Control — Access Risk Analysis (user-level risk)
HIGH P3 · 42 Job runs RSBDCOS0 or unreviewed custom code under a privileged user JOBCMD-JOB-003 ▶
Security Risk
This step either runs RSBDCOS0 - the standard SAP report that executes an operating-system command directly - or runs a custom Z/Y program under a privileged step user. RSBDCOS0 takes an OS command as input and runs it as <sid>adm, entirely bypassing the SM69 external-command allowlist and its S_LOG_COM checks. Scheduling RSBDCOS0 in a job is a classic backdoor pattern: it needs no SM69 catalog entry and leaves minimal trace. A custom Z/Y report under SAP*/DDIC/SAP_ALL is equally dangerous - it can contain arbitrary logic and runs with unrestricted authority, unreviewed. Such custom code can itself reach the OS via CALL 'SYSTEM', OPEN DATASET, or SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE. Attack scenario: an attacker with batch-admin rights schedules RSBDCOS0 with an OS-command payload, or slips a malicious Z-report into an existing privileged job. On the next run the command executes as <sid>adm - data theft, persistence, or destruction - bypassing the command catalog and its audit. Because RSBDCOS0 is a standard SAP report, it does not stand out the way a custom program might. Business impact: direct, catalog-bypassing OS execution on the S/4HANA app server, under a powerful identity. An RSBDCOS0 entry in a job schedule is a strong indicator of an implanted backdoor. DB-layer and ABAP-application controls do not see the OS action, so detection depends on OS/job monitoring. Real incident: RSBDCOS0 found scheduled under DDIC in a compromised system, running reverse-shell commands nightly; it had never been part of any legitimate job (see SAP Note 2443193 on RSBDCOS0 behaviour).
Affected Items (2)
  • JOB_FI_CLOSE -> custom report ZFI_CLOSE under privileged user DDIC
  • JOB_OSCMD -> RSBDCOS0 (direct OS command, bypasses SM69) — user ZJOBSVC
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify: SM37 / SE16 TBTCP where PROGNAME = 'RSBDCOS0', and Z*/Y* programs whose step user (AUTHCKNAM) is SAP*/DDIC/SAP_ALL. 2. Treat any RSBDCOS0 schedule as a potential backdoor - before deleting, capture who created it (SDLUNAME, change docs) and review the Security Audit Log (SM20 / RSAU_READ_LOG) and system log (SM21). 3. Delete the RSBDCOS0 job step (SM36/SM37) once evidence is preserved. 4. Restrict authorization to run RSBDCOS0: it is protected by S_PROGRAM (its authorization group) and by S_LOG_COM at the OS layer - remove broad S_PROGRAM/S_DEVELOP/SA38 grants. 5. Confirm remaining holders with SUIM and report RSUSR008_009_NEW (users with critical authorizations). 6. Code-review the flagged custom Z/Y batch programs (SE38/SE80) for OS access - CALL 'SYSTEM', OPEN DATASET, SXPG_COMMAND_EXECUTE. 7. Reassign those custom steps to a least-privilege type B step user (see JOB-001). 8. Where OS interaction is genuinely required, route it through a reviewed, tightly-scoped SM69 command under S_LOG_COM control instead of RSBDCOS0. 9. Enable/monitor the Security Audit Log (SM19 / RSAU_CONFIG) to alert on RSBDCOS0 execution and suspicious report starts. 10. Verify: SE16 TBTCP shows no armed RSBDCOS0 step and no Z/Y step under a privileged user. 11. Rollout caution: a rare legitimate use of RSBDCOS0 may exist - confirm with Basis before deletion and keep evidence; changing custom-program step users can break the job, so capture required authorizations (STAUTHTRACE) first and test in DEV/QA.
References
  • SAP KBA 2443193 — Report RSBDCOS0: execute OS command from SAP GUI (SM69-allowlist bypass)
  • SAP Help — Background processing security

Security Risk
2 emergency-access (firefighter) session(s) were used with no reason code / justification recorded. Firefighter IDs grant broad privileged access; SOX ITGC and the SAP GRC EAM control model require that every use is justified up-front and the log reviewed after the fact. Unjustified privileged sessions are the classic gap auditors cite for emergency access.

  • FF_FIN_02 used by MSMITH @ 20260701

Maintain EAM Reason Codes and make reason-code entry mandatory in the Superuser/EAM logon workflow so sessions cannot start without a justification. Review the listed sessions with the firefighter owner and record the business justification retroactively.

HIGH P3 · 42 Posting periods open too wide with no authorization-group control FIN-PP-001 ▶
Security Risk
2 posting-period variant setting(s) leave the period open for all account types across a full year or more (or into the far future) with no authorization group (T001B-BRGRU) restricting who may post. Open posting periods are the primary financial cutoff/completeness control: wide-open periods let entries be posted or back-dated into closed/future periods, defeating period-end cutoff and enabling manipulation of which period results land in — a core SOX financial-reporting concern (PCAOB AS 2201).

  • variant 2000: all account types, periods 1-16/2025-2027, no auth group
Remediation — Step by Step
In OB52 (posting period variant, T001B) keep only the current open period(s) open, close prior periods, and set an authorization group on the second/special period range so only the close team (S_TABU_DIS / posting-period auth) can post to it. Review the wide-open variants above.

Security Risk
2 FI tolerance group(s) have a per-document limit that is unset or effectively unlimited. The tolerance group is the preventive cap on how much a user can post/clear in one document; an unset or huge limit means no monetary control on individual postings, so errors or fraudulent entries of any size pass unchecked (a SOX preventive-control gap).

  • group SUPER: per-document limit 9,999,999,999

In OBA4 set realistic per-document and per-open-item amount limits on each FI tolerance group appropriate to the roles assigned, and confirm the default (blank) group is not the one granting unlimited posting.

Security Risk
Sensitive-fields dual control (FK08/FD08, table T055F) is configured but no PAYMENT-relevant fields (bank account, bank key, IBAN, payment method) are among them. When a vendor/customer bank account or payment method can be changed by ONE person with no second-person confirmation, an attacker or insider can silently redirect payments to their own account (the classic vendor-bank-change payment fraud). Dual control over payment master data is a key SOX anti-fraud control.

  • NAME1
Remediation — Step by Step
In FK08 (vendor) / FD08 (customer) mark the bank-detail and payment-method fields (LFBK-BANKN/BANKL/BANKS, IBAN, ZWELS, house bank) as 'sensitive' so a change locks the master record until a second, segregated user confirms it (FK09/FD09).

Altering payment routing on an already-approved/posted document bypasses the approval that authorised it and undermines the immutability of the financial record — a SOX record-integrity gap and a payment-fraud vector.

  • BVTYP (K) changeable after clearing

HIGH P3 · 24 Missing authorization check in custom ABAP — Z_MM_PO_UPLOAD ATC-AUTHCHK ▶
Security Risk
This was reported by SAP's own code analysis (ABAP Test Cockpit / Code Vulnerability Analyzer) running inside the system, not by this product's scanner. The statement performs a privileged action — reading, writing or deleting business data, calling out to another system, or starting a transaction — without an authorization check that governs it. Authorization in ABAP is not enforced by the database or the runtime; it happens only where a developer writes AUTHORITY-CHECK. A missing check is therefore not a weakened control but an absent one. Any user who can reach the code path can perform the action, regardless of their role, and the failure is invisible in role reviews because there is no role to review.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_MM_PO_UPLOAD (CLAS) line 22
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Open the object in ADT or SE80 and read the reported statement in context — the line number came from a scan and moves as the code is edited. 2. Add an AUTHORITY-CHECK before the action, against the authorization object that actually governs it — for business data that is the object the standard transaction checks, not a convenient generic one. 3. Check SY-SUBRC immediately after and stop processing when it is non-zero; an unchecked AUTHORITY-CHECK is the same as no check. 4. Maintain the authorization proposal for the object so the check appears in role maintenance and can be reviewed. 5. Verify by executing the path as a user who should be refused, and confirm the refusal. 6. Wire the check into the transport release path so the same defect class cannot be reintroduced by the next change.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — secure custom code
  • CWE-862
MEDIUM P3 · 36 Parameter rfc/allowoldticket4tt non-compliant PARAM-rfc/allowoldticket4tt ▶
Security Risk
rfc/allowoldticket4tt governs whether the SAP system still accepts the old-format tickets/assertions used by the legacy trusted-RFC (trusted/trusting-system) mechanism. Note the parameter is text-valued (values such as 'no', 'both', 'yes'), not the numeric 0/1 the scanner compares against, but the security intent is sound: as long as old-format trusted-RFC tickets are accepted, the system remains vulnerable to the weaknesses that the reworked trusted/trusting concept was designed to fix. The legacy method did not uniquely bind the ticket to a specific source system, which is the root of CVE-2023-0014 (addressed by SAP Security Notes 3089413 and 3318850): an attacker able to capture the authentication from normal communication between trusting SAP systems can replay it to impersonate the trusted source system and log on to the trusting system with elevated rights, without knowing any password. In a connected S/4HANA landscape with trusted-RFC relationships (e.g., Solution Manager to managed systems, or hub-and-spoke S/4 to satellites), a single foothold plus captured trusted-RFC traffic can be pivoted into privileged access on multiple systems - a classic lateral-movement and privilege-escalation chain. Business impact: multi-system compromise, fraud, and data breach spanning the landscape. Compliance impact: leaving weak crypto/legacy tickets enabled contradicts SAP's security notes and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident would look like a trusted-system logon on a production system that no legitimate source actually initiated.
Affected Items (1)
  • rfc/allowoldticket4tt = 1
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current value in RZ11 for rfc/allowoldticket4tt (secure target is 'no'; a temporary migration value of 'both' may be needed while old and new methods coexist). 2. First implement the reworked trusted/trusting-RFC method: apply SAP Security Notes 3089413 and 3318850 and prerequisites, then re-establish trust relationships using the new migration in transactions SMT1 (trusted) and SMT2 (trusting). 3. Migrate every trusted-RFC connection in the landscape to the new method; use the relevant migration/report guidance in the notes to confirm each relationship is upgraded on both sides. 4. Only after all connections are migrated, set rfc/allowoldticket4tt = no in the DEFAULT profile (DEFAULT.PFL) via RZ10 so old-format tickets are rejected system-wide. 5. Also review rfc/selftrust = 0 and the trusted-system entries in table RFCSYSACL for stale or overly broad trust. 6. Save/activate the profile and restart the instances during a maintenance window. 7. Verify with RSPARAM that the value is 'no' and test each trusted-RFC destination (SM59) still authenticates under the new method. 8. Roll out carefully across the whole landscape in coordination with every trusting/trusted partner - setting 'no' prematurely will break connections still on the old method, so migrate all sides first. 9. Monitor trusted-system logons via the Security Audit Log for anomalies during and after cutover. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm the legacy-ticket acceptance is disabled.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)

This check reports only a deviation from the value SAP mandates. Current value: '1'. The ECS standard value is '0'. SAP permits no exception to this value.

Set icf/set_HTTPonly_flag_on_cookies to the ECS standard value. Re-export the profile parameters (RSPARAM) afterwards and confirm the active value on every instance.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 RFC destinations to external/non-RFC hosts NET-002 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags RFC destinations whose target host falls outside the recognized internal RFC-1918 ranges, i.e. destinations that point to external or unrecognized systems. Each such destination is a potential data-egress channel and a trust boundary where credentials and business payloads may cross an untrusted network. In an S/4HANA RISE model some external targets are legitimate (BTP services reached through the SAP Cloud Connector, sanctioned SaaS endpoints), but an unmanaged or undocumented external destination is exactly what an attacker or a malicious insider would create to redirect traffic. The abuse scenario has two shapes. First, an actor who can maintain destinations repoints or creates a destination toward an attacker-controlled host; if the destination stores logon data or uses basic auth, the logon handshake and payload are delivered straight to the attacker, harvesting credentials and data. Second, a legitimate-looking external destination silently exfiltrates business data (HR, payroll, customer master, pricing) to a third party, or acts as a man-in-the-middle relay. Because RFC and HTTP destinations can carry sensitive fields, an uncontrolled external endpoint is also an uncontrolled cross-border data flow, which raises GDPR sub-processor and data-residency concerns and undermines the RISE shared-responsibility boundary. The business impact ranges from silent data breach to compliance failure for undeclared data transfers. A real incident often looks like a destination to an unfamiliar public IP that, on investigation, has been quietly siphoning master data for months, discovered only because network egress logging finally flagged the connection.
Affected Items (6)
  • ARIBA_CLOUD → ariba.cloud.sap.com (type: W)
  • SF_EC_CONNECT → api.successfactors.com (type: W)
  • VENDOR_PORTAL → 203.0.113.55 (type: 3)
  • LEGACY_ECC → 198.51.100.22 (type: 3)
  • BTP_DESTINATION → mysubaccount.authentication.eu10.hana.ondemand.com (type: W)
  • BANK_INTERFACE → 192.0.2.100 (type: T)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate all destinations in SM59 (or table RFCDES) and extract the target host for each connection type. 2. Compare every target against an approved allow-list of internal subnets plus sanctioned SaaS and BTP endpoints; treat anything else as an exception to be justified. 3. For each external host, obtain documented business justification and interface-owner sign-off and record it in the interface register. 4. Ensure every external connection is encrypted: type 3 and T destinations via SNC, and HTTP destinations (type G/H) via HTTPS with server-certificate validation using certificates imported in STRUST. 5. For BTP or cloud targets in RISE, route through the SAP Cloud Connector with an explicit resource allow-list rather than configuring direct outbound destinations. 6. Constrain the gateway: maintain secinfo and reginfo (via SMGW or the ACL files) to restrict which external programs may register or be started. 7. Enforce network-layer egress firewall rules so only approved destinations can be reached. 8. Deactivate and delete obsolete or unowned external destinations, and restrict SM59 maintenance authorization to Basis. 9. Verify by re-scanning and confirming every remaining external destination is on the allow-list and encrypted; test changes in non-production with the interface owner before touching production.
References
  • SAP Note 1480644
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Default SAP IDP trust still active: sap.default RISE-001 ▶
Security Risk
The default SAP identity provider (SAP ID Service, origin sap.default / sap.ids) is still enabled as a logon-capable trust on the BTP subaccount, alongside or instead of the corporate IdP. SAP ID Service is a public, internet-facing identity store that anyone holding an S-user or a self-registered P-user can access; it is NOT governed by the organization's joiner/mover/leaver process, corporate password policy, MFA enforcement, or conditional-access rules. While it remains 'Available for User Logon', an attacker who obtains or self-provisions an SAP ID Service account and is granted (or inherits, via shadow-user creation) any role collection can authenticate to BTP apps and, through destinations and principal propagation, reach the connected S/4HANA backend, completely bypassing the corporate IdP, its MFA, and its central deprovisioning. Because the default IdP survives corporate-IdP outages and is routinely forgotten after a custom-IdP go-live, it becomes a durable, low-visibility backdoor. In a real incident, a former contractor whose corporate account was disabled still logs on through SAP ID Service, or a phished S-user password is replayed against the subaccount; the SOC sees a 'valid' BTP logon with no failed corporate-IdP events, and the actor pivots to Fiori launchpad tiles exposing financial or HR data. From a compliance standpoint this defeats SOX access-control assertions and GDPR least-privilege/deprovisioning obligations, and it is a standard SAP Security Baseline audit finding. The weakness is architectural, not a single stolen password: it is a permanently-open alternate authentication path that neither central IAM nor the SIEM has full visibility over.
Affected Items (1)
  • Trust: SAP ID Service (origin: sap.default)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the corporate IdP (SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication, IAS) is fully configured and tested end-to-end for the subaccount before touching the default trust. 2. In the BTP Cockpit open the affected Subaccount -> Security -> Trust Configuration. 3. Locate the 'Default Identity Provider' entry (SAP ID Service, origin sap.default/sap.ids) and choose the Edit (pencil) icon. 4. Uncheck 'Available for User Logon' and Save. Note: the default IdP cannot be deleted - hiding it from logon is the SAP-supported hardening step; it stays as an administrative fallback only. 5. Repeat for every subaccount (DEV/QA/PROD) and for both the platform and application trust where applicable. 6. If you administer via CLI, verify and set with 'btp list security/trust' and 'btp update security/trust'. 7. Synchronise the trust list into any SAP Cloud Connector: Cloud To On-Premise -> Principal Propagation -> Synchronize, so the on-prem trust list matches BTP. 8. Verify: open the subaccount/application logon URL in a fresh private browser session and confirm the SAP ID Service tile no longer appears and only the corporate IdP is offered. 9. Verify no active role collections remain assigned to sap.default shadow users (Security -> Users, filter by origin) and clean up any found. 10. Rollout caution: retain one break-glass platform administrator reachable via the global account or a separately governed emergency path BEFORE disabling default logon, and perform the change in a non-production subaccount first to avoid a lock-out.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 Automatic shadow user creation enabled for SAP ID Service RISE-002 ▶
Security Risk
The trust is configured to auto-create BTP shadow users on first logon (createShadowUsers / auto_create_shadow_users = true). A shadow user is the local BTP representation that carries role-collection assignments; with on-the-fly creation the mere ability to authenticate at the trusted IdP is enough to materialise an account in the subaccount with no approval or provisioning workflow. This collapses the crucial separation between 'can authenticate' and 'is authorized to use this system'. The danger is amplified when the IdP is a large corporate directory (every employee can now instantiate an account in a Finance or HR subaccount) or when a permissive default IdP is also enabled. If any 'default' role collection is assigned at the subaccount level or via IdP group-to-role-collection mapping, freshly created shadow users may immediately inherit access. Attack scenario: an internal user outside the ERP population, or an attacker who has compromised any federated identity, logs on once; a shadow user is silently created and, via group mapping, receives access to OData APIs or Fiori apps - with no request ticket, no approver, and no joiner record to trip detection. The outcome is uncontrolled user-base growth, orphaned and over-entitled accounts, broken segregation-of-duties and named-user licence compliance, and an audit finding that user provisioning is ungoverned. A breach looks like dozens of never-approved shadow users appearing in the user list, several holding sensitive role collections that no one can trace to a request, discovered only during an access recertification.
Affected Items (1)
  • Trust: SAP ID Service — auto_create_shadow_users = true
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Decide the target model: explicit provisioning via SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Provisioning (IPS/SCIM) rather than logon-time auto-creation. 2. In BTP Cockpit -> Subaccount -> Security -> Trust Configuration, edit the relevant trust and set shadow-user creation to a controlled value (disable automatic creation where exposed); via CLI use 'btp update security/trust' with the auto-create-shadow-users parameter set to false. 3. In the corporate IdP (IAS admin console) restrict the BTP/XSUAA application's User Access to 'Only Corporate Users' or 'Private' so only assigned users can authenticate. 4. Remove any broad 'default' role-collection assignment at the subaccount and replace it with explicit, request-based assignment under Security -> Role Collections. 5. Configure IPS jobs (or SCIM) to provision only entitled users and to deprovision leavers, tied to an approval workflow. 6. Clean up existing shadow users: Security -> Users, identify auto-provisioned accounts, revoke unneeded role collections and delete orphans. 7. Verify: attempt logon with a deliberately non-entitled test identity and confirm no shadow user is created and access is denied. 8. Reconcile the BTP user list against the authoritative HR/IGA source and document any exceptions. 9. Rollout caution: coordinate with app/integration owners so legitimate first-time users are pre-provisioned before you disable auto-creation, and pilot in a non-production subaccount to avoid locking out real users.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 Communication arrangements with excessive service scope RISE-003 ▶
Security Risk
One or more communication arrangements bundle a large number of inbound/outbound services (more than ten) under a single communication scenario and a single communication user. In S/4HANA a communication arrangement instantiates an SAP-delivered scenario (SAP_COM_*) and grants the bound communication user access to every API/service the scenario contains. When a scenario is broad, or several are consolidated onto one arrangement/user, a single credential can call dozens of OData/SOAP APIs spanning finance, procurement, sales and master data. This violates least privilege and dramatically enlarges the blast radius: if that one credential leaks (hard-coded in middleware, committed to a repo, or exposed in logs) the attacker inherits the union of all those services at once - read/write of business partners, posting of journal entries, creation of purchase or sales orders. It also destroys traceability, because activity from many logically distinct integrations all appears under the same arrangement and user, so an incident cannot be scoped to one interface. Attack scenario: a developer stores the arrangement's client secret in a CI pipeline; it is exfiltrated; the attacker enumerates the arrangement's services and posts fraudulent supplier bank-detail changes via API_BUSINESS_PARTNER while simultaneously pulling GL data via API_JOURNAL_ENTRY, all with one token. Compliance impact spans SoD violations, SOX ITGC failures over interface access, and an inability to contain the breach. Auditors flag this as a classic over-entitlement/least-privilege interface finding.
Affected Items (1)
  • SF_EMPLOYEE_SYNC (scenario: SAP_COM_0008, 12 services)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory arrangements in the 'Maintain Communication Arrangements' Fiori app and list every service active under each (Inbound/Outbound Services sections). 2. For each arrangement, confirm which services the connected system actually consumes; set the unneeded individual inbound/outbound services inactive within the arrangement. 3. Split multi-purpose arrangements into separate arrangements per integration scenario / per external system, each bound to the narrowest suitable SAP_COM_* scenario. 4. Assign a dedicated communication user to each arrangement (see RISE-006) so scope and identity are 1:1 with the integration. 5. Prefer narrower SAP-delivered scenarios over broad ones; do not extend a scenario's services beyond documented need. 6. For S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition / on-prem equivalents, review activated OData services in transaction /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE and web-service bindings in SOAMANAGER, removing unused ones. 7. Verify: re-open each arrangement and confirm the service count reflects only required services; regression-test each integration after pruning. 8. Document each arrangement's business owner, consuming system and service list for audit evidence. 9. Rollout caution: coordinate with interface owners and change management; deactivate services in a test tenant first, because removing a service in active use will break the integration.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 Communication users shared across many arrangements RISE-006 ▶
Security Risk
A single communication (technical/system) user is reused across more than three arrangements. Sharing one identity across many integrations breaks accountability and multiplies blast radius. Because all those interfaces authenticate as the same principal, backend and gateway logs cannot distinguish which integration performed a given call, so forensic attribution during an incident is effectively impossible and SoD analysis is muddied. The shared user typically accumulates the union of authorizations required by all the arrangements it serves, becoming an over-privileged account whose single credential unlocks a wide swath of APIs. If that one secret leaks or must be rotated, every dependent interface is simultaneously at risk or disrupted, which discourages timely rotation and encourages long-lived static secrets. Attack scenario: a shared communication user's password/secret is exposed in one poorly secured middleware system; the attacker now wields access to all the finance, procurement and master-data services aggregated on that user, and defenders cannot tell which interface was abused because every call carries the identical identity. Compliance impact includes failure of SOX ITGC around unique user identification and audit trail, GDPR accountability gaps, and standard audit findings on shared/technical-account governance. A real incident looks like the credential appearing in traffic from an unexpected system while the legitimate interfaces continue using the same account, effectively camouflaging the intrusion inside normal integration noise.
Affected Items (1)
  • SF_COMM_USER — used in 4 arrangements: SF_EMPLOYEE_SYNC, VENDOR_INVOICE_API, CRM_INTEGRATION, TAX_ENGINE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the 'Maintain Communication Users' Fiori app list all communication users and cross-reference them to arrangements via 'Maintain Communication Arrangements'. 2. Create a dedicated communication user per integration scenario / per external system (Maintain Communication Users -> New). 3. Re-point each arrangement to its own dedicated user in the 'Maintain Communication Arrangements' app and remove the shared user from arrangements it should no longer serve. 4. Grant each new user only the scope of its single arrangement (least privilege) so its authorizations are no longer the union of many interfaces. 5. Prefer OAuth 2.0 client credentials / X.509 per user over shared static passwords, and store each interface's secret separately in a secrets manager. 6. For Private Edition/on-prem technical users, review type and usage via SU01/SUIM and table USR02 (user type Communications/System) and split shared service users similarly. 7. Establish a secret-rotation schedule now that rotation impacts only one interface at a time. 8. Verify: confirm each arrangement shows a unique communication user and that backend logs now attribute calls to distinct users; regression-test each interface after the change. 9. Rollout caution: coordinate credential cutover with each interface owner and stage in non-production - repointing to a new user requires the calling system to adopt the new credential simultaneously.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 BTP users without corresponding S/4HANA account IAM-XID-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags SAP BTP subaccount users that have no matching identity in the S/4HANA user master. In a RISE landscape, BTP is the extension and integration layer that often reaches back into the S/4 backend through destinations, APIs and the Cloud Connector. A BTP user with no S/4 counterpart may be a legitimate external developer or consultant, but it may equally be an orphaned account left after a project, a shadow identity created directly in BTP outside central governance, or a leaver who was removed from S/4 but not from BTP. The danger is that these accounts fall outside the joiner-mover-leaver process and periodic reviews that govern S/4 users, so they persist unnoticed and unreviewed. The abuse scenario: an external contractor's BTP account remains active after engagement end, still holding role collections that allow access to apps, APIs or destinations that proxy into backend data — the contractor (or anyone who obtains the credentials) can continue to reach business functions with no S/4 login ever appearing. Impact is unmanaged standing access, potential data exposure through BTP services, and a governance gap that identity audits will flag. A real incident looks like a former consultant retaining BTP access months after leaving, used to pull data through an OData API that routes to S/4.
Affected Items (10)
  • JSMITH@COMPANY.COM (roles: Subaccount Viewer, Launchpad_User)
  • AGARCIA@COMPANY.COM (roles: Subaccount Viewer)
  • MWILSON@COMPANY.COM (roles: Subaccount_Admin, Security_Admin, Destination_Admin)
  • DLEE@COMPANY.COM (roles: Launchpad_User)
  • LWANG@COMPANY.COM (roles: Global_Account_Admin, Subaccount_Admin, Security_Admin)
  • EXT_CONSULTANT1@PARTNER.COM (roles: Subaccount_Admin, Space_Developer)
  • EXT_DEVOPS@VENDOR.IO (roles: Space_Developer, Connectivity_Admin)
  • OLD_ADMIN@COMPANY.COM (roles: Subaccount_Admin)
  • TNGUYEN@COMPANY.COM (roles: Launchpad_User)
  • TEST_USER_BTP@COMPANY.COM (roles: Subaccount Viewer)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Export the BTP subaccount user and role-collection list (BTP cockpit > Security > Users, or via the SCIM/authorization API) and reconcile against the S/4 user master to review each BTP-only account. 2. For each, confirm business justification with the responsible team; remove orphaned or unrecognized accounts in the BTP cockpit. 3. Establish centralized identity governance across S/4 and BTP using SAP Cloud Identity Services — Identity Authentication (IAS) as the single IdP and Identity Provisioning (IPS) with SCIM to provision/deprovision consistently. 4. Bring external/consultant identities into the same lifecycle (sponsored accounts with expiry) rather than standalone BTP entries. 5. Add BTP users to the periodic access review scope so BTP-only identities are re-justified each cycle. 6. Verify by re-running the comparison after cleanup and confirming remaining BTP-only users are documented exceptions. 7. Rollout caution: confirm an account is truly orphaned (not a needed technical/integration user) before deletion, coordinate with the extension/development team, and change in a controlled window to avoid breaking running BTP apps or destinations.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 Federated identities are auto-created with no evidence of de-provisioning IAM-FED-004 ▶
Security Risk
2 trust configuration(s) create a BTP identity automatically the first time a user authenticates, and nothing in the supplied exports evidences an automated provisioning integration (SAP Cloud Identity Services / Identity Provisioning, or any SCIM client) that would remove those identities again. Shadow-user creation is one-directional: disabling a person's account in the corporate directory does not delete the BTP principal it created, nor its role collections, nor tokens already issued to it. After an HR leaver event the identity therefore survives — invisible to the corporate directory that everyone reviews, and reachable through any trust or local credential that does not consult it. This is the commonest way a federated SAP landscape ends up with access that belongs to nobody. Note this reports what the exports could not show: if provisioning IS configured, the export that carries it was not supplied.
Affected Items (2)
  • Trust: sap.default — shadow users created automatically
  • Trust: corp-aad-tenant — shadow users created automatically
Remediation — Step by Step
Wire de-provisioning, then evidence it. Configure SAP Cloud Identity Services (Identity Provisioning) or another SCIM client to read the authoritative HR/directory source and to DELETE or deactivate BTP shadow users when the source identity is disabled — read-only provisioning that only creates is the failure this finding describes. Confirm the job runs on a schedule and that its failures alert somebody. Until it exists, reconcile BTP users against the corporate directory on the same cadence as your access reviews and remove identities with no active source record. Re-run the scan with the communication arrangement or IAS provisioning configuration included in the export so the control can be seen.

MEDIUM P3 · 34 Stale Cloud Connector backends (90+ days unused) BTP-CC-007 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found Cloud Connector backend mappings that are stale - unused beyond the idle threshold or in a disabled/inactive/disconnected state. Stale mappings are a quiet but real risk because they represent standing configuration for connections nobody uses or monitors. A disabled or long-idle backend often still carries its full resource allowlist and its associated technical user on the on-premise side, and it may point to a system that has been decommissioned, migrated, or repurposed. The danger emerges when such an entry is re-enabled (accidentally, or by an attacker who has gained SCC admin or has compromised a bound app) and suddenly re-exposes a system that has drifted out of the patch and monitoring baseline. Idle mappings also inflate the attack surface and management burden addressed in BTP-CC-003, and they undermine the accuracy of the connectivity inventory auditors rely on. Business impact is an accountability and hygiene gap: connections exist between the cloud and internal systems with no owner, no business justification, and no assurance the target is still hardened. In a real incident, an attacker enumerating the SCC configuration finds a dormant mapping to a legacy, unpatched host that has fallen off the operations team's radar and uses it as an entry point.
Affected Items (3)
  • ECC_Legacy — last used: 2024-03-15 (882d ago)
  • BW_Reporting — last used: 2025-02-28 (532d ago)
  • Dev_System_Old — last used: 2023-11-01 (1017d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the SCC admin UI, review the 'Cloud To On-Premise' mappings and the SCC 'Monitoring' data for last-access/connection state per backend. 2. Identify mappings idle beyond your threshold (for example 90 days) or in DISABLED/INACTIVE/DISCONNECTED state. 3. Confirm with the connection owner and CMDB whether the target system is still in use. 4. Delete mappings for decommissioned or genuinely unused backends, and remove their now-orphaned technical users on the on-premise side (SU01) and any dedicated ICF exposure (SICF). 5. For backends that are temporarily idle but still required, document the justification and owner rather than leaving them unmanaged. 6. Export/archive the SCC configuration before deleting so it can be reinstated if needed. 7. Enable SCC audit logging to the SIEM so any future re-enablement of a mapping is alerted. 8. Establish a recurring review (quarterly) of idle and disabled mappings. 9. Verify by re-exporting the configuration and confirming the stale entries are gone and the backend count is minimal. 10. Rollout caution: coordinate with interface owners and check for low-frequency scheduled jobs (month-end, year-end interfaces) before deleting, since 'idle for 90 days' can still mean an annual process.
