MEDIUM P3 · 34 Orphaned service bindings (deleted/failed instances) BTP-SB-003 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found orphaned service bindings - bindings or service keys that reference a service instance which is deleted, failed, deprovisioned, or in an error state. Orphaned credentials are dangerous because deleting or failing a service instance does not always guarantee that previously issued credentials are invalidated or cleaned up, and even when access is broken, the credential material (clientid/clientsecret, certificates, URLs) may still exist in application configs, secret stores, logs and repositories. This leaves standing, unmanaged secrets with no clear owner and no lifecycle: they are not rotated, not monitored, and not part of any access review, yet they may grant access to a re-created instance with the same name or to residual data. Attack scenario: an attacker or careless operator recreates a service instance with a familiar name and an old, leaked binding secret unexpectedly regains validity, or the orphaned credential still resolves against backing infrastructure that was not fully torn down, giving unaudited access. More broadly, orphaned bindings pollute the inventory that governance and audit depend on, masking which identities can reach which services. Business impact is unmanaged machine access and a hygiene/compliance gap under the SAP Security Baseline and ISO 27001 access-management controls. A real incident emerges when a forgotten binding, long presumed dead, is found to still authenticate during an investigation.
Affected Items (1)
  • old-test-binding (service: xsuaa) — instance status: DELETED
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List all service bindings/keys and correlate each to its service instance state using the BTP cockpit, btp CLI, or Service Manager API. 2. Identify bindings whose instance status is DELETED, FAILED, DEPROVISIONED, or ORPHANED. 3. Delete the orphaned bindings/service keys explicitly (btp CLI / Service Manager API / `cf delete-service-key`). 4. Remove the corresponding secret references from application configuration, the Credential Store, CI/CD variables and any repositories. 5. For instances stuck in FAILED state, resolve or purge the instance itself so no dangling backing resources remain. 6. Implement deprovisioning hooks/automation so bindings are always deleted before or with their parent instance. 7. Rotate/revoke any credential that may have leaked while orphaned. 8. Enable BTP Audit Log and alert on token issuance for identities tied to deleted instances. 9. Verify by re-running the inventory and confirming no binding references a non-active instance, and confirm the old credential no longer authenticates. 10. Rollout caution: before deletion, confirm the instance is genuinely retired (not merely mid-recreation) with the owning team, to avoid removing a binding that an in-flight redeploy still needs.
References
  • SAP BTP — Service Instance Lifecycle
MEDIUM P3 · 34 BTP destinations with proxy type mismatch BTP-DST-003 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found BTP destinations whose ProxyType does not match the nature of their target URL - for example ProxyType=OnPremise pointing at an apparently internet URL, or ProxyType=Internet pointing at an apparently on-premise address. ProxyType controls the network path the connectivity service uses: OnPremise routes the call through the Cloud Connector tunnel into the corporate network, while Internet routes it directly out to public endpoints. A mismatch is a symptom of misconfiguration that carries security consequences. If a destination that should traverse the controlled Cloud Connector path is instead set to Internet, traffic to what is meant to be an internal system may be pushed onto the public internet, exposing it outside the intended trust boundary. Conversely, an Internet target incorrectly flagged OnPremise can be used to probe or reach internal hosts through the tunnel, contributing to SSRF-style pivoting if the URL is attacker-influenced. Beyond security, mismatches cause intermittent routing failures that operators may 'fix' by relaxing other controls. Attack scenario: a destination whose ProxyType and URL disagree either leaks internal-bound traffic to the internet or provides an unexpected route into the on-premise network that bypasses the assumptions built into firewall and Cloud Connector rules. Business impact is unintended network exposure and weakened segmentation; the finding also flags configuration drift that undermines an accurate connectivity inventory. A real incident may involve internal data being sent to a public endpoint because a destination was mislabeled.
Affected Items (2)
  • Test_System_Old → https://10.0.3.10/sap/opu — ProxyType=Internet but URL appears on-premise
  • Analytics_DWC → https://mycompany.eu10.hcs.cloud.sap — ProxyType=Internet but URL appears on-premise
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, Connectivity > Destinations, list destinations and compare each ProxyType against its URL/host. 2. For destinations targeting on-premise systems reachable via the Cloud Connector, set ProxyType=OnPremise and confirm the virtual host matches an SCC mapping. 3. For destinations targeting public/cloud endpoints, set ProxyType=Internet. 4. For SAP Private Link targets, use ProxyType=PrivateLink where applicable. 5. Correct any destination where the URL indicates a different network path than the configured ProxyType. 6. Verify each corrected destination with 'Check Connection' and confirm it resolves through the intended path (SCC monitoring shows the call for OnPremise; it should not appear there for Internet). 7. Cross-check that OnPremise destinations only reference virtual hosts that exist in the Cloud Connector allowlist, closing any route to undocumented internal hosts. 8. Ensure destination URLs are not built from unvalidated user input to prevent SSRF via the connectivity proxy. 9. Re-run the scanner to confirm no proxy-type mismatches remain. 10. Rollout caution: change and test in a non-production destination first and coordinate with interface owners, since altering ProxyType changes routing and can break a working integration if the corresponding SCC mapping or public egress is not in place.
References
  • SAP BTP Destination Service — Proxy Configuration
MEDIUM P3 · 34 IAS applications without conditional authentication rules BTP-IAS-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication (IAS) applications with no conditional authentication (authentication) rules defined. Conditional authentication is the IAS mechanism that varies the authenticating identity provider and the required assurance based on context - user group, corporate versus external network (IP range), authentication method, and the specific application. Without any rules, every user of the application authenticates through a single, uniform flow regardless of who they are, where they connect from, or how sensitive the operation is. This flattens the risk posture: an administrator signing in from an untrusted network is treated identically to a read-only user on the corporate LAN, and there is no ability to route privileged access to a stronger IdP or to block risky contexts. Attack scenario: an attacker who has phished or password-sprayed a credential can authenticate to the application from anywhere, because no rule forces a stronger factor or restricts the source for that user group; the same weakness prevents the organization from confining admin logon to trusted networks. Business impact is a missed opportunity to enforce risk-appropriate access on business-critical Fiori/BTP applications, weakening defense against account takeover and failing least-privilege and adaptive-access expectations in the SAP Security Baseline and identity-governance frameworks. A real incident looks like a compromised standard credential used to reach a sensitive application from an anomalous location that a conditional rule would have challenged or denied.
Affected Items (4)
  • BTP_Admin_Cockpit (type: standard)
  • Integration_Suite (type: standard)
  • Build_WorkZone (type: standard)
  • Custom_App_Portal (type: standard)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Log on to the IAS administration console (https://<tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/admin) with an administrator account. 2. Go to Applications & Resources > Applications and select each business-critical application. 3. Open Authentication and Access > Conditional Authentication. 4. Define rules that select the identity provider and assurance based on context: user group/type, IP range (corporate vs external), and authentication method. 5. Route privileged/admin user groups to a stronger flow (e.g. corporate IdP plus MFA) and, where appropriate, restrict or block untrusted sources. 6. Set a safe default action for users not matching a rule. 7. Combine with the IP-range restriction (see BTP-IAS-002) and MFA (see BTP-IAS-003) for layered adaptive access. 8. Save and test with representative accounts (an admin from an external IP, a standard user from the corporate range) to confirm the rules route correctly. 9. Verify via the IAS login/audit logs that authentications are matching the intended rules. 10. Rollout caution: validate rules against a test/pilot application or user group first, since an over-restrictive conditional rule can lock out legitimate users or the administrators themselves - keep an emergency-access administrator path.
References
  • SAP IAS — Conditional Authentication
MEDIUM P3 · 34 IAS applications without IP-based access restrictions BTP-IAS-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found IAS applications with no IP-based access restrictions configured, meaning users can authenticate to the application from any network location on the internet. For business applications - especially administrative consoles, backend/technical apps, and privileged BTP tooling - unrestricted source access removes a simple but effective control that limits where credentials can be used. Without an IP allowlist, a stolen credential or session is usable from anywhere, and the organization cannot confine sensitive access to corporate networks or approved VPN ranges. Attack scenario: after phishing or purchasing a valid credential, an attacker authenticates to the application directly from their own infrastructure; because no IP rule constrains the source, the only remaining barrier is the password (and MFA, if configured). For internet-exposed admin or integration applications this materially widens the window for credential-stuffing, password-spray and account-takeover attacks and enables access from geographies the business never operates in. Business impact is elevated account-takeover risk on cloud applications and a gap against network-based access controls expected by the SAP Security Baseline and many regulatory regimes for privileged access. A real incident presents as successful logons to a sensitive application from foreign or hosting-provider IP ranges that a network restriction would have blocked outright.
Affected Items (5)
  • S4HANA_Fiori_Launchpad (type: standard)
  • Integration_Suite (type: standard)
  • Build_WorkZone (type: standard)
  • Analytics_Cloud (type: standard)
  • Custom_App_Portal (type: standard)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the IAS admin console, open Applications & Resources > Applications and select each application, prioritizing admin/backend/privileged apps. 2. Under Authentication and Access, configure an allowed IP range (via the IP-range restriction or a Conditional Authentication rule that permits only corporate/VPN CIDR ranges). 3. At minimum, restrict administrative and technical applications to corporate egress IPs or the approved VPN ranges; apply broader-but-still-bounded ranges to general user apps as feasible. 4. Coordinate the exact CIDR list with the network team, accounting for VPN, proxy egress, and office locations. 5. Combine IP rules with MFA and conditional authentication so remote users can still be granted access under stronger assurance rather than a blanket allow. 6. Save and test from an in-range and an out-of-range client to confirm enforcement. 7. Verify via IAS login/audit logs that out-of-range attempts are blocked and in-range succeed. 8. Document the allowlist and its owner, and review it when network egress changes. 9. Rollout caution: pilot on a non-critical application first and confirm all legitimate source ranges (including cloud/CI egress and mobile VPN) are included before applying to production, to avoid locking out valid users or administrators - retain an emergency-access path.
References
  • SAP IAS — IP Range Restrictions
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Security-critical BTP services entitled but not provisioned BTP-ENT-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found security-critical BTP services that are entitled but not provisioned - services such as Audit Log (Management/Viewer), Credential Store, Malware Scanner, Cloud Logging, and Alert Notification that are available to the account yet have no running instances. Unlike ordinary unused entitlements, these are controls the organization should be actively using, so their absence is a gap in the security baseline rather than merely idle capability. Without the Audit Log service properly consumed and retained, security-relevant events and configuration changes are not durably captured for investigation or compliance. Without the Credential Store, applications tend to embed secrets in code or destinations (feeding findings like BTP-CPI-003 and BTP-DST-001). Without the Malware Scanner, file uploads into BTP apps are not screened, and without Cloud Logging/Alert Notification, telemetry never reaches the SIEM and no one is alerted to incidents. Attack scenario: an attacker operating in a subaccount that lacks audit logging and alerting can perform reconnaissance, privilege changes, and data access with little chance of detection or forensic reconstruction, because the very services that would record and surface the activity were never turned on. Business impact is a monitoring and secret-management blind spot that undermines incident response and fails SOX, GDPR and ISO 27001 logging/monitoring requirements as well as the SAP Security Baseline's essential-services guidance. A real incident is one that goes undetected or cannot be reconstructed because the audit and logging controls were entitled but never provisioned.
Affected Items (6)
  • auditlog/premium — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • credstore/standard — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • malware-scanner/cav — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • cloud-logging/standard — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • alert-notification/standard — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • privatelink/standard — entitled: 2, used: 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, identify the security-critical entitlements with no instances (Audit Log, Credential Store, Malware Scanner, Cloud Logging, Alert Notification). 2. Provision and configure the Audit Log service in every subaccount and set an appropriate retention (via the Audit Log Retention API / Audit Log Management service) to meet compliance requirements; forward logs to your SIEM. 3. Provision the Credential Store and migrate embedded secrets from destinations and iFlows into it (supports remediation of BTP-DST-001 and BTP-CPI-003). 4. Provision the Malware Scanning service and integrate it into any application flow that accepts file uploads. 5. Provision Cloud Logging (and Alert Notification) to stream telemetry and route alerts to the operations/SOC tooling. 6. Assign clear ownership for each service and confirm the consuming applications are bound and functioning. 7. Verify each service is running (Instances and Subscriptions) and producing output - confirm audit events appear in the SIEM and a test alert fires. 8. Add these services to the standard subaccount provisioning blueprint so new subaccounts inherit them by default. 9. Rollout caution: enable audit logging and forwarding first (highest value, lowest risk), then roll out credential-store and scanner integration in coordination with app teams; validate SIEM ingestion volumes so log forwarding does not overwhelm downstream systems.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Recommendations — Essential Services
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Event Mesh queues subscribing to foreign namespaces BTP-EM-003 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found Event Mesh queues subscribing to topics in a namespace different from the queue's own namespace. In Event Mesh, the message namespace is an isolation construct that scopes events to a business domain, application, or environment. A cross-namespace subscription means events are flowing from one domain into a consumer belonging to another, which may be entirely intentional in a deliberately shared architecture but is often a sign of misconfiguration or scope creep that erodes domain isolation. The risk is that events - which can carry sensitive business or personal data - cross a boundary that governance, data-classification, or regulatory separation intended to keep distinct (for example HR events reaching a logistics domain, or production events reaching a non-production consumer). Undocumented cross-namespace flows also complicate impact analysis and incident response, because a change or breach in one domain can propagate through unexpected event paths into another. Attack scenario: a consumer in a lower-trust namespace subscribes to a higher-sensitivity namespace's topics and quietly receives data it should not, or a mistaken subscription bridges production and non-production, allowing test/compromised consumers to observe real business events. Business impact is data-segregation and confidentiality risk (a GDPR and data-governance concern) and loss of the clean domain boundaries the architecture assumed. A real incident is the discovery, during an audit or investigation, that sensitive events were being delivered across a namespace boundary nobody had approved.
Affected Items (8)
  • Queue: s4hana/salesorder/created — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/s4)
  • Queue: integration/events/all — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/s4)
  • Queue: integration/events/all — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/s4)
  • Queue: finance/journal/posted — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/s4)
  • Queue: cross_domain/ariba — subscribes to foreign namespace: ariba (own: sap/s4)
  • Queue: cross_domain/ariba — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/s4)
  • Queue: hr/employee/all — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/sf)
  • Queue: hr/employee/all — subscribes to foreign namespace: sap (own: sap/sf)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the Event Mesh dashboard / Management API, list queues with their namespace and the namespaces of their subscribed topics. 2. For each cross-namespace subscription, confirm with the domain/application owners whether the cross-domain event flow is intentional and approved. 3. Remove unintended cross-namespace subscriptions and re-scope the consumer to its own namespace's topics. 4. For flows that are legitimately cross-domain, document the data classification, purpose, and owner of the shared events, and confirm access is authorized (see BTP-EM-002). 5. Where isolation is required (for example production vs non-production, or regulated vs general data), use separate Event Mesh instances rather than cross-namespace subscriptions. 6. Ensure queue access policies and subscription scopes enforce the intended boundaries. 7. Save and test that only approved namespaces are consumed. 8. Verify via monitoring that cross-namespace delivery matches the documented, approved flows only. 9. Establish periodic review of namespace subscriptions. 10. Rollout caution: validate in non-production and coordinate with both the producing and consuming domain owners before removing a subscription, since an undocumented cross-namespace flow may support a real (if unsanctioned) integration that would break.
References
  • SAP Event Mesh — Namespace Isolation
MEDIUM P3 · 34 CPI credentials using basic/plaintext authentication BTP-CPI-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found CPI security material using basic username/password or plaintext credential types (PLAIN_TEXT, USER_CREDENTIAL, BASIC). Basic-auth and plaintext credentials are static shared secrets: they do not expire on their own, cannot be scoped or revoked granularly, and are transmitted (over TLS) as reusable passwords. Compared with modern OAuth 2.0 client credentials or X.509 certificate-based authentication, they offer weaker assurance, no built-in short lifetime, and poorer attribution, and they encourage credential reuse across systems. In an integration context these credentials often reach sensitive targets (backends, databases, partner SFTP/AS2 endpoints), so a compromised static password provides straightforward, persistent access. Attack scenario: an attacker who obtains a basic credential - through an export, a log, a transported artifact, or over-broad tenant access - authenticates directly to the target system as the integration user and operates with its authorizations, with no token expiry to limit the window and no certificate binding to constrain where it can be used. Static basic credentials are also more likely to be reused, so one leak can unlock several endpoints. Business impact is elevated risk of durable unauthorized access to backends and partners, weaker auditability, and a gap against the SAP Security Baseline and CPI security best practices, which call for token- or certificate-based authentication. A real incident involves a shared basic-auth integration password being reused by an attacker against the backend it was meant only for CPI to reach.
Affected Items (3)
  • SF_EC_Credential (type: USER_CREDENTIAL) — consider migrating to OAuth or certificate
  • Ariba_API_Key (type: PLAIN_TEXT) — consider migrating to OAuth or certificate
  • Legacy_ECC_Basic (type: BASIC) — consider migrating to OAuth or certificate
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, Manage Security > Security Material, list credentials of type User Credentials/Basic/plaintext. 2. For each, determine whether the target endpoint supports OAuth 2.0 (client credentials or SAML bearer) or X.509 client-certificate authentication. 3. Migrate to OAuth2 Credentials or certificate-based authentication: create the corresponding security material and update the iFlow receiver channel's authentication accordingly. 4. For backend ABAP/S4 targets, prefer OAuth2SAMLBearer or certificate-based flows over basic auth; configure the trust on the backend as needed. 5. Use the BTP Credential Store service for centralized secret management where applicable. 6. Where basic auth is genuinely unavoidable (legacy partner), minimize the account's privileges at the target and rotate it frequently (see BTP-CPI-001). 7. Remove the obsolete plaintext/basic security material once the new method works. 8. Verify by deploying and executing the affected iFlow and confirming successful authentication via the new mechanism, checking Monitor Message Processing. 9. Rollout caution: test the new authentication in a non-production tenant and coordinate with each target/partner owner (OAuth client registration or certificate trust must be set up on their side first) to avoid interrupting production message flows.
References
  • SAP CPI Security Best Practices
MEDIUM P3 · 34 BTP subaccounts using default SAP IDP only BTP-GOV-002 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found BTP subaccounts relying solely on the default SAP Identity Provider (SAP ID service / sap.default / sap.ids) without a custom corporate identity provider configured. When a subaccount trusts only the default SAP IdP, users authenticate with SAP IDs (self-registered or SAP-managed accounts) rather than corporate credentials governed by the enterprise identity system. This bypasses centralized identity governance: corporate password and MFA policies, conditional access, joiner-mover-leaver deprovisioning, and central logging do not apply. The most acute risk is lifecycle: when an employee leaves, their corporate account is disabled centrally, but an SAP-ID-based account in the subaccount may persist, leaving orphaned access. Default-IdP accounts also typically escape the organization's MFA and conditional-access enforcement and are not covered by central access reviews. Attack scenario: a former employee or contractor whose corporate identity was deprovisioned retains a still-active SAP-ID login to the subaccount and re-enters to access data or systems; or an attacker targets the weaker, self-service default-IdP authentication (often lacking enterprise MFA/conditional access) to compromise an account, because the strong controls enforced on corporate identities are absent. Business impact is fragmented identity governance, orphaned/unmanaged access, weaker authentication assurance, and non-compliance with SOX access-management, GDPR accountability, and the SAP Security Baseline recommendation to federate BTP to a corporate IdP (typically via SAP IAS). A real incident involves access via a default-IdP account that should have been deprovisioned or that never met corporate authentication standards.
Affected Items (2)
  • Development (sa-dev-003, region: eu10)
  • Sandbox (sa-sbx-004, region: us10)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, for each subaccount open Security > Trust Configuration and review the configured identity providers. 2. Establish trust to a corporate IdP: configure SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication (IAS) as the trusted IdP for the subaccount, and configure IAS to federate to the corporate IdP (Azure AD/Entra ID, Okta, etc.) as a Corporate Identity Provider (proxy IdP model). 3. Use IAS as the single proxy so conditional authentication, MFA, and IP restrictions are enforced consistently across all subaccounts. 4. Once the corporate/IAS trust is validated, disable or restrict new logins via the default SAP ID service where business scenarios allow, keeping it only for genuine external users if needed. 5. Ensure joiner-mover-leaver provisioning flows through the corporate IdP / Identity Provisioning so access is deprovisioned centrally. 6. Map role collections to corporate groups delivered via the federated assertion. 7. Test SSO end-to-end with a corporate account and confirm MFA/conditional rules apply. 8. Verify that a deprovisioned corporate user can no longer authenticate to the subaccount. 9. Add corporate-IdP trust to the standard subaccount setup blueprint. 10. Rollout caution: configure and test the new trust in a non-production subaccount first and retain an emergency-access administrator (a platform user not dependent on the new federation) before restricting the default IdP, to avoid a lockout during cutover.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — Identity Federation
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Applications still using XSUAA authentication (not migrated to IAS) BTP-MIG-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found applications still using XSUAA-based authentication (auth/trust type XSUAA or LEGACY) rather than SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication (IAS). XSUAA (the Authorization and Trust Management service) remains valid for authorization and token issuance, but SAP's strategic direction is to front user authentication with IAS and use XSUAA behind it for authorization, establishing trust between IAS and XSUAA. Applications that authenticate users directly against XSUAA without IAS in front miss the advanced, centralized security capabilities IAS provides: conditional authentication, risk-based authentication, corporate-IdP federation, consistent MFA enforcement, and centralized policy and branding across applications. The result is fragmented, weaker, and less adaptive authentication for those apps, and inconsistent policy compared with IAS-fronted applications. Attack scenario: because an XSUAA-only app cannot enforce the conditional/risk-based rules and consistent MFA that IAS applies, a compromised credential can be used against it under weaker conditions than the organization enforces elsewhere - for example without the IP-based challenge or step-up MFA an IAS policy would impose - making it the soft target among the application portfolio, particularly if it is an administrative or sensitive app. Business impact is inconsistent authentication assurance across the landscape, reduced ability to enforce adaptive access and central identity governance, and misalignment with SAP's recommended architecture and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident involves an attacker preferentially targeting the XSUAA-only application because it lacks the stronger, centrally managed authentication controls applied to migrated apps.
Affected Items (2)
  • Integration_Suite — auth: XSUAA, trust: XSUAA
  • Build_WorkZone — auth: XSUAA, trust: LEGACY
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory applications and their authentication/trust configuration to confirm which still authenticate directly via XSUAA (LEGACY trust) without IAS in front. 2. Establish trust between SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) and the subaccount's XSUAA/Authorization and Trust Management service, following the SAP guide for establishing trust between the Authorization and Trust Management service and Identity Authentication. 3. Configure IAS as the authenticating identity provider (with the corporate IdP federated behind it) so users authenticate through IAS while XSUAA continues to handle authorization/role collections. 4. Migrate applications to use the IAS-fronted flow, prioritizing administrative and security-sensitive applications first. 5. Apply IAS conditional authentication, risk-based authentication, IP restrictions, and MFA to the migrated applications (see BTP-IAS-001/002/003). 6. Validate role-collection mapping continues to work via the IAS-to-XSUAA trust after cutover. 7. Test each migrated application's login and authorization end-to-end in non-production. 8. Verify via IAS login/audit logs that authentication now flows through IAS and that the intended policies are enforced. 9. Decommission the direct XSUAA-only authentication path once migration is confirmed. 10. Rollout caution: perform the trust establishment and app migration in a non-production subaccount first, coordinate with application owners, and keep an emergency-access path, since changing the trust/authentication chain can disrupt user login and role assignment if role-collection mappings are not correctly re-established before cutover.
References
  • SAP BTP — Migration from XSUAA to Identity Authentication
  • SAP Blog — Establishing Trust Between IAS and BTP
MEDIUM P3 · 34 IDOC file ports with insecure directory paths INTG-IDOC-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags IDOC file ports (WE21) whose output directory is a commonly accessible or temporary path such as /tmp, /var/tmp, C:\temp, /usr/sap, or /sapmnt. File ports write IDOC content to the file system as flat files that other processes then pick up; if that directory is world-readable or shared, the IDOC data is exposed to any OS user or process on the host. IDOC files can contain the same sensitive content as any other IDOC - financial documents, master data, HR records - so a weak directory is an offline data-leak channel that bypasses all SAP application-layer authorization. Attack scenario: a low-privileged OS account (or a compromised co-hosted application) reads the /tmp spool directory and harvests every IDOC written there, or worse, modifies an outbound IDOC file before the downstream job consumes it, injecting fraudulent orders or payments. World-writable temp locations also invite tampering, symlink attacks, and race conditions during file creation. Storing IDOCs under /usr/sap or /sapmnt risks mixing business data into shared SAP mount points that may be broadly accessible across the landscape or backed up to less-controlled locations. Business impact: confidentiality breach and potential data integrity/fraud, plus a file-system-permission audit failure against the SAP Security Guide and hardening baselines. A real incident looks like sensitive IDOC files found in a shared temp path during a host review, or downstream postings that do not match what SAP believes it sent. Because file ports run unattended, exposure persists silently until cleanup or discovery. This is rated medium because exploitation requires local/OS access, but it is a genuine and preventable data-at-rest exposure.
Affected Items (2)
  • FILE_BANK (type: FILE) — path: /tmp/idoc_bank/inbound
  • FILE_ARCHIVE (type: FILE) — path: /sapmnt/PRD/idoc_archive
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In WE21, open each flagged file port and note its configured directory (and any logical file path from transaction FILE). 2. Repoint the port to a dedicated, access-controlled directory owned by the SAP administrator account, outside /tmp, /var/tmp, /usr/sap, and /sapmnt. 3. Set restrictive OS permissions on that directory (owner <sid>adm, mode 700 / no group or world access) so only the SAP work processes can read and write it. 4. If a logical file name is used, harden it in transaction FILE and validate against the physical path, and review sapftp/sapgui file access parameters. 5. Ensure the directory is on a volume that is not a broadly shared network mount and is covered by controlled, encrypted backups. 6. Add file-system monitoring/alerting for unexpected readers of the directory. 7. Where feasible, migrate the file-based interface to a transport-secured port (SFTP, or an RFC/HTTP port with SNC/TLS) to remove the at-rest exposure entirely. 8. Verify by writing a test IDOC (WE19) and confirming the file lands only in the secured directory with correct ownership/permissions. 9. Verify no residual sensitive IDOC files remain in the old temp path, and securely purge them. 10. Roll out in non-prod first and coordinate with the downstream file-pickup job owner so the new path is consumed correctly. Caution: changing the path without updating the downstream job will silently break the interface - synchronise both sides.
References
  • SAP Security Guide — File System Permissions
MEDIUM P3 · 34 IDOC partner profiles configured for sensitive message types INTG-IDOC-004 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags IDOC partner profiles (WE20) configured for sensitive message types - HR master (HRMD_A), payment orders (PEXR2002), bank statements (FINSTA01), customer/vendor/material master (DEBMAS, CREMAS, MATMAS), accounting documents (ACC_DOCUMENT), orders (ORDERS), and goods movements (WMMBXY). These IDOC types carry the organization's most sensitive and highest-impact data, so any weakness in their transport, authorization, or monitoring translates directly into privacy, fraud, or integrity risk. The finding itself is not proof of misconfiguration, but it marks interfaces that demand elevated controls: encryption in transit, strict partner authorization, and active monitoring. Attack scenario: if such a profile is combined with an unencrypted port, an attacker can intercept and alter a PEXR2002 to redirect a payment, or read an HRMD_A to harvest employee PII; if combined with weak partner-user authorization, a spoofed partner can inject fraudulent CREMAS (vendor) records to enable invoice fraud. Vendor/customer master injection (CREMAS/DEBMAS) is a well-known fraud vector - create a fake vendor, then post and pay an invoice to it. Business impact: financial fraud, GDPR exposure for HR/customer data, and SOX-relevant integrity issues on master data and postings. A real incident looks like a fraudulent vendor bank change delivered by IDOC, or bulk PII leaving via an HR interface, discovered only after payment or breach. Because these flows are automated and high-volume, malicious or erroneous IDOCs post quickly and at scale. This is rated medium as a flag for scrutiny, but the underlying data class makes it a priority for defence-in-depth.
Affected Items (7)
  • Partner: ARIBA_CLOUD (LS) — ORDERS via port TRFC_ARIBA (OUTBOUND)
  • Partner: SF_EC (LS) — HRMD_A via port HTTP_SF (OUTBOUND)
  • Partner: BANK_01 (KU) — FINSTA01 via port FILE_BANK (INBOUND)
  • Partner: BANK_01 (KU) — PEXR2002 via port FILE_BANK (OUTBOUND)
  • Partner: VENDOR_X (LI) — CREMAS via port XML_VENDOR (INBOUND)
  • Partner: BW_SYSTEM (LS) — WMMBXY via port TRFC_BW (OUTBOUND)
  • Partner: CPI_BROKER (LS) — ACC_DOCUMENT via port HTTP_CPI (OUTBOUND)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In WE20, list each partner profile carrying a sensitive message type and record the direction, port, and process code. 2. Confirm each of these interfaces uses encrypted transport - SNC for RFC/tRFC ports or TLS/HTTPS for HTTP ports (see INTG-IDOC-001). 3. Verify the partner's technical/communication user is least-privileged and authorized only for these specific message types (auth objects B_ALE_RECV, S_IDOCDEFT), not broadly. 4. Validate that the receiving/sending partner is genuinely authorized for the data classification (e.g. PII, financial) per data-governance policy. 5. For master-data types prone to fraud (CREMAS/DEBMAS), enforce dual-control or downstream review on bank-account and critical field changes. 6. Enable IDOC monitoring and alerting for these message types (failed and successful) using SM58, WE05/WE02 review, and BD87 for reprocessing control. 7. Ensure IDOC processing errors route to a monitored workflow rather than silently queueing. 8. Verify by sending a controlled test IDOC (WE19) end to end and confirming encryption, authorization, and alerting all trigger correctly. 9. Add these interfaces to the SIEM feed so anomalies correlate with other security events (see INTG-MON-002). 10. Review the partner list periodically as part of interface governance. Caution: make monitoring/alerting changes in non-prod first to tune thresholds and avoid alert fatigue on high-volume flows.
References
  • SAP IDOC Security — Sensitive Data Handling
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Webhooks delivering events to external/third-party endpoints INTG-WH-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags webhooks that deliver business events to endpoints outside the recognized corporate/BTP domains (i.e. external third-party destinations). Outbound webhooks to external domains are a data-egress channel: every triggered event carries business data across the corporate trust boundary to a third party, whether or not that flow was formally reviewed or authorized. The risk is twofold - the destination may not be authorized to receive the data classification involved, and an external endpoint is outside the organization's control, so its security posture and data handling cannot be assured. Attack scenario: an insider or a compromised integration account registers (or repoints) a webhook to an attacker-controlled external URL, quietly exfiltrating a continuous stream of order, customer, or financial events; because it is 'just another webhook', it can blend into normal integration traffic and evade notice for a long time. Even without malice, an unreviewed external webhook can constitute an unlawful transfer of personal data to a third country or unapproved processor. Business impact: data leakage and GDPR/data-residency violations (unauthorized processor / cross-border transfer), loss of confidential business intelligence, and audit findings on data-flow governance. A real incident looks like sensitive event data discovered flowing to an unknown external domain, or a regulator query about a transfer no one approved. This is rated medium because external delivery can be entirely legitimate - the point is that each such flow must be explicitly authorized and constrained. Unreviewed external egress is the concern, not external delivery per se.
Affected Items (5)
  • SalesOrder_Created → https://integration.company.com/hooks/so-created
  • Vendor_Updated → http://middleware.company.com/hooks/vendor
  • Payment_Processed → https://external-bank-api.com/webhooks/payment-notify
  • Invoice_Approved → https://ariba.procurement.com/callback/invoice
  • Test_Hook_Old → https://test.company.com/hooks/test
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the list of external-destination webhooks flagged and map each to a business owner and a documented purpose. 2. For each, confirm formal authorization: is the third party an approved processor, and does the data classification permit egress and (if PII) cross-border transfer under GDPR? 3. Remove or repoint any webhook that lacks authorization or whose destination cannot be justified. 4. For approved flows, minimize the payload to only the fields the third party genuinely needs (data minimization). 5. Constrain the destination: enforce HTTPS (INTG-WH-001), HMAC signing (INTG-WH-002), and, where the platform supports it, IP allowlisting to the partner's published ranges. 6. Record each authorized external flow in the data-flow/RoPA register with legal basis and DPA reference. 7. Establish an approval gate so new external webhook registrations require security/privacy sign-off. 8. Verify by reviewing delivery logs that events go only to the approved external endpoints and nowhere else. 9. Feed webhook registration changes and delivery destinations into the SIEM to detect unauthorized repointing. 10. Re-review external webhooks periodically as part of integration governance. Caution: coordinate with the interface/business owner before disabling any external webhook, as legitimate partner integrations may depend on it - stage in non-prod and confirm impact first.
References
  • Data Classification — Outbound Event Controls
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Integration events not forwarded to SIEM INTG-MON-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags that integration monitoring events are not forwarded to a SIEM. The SIEM is where security-relevant signals from across the estate are correlated; if integration events (CPI runtime logs, API Management access logs, Event Mesh audit logs, Cloud Connector logs, gateway/RFC and IDOC events) never reach it, the integration layer becomes a blind spot for the security operations center. Without SIEM correlation, an attack that spans the integration layer and other systems - for example an OAuth token abused at the API gateway and then used to pivot into S/4HANA - cannot be detected as a single campaign, because no single tool sees both halves. This also breaks threat-hunting, incident forensics, and the ability to meet detection/response SLAs, because the relevant logs are siloed in each BTP service with short retention and no cross-correlation. Attack scenario: an attacker abuses an API and an RFC destination; each component may log locally, but with no central correlation the individual events look benign and no analyst ever connects them, so the intrusion progresses undetected until impact. Business impact: extended attacker dwell time, failed incident detection/response, weaker forensic capability, and non-compliance with monitoring/logging expectations (SAP Security Baseline, SOX, and many regulatory regimes). A real incident looks like a post-breach investigation where the integration logs needed to reconstruct the attack were never centralized or had already aged out. This is rated medium because it is a visibility/coverage gap rather than a direct vulnerability, but it materially weakens detection across the landscape. Centralizing integration telemetry is a foundational SOC capability.
Affected Items (1)
  • SIEM integration: not configured
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enable audit/access logging on each integration component: Cloud Integration (CPI) runtime and audit logs, API Management access logs, Event Mesh audit logs, Cloud Connector logs, and the BTP Audit Log service. 2. On the S/4HANA side, ensure the Security Audit Log (RSAU/SM19/SM20) and gateway logs are active and captured. 3. Use the BTP Audit Log Retrieval API / Cloud Integration or a log-forwarding iFlow to ship these logs to the enterprise SIEM (e.g. Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, QRadar). 4. Normalize and map the events to your detection content so auth failures, quota breaches, and registration/program-start events become alertable. 5. Set retention in the SIEM to meet policy/regulatory requirements, since native BTP retention is short. 6. Build correlation rules linking API/OAuth events to backend S/4HANA activity for cross-layer detection. 7. Verify end to end by generating a test event (e.g. a failed API auth) and confirming it appears in the SIEM within the expected latency. 8. Confirm no sensitive payload data is over-collected; forward metadata, not full business payloads, where possible. 9. Assign SOC ownership and alerting/response runbooks for the new data sources. 10. Review coverage periodically as new integration services are added. Caution: validate the log-forwarding pipeline in non-prod first and monitor its own health - a silently broken forwarder recreates the blind spot without anyone noticing.
References
  • SAP BTP — SIEM Integration with Alert Notification
MEDIUM P3 · 34 CPI global variables with potentially sensitive names INTG-CPI-DS-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags CPI global Variables whose names suggest they hold credentials, tokens, or personal data. Global variables in Cloud Integration are intended for lightweight state (counters, last-run timestamps, correlation ids), are not encrypted, and are readable through the CPI monitoring/management API; they are the wrong place for any secret or sensitive value. A credential or token stored in a global variable is effectively a plaintext secret sitting in the integration tenant, accessible to anyone with monitoring/management authorization and to any process that can reach the management API. Attack scenario: an operator or an attacker with CPI monitoring access (or a compromised management credential) lists the global variables and reads a stored API token or password; if that token is still valid, they reuse it to call the backend system it protects, escalating from tenant access to backend access. Because variables persist across iFlow executions, the secret remains available indefinitely until explicitly overwritten, and it may also appear in traces or exported tenant content. Business impact: credential/PII exposure, potential onward system compromise via reused tokens, and non-compliance with SAP CPI credential-management guidance and general secrets-handling policy. A real incident looks like a valid backend token recovered from a CPI variable and then used to access the target system, or PII found in variable content during review. This is rated medium because exploitation requires tenant access, but a stored valid secret is a direct escalation path. Secrets must live in Security Material, never in variables.
Affected Items (2)
  • Variable: SF_API_Password — may contain sensitive data
  • Variable: bank_secret_key — may contain sensitive data
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, open Monitor → Manage Stores → Variables and identify each flagged global/local variable. 2. For any variable holding a credential, token, or key, remove that usage from the iFlow and store the secret in Monitor → Manage Security → Security Material (User Credentials, Secure Parameter, or OAuth2 Credentials). 3. Update the iFlow to fetch the secret at runtime from Security Material (e.g. via the credential name) rather than from a variable. 4. For any variable holding PII, redesign the flow to avoid persisting personal data in a variable; use an encrypted data store if persistence is genuinely required. 5. Delete the existing sensitive variable values after migration. 6. Rotate any credential/token that was exposed in a variable, since it must be treated as compromised. 7. Restrict CPI monitoring/management roles so variable access is limited to authorized administrators. 8. Verify by listing variables via the monitor/API and confirming no secret/PII values remain, and that the iFlow still authenticates correctly using Security Material. 9. Add a design-review check so future iFlows never store secrets in variables. 10. Promote via transport to the productive tenant after non-prod testing. Caution: changing where a running interface reads its credentials can break it if mis-sequenced - test the reconfigured iFlow end to end in non-prod before production cutover.
References
  • SAP CPI — Credential Management Best Practices
MEDIUM P3 · 34 OAuth clients unused for 180+ days INTG-OAUTH-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags OAuth clients that have not been used within the configured window (default 180 days), i.e. stale/unused client registrations. Every registered OAuth client is a live credential that can obtain tokens; an unused client is standing privilege with no offsetting business value, and because nobody is watching it, its abuse is unlikely to be noticed. Stale clients are a favored persistence and initial-access vector: their secrets are often old, never rotated, and may be sitting in decommissioned systems, old CI pipelines, backups, or documentation from which an attacker can recover them. Attack scenario: an attacker finds an old client secret in an archived repository or a retired server image, and because the client was never deleted, requests a valid token and quietly accesses whatever the client is scoped for; since the client is 'unused', no baseline of normal activity exists to make the sudden usage look anomalous, so it blends in. Stale clients also accumulate whatever scope weaknesses they were created with (see INTG-OAUTH-001), so a forgotten client can carry broad privileges indefinitely. Business impact: unmonitored credential exposure, a ready-made persistence mechanism for attackers, and governance/audit findings on identity lifecycle management. A real incident looks like a long-dormant client suddenly issuing tokens from an unexpected source, discovered (if at all) only after the access is abused. This is rated medium because it is latent rather than actively exploited, but stale machine identities are a common breach root cause. Disciplined client lifecycle management removes the exposure.
Affected Items (6)
  • sb-cpi-prod — last activity: 2025-03-01 (531d ago)
  • sb-apim-admin — last activity: 2025-02-20 (540d ago)
  • sb-portal-app — last activity: 2025-03-01 (531d ago)
  • sb-test-legacy — last activity: 2023-11-01 (1017d ago)
  • sb-sf-replication — last activity: 2025-03-01 (531d ago)
  • sb-ariba-sync — last activity: 2025-02-28 (532d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the flagged stale clients with their last-used/created dates from the BTP cockpit / XSUAA service instances and service keys. 2. For each, contact the owning team to confirm whether the client is still needed. 3. Delete confirmed-obsolete clients (remove the service key / client registration) and revoke their secrets. 4. For clients that are legitimately low-frequency (e.g. periodic batch), document the justification and exempt them from the staleness rule rather than deleting. 5. Rotate secrets on retained clients and verify their scopes are still minimal (cross-check against INTG-OAUTH-001). 6. Implement an OAuth client lifecycle process: periodic (e.g. quarterly) review, mandatory owner, and expiry/rotation policy. 7. Where supported, prefer short-lived, certificate-based (mTLS/X.509) client authentication over long-lived static secrets. 8. Verify by confirming deleted clients can no longer obtain tokens (token request fails) and that no interface breaks. 9. Feed token-issuance events into the SIEM so future dormant-then-active clients are alertable. 10. Re-run the audit to confirm the stale count is reduced. Caution: confirm true inactivity over a sufficiently long window and with the owner before deleting - a client may be dormant only because its business process is seasonal; stage in non-prod where feasible.
References
  • OAuth Client Governance — Credential Lifecycle
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Integration connections to deprecated/legacy systems INTG-TOPO-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags integration connections that involve systems whose names indicate deprecated or end-of-life platforms (e.g. ECC, R/3, older BW/CRM/SRM, XI/PI 7.x, or LEGACY/OLD/DECOM markers). Connections to legacy/EOL systems are risky because such systems are frequently out of mainstream maintenance, no longer receive security patches, and often run weaker protocols and authentication than current S/4HANA/BTP components. A deprecated system on the other end of an interface effectively lowers the security level of the whole connection to that of its weakest participant, and it may retain outdated trust relationships (e.g. old trusted-RFC or shared technical users) into current systems. Attack scenario: an attacker targets the unpatched legacy system (which may carry known, unpatched vulnerabilities), compromises it more easily than the hardened S/4HANA core, and then uses the existing integration trust - a trusted RFC destination, a shared service account, or an open gateway link - to pivot from the weak legacy box into the current production landscape. Legacy systems slated for decommission are also commonly under-monitored, so activity there raises fewer alerts, giving the attacker a quiet staging ground. Business impact: increased breach likelihood via the weakest link, lateral movement into current systems, and audit findings on running unsupported software connected to production. A real incident looks like an intrusion that begins on an EOL system and moves into S/4HANA through a long-standing interface that everyone assumed was low-risk. This is rated medium: the connection may be a genuine transitional need, but each such link must be justified and compensated. Decommissioning or isolating legacy endpoints is the durable fix.
Affected Items (3)
  • S4HANA_PROD → ECC_LEGACY (system: ECC_LEGACY)
  • ECC_LEGACY → CPI_BROKER (system: ECC_LEGACY)
  • S4HANA_PROD → CRM_OLD_5.0 (system: CRM_OLD_5.0)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Validate each flagged connection: confirm which endpoint is legacy/EOL and whether the connection is still business-required (some 'ECC'/'PI' names may be labels rather than active EOL systems - verify). 2. For genuinely unneeded connections, remove the destination (SM59) and the corresponding partner/interface configuration. 3. For connections that must remain during transition, apply compensating controls: SNC/TLS encryption (INTG-TOPO-001), a dedicated least-privileged technical user (never a trusted-RFC or admin account), and network isolation of the legacy system. 4. Remove any trusted-RFC relationships (SMT1/SM59 trusted option, S_RFCACL) between legacy and current systems so a legacy compromise cannot assume identities on the current side. 5. Prioritize migration/decommission of the legacy endpoint in the roadmap and set a target date. 6. Increase monitoring on the legacy connection and forward its logs to the SIEM (INTG-MON-002). 7. Confirm the legacy system's own patch/support status and quantify the risk of retaining it. 8. Verify by testing that the remaining connection is encrypted, least-privileged, and free of trusted-RFC. 9. Document each retained legacy connection with its business justification, compensating controls, and decommission date under change control. 10. Re-review at each roadmap milestone. Caution: legacy interfaces often underpin critical but poorly-documented processes - confirm real usage before removal, test in non-prod, and coordinate with business owners so a needed cutover interface is not severed prematurely.
References
  • SAP — System Decommissioning Security Checklist
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Fiori spaces with public visibility FIORI-SPACE-001 ▶
Security Risk
With SAP Fiori 3 / FES 2020+ the Launchpad content model moved from groups to Spaces and Pages, where a space is a role-scoped navigation container and a page arranges the tiles. This check flags spaces whose visibility is PUBLIC/EVERYONE/ALL or that carry no role assignment at all. A space is meant to reach users only through a business role: in PFCG the space is added to the role menu (Menu > Other > Launchpad-Space) and enforced by the S_UI2_SPACE and S_UI2_PAGE authorization objects. A public space bypasses this and pushes its pages, and every tile on them, to the entire authenticated population, while a space with no role assignment is either dead content or content that leaks through a default assignment. The effect mirrors the public-catalog problem one layer up: it enlarges the visible application surface for every user and can surface sensitive tiles to people never provisioned for the underlying transactions. Abuse scenario: an ordinary user logs in and finds pages full of tiles intended for finance or HR power-users; they probe each tile, and any whose backend OData check is weak (see FIORI-ODATA-001/002) becomes an escalation path, while the rest hand the attacker a free map of the system's capabilities for later targeting. Business impact: least-privilege and SoD erosion, unnecessary information disclosure, and audit findings against the SAP Security Baseline role-based access requirement. A real incident looks like a page of privileged tiles appearing for the whole company after a space was published without a role restriction.
Affected Items (2)
  • Admin_Space — visibility: PUBLIC
  • Default_Space — visibility: EVERYONE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify the flagged spaces using the Manage Launchpad Spaces app (Fiori ID F4834) and Manage Launchpad Pages, or the Launchpad Content Manager transaction /UI2/FLPCM_CUST. 2. For every space set visibility to role-based and remove any PUBLIC/EVERYONE setting; assign the space to the correct business role(s) in PFCG via Menu > Other > Launchpad-Space. 3. Regenerate the role authorization profile so S_UI2_SPACE and S_UI2_PAGE restrict to the intended space/page IDs, and run SU24 sync if defaults were adjusted. 4. Delete or deactivate orphan spaces that have no legitimate role owner rather than leaving them unassigned. 5. Confirm the pages within each space reference only catalogs the same role authorizes, keeping catalog, space and page assignments consistent. 6. Clear the Launchpad caches (transaction /UI2/CACHE_DEL) and recalculate the app index with /UI5/APP_INDEX_CALCULATE so the visibility change takes effect. 7. Verify: log on as a representative non-privileged user and confirm the previously public space and its tiles are gone; use SUIM to list which roles grant S_UI2_SPACE for that space ID. 8. Rollout caution: changing space visibility changes what every affected user sees on their home page, so stage in DEV/QA, transport, coordinate with content owners and end-user communications, and validate with a pilot group before the production import.
References
  • SAP Fiori — Spaces and Pages Configuration
MEDIUM P3 · 34 HANA encryption uses internal/default root key management CRYPTO-HANA-003 ▶
Security Risk
HANA encryption is enabled but the root keys are managed internally/locally (root key type INTERNAL/DEFAULT/LOCAL), i.e. the master root keys are protected only by HANA's own Secure Store in the File System (SSFS) on the same host rather than by an external key management system. Encryption is only as strong as the protection and governance of its root keys, and internal management concentrates key and data on the same platform. The weakness: the instance SSFS holding the data/log/backup root keys resides on the HANA host, so an OS-level administrator, a host compromise, or anyone who obtains both a volume/backup copy and the SSFS can potentially recover the keys and decrypt the data - there is no cryptographic separation of duties between whoever runs the database and whoever controls the keys. It also complicates centralised, auditable key rotation and HSM backing. In a RISE/regulated context, external key management (SAP Data Custodian Key Management Service, or a hyperscaler KMS integration) is the recommended pattern precisely because it separates key custody from data custody, provides HSM-backed keys, centralised rotation, and independent access logging - which are often contractual or regulatory expectations (e.g. customer-controlled keys / BYOK). Attack/abuse scenario: a privileged insider or an attacker with host-level access copies the data volume and the co-located SSFS, moves both off-platform, and decrypts at leisure - something external key custody with strict access control and logging would prevent or at least make detectable. Business impact: weaker assurance over the confidentiality control, inability to demonstrate key/data separation to auditors, and slower/incomplete key rotation. Rated Medium: encryption is present, but key governance is below best practice and may not satisfy stricter compliance or customer BYOK requirements. A realistic finding is an auditor noting that HANA root keys are host-local with no external KMS and no enforced rotation.
Affected Items (1)
  • Root key management: INTERNAL
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Determine the current root-key custody: review the encryption configuration and query ENCRYPTION_ROOT_KEYS to confirm keys are held in the instance SSFS with internal/default management. 2. Evaluate an external key management option appropriate to the platform - SAP Data Custodian Key Management Service, or local key management (LKM) integrated with a hyperscaler KMS/HSM (Azure Key Vault, AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) - per the SAP HANA Administration/Security Guide. 3. In RISE, engage SAP ECS to scope and implement external/customer-managed keys, since the underlying platform and SSFS are provider-operated; agree the BYOK model and responsibilities. 4. Implement the chosen external key management configuration and migrate/re-wrap the root keys according to the guide, keeping verified backups at every step. 5. Establish root-key rotation: ALTER SYSTEM PERSISTENCE ENCRYPTION CREATE NEW ROOT KEY WITHOUT ACTIVATE; back it up; then ALTER SYSTEM PERSISTENCE ENCRYPTION ACTIVATE NEW ROOT KEY; (repeat for LOG and BACKUP encryption). 6. Verify the new key status in ENCRYPTION_ROOT_KEYS and confirm the data/log/backup remain readable after activation. 7. Ensure the SSFS master key and any external-KMS credentials are backed up and access-controlled separately from the database, with rotation logged. 8. Rollout caution: test the full key-rotation and recovery procedure in a non-production HANA system first, and confirm you can restore from a backup taken under the new keys before relying on it in production.
References
  • SAP HANA — External Key Management
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Detailed connect errors exposed to clients HANADB-PARAM-002 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that [password policy] detailed_error_on_connect is set to true, causing the database to return specific authentication-failure reasons to the client - distinguishing 'user does not exist' from 'wrong password' from 'user is locked/deactivated'. This is an information-disclosure weakness that directly enables user enumeration: an attacker can probe login names and learn which accounts exist, which are locked, and which are valid, live targets, then focus password-guessing and spraying on real, unlocked accounts. It also leaks account-state intelligence useful for social engineering. The secure default is false (a single generic message), but the parameter is sometimes switched on to aid troubleshooting and then left on in production. Attack scenario: an adversary scripts connection attempts against a list of likely usernames; with detailed errors on, they rapidly build an accurate inventory of valid accounts and their lock state, dramatically improving the efficiency of a subsequent brute-force or targeted phishing campaign. Business and compliance impact: it facilitates credential attacks and reconnaissance and is a recognised hardening gap in the CIS SAP HANA benchmark, contributing to broader confidentiality and access-control risk. A real incident looks like pre-attack reconnaissance logs showing systematic login probing that successfully mapped valid HANA users because detailed connect errors were enabled.
Affected Items (1)
  • detailed_error_on_connect = true
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value: SELECT KEY, VALUE FROM M_INIFILE_CONTENTS WHERE KEY='detailed_error_on_connect'; (section [password policy]). 2. Set it to false: ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('indexserver.ini','SYSTEM') SET ('password policy','detailed_error_on_connect')='false' WITH RECONFIGURE; (use nameserver.ini for the system DB). 3. Confirm clients now receive only a generic 'authentication failed' message. 4. Keep detailed errors only in non-production, and only temporarily while troubleshooting a specific issue - revert immediately afterwards. 5. Pair this with account lockout (maximum_invalid_connect_attempts) and connect auditing so enumeration and brute-force attempts are both throttled and detected. 6. Verify: re-query M_INIFILE_CONTENTS (value 'false'), then attempt a login with a bad username and separately with a bad password and confirm the client-side message is identical and generic in both cases. 7. Rollout caution: turning this off makes helpdesk troubleshooting slightly harder - direct admins to the server-side trace/audit for the real failure reason rather than the client message; test in non-production and, in RISE, coordinate the change with SAP ECS.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — detailed_error_on_connect
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Error Disclosure
MEDIUM P3 · 34 RFC Gateway proxy ACL (gw/prxy_info) not configured TRUST-008 ▶
Security Risk
Profile parameter gw/prxy_info is empty and gw/acl_mode_proxy is not 1, so no proxy ACL (prxyinfo) is loaded and the built-in default permits any source gateway to proxy RFC traffic to any destination system. The RFC gateway can proxy (relay) RFC requests between gateways and systems. Without a prxyinfo ACL, the gateway acts as an open RFC relay: an attacker can use it as a pivot to reach and call RFMs on other systems it could not otherwise contact, defeating network segmentation. Combined with weak reg_info/sec_info ACLs this feeds the well-known gateway relay and RCE chains. Attack scenario: an attacker who can reach the gateway port (33NN) proxies RFC calls through it to internal target systems, or launders malicious registered-server traffic, expanding reach and evading network controls. The severity is Medium here because modern kernels with gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1 auto-generate restrictive default proxy rules, which mitigates an empty prxyinfo file; the risk is highest on older kernels or where the mode is off. Business impact: lateral movement, an expanded RFC attack surface, and defense evasion across the landscape. A real incident looks like gateway logs (SMGW) showing proxied connections to unexpected destination systems.
Affected Items (1)
  • gw/prxy_info = (empty)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In SMGW use Goto -> Expert Functions to review the current ACL/proxy status, and check gw/prxy_info, gw/acl_mode_proxy, gw/reg_info and gw/sec_info in RZ11. 2. Create a prxyinfo ACL file with explicit rules (P/D source-host dest-host) that permit only the required proxy flows and deny everything else by default. 3. In RZ10 point gw/prxy_info at that file and set gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1 (per SAP Notes 910918 and 3224889) so restrictive defaults apply even with a minimal file. 4. Secure the companion gateway ACLs at the same time: gw/reg_info, gw/sec_info and gw/acl_mode = 1 — the gateway ACLs work as a set. 5. Reload the ACLs (SMGW can re-read the ACL files) or restart to activate. 6. Verify: SMGW shows the prxyinfo file loaded, a non-permitted proxy route is denied on test, and gateway logging records the blocked attempts. Caution: proxy ACLs can break legitimate cross-gateway scenarios (certain SLD/PI and registered-server flows) — inventory proxy flows first, test in non-production, and keep the previous configuration for rollback.
References
  • SAP Note 910918 — Parameter gw/prxy_info
  • SAP Note 3224889 — gw/acl_mode_proxy default settings
  • SAP Security Baseline — RFC Gateway ACLs
MEDIUM P3 · 34 RFC Gateway default ACL not enforced (gw/acl_mode) BASELINE-007 ▶
Security Risk
The RFC Gateway brokers registration of external RFC server programs (registered and started programs) and their access to the system. That access is meant to be governed by the secinfo (who may start/use programs) and reginfo (which external programs may register) ACL files. gw/acl_mode sets the DEFAULT behaviour when those ACL files are absent: value 0 is permissive, so with no reginfo/secinfo the gateway lets external programs register and be started, i.e. an open gateway; value 1 applies a restrictive default (only same-host/internal) that closes the gap when ACLs are missing. An open gateway is the classic critical SAP exposure: a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can reach the gateway port (33xx, or 48xx with SNC) can register a malicious RFC server program or invoke started programs, leading to arbitrary OS command execution on the SAP host. This is the 10KBLAZE / 'SAP Gateway to Heaven' class of attack described in CISA Alert AA19-122A (addressed by secinfo/reginfo ACLs rather than a CVE). Attack scenario: the attacker registers a rogue program via the gateway and calls it to run OS commands as the <sid>adm user, achieving full remote code execution, database access and lateral movement, with no SAP credentials required. Business and compliance impact is unauthenticated RCE on production SAP, total loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability, and a ransomware or data-theft entry point, i.e. a headline-grade breach. It manifests as unexpected registered programs in the gateway monitor (SMGW) and OS processes/commands spawned by the gateway or work process.
Affected Items (1)
  • gw/acl_mode = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value via RSPARAM/RZ11 for gw/acl_mode and set gw/acl_mode = 1 in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10). Note that gw/acl_mode=1 only takes effect while explicit ACL files are absent; the real control is the ACLs themselves (SAP Note 1408081). 2. Create and maintain the ACL files and point the parameters at them: gw/sec_info = <path>/secinfo and gw/reg_info = <path>/reginfo, using the SAP secinfo/reginfo generator (SAP Notes 1408081 / 1425765 and the CISA AA19-122A guidance). 3. Start deny-by-default, then add only the specific registered/started programs your interfaces need (SAP standard entries, PI/PO adapters, external RFC servers) with explicit host lists. 4. Set gw/reg_no_conn_info appropriately (SAP Note 1444282) and enable gateway logging (gw/logging) to monitor registrations. 5. Use transaction SMGW (Goto > Expert Functions > External Security) to display/reload secinfo/reginfo without a restart; the gw/acl_mode change itself needs an instance/gateway restart. 6. Verify in SMGW that unauthorized program registration is rejected (Logged-On Clients / registered programs list) and review the gateway log for denied registrations. Caution: mis-scoped ACLs break legitimate RFC server programs (PI/PO, external tax/output systems). Build the lists from a monitored baseline (gw/logging) in non-prod and coordinate with all RFC interface owners before enforcing in production.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — gw/acl_mode
  • SAP Note 1408081
  • CISA AA19-122A (10KBLAZE)
MEDIUM P3 · 34 Destructive / exfiltration OS command defined as a standing command JOBCMD-CMD-004 ▶
Security Risk
The external-command catalog contains a standing, SM49-callable command that wraps a destructive or data-movement utility. Examples flagged here: rm/del/erase/format/dd/mkfs/shred/rmdir (destruction) or curl/wget/tftp/ftp/nc/ncat/scp/rsync and reg/net/sc/certutil/bitsadmin/openssl/base64 (download/exfiltration/tampering). Unlike an injection flaw, this needs no cleverness - the dangerous primitive is already built and allowlisted. Anyone holding S_LOG_COM for it, or any job step that calls it, has a ready-made tool for destruction, payload download, or exfiltration. Attack scenario A: 'ZFTP' = curl lets an attacker pull a payload onto the host or push /usr/sap/<SID> data to an external server as <sid>adm. Attack scenario B: 'ZCLEAN' = rm -rf can wipe interface directories or delete forensic evidence. All of this runs under the trusted SAP service identity and largely outside DB-level auditing. Business impact: data theft (finance/HR extracts staged on the host), ransomware-style destruction of SAP directories, or anti-forensic log deletion. Network utilities also enable lateral movement from the SAP host into the wider datacentre. The exposure is chronic: the primitive sits in the catalog indefinitely until someone removes it. These entries frequently survive as leftovers from migration or interface projects that were never cleaned up. Real incident: a 'temporary' curl command left in SM69 after a data-migration project became the exfiltration channel in a later intrusion because no one had removed it.
Affected Items (1)
  • ZWGET -> /usr/bin/wget (wget)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory: SM69 / SE16 SXPGCOSTAB -> identify commands whose OPCOMMAND base is a destructive or network/data-movement utility (rm, dd, format, shred; curl, wget, ftp, tftp, nc, scp, rsync; reg, net, sc, certutil, bitsadmin, openssl, base64). 2. For each, require a documented operational owner and business need from change records; if none exists, delete the command in SM69. 3. Before deleting, confirm no armed job step references it (TBTCP field EXTCMD via SE16 / SM37). 4. Where genuinely required (e.g., an approved file transfer), replace the generic utility with a tightly-scoped wrapper: fixed source/target, ADDPAR off, absolute non-writable path. 5. Prefer a governed interface/middleware (PI/PO/CPI, managed file transfer) over an ad-hoc OS command for data movement. 6. Restrict execution: minimal S_LOG_COM (fields COMMAND, OPSYSTEM, HOST) via PFCG; list holders with SUIM and remove broad grants. 7. Enable SM49/gateway execution logging and alert on any use of the remaining sensitive commands. 8. Verify: SE16 SXPGCOSTAB no longer lists removed commands and SM49 confirms they can no longer be executed. 9. Periodically re-scan the catalog so new destructive commands do not accumulate. 10. Rollout caution: some of these support legitimate housekeeping/interface jobs - coordinate removal with Basis/job owners and stage in DEV/QA so nightly cleanup or transfers are not broken.
References
  • SAP Help — External OS Commands (SM69)
  • Onapsis / CISA — SAP OS command abuse
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Dormant accounts (90+ days inactive) USR-003 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags unlocked accounts (USR02-UFLAG = 0) whose last logon date (USR02-TRDAT) is older than the configured threshold (default 90 days). Dormant accounts are latent attack surface: they are typically leavers, movers, ex-consultants or old test IDs whose owners no longer watch them, yet they still carry their roles and authorizations. Attack scenario: an attacker who phished or purchased old credentials, or who guesses a weak never-rotated password, logs in with a dormant account nobody monitors; because the legitimate owner is gone, the intrusion generates no user complaint and can persist for months. Dormant privileged accounts are worse, as a dormant Basis or finance user yields instant high privilege. In an outsourced/RISE landscape with rotating consultants, orphaned external accounts are common and easy to miss. Business impact: unauthorized transactions, quiet data exfiltration, and a failed access-recertification and termination control (SOX ITGC), plus GDPR concerns where the dormant ID can still read personal data. A real incident looks like a logon on a long-idle ex-employee ID from a new IP outside business hours, followed by report execution and downloads of customer or payroll data. Even absent compromise, dormant accounts inflate the named-user license count and the audit-review burden and dilute the reliability of periodic reviews.
