  • ZJOBSVC (last logon: 20250401, 500d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Produce the authoritative list with RSUSR200 (users by logon date and password change) or RSUSR006, selecting last logon (TRDAT) older than the policy threshold and lock status = unlocked. 2. Reconcile against HR leavers and the joiner-mover-leaver feed to confirm which owners have left or changed roles. 3. Lock confirmed dormant accounts in SU01, or in bulk with SU10 (mass administrator lock), and set a validity end date so they cannot be silently reused. 4. After a defined grace period (for example 30-60 days locked with no business objection), delete or archive the users and reclaim their roles. 5. Automate detection by scheduling RSUSR200/RSUSR006 as a periodic background job in SM36, and/or use SAP GRC User Access Review for recurring recertification. 6. Establish a formal quarterly user-access review with business-owner sign-off, and integrate deprovisioning with the leaver process (ideally via SAP IPS or GRC). 7. Set login/password_max_idle_productive so unused productive passwords expire automatically, shrinking the dormant-but-usable window. 8. Verify by re-running RSUSR200 to confirm the previously dormant IDs are locked or removed, and confirm no successful logon occurred after lock via SM20 / RSAU_READ_LOG. 9. Caution: some dormant-looking IDs are legitimate technical or break-glass accounts, so confirm user type and purpose before locking to avoid breaking an interface. 10. Communicate with business owners before locking to avoid disrupting seasonal or infrequent but valid users.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 2.5
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Dialog users with stale passwords (>180 days) USR-008 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags unlocked dialog users (type A) whose password has not changed in more than the policy window (USR02-PWDCHGDATE older than the threshold, default 180 days). This usually means password expiry is not enforced (login/password_expiration_time = 0 or too high) or these users are exempt. Stale, long-lived passwords are more likely to have been exposed via phishing, reuse across systems, a prior breach dump, or shoulder-surfing, and the longer they persist the larger the window for offline cracking of a captured hash. Where weak downward-compatible hashing is still active (login/password_downwards_compatibility not disabled, legacy BCODE hashes present), captured hashes crack quickly. Attack scenario: an attacker obtains an old credential through credential-stuffing from a public breach, a phishing capture, or a cracked USR02 hash, and because the password was never rotated it still authenticates for interactive SAP GUI/Fiori logon, letting the attacker operate as that business user. Long-lived passwords also undermine the assumptions behind lockout and audit controls. Business/compliance impact: account takeover, fraud and data access under a real user's identity, and direct policy, SOX and CIS findings on password lifecycle. A real incident: a finance clerk's years-old password, reused on a breached website, is replayed against the Fiori launchpad and used to run a payment proposal. In RISE/BTP many dialog logons should be moving to SSO via SAP Cloud Identity (IAS), which changes but does not remove this control for accounts still using local passwords.
Affected Items (12)
  • SAP* (password age: 1170d)
  • DDIC (password age: 956d)
  • JSMITH (password age: 559d)
  • AGARCIA (password age: 545d)
  • MWILSON (password age: 956d)
  • SVC_RFC_01 (password age: 1170d)
  • RFC_BILLING (password age: 956d)
  • BATCH_FIN (password age: 1140d)
  • INT_ARIBA (password age: 896d)
  • DLEE (password age: 540d)
  • TNGUYEN (password age: 1201d)
  • LWANG (password age: 545d)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current policy by checking login/password_expiration_time, login/password_max_idle_productive, login/min_password_lng, the login/min_password_* complexity parameters, and login/password_downwards_compatibility via RZ11 / report RSPFPAR. 2. Set an enforced rotation window (for example login/password_expiration_time = 90) and adequate length/complexity in RZ10 (DEFAULT profile), activate it, and set login/password_compliance_to_current_policy = 1 so existing non-compliant passwords must change at next logon. 3. Disable weak legacy hashes by setting login/password_downwards_compatibility = 0 (after confirming no old kernels/systems depend on it) so only strong PWDSALTEDHASH is stored, and clean up history per SAP guidance. 4. Identify stale accounts with RSUSR200 (by password change date) and, for those past the threshold, force a change by setting a new productive/initial password via SU01 or SU10 with change-at-next-logon. 5. Reduce password dependence by adopting SSO: SAML/OIDC via SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) for Fiori, or SNC/Kerberos for SAP GUI, so interactive logon uses a central identity with MFA rather than static SAP passwords. 6. Configure lockout parameters login/fails_to_user_lock and login/failed_user_auto_unlock to blunt credential-stuffing. 7. Verify by re-running RSUSR200 and RSPFPAR to confirm no dialog user exceeds the age threshold and the parameters are active at runtime, then test a logon to confirm the change-at-next-logon prompt fires. 8. Enable Security Audit Log monitoring for repeated failed logons and logons after long inactivity. 9. Caution: forcing mass password changes can generate helpdesk load and break any dialog account misused as a technical account, so first re-type genuine technical IDs (see USR-004) to exclude them and communicate the change to users. 10. Roll out complexity/expiry changes in a maintenance window and confirm no critical interface relies on a never-expiring dialog password.

MEDIUM P4 · 22 Parameter login/min_password_digits non-compliant PARAM-login/min_password_digits ▶
Security Risk
login/min_password_digits enforces the minimum number of numeric characters a new password must contain; the default is 0, meaning purely alphabetic (often dictionary-word) passwords are permitted. Without a digit requirement, users overwhelmingly choose predictable words, names or seasonal patterns, which fall immediately to dictionary and rule-based cracking and to targeted online guessing. Combined with a short min length this collapses effective password entropy far below the nominal length. In an S/4HANA landscape any remaining password-based dialog, service or communication users become the weak link: an attacker running a dictionary attack against the logon (or cracking a USR02 hash dump offline) recovers such passwords in seconds. The abuse path is straightforward - enumerate valid user IDs (via SU01 error differences, RFC, or leaked lists), spray common words, and log on as a legitimate user. Because the logon is credential-valid it bypasses many detective controls unless the Security Audit Log is active. Business impact includes account takeover, segregation-of-duties bypass, and fraudulent transactions attributable to the victim. Compliance impact: fails CIS SAP password-complexity benchmarks and the SAP Security Baseline. A real incident would appear as a successful logon following a burst of failed attempts, tied to an account whose password was a single dictionary word with no digit.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/min_password_digits = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the current value in RZ11 for login/min_password_digits. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/min_password_digits >= 1 (a value of 1-2 is typical; do not over-constrain, which pushes users to predictable substitutions). 3. Harden the companion parameters in the same change: login/min_password_letters >= 1 and login/min_password_specials >= 1, and ensure login/min_password_lng >= 8. 4. Optionally maintain a prohibited-password list in table USR40 (via SM30) to block trivial patterns such as the company name. 5. Save and activate the profile; login/* parameters are dynamic but persist them in the profile for durability. 6. Set login/password_compliance_to_current_policy = 1 so existing weak passwords are forced to comply on next change. 7. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and per-instance with RZ11. 8. Communicate the new complexity rule to end users and the service desk ahead of rollout. 9. Test in DEV/QA first to confirm no automated/interface logons rely on non-compliant fixed passwords. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm the parameter is compliant.
References

MEDIUM P4 · 22 Parameter login/min_password_specials non-compliant PARAM-login/min_password_specials ▶
Security Risk
login/min_password_specials sets the minimum number of special (non-alphanumeric) characters required in a password; the default is 0. Requiring at least one special character meaningfully expands the character set an attacker must brute-force and defeats simple dictionary and mask attacks that assume alphanumeric-only passwords. With the value at 0, users default to word-plus-number patterns that modern cracking rules exhaust rapidly, so despite a nominal length the real strength is low. In S/4HANA landscapes this matters most for the residual password-based dialog, communication and RFC users that persist even after SSO adoption; those are exactly the accounts adversaries target for reuse and lateral movement. Concrete abuse: after obtaining a USR02 hash export (via excessive table-read authorizations, a database/backup exposure, or SQL injection in custom ABAP), the attacker runs rule-based cracking; passwords lacking special characters fall first, yielding plaintext credentials for direct logon. The resulting access is credential-valid and blends into normal traffic. Business impact includes account takeover, SoD circumvention, and fraudulent or unauthorized transactions performed under a legitimate identity. Compliance impact: non-conformance with CIS SAP and SAP Security Baseline complexity guidance and typical ITGC standards. A real incident would show a legitimate-looking logon whose credential was later found to be a simple word-plus-digit password with no special character requirement in force.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/min_password_specials = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current value in RZ11 for login/min_password_specials. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/min_password_specials >= 1. 3. Apply as part of the complete complexity policy (digits >= 1, letters >= 1, length >= 8) so the controls reinforce rather than push users to predictable substitutions. 4. Optionally block trivial/predictable passwords via table USR40 (SM30). 5. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; login/* parameters are dynamic but persist them in the profile. 6. Force legacy passwords to comply with login/password_compliance_to_current_policy = 1. 7. Verify with RSPARAM (active value) and RZ11 (per instance). 8. Warn users and the service desk that new passwords must contain a special character before enforcing. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA and check that no automated logon uses a fixed non-compliant password. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm the parameter is compliant.

MEDIUM P4 · 22 Parameter login/password_expiration_time non-compliant PARAM-login/password_expiration_time ▶
Security Risk
login/password_expiration_time defines, in days, how long a password remains valid before the user must change it; the SAP default is 0, which means passwords never expire. When passwords never expire, a single credential compromise is effectively permanent: a password captured months ago from a phishing lure, a keylogger, a reused-credential breach, or an old USR02 hash dump remains valid indefinitely, and terminated employees or rotated contractors may retain working credentials well past their access-review date. In S/4HANA RISE landscapes this is most acute for password-based dialog and communication users that are not integrated with SSO/central IdP-driven rotation. Attack scenario: an adversary obtains a credential once (breach dump, malware, or hash crack), and because it never expires, they can return at any time to log on as that user, exfiltrate data or post transactions, with the access indistinguishable from normal use. Long-lived static passwords on technical/RFC users are especially prized for durable persistence. Business impact: prolonged undetected access, fraud, data breach, and failure of the periodic-credential-rotation control that auditors expect. Compliance impact: violates CIS SAP benchmark 1.1.6, the SAP Security Baseline, and SOX/ISO password-lifecycle controls. A real incident would look like a dormant account reactivating months after an employee left, or credentials from an old breach still granting access.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/password_expiration_time = 180
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the current value in RZ11 for login/password_expiration_time. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/password_expiration_time to 90 or fewer days (per policy; many organisations use 60-90). 3. Pair this with login/password_max_idle_productive to invalidate productive passwords that go unused, and login/min_password_diff to force meaningful changes. 4. For technical/RFC/communication users where interactive rotation is impractical, prefer SNC/certificate-based authentication or move them to SSO rather than exempting them from expiry. 5. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; login/* parameters are dynamic but keep them in the profile so they persist across restarts. 6. Communicate the change well ahead of time - a large first-wave password-reset spike is expected once expiry is enabled. 7. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and confirm on all instances via RZ11. 8. Identify accounts that would break on rotation (interface users) beforehand via SUIM and plan alternative authentication for them. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA and coordinate with interface owners before production enforcement. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm compliance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Parameter login/password_max_idle_initial non-compliant PARAM-login/password_max_idle_initial ▶
Security Risk
login/password_max_idle_initial controls how many days an initial (administrator-set or reset) password remains usable if it is never used to log on; after that window the initial password becomes invalid and must be reset again. The default is effectively unbounded/large, which means a password an administrator set during user creation or a help-desk reset can sit unused and valid for a long time. This is dangerous because initial passwords are the weakest link in the lifecycle: they are frequently a predictable pattern (a standard 'welcome' string, the SID, or a formula the help desk reuses), they are transmitted over email/tickets, and they are known to at least one other person. If such an initial password is not consumed and expired quickly, an attacker who learns it - by guessing the help-desk convention, reading a ticketing system, or intercepting the notification - can activate a dormant or newly-created account before the legitimate user ever logs on. In S/4HANA onboarding at scale, many freshly created accounts may sit with initial passwords, presenting a broad set of easily-activated identities. Business impact: account takeover of new or reset users, including potentially privileged ones, and creation of a persistence foothold. Compliance impact: fails CIS SAP 1.1.7 and SAP Security Baseline initial-password guidance. A real incident would look like a never-onboarded or long-idle account being logged into using its original help-desk password.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/password_max_idle_initial = 30
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the current value in RZ11 for login/password_max_idle_initial. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/password_max_idle_initial to a short window, 14 days or fewer (7 or less is stronger), so unused initial passwords expire quickly. 3. Also set login/password_max_idle_productive to a sensible limit for productive passwords that go unused. 4. Standardise on strong, unique initial passwords (avoid a fixed help-desk pattern) and require change-on-first-logon, which SAP enforces for admin-set passwords by default. 5. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; these login/* parameters are dynamically switchable but keep them in the profile. 6. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and per-instance with RZ11. 7. Use SUIM/RSUSR200 to identify existing users still on an initial password and follow up on stale ones. 8. Coordinate with the onboarding/service-desk team so newly created accounts are activated within the shortened window. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA to confirm the shortened window does not disrupt batch user provisioning. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm compliance.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Parameter login/password_history_size non-compliant PARAM-login/password_history_size ▶
Security Risk
login/password_history_size defines how many previous passwords the system remembers and forbids a user from reusing. When the history is too small (or 0), users cycle back to a handful of familiar passwords - or immediately re-set the same password after a forced expiry - which defeats the purpose of password rotation entirely. The security value of expiry (login/password_expiration_time) depends on this control: without a meaningful history, a mandatory 90-day change becomes theatre because the user simply reverts to the old, possibly already-compromised, password. In an S/4HANA environment this means a credential leaked in a prior breach or cracked from an old hash dump can be reinstated by the user at the next change, restoring the attacker's access. It also enables the well-known trick of changing the password N times rapidly to flush the history and return to a favourite. Attack scenario: an adversary holding a previously valid credential waits for rotation and finds the same password back in use because history was too shallow to block it. Business impact: rotation controls provide false assurance, compromised credentials persist, and auditors may rely on an ineffective control. Compliance impact: weakens conformance with CIS SAP 1.1.8 and the SAP Security Baseline password-reuse expectation. A real incident would look like a compromised password reappearing on an account shortly after a mandated change, granting renewed access. This is rated lower severity but materially undermines the other password controls.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/password_history_size = 3
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the current value in RZ11 for login/password_history_size. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/password_history_size to at least 5 (values of 5-24 are common; higher is stronger). 3. To close the rapid-cycling loophole, set login/password_change_waittime to a small positive value (e.g. 1 day) so users cannot change the password many times in a row to flush history. 4. Ensure login/min_password_diff > 0 so a new password must differ meaningfully from the old one. 5. Keep this aligned with login/password_expiration_time so rotation and reuse-prevention reinforce each other. 6. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; login/* parameters are dynamic but persist them in the profile. 7. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and confirm across instances via RZ11. 8. Communicate to users that recent passwords cannot be reused. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA before enforcing in production. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm the parameter is compliant.
References
  • SAP Note 3250501 — mandatory hardening for AS ABAP in SAP ECS (v46, 2026-05-15)
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Parameter icm/security_log non-compliant PARAM-icm/security_log ▶
Security Risk
Sets the detail level of the ICM security log — the web tier's record of rejected and suspicious requests. Below the mandated level, attacks on the HTTP channel are not recorded in enough detail to reconstruct. Current value: 'LOGFILE=dev_icm_sec LEVEL=1 MAXSIZEKB=1000'. The ECS standard value is 'LEVEL=3'. SAP permits no exception to this value. Checked here: LEVEL >= 3. Verified: the security-log LEVEL. Not verified: the log file name or size limit, which are per-host.

Configure icm/security_log at or above the mandated LEVEL, with a log file and rotation. In an ECS/RISE tenant profile parameters are maintained by SAP: raise a service request quoting SAP Note 3250501 rather than attempting the change in RZ10. Re-export the profile parameters (RSPARAM) afterwards and confirm the active value on every instance.

MEDIUM P4 · 22 Users with excessive firefighter usage (>5 sessions) IAM-FF-005 ▶
Security Risk
This flags users who invoked emergency/firefighter access more often than the configured monthly threshold (default 5 sessions). Emergency access is meant to be exceptional — for genuine, unforeseen incidents. When a user relies on it repeatedly, it signals that firefighter access has become a routine substitute for properly designed day-to-day roles, which erodes the whole model: frequent use normalizes privileged access, dilutes controller scrutiny (reviewers become desensitized to yet another session), and expands the time these users spend operating with broad, SAP_ALL-class authorizations. The abuse angle is subtle rather than a single break-in: a user who is 'always firefighting' effectively holds standing elevated access under the guise of emergencies, blending routine work into privileged sessions where individual actions get less attention, and gaining ongoing capability to act beyond their assigned role. Impact is heightened privilege-misuse exposure and a weakened control narrative for audit — a recertification reviewer will question why standing needs are met through emergency access. It also masks a role-design gap. A real incident looks like a power user who quietly runs most of their job through firefighter IDs, so a fraudulent action hides among dozens of 'normal' emergency sessions nobody scrutinizes closely.
Affected Items (1)
  • JSMITH — 6 sessions (max: 5/month)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review each high-frequency user's firefighter usage in the GRC EAM log to understand what recurring tasks are driving the check-outs. 2. Where the need is legitimate and recurring, redesign the user's permanent role in PFCG to cover it (least privilege) so emergency access is no longer the routine path. 3. Reserve firefighter IDs strictly for genuine emergencies and set/enforce a monthly usage expectation; flag outliers for owner review. 4. Tighten the scope of firefighter IDs so they are not a catch-all superuser — provision task-specific firefighter roles where possible. 5. Track firefighter-usage trends over time and feed them into periodic access review so recurring users are re-justified or re-provisioned. 6. Verify by re-running the analysis after role redesign and confirming usage frequency drops below the threshold. 7. Rollout caution: validate the redesigned permanent role in QA and confirm it does not itself create a SoD conflict, and coordinate with the process owner before removing the user's reliance on emergency access.
References
  • SAP GRC — Firefighter Usage Optimization
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Role assignments without expiry dates IAM-EXP-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags role assignments with no expiration date (validity-to open-ended, e.g. 31.12.9999) in AGR_USERS. Indefinite role assignments defeat time-based access governance: access that never expires accumulates silently as people change jobs, cover for colleagues, or complete projects, producing the classic 'privilege creep' where long-tenured users end up with far more access than their current role needs. Because the assignment never lapses, it also bypasses one of the simplest recertification levers — forcing periodic renewal by design. The abuse scenario is opportunistic: a user who retains an old, forgotten but still-valid role can use residual access (e.g. to a financial transaction or sensitive table) long after any business need ended, and because nothing ever prompted a review, the access is invisible to controls. Impact is an ever-growing attack surface and SoD-conflict likelihood, plus an ITGC/SOX weakness because recertification cannot be evidenced as effective when assignments are perpetual. A real incident looks like a mover-not-leaver who accumulated financial and admin roles across several transfers — none time-boxed — and exploited a legacy authorization that should have expired years earlier, discovered only during a belated access review.
Affected Items (14)
  • JSMITH → Z_FI_ACCOUNTANT (valid to: indefinite)
  • JSMITH → Z_FI_PAYMENT (valid to: indefinite)
  • MWILSON → Z_FI_GL_ADMIN (valid to: indefinite)
  • MWILSON → Z_FI_VENDOR_MAINT (valid to: indefinite)
  • DLEE → Z_SD_BILLING (valid to: indefinite)
  • LWANG → Z_BC_USER_ADMIN (valid to: indefinite)
  • LWANG → Z_BC_ROLE_ADMIN (valid to: indefinite)
  • LWANG → Z_BC_TRANSPORT (valid to: indefinite)
  • TNGUYEN → Z_HR_MASTER_DATA (valid to: indefinite)
  • SVC_RFC_01 → Z_RFC_FULL (valid to: indefinite)
  • BATCH_FIN → Z_BATCH_FI_PROC (valid to: indefinite)
  • INT_ARIBA → Z_INT_ARIBA (valid to: indefinite)
  • API_GATEWAY → Z_API_GW_FULL (valid to: indefinite)
  • TECH_MONITOR → Z_MONITORING (valid to: indefinite)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Quantify the population from AGR_USERS (SE16N: entries with TO_DAT = 99991231) and prioritize privileged and financially significant roles. 2. Set validity-end dates on assignments: use PFCG (user tab) or mass maintenance via SU10 to apply a policy-based expiry, or drive it through SAP Identity Management / GRC Access Request Management for automated enforcement. 3. Define and document a maximum validity policy (e.g. 12 months for business roles; longer, justified periods for technical/service accounts). 4. Implement periodic recertification (GRC User Access Review campaigns) so renewals require explicit re-approval rather than defaulting to perpetual. 5. For assignments provisioned via GRC ARM, enforce mandatory validity end-dates at request time. 6. Verify by re-extracting AGR_USERS and confirming the count of open-ended assignments has dropped to the approved exceptions only. 7. Rollout caution: do not blanket-expire technical/RFC/service users that would break interfaces — coordinate with interface owners, exempt and document them, and stage changes in QA before production.

MEDIUM P4 · 22 Access reviews marked complete but with incomplete coverage IAM-REV-002 ▶
Security Risk
This flags access-review campaigns marked as completed/closed but whose recorded completion percentage is below 100%. A campaign closed with incomplete coverage gives false assurance: the control's output says 'access has been reviewed and validated' when in fact a subset of users, roles or line-items was never examined. Those unreviewed items retain whatever access they had, unvalidated, while the audit record claims otherwise — which is arguably worse than a visibly-overdue campaign because it hides the gap. The scenario: reviewers work through most items, the campaign is administratively closed to meet a deadline, and the skipped items (often the hardest or most privileged) are exactly where inappropriate access hides — a leaver's residual role or a SoD-conflicting grant slips through under the cover of a 'completed' review. Impact is a misstated control result: for SOX/ITGC this undermines the reliability of the recertification evidence and can be a more serious finding than lateness, because it calls the control's integrity into question. A real incident looks like an auditor reconciling the campaign's item count to its attestations, finding a shortfall behind a 'closed' status, and expanding testing on the assumption that other campaigns may be similarly incomplete.
Affected Items (1)
  • Q1 2025 HR/Payroll Access Review — status: COMPLETED, completion: 85.0%
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Reopen each affected campaign in GRC Access Control and identify the specific line-items/users that were not reviewed. 2. Complete the review of all outstanding items so coverage reaches 100%, with reviewers explicitly deciding keep/remove on each. 3. Investigate why items were skipped (reviewer unavailability, unassigned owners, data errors) and fix the root cause. 4. Enforce completion rules in GRC ARM/UAR so a campaign cannot be set to Completed/Closed while any item is unactioned. 5. Add a reconciliation check that compares attested items to total scope before allowing closure. 6. Verify by re-extracting campaign data and confirming closed campaigns show 100% completion. 7. Rollout caution: closing the enforcement gap may surface a backlog of genuinely incomplete campaigns — plan reviewer capacity, and communicate that 'closed' now means fully reviewed so deadlines are met by doing the work, not by early closure.
References
  • SOX — Access Review Completeness Requirements
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Access review campaigns without assigned reviewer IAM-REV-003 ▶
Security Risk
This flags access-review campaigns with no assigned reviewer or owner. A recertification campaign only produces a control outcome if a responsible person actually performs the review; an unowned campaign is inert — nobody is accountable for examining the access, so it will simply never be completed, silently defeating the periodic-review control for whatever population it covers. The weakness is organizational rather than technical, but its effect is a coverage hole: the users or roles in that campaign go unreviewed indefinitely while the program assumes they are covered. The scenario: a campaign is generated for a business area whose owner left or was never mapped, so it sits with no reviewer; access that should be re-attested (including privileged or SoD-relevant grants) is never looked at, and the gap is invisible unless someone checks for unassigned ownership. Impact is unreviewed standing access plus an ITGC/SOX gap — auditors expect every in-scope population to have a named accountable reviewer, and unowned campaigns indicate the review program is not comprehensively assigned. A real incident looks like a whole department's access going years without recertification because its review campaign was never assigned an owner, discovered when someone finally maps campaigns to responsible managers.
Affected Items (2)
  • Q1 2025 Procurement Access Review
  • Q1 2025 BTP Access Review
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Assign a named reviewer/owner to each unassigned campaign, based on business-process or role ownership (the business manager for user access, the role owner for role content). 2. Configure automatic reviewer determination in GRC ARM/UAR using the organizational structure (manager hierarchy) or role-owner mapping so campaigns are never generated without an owner. 3. Ensure role and user-manager ownership data is maintained (GRC role owner assignment; up-to-date manager relationships in the HR/identity source). 4. Add a pre-launch check that blocks or flags any campaign lacking a reviewer before it starts. 5. Complete the now-assigned reviews so the previously unowned population is finally recertified. 6. Verify by re-extracting campaign metadata and confirming every campaign has an assigned reviewer. 7. Rollout caution: validate that auto-assigned owners are correct (a stale manager mapping can route reviews to the wrong person), and coordinate with HR to keep the org structure current so future assignment stays accurate.
References
  • SAP GRC ARM — Reviewer Assignment
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Custom roles without designated owners IAM-ROLE-002 ▶
Security Risk
This flags custom (Z/Y) roles that have no designated owner. Role ownership is the linchpin of access governance: the owner is the accountable person who approves who may hold the role, attests to its content during recertification, and authorizes changes to its authorizations. An ownerless role has no one to include it in access-review campaigns and no one accountable for its scope, so it drifts — authorizations get added over time through copy-and-modify maintenance with no owner challenging the growth, and the role never gets re-attested because there is nobody to attest. The scenario is progressive over-provisioning: an ownerless Z-role gradually accumulates powerful or conflicting authorizations and is assigned to more users, all without governance, becoming a concentration of unmanaged access that no review ever validates. Impact is elevated privilege-creep and SoD risk plus a direct recertification gap — GRC User Access Reviews and role-content reviews depend on a named owner, so ownerless roles are effectively outside the control. For SOX/ITGC, undefined ownership and accountability is a recognized deficiency. A real incident looks like a widely-assigned custom role with no owner turning out to contain excessive authorizations that were never reviewed because no campaign could route to a responsible approver.
Affected Items (12)
  • Z_FI_GL_ADMIN
  • Z_FI_VENDOR_MAINT
  • Z_MM_GR_POSTER
  • Z_MM_BUYER_TEMP
  • Z_HR_PAYROLL
  • Z_RFC_FULL
  • Z_BATCH_FI_PROC
  • Z_INT_ARIBA
  • Z_API_GW_FULL
  • Z_LEGACY_ROLE_01
  • Z_DECOM_2023
  • YTEST_ROLE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract custom roles lacking an owner (from role metadata / GRC role master or CREATED_BY as a stopgap) to build the work list. 2. Assign a business owner to every custom role — ideally the business-process lead who uses it, not an IT administrator — using GRC Business Role Management role-ownership features or a maintained RACI/role catalog. 3. Make owner assignment a mandatory step in the role-creation and change procedure so no new custom role goes live without one. 4. Wire ownership into recertification so each owner attests to their roles' content and assignments each cycle (GRC UAR / role-content review). 5. Prioritize privileged and high-assignment roles for immediate owner assignment. 6. Verify by re-extracting role ownership data and confirming all custom roles now have a named owner. 7. Rollout caution: confirm assigned owners accept and understand the accountability (approvals, attestations) rather than assigning nominally; validate that owners map to current staff, since a stale owner is as ineffective as none.
References
  • ISACA COBIT — Role Ownership and Accountability
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Users assigned to non-existent or deleted roles IAM-ORPH-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags user-role assignments that reference roles which no longer exist in the role catalog (present in AGR_USERS but not in AGR_DEFINE/role_details). These orphaned assignments are the residue of roles that were deleted without cleaning up the user linkages. While a truly deleted role usually conveys no live authorizations, orphaned assignments corrupt the integrity of the access model and create several concrete risks. First, they make 'who has what' unreliable — reporting, SoD analysis and access reviews operate on a user-role table that references phantom roles, undermining audit assertions. Second, they create a reactivation hazard: if a role name is later recreated (e.g. a role with the same technical name is rebuilt for a different purpose), every user still carrying the orphaned assignment silently inherits the new role's authorizations without any provisioning or approval — an unintended, unreviewed grant. Third, they indicate a broken role-deletion process, which itself is a control weakness. Impact is data-integrity and potential unauthorized-access risk, plus audit exceptions on access-baseline accuracy. A real incident looks like a decommissioned role name being reused months later, instantly granting the new (possibly privileged) access to a set of users who were never provisioned for it, discovered only when someone notices unexpected access tied to a recreated role.
Affected Items (20)
  • ADMIN1 → Z_BASIS_SUPER
  • CONTRACTOR7 → Z_BASIS_SUPER
  • DEV1 → Z_DEV_UNRESTRICTED
  • BATCH1 → Z_TABLE_ADMIN
  • ARAFRAUD1 → Z_ARA_VENDOR
  • ARAFRAUD1 → Z_ARA_PAY
  • ARAFRAUD2 → Z_ARA_GLMASTER
  • ARAFRAUD2 → Z_ARA_GLPOST
  • ARAFRAUD3 → Z_ARA_USERADMIN
  • ARAFRAUD3 → Z_ARA_ROLEADMIN
  • ARAFRAUD4 → Z_ARA_HRMASTER
  • ARAFRAUD4 → Z_ARA_PAYROLL
  • ARAMULTI → Z_ARA_VENDOR
  • ARAMULTI → Z_ARA_PAY
  • ARAMULTI → Z_ARA_GLMASTER
  • ARAMULTI → Z_ARA_GLPOST
  • ARAMULTI → Z_ARA_USERADMIN
  • ARAMULTI → Z_ARA_ROLEADMIN
  • ARACLEAN → Z_ARA_VENDOR_DISP
  • ARACLEAN → Z_ARA_PAY
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the orphaned assignments by reconciling AGR_USERS (SE16N) against AGR_DEFINE — assignments whose AGR_NAME has no matching role definition. 2. Remove the orphaned assignments: use SU10 mass maintenance or targeted SU01 changes to strip the non-existent roles from affected users. 3. Run PFUD (user master comparison, background report RHAUTUPD_NEW) so user buffers/profiles are reconciled after cleanup. 4. Run PRGN_COMPRESS_TIMES to compress and tidy AGR_USERS, reviewing its log. 5. Fix the root cause: adopt a role-decommission procedure that removes all user assignments before or as part of deleting the role, so orphans are not created again. 6. Verify by re-reconciling AGR_USERS to AGR_DEFINE and confirming no assignment references a missing role. 7. Rollout caution: before deleting assignments, confirm the role is genuinely deleted (not merely missing from the extract); test the mass change in QA, take a backup of AGR_USERS, and coordinate with role owners in case a role is due to be recreated intentionally.
References
  • SAP Note 1763498
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Several identity providers can authenticate users into one subaccount IAM-FED-001 ▶
Security Risk
2 trust configuration(s) in this subaccount can interactively authenticate users. Every one of them is an independent policy engine: multi-factor enforcement, conditional access, session lifetime, and joiner/mover/leaver de-provisioning are all decided by the identity provider behind the trust, not by BTP. The effective assurance of the subaccount is therefore the weakest of these paths, not the strongest, and an attacker chooses which one to attack. Second logon paths are rarely deliberate — they are usually a legacy SAML tenant kept 'until the migration finishes', a partner IdP from a project that ended, or a test trust nobody removed. Each is listed below so the owner can confirm it is intended and carries the same controls as the primary corporate provider.
Affected Items (2)
  • sap.default (SAP ID Service)
  • corp-aad-tenant (Corporate Azure AD)
Remediation — Step by Step
Confirm every trust listed is still required. Remove or set to inactive any trust left over from a migration, a pilot or an ended partner engagement (BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Security → Trust Configuration). For each trust that must stay, verify at the identity provider that it enforces the same multi-factor and conditional-access policy as the primary corporate provider, and that it is included in the same joiner/mover/leaver process — a trust whose IdP does not de-provision leavers keeps access alive after the corporate account is closed.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — Trust Configuration
  • SAP Security Baseline — Identity Federation
MEDIUM P4 · 22 RAL log channels with retention below 365 days DPP-RAL-003 ▶
Security Risk
RAL records are only useful for forensic and subject-access purposes if retained long enough to cover the period a regulator, auditor, or investigation cares about. This finding flags RAL log channels whose retention is shorter than the configured minimum (default 365 days) and/or that have no archiving. Data-protection incidents are frequently discovered months after the fact; insider data theft dwell time and the typical lag before a subject complaint or regulatory inquiry both often exceed a year. If RAL logs roll off after, say, 90 days, the organization cannot answer 'who accessed this person's data over the last year', cannot reconstruct the scope of a breach that began before the retention window, and cannot demonstrate accountability under GDPR Art.5(2). Short retention also conflicts with sector obligations (e.g. financial-services record-keeping) that may require multi-year audit trails. Conversely, retention must be balanced against Art.5(1)(e) storage-limitation, so the target is a defensible, documented period, not indefinite. Business impact: an investigation into suspected PII misuse stalls because evidence was already purged, weakening the organization's legal position and potentially converting a defensible position into an assumed worst-case breach for notification purposes.
Affected Items (2)
  • HR_ACCESS_LOG — retention: 180d (min: 365d)
  • FINANCE_ACCESS_LOG — retention: 90d (min: 365d)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Agree the required RAL retention with the DPO/compliance, aligning to regulatory and internal-audit needs (commonly at least 365 days). 2. In SRALMANAGER, review each log channel/log-storage configuration and its current retention/TTL. 3. Increase retention to the agreed minimum for every channel handling personal data. 4. Enable archiving for long-term storage: use SAP data archiving (transaction SARA) / ILM so RAL logs are moved to compliant storage rather than deleted. 5. If using ILM, define an ILM policy in IRMPOL for the RAL log object with the agreed retention and a destruction rule. 6. Ensure log storage (HANA/DB) is sized for the extended retention to avoid premature deletion or logging failure. 7. Restrict deletion of RAL logs to authorized administrators and log those deletions. 8. Verify: inspect the oldest available RAL entry per channel and confirm it meets the retention target. 9. Document the retention decision and its legal basis in the ROPA to satisfy storage-limitation. 10. Caution: longer retention grows storage - coordinate with Basis capacity planning and, in RISE, with the SAP-managed storage sizing/contract.
References
  • GDPR Article 5(1)(e) — Storage Limitation
MEDIUM P4 · 22 ILM policies with retention exceeding 10 years DPP-ILM-001 ▶
Security Risk
SAP ILM policies (maintained in IRMPOL) define how long each data object is retained before it may be blocked or destroyed. Retention periods that exceed a defensible maximum (default flagged at 10 years) mean personal data - HR records, business-partner and customer PII, financial documents - is kept far longer than the processing purpose or statutory requirement justifies, violating GDPR/DPDP storage-limitation and data-minimization. Over-retention is dangerous because every extra year of retained PII enlarges the breach blast radius: data that should have been destroyed is still present to be stolen, misused, or subpoenaed. It also creates direct compliance exposure - a regulator can fine an organization simply for holding data with no lawful justification, independent of any breach. Abuse scenario: an attacker who compromises the system, or an over-privileged internal user, accesses decades of historical personnel and customer records that ought to have been erased; a subsequent subject-access or erasure request then reveals the organization is holding data it had no basis to keep. In RISE, excessive retention also inflates the managed-database footprint and cost. A real incident looks like a complaint or audit discovering ex-employees' or former customers' full records retained a decade past their lawful period, triggering enforcement and mandatory bulk deletion.
Affected Items (2)
  • HR_Payroll_Retention (object: PA0008) — retention: 15 years (max: 10)
  • Customer_Master (object: KNA1) — retention: 99 years (max: 10)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In transaction IRMPOL, list all ILM policies/retention rules and note each object's retention period and unit. 2. For each flagged object, obtain the governing statutory retention (e.g. tax/commercial-law periods) from Legal/Tax and the DPO. 3. Reduce the ILM retention period to the minimum necessary; where multiple rules apply, use the shortest defensible period per data category. 4. Where a long period is genuinely required by law, document the specific legal basis and retain that justification in the ROPA. 5. Configure Residence and Retention periods correctly (residence in the live DB vs. retention post-archiving) so data is archived then destroyed on schedule. 6. Ensure a destruction rule/end action is set so data is actually removed at end of retention (see DPP-ILM-002). 7. Transport the corrected policy through the landscape via change management. 8. Verify: simulate the retention calculation for sample records (ILM/SARA preprocessing) and confirm destruction dates now fall within policy. 9. Schedule ILM destruction runs (SARA / ILM destruction) to clear the backlog of over-retained data after approval. 10. Caution: destruction is irreversible - validate legal holds/e-discovery flags first and run in a controlled cycle with DPO sign-off.
References
  • GDPR Article 5(1)(e) — Storage Limitation
  • DPDP Act 2023 Section 8(7) — Data Retention
MEDIUM P4 · 22 ILM policies without automatic data destruction DPP-ILM-002 ▶
Security Risk
An ILM policy that relies on manual destruction, or has no destruction method configured, means data reaches end-of-retention but is never actually deleted - it simply accumulates. This defeats the purpose of ILM: the retention clock is set but nothing enforces erasure, so personal data is retained indefinitely in practice. Manual destruction processes are notoriously unreliable - they depend on someone remembering to run them, are deprioritized under operational pressure, and produce inconsistent, undocumented outcomes. The result is data hoarding: former employees', customers', and vendors' PII persists years past its lawful window, enlarging breach exposure and creating standing GDPR Art.5(1)(e)/Art.17 non-compliance. Abuse scenario: because destruction never runs, an attacker or insider who gains database or SE16 access finds a rich trove of historical personal and financial data that should have been gone; and when an erasure request arrives, staff must hunt and manually purge records across tables and archives, frequently missing residual copies. Business impact: audit findings for ineffective data-lifecycle controls, inability to prove erasure, and inflated storage/cost in the managed RISE database. A real incident is an auditor sampling 'destroyed' data objects and finding the records still fully present because destruction was never automated or executed.
Affected Items (3)
  • HR_Payroll_Retention (object: PA0008) — destruction: MANUAL
  • Customer_Master (object: KNA1) — destruction: NONE
  • Vendor_Master (object: LFA1) — destruction: REVIEW
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In IRMPOL, identify each policy whose destruction/end action is MANUAL, REVIEW, NONE, or blank. 2. Define an automatic destruction rule (end action) for each ILM object so data is destroyed when retention expires. 3. Ensure the corresponding ILM/archiving object is configured in SARA (Archive Administration) with write, delete/store, and destruction steps. 4. Activate the ILM_BLOCKING / ILM business functions as required so blocking and destruction are supported. 5. Schedule periodic ILM destruction runs (SARA / ILM destruction jobs) in the batch calendar rather than ad-hoc manual execution. 6. Implement four-eyes approval for destruction of regulated data, logged for accountability. 7. Integrate legal-hold checks so objects under litigation hold are excluded from automatic destruction. 8. Verify: run a destruction preview/simulation, confirm eligible records are selected, and after execution confirm they are physically removed. 9. Reconcile destruction logs against the ROPA and retention schedule periodically. 10. Caution: destruction is irreversible - pilot in a non-production copy, confirm no active business/legal dependency, and obtain DPO sign-off before enabling in production.
References
  • SAP ILM — Data Destruction Configuration
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Expired purposes of processing still active DPP-POP-002 ▶
Security Risk
A purpose of processing that has passed its expiry/valid-to date but is still marked active means personal data continues to be processed under a purpose that no longer has a lawful basis - the justification lapsed but processing did not stop. This violates purpose-limitation (Art.5(1)(b)): data collected for a now-expired purpose should be blocked or deleted, not left in active use. It is dangerous because it is silent - the expiry passed, but nothing enforced a stop, so the data keeps being read, reported on, and shared as though still lawful. Abuse/impact scenario: a consent-based marketing purpose expired, yet campaigns still pull that customer data; or a fixed-term project's processing purpose ended, yet the project's personal data remains fully accessible and in use. A subject who withdrew or whose consent lapsed continues to have their data processed - exactly the kind of violation that generates complaints. Business impact: unlawful continued processing, purpose-limitation findings, and - for consent-based purposes - processing after consent expiry, a common and heavily fined violation. A real incident: a regulator samples processing purposes, finds several past expiry but still active with data flowing, and issues an enforcement notice plus mandatory blocking.
Affected Items (3)
  • Purpose: Marketing Communications — expired: 20241231, status: ACTIVE
  • Purpose: Health & Safety Records — expired: 20250630, status: ACTIVE
  • Purpose: Legacy CRM Migration — expired: 20240101, status: ACTIVE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, list purposes past their expiry/valid-to date that remain in active status. 2. Deactivate each expired purpose in the DPP purpose configuration/register (set status to expired/closed). 3. Trigger end-of-purpose processing so data tied to the expired purpose is blocked (BUPA_PRE_EOP / CVP_PRE_EOP for BP data; ILM blocking for other objects). 4. Review the affected data for deletion eligibility and schedule ILM destruction where no other purpose or legal hold applies. 5. Where processing must continue, establish and document a new valid purpose and legal basis before re-enabling - do not simply extend the old one without justification. 6. Update the ROPA to reflect the closed purposes and any resulting blocking/deletion. 7. Implement automated expiry monitoring/alerts so purposes are reviewed before they lapse rather than after. 8. Verify: confirm the expired purposes now show inactive and that data under them is blocked/no longer processed (test a sample record). 9. For consent-based purposes, confirm downstream systems (marketing/BTP) also stopped processing. 10. Caution: coordinate with business owners before blocking to avoid disrupting a still-valid activity that was merely mis-dated, and involve the DPO in deletion decisions.
References
  • GDPR Article 5(1)(b) — Purpose Limitation
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Known sensitive fields missing from data classification inventory DPP-FIELD-003 ▶
Security Risk
The scanner compares SAP's well-known sensitive fields (the HIGHLY_SENSITIVE_FIELDS set - HR fields like PERNR/GBDAT/BANKN/BETRG, special-category RACKY ethnicity/CONFG religion/GESCH gender, BP/customer PII, tax IDs, financial amounts) against the organization's classification inventory and flags those absent. Fields missing from the inventory are, by definition, unmanaged: they do not get RAL, masking, or retention/erasure treatment, because the privacy program does not know they exist as PII. This 'you cannot protect what you have not classified' gap is dangerous because it silently undermines all other controls - a field like GBDAT (date of birth) or ICNUM (national ID) that is not inventoried falls through every downstream protection. Special-category fields (race, religion) are especially serious: processing them requires Art.9 conditions, and if they are not even classified the organization almost certainly lacks the required safeguards and legal basis. Abuse/impact scenario: sensitive attributes are read, exported, copied to non-prod, and retained indefinitely with no control because they were never recognized as PII; a later data-mapping exercise or breach reveals the organization was processing special-category data it never accounted for. Business impact: incomplete ROPA/data map (Art.30), unprotected special-category data (Art.9), and audit findings of an inaccurate inventory. A real incident: a DPIA or breach investigation discovers unclassified national-ID or ethnicity fields in active use with none of the mandated protections.
Affected Items (19)
  • PERNR: Personnel number
  • PERID: Personal ID number
  • ICNUM: National ID / passport
  • NATIO: Nationality
  • BANKL: Bank routing number
  • SWIFT: SWIFT/BIC code
  • LGART: Wage type
  • GESCH: Gender
  • RACKY: Ethnicity/race
  • CONFG: Religion
  • PSTLZ: Postal code
  • NAME2: Name line 2
  • STCD2: Tax ID 2
  • LIFNR: Vendor number
  • WRBTR: Transaction amount
  • DMBTR: Local currency amount
  • BELNR: Document number
  • HKONT: GL account
  • SAESSION_COOKIE: Session identifiers
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, take the list of known-sensitive fields absent from the inventory. 2. Add each to the personal-data classification inventory with the correct sensitivity level (PII vs. special category). 3. Flag special-category fields (ethnicity RACKY, religion CONFG, gender GESCH, health) for Art.9 handling and confirm a lawful condition exists. 4. Use automated personal-data discovery/classification tooling to find further undocumented PII across custom tables and Z-fields, not just the standard list. 5. For each newly classified field, trigger the downstream controls: RAL (DPP-FIELD-001), non-prod masking (DPP-FIELD-002), and ILM retention (DPP-ILM-004). 6. Update the ROPA/data map to reflect the added fields and their processing purposes. 7. Assign data owners for the newly classified fields. 8. Verify: re-run the classification/inventory comparison and confirm no known-sensitive field remains unclassified. 9. Establish a periodic re-scan so newly added custom fields are classified going forward. 10. Caution: special-category data may require immediate remediation (basis, safeguards) - escalate those to the DPO rather than just cataloguing them, and confirm cross-border implications (DPP-RES-002).
References
  • SAP DPI — Personal Data Discovery & Classification
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Data subject requests without documentation DPP-DEL-003 ▶
Security Risk
The accountability principle (Art.5(2)) requires controllers not only to comply but to demonstrate compliance. Data-subject requests with no documentation or justification recorded mean the organization cannot prove what was requested, how identity was verified, what actions were taken, which exemptions were applied, or when it completed - even if the underlying work was done correctly. This is dangerous because in a regulatory challenge, undocumented compliance is treated as non-compliance: the burden of proof is on the controller, and 'we did it but kept no record' is not a defense. Abuse/impact scenario: a regulator or data subject disputes how a request was handled - e.g. alleges an erasure was incomplete or that identity was not verified before disclosure - and the organization has no audit trail to rebut the claim; or a disclosure was made to an imposter and there is no record of the identity check that should have prevented it. Missing documentation also prevents internal quality control and trend analysis of request handling. Business impact: failed accountability audits, inability to defend against complaints, and exposure to claims of mishandling. A real incident: during an investigation the organization cannot produce the case file for a contested request, and the regulator infers it was mishandled, tipping the outcome against the controller.
Affected Items (5)
  • Request DSAR-2025-003 (DELETION, subject: vendor_9012) — no documentation/justification recorded
  • Request DSAR-2025-005 (RECTIFICATION, subject: customer_7890) — no documentation/justification recorded
  • Request DSAR-2025-006 (DELETION, subject: prospect_1111) — no documentation/justification recorded
  • Request DSAR-2025-007 (ACCESS, subject: employee_2222) — no documentation/justification recorded
  • Request DSAR-2025-008 (DELETION, subject: customer_3333) — no documentation/justification recorded
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, identify requests lacking documentation and reconstruct records where possible from system logs and handler recollection. 2. Define a mandatory documentation template for every request capturing: identity-verification evidence, request scope/type, data located, actions taken, exemptions/legal holds applied, and completion confirmation with timestamps. 3. Backfill documentation for the flagged requests to the extent reconstructable, and flag any that cannot be evidenced. 4. Store request case files in a controlled repository with appropriate access restrictions and retention. 5. Make documentation a required, enforced step in the request workflow so a request cannot be closed without it. 6. Link technical evidence (RAL / Security Audit Log entries, ILM deletion logs, IRF disclosure output) to each case file. 7. Assign the DPO/privacy team ownership of case-file completeness and periodic review. 8. Verify: sample recent closed requests and confirm each has a complete, retained record. 9. Retain documentation per the organization's accountability/retention policy. 10. Caution: request documentation itself contains personal data - apply access controls and its own retention limit so the accountability records do not become a new over-retention/exposure problem.
References
  • GDPR Article 5(2) — Accountability Principle
  • DPDP Act 2023 Section 8(8) — Records of Processing
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Systems without data classification assignment DPP-LAND-001 ▶
Security Risk
Systems in the landscape with no data-classification level assigned (Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted) lack the foundational label that drives every protective control - encryption strength, access-control tightness, monitoring/logging depth, backup handling, and whether production PII is even permitted. Without classification, the organization cannot consistently decide how a system must be protected, so controls are applied ad hoc and gaps go unnoticed. This is dangerous because an unclassified system that in fact holds Restricted/PII data may be treated with Internal-grade controls - weak access, no RAL, no masking obligation - creating exactly the exposure the earlier findings describe, but invisibly, because nobody flagged the system as sensitive. Abuse/impact scenario: an unclassified QA or peripheral system that actually contains production personal or financial data is left with lax access and no monitoring; an attacker or insider targets it precisely because it is under-protected, and the breach is severe because the data is sensitive despite the system's un-labeled status. Classification gaps also break audit and ISO 27001 information-classification requirements. Business impact: inconsistent security posture, mis-prioritized controls and monitoring, and audit findings against information-classification policy. A real incident: a breach post-mortem finds the compromised system held sensitive data but had never been classified, so it received none of the controls its data warranted.
Affected Items (1)
  • TRN (env: TRAINING)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. From the finding, list every system without a classification and, for each, determine the highest sensitivity of data it holds (does it contain production PII/financial data?). 2. Assign a classification level to each system per the corporate scheme (e.g. Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted), aligned to ISO 27001 information-classification practice. 3. Record the classification in the authoritative landscape/CMDB source (e.g. SAP Solution Manager LMDB / SLD system attributes) so it is maintained and visible. 4. Map each classification to a control baseline: access-control strictness, encryption, RAL/audit logging, masking obligations, and backup handling. 5. For systems now classified Confidential/Restricted, verify the corresponding controls are actually in place (RAL, non-prod masking, tightened authorizations) and remediate gaps. 6. Cross-check against production-copy flags (DPP-MASK-002) so any classified-sensitive non-prod system gets masking. 7. Establish governance so no new system is provisioned/promoted without a classification (a gate in the build/RISE onboarding process). 8. Verify: reconcile the landscape so every system carries a classification and its controls match the assigned level. 9. Review classifications periodically and on significant data-scope changes. 10. Caution: classification must reflect actual data content, not assumptions - validate with data/process owners and treat 'unknown' as high-sensitivity until confirmed to avoid under-protecting.
References
  • ISO 27001 — Information Classification
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Transport imports outside normal change windows (weekends) CODE-TMS-004 ▶
Security Risk
Transports were imported into the target system on weekends / outside normal change windows. Off-hours imports are not inherently malicious, but they are a recognized indicator of change-control weakness: they often coincide with reduced oversight, absent approvers, skipped CAB review, and thin monitoring, which is precisely when unauthorized or emergency-disguised changes are most likely to slip through. The danger is reduced detective control. A change made at 02:00 on a Sunday is less likely to be observed, correlated, or challenged in real time; if it is malicious or erroneous, the window before anyone notices is longer, increasing dwell time and impact. Attackers and malicious insiders deliberately choose low-staffing windows for exactly this reason. Abuse scenario: an insider schedules or manually triggers a production import during a weekend maintenance slot, relying on the absence of the normal approval/monitoring staff to land a change (e.g., a config or role modification) that would draw scrutiny during business hours. By the time it is reviewed on Monday, the change has already executed against live data. Business impact: weakened change-window governance, potential SOX finding if off-hours changes lack the same approval rigor, and slower incident detection. A real incident is a problematic production change that was imported outside the sanctioned window and correlated only after downstream effects appeared, having evaded timely review.
Affected Items (6)
  • DEVK900100 → QAS — imported: 2025-02-15 (weekend)
  • DEVK900102 → QAS — imported: 2025-02-22 (weekend)
  • DEVK900103 → PRD — imported: 2025-03-01 (weekend)
  • DEVK900104 → QAS — imported: 2025-03-01 (weekend)
  • DEVK900105 → QAS — imported: 2025-03-02 (weekend)
  • DEVK900105 → PRD — imported: 2025-03-02 (weekend)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the off-hours/weekend imports from the transport history and reconcile each against an approved change record and an authorized maintenance window. 2. Define and publish formal change windows and change-freeze periods in the change policy (and in ChaRM / SAP Cloud ALM if used). 3. Require an explicit emergency/exception approval for any import outside the standard window, captured before the import. 4. For each flagged import, confirm it had valid emergency justification; document a post-implementation review for those that did, and raise exceptions for those that did not. 5. Ensure off-hours imports still pass the same QA Approval Procedure and four-eyes controls as business-hours imports - the window must not lower the bar. 6. Enable/verify the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG) and alert on production imports occurring outside defined windows (e.g., via monitoring on STMS import events). 7. Restrict production import authorization to the on-call operations team and log all activity. 8. Verify the control by reviewing the next scheduled off-hours change and confirming approval + review evidence exists before and after. 9. Coordinate window definitions with application/interface owners so legitimate batch/maintenance work is scheduled and pre-approved. 10. Report the reconciliation results (justified vs. unjustified off-hours imports) to the change/GRC owner.
References
  • ITIL — Change Window Management
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Critical object types without change documents CODE-CHG-001 ▶
Security Risk
Change documents are absent for one or more critical object types (e.g., USER/PFCG role changes, T000 client config, TADIR repository directory, RFCDES RFC destinations, CDHDR itself). Missing change history for these objects means either that change logging is switched off for them or that the audit export is incomplete - in both cases the forensic trail for the most security-relevant objects in the system is broken. The danger is loss of detective and forensic control precisely where it matters most. User and role changes, RFC destination changes, and client/config changes are the actions an attacker or malicious insider takes to escalate privilege, create backdoors, or open the system - and if these are not logged, such actions become invisible. An attacker who knows logging is off for these objects can operate with impunity. Abuse scenario: an insider grants themselves a powerful role or creates a trusted RFC destination to a target system; with change documents/table logging disabled for PFCG/RFCDES, no CDHDR/CDPOS or DBTABLOG record is produced, so a later review finds no evidence the change ever happened, defeating both real-time detection and post-incident investigation. Business impact: inability to detect or investigate privilege escalation and configuration tampering, and failure of SOX/GDPR requirements for an auditable change trail. A real incident is discovered late (or never) because the very objects used in the attack had no change history, forcing reliance on incomplete secondary evidence.
Affected Items (5)
  • PFCG: Role changes
  • CDHDR: Change document header manipulation
  • T000: Client configuration changes
  • TADIR: Repository object directory changes
  • RFCDES: RFC destination changes
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm whether the gap is a logging gap or an export gap: check whether change documents/table logging are actually active for the listed object types before assuming missing data. 2. Verify the system-wide table-logging switch: parameter rec/client (check via RZ11/RSPFPAR) must be set to log the production client (e.g., ALL); coordinate the value and any restart with SAP ECS under RISE. 3. For sensitive tables, ensure 'Log data changes' is enabled in the technical settings (SE13) so changes are captured in DBTABLOG and viewable via SCU3. 4. Confirm change-document objects are active for user/role/config changes (SU01/PFCG changes are logged in CDHDR/CDPOS by standard; validate they are present). 5. Enable and configure the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG; read via SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG) to record security events for users, RFC, and debugging as a complementary trail. 6. For any object type where logging was genuinely off, enable it and document the change-control baseline of logged objects. 7. Re-run the data export to ensure completeness, then re-assess coverage against the critical object list. 8. Verify by making a test change to a covered table/object and confirming a corresponding record appears in SCU3/DBTABLOG or CDHDR/CDPOS. 9. Protect the logs: restrict deletion authorizations (table logging deletion, RSAU log admin) so the trail cannot be tampered with. 10. Report the corrected logging baseline to GRC/audit and re-check after client copies, which can reset technical settings.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Change Document Logging
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Change documents with empty or system user attribution CODE-CHG-002 ▶
Security Risk
Change documents are attributed to empty, BATCH, SYSTEM, or DDIC users. When changes to business or configuration data are recorded against a generic/technical identity rather than a named person, the audit trail cannot establish who actually made the change. This breaks non-repudiation and undermines every downstream investigation and SOX control that depends on user attribution. The danger is twofold. First, legitimate automation running under a shared generic account produces changes no one can be held accountable for. Second, an attacker or insider can deliberately hide behind a generic/technical user (or a job that runs as one) so that malicious changes appear as anonymous system activity, frustrating detection and attribution. DDIC in particular is a powerful standard account whose use for data changes is a red flag. Abuse scenario: an insider schedules or triggers a data/config change through a batch job or a shared technical user so the change document shows only 'BATCH'/'SYSTEM'; during a fraud investigation the change is real and damaging, but it cannot be pinned to any individual, so accountability - and the ability to prosecute or remediate access - is lost. Business impact: failure of SOX Section 404 change-attribution controls, weakened forensic readiness, and potential masking of fraud. A real incident is a confirmed unauthorized change whose change document names only a generic user, leaving investigators unable to prove who performed it and forcing reliance on circumstantial system logs.
Affected Items (2)
  • MATERIAL #0001234575 — user: empty, tcode: MM01, date: 20250215
  • VENDOR #0001234580 — user: BATCH, tcode: , date: 20250220
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the change documents attributed to empty/BATCH/SYSTEM/DDIC users and identify, for each, the originating program, job, or interface. 2. For legitimate automation, replace shared generic users with named service/system accounts of type 'System' or 'Communication' (SU01), one per interface/job, so activity is attributable. 3. Ensure background jobs (SM36/SM37) are defined to run under a specific named service account rather than a generic one; update the job steps accordingly. 4. Lock down and stop using DDIC and other standard users for routine changes; restrict and monitor DDIC per SAP Security Baseline, and rotate its password. 5. For system-to-system (RFC/IDoc/OData) flows, configure dedicated technical users per connection so inbound changes carry a traceable identity. 6. Verify the Security Audit Log (SM19/RSAU_CONFIG) captures logon and change events for these technical users to reinforce attribution. 7. Investigate any empty-user or DDIC change that cannot be tied to a known job as a potential incident and escalate. 8. Verify remediation by triggering the affected job/interface and confirming the resulting change document now shows the named service account. 9. Coordinate the account changes with interface/job owners and test in QA to avoid breaking automated flows. 10. Report the cleaned-up attribution model and residual generic-user usage to GRC/audit.
References
  • SOX Section 404 — Change Audit Trail
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Unregistered SAP standard modifications CODE-MOD-001 ▶
Security Risk
SAP standard objects have been modified without registration against an SAP Note / correction number (no SSCR / Modification Assistant record). Unregistered modifications are undocumented deviations from SAP standard: no one knows why the change was made, what it affects, or whether it is still needed, and the Modification Adjustment tools (SPAU/SPDD) rely on registration to surface them at upgrade time. The security danger is that undocumented modifications can silently alter standard behavior - including security-relevant logic - and are easily lost or mishandled during Support Package and upgrade cycles. A modification that weakens a standard check may be reintroduced or dropped unpredictably, and because it is unregistered, it evades the structured upgrade review, potentially re-opening a vulnerability or breaking a control without anyone noticing. Abuse/failure scenario: during an S/4HANA upgrade or SP import, an unregistered modification to a standard program is either overwritten (removing a needed control or fix) or blindly re-applied (reintroducing a weakness), and because it never appeared in the modification browser, it is not reviewed - leaving the system in an unknown, possibly insecure state. Business impact: upgrade instability, unmanaged security drift, and a governance/audit finding that the organization cannot account for changes to standard code. A real incident is a post-upgrade defect or security regression traced to an unregistered modification that the upgrade process could not properly adjust because it was never registered.
Affected Items (4)
  • SAPLSU01 (type: PROG, by: LWANG) — no SAP Note / registration
  • SAPMHTTP (type: PROG, by: FORMER_DEV) — no SAP Note / registration
  • SAPLAUTH (type: PROG, by: LWANG) — no SAP Note / registration
  • SAPLSTMS (type: PROG, by: ADMIN) — no SAP Note / registration
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Enumerate the modified standard objects via the Modification Browser (transaction SE95) and SPAU/SPDD, and cross-check against the flagged list. 2. For each modification, establish and document the business reason, the exact behavior change, and whether it is still required. 3. Bring modifications under the Modification Assistant so they are tracked and adjustable at upgrade; register them properly (SE95) rather than leaving them as raw, unregistered changes. 4. Where the functionality can be achieved via a supported extension point, replace the modification with a BAdI / enhancement-framework / user-exit implementation and revert the core modification. 5. Retire modifications that are no longer needed by resetting the object to SAP standard. 6. Give special scrutiny to any modification touching security-relevant standard code and route it through CODE-MOD-002 handling. 7. Ensure all modifications are captured in transports and documented in the change record so they survive and are reviewed at the next SP/upgrade (SPAU). 8. Verify by re-running SE95/SPAU and confirming every remaining modification is registered and documented. 9. Test reverted/replaced logic in QA to confirm no functional regression before transporting DEV->QA->PRD. 10. Record the modification register as audit evidence and review it before each upgrade project.
References
  • SAP Note 7920 — Modification Assistant
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Security Audit Log integrity protection not active (rsau/integrity = 0) LOG-AUD-011 ▶
Security Risk
Profile parameter rsau/integrity = 0. Without the tamper-evident (integrity) audit log format, a local attacker or administrator can alter or delete audit records to cover their tracks, undermining the chain of custody that makes the SAL usable as forensic evidence.
Affected Items (1)
  • rsau/integrity = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
Set rsau/integrity = 1 to enable the integrity-protected audit log format.
References
  • SAP Note 2033317 — Security Audit Log integrity protection
  • SOX ITGC — log integrity / chain of custody
MEDIUM P4 · 22 SIEM missing critical log source forwarding LOG-SIEM-002 ▶
Security Risk
Here a SIEM connector is active but only a subset of the required log sources is being forwarded - the module checks for SM20 (Security Audit Log), SM21 (system log), CDHDR (change documents), BTP_AUDIT (BTP audit log), ICM_LOG (HTTP access), and GATEWAY_LOG (RFC gateway). Partial coverage yields partial visibility, and each missing source is a specific, exploitable detection hole. Concrete gaps: if SM20 is forwarded but CDHDR is not, the SOC sees logons but not the actual configuration and master-data changes, so a fraudulent vendor bank-detail change in LFA1 followed by a payment run goes undetected. If ICM access logging is missing, web-tier attacks against the Fiori launchpad and OData services - path traversal, injection, credential stuffing - are invisible. If the gateway log is absent, RFC gateway attacks (reg_info/sec_info bypass, registration of rogue external programs) are unseen. If the BTP audit log is not forwarded, high-impact cockpit actions (role-collection assignment, destination edits, service-key creation) are untracked. In a hybrid S/4HANA RISE plus BTP landscape, attackers pivot across these tiers, so uneven coverage lets them pick the unmonitored path. Business and compliance impact: incomplete monitoring undermines the SAP Security Baseline, weakens SOX change-tracking evidence, and slows breach detection. A realistic incident is an OData injection via an exposed service that never reaches the SIEM because ICM logging was never forwarded, resulting in an undetected data breach.
Affected Items (3)
  • BTP_AUDIT: BTP Audit Log
  • ICM_LOG: ICM Access Log (HTTP)
  • GATEWAY_LOG: Gateway security log
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory the required sources and confirm each is both generated and forwarded: SAL (SM20), system log (SM21), change documents (CDHDR/CDPOS), ICM HTTP access log, RFC gateway log, and BTP audit log. 2. Enable ICM access logging via RZ10 parameter icm/HTTP/logging_0 (define log file and fields); enable gateway logging via the gw/logging parameters and review in SMGW. 3. Ensure change documents are extracted (via ETD/extractor) and system log is syslog-forwarded. 4. For BTP, enable Audit Log Retrieval and route Alert Notification Service events by webhook to the SIEM. 5. Map every source into SIEM ingestion with a clear source label, and build parsers per source. 6. Verify each source individually by generating a representative event (an HTTP request, an RFC call, a config change) and confirming it lands in the SIEM. 7. Rollout caution: HTTP and gateway logging can be high-volume, so tune the captured fields, and coordinate gateway/ICM parameter changes with interface owners and SAP RISE operations. Reference the SAP Security Baseline and SAP SIEM integration guidance.
References
  • SAP SIEM Integration — Log Source Configuration
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Log retention below 365-day minimum LOG-RET-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding means one or more security log types retain data for fewer than the configured minimum (default 365 days). Short retention directly limits forensic reach, and that matters because sophisticated attacks and internal fraud are frequently discovered months after the fact - industry dwell times routinely exceed 200 days. If the Security Audit Log rotates after 30-90 days, then by the time a breach or fraud surfaces the evidence has already been overwritten. The consequences are concrete: investigators cannot scope the breach (what was accessed, by whom, over what period), auditors cannot obtain evidence that SOX controls operated throughout the audit period, and the organisation cannot meet GDPR accountability obligations. In RISE and BTP the risk is heightened because the BTP Audit Log Retrieval service retains only about 90 days by default - longer retention requires an explicit export - and local SAL files are overwritten once rsau/max_diskspace is reached. Attack/abuse scenario: an insider commits fraud in January; a routine SOX walkthrough in Q4 requests the change history for a critical role or a vendor bank-detail change; the logs were purged after 90 days, so the control cannot be evidenced. This becomes an audit control deficiency and, if pervasive, a potential material weakness. A real incident also looks like an external breach notification arriving five months late, with SAP logs already gone, making impact assessment impossible and regulatory fines more likely.
Affected Items (3)
  • Security Audit Log (SM20): 90d (min: 365d)
  • System Log (SM21): 60d (min: 365d)
  • ICM Access Log: 30d (min: 365d)
Remediation — Step by Step
