1. Define a documented retention standard for security logs - at least 365 days, and longer where SOX, GDPR, or legal hold require it (align the exact figure with Legal/Compliance). 2. For the Security Audit Log, switch recording to the database in RSAU_CONFIG for durable retention (or substantially increase rsau/max_diskspace/local for file-based recording). 3. Use RSAU_ADMIN to manage and reorganise SAL data, and set up archiving via SARA for long-term storage. 4. For change documents and table logs, schedule archiving (SARA archive objects) rather than deletion. 5. For BTP, schedule periodic Audit Log Retrieval API exports to long-term storage (SIEM or object store), since the native retention is only ~90 days. 6. Verify the fix by confirming the oldest retrievable event date for each log type meets the standard. 7. Rollout caution: plan storage capacity for the increased volume, and balance retention against GDPR data-minimisation so personal data is not held longer than justified. Reference the SAP Security Baseline retention guidance and SOX log-retention requirements.
References
  • SOX — Log Retention Requirements
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Accounts with excessive logon failures LOG-LOGON-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags accounts with a high absolute number of logon failures (at or above the threshold, default 20) but without the extreme ratio that signals an obvious brute-force attack. The cause is often a misconfigured service or RFC account with a stale password hammering the system, a human user immediately after a password reset, or slow, low-volume password guessing. All three are anomalies that deserve attention. A stale-credential technical account is a real operational risk: repeated failed RFC logons can trip login/fails_to_user_lock and lock the account, taking down an interface (for example a nightly order or payment job) and causing a business outage. Simultaneously, a steady background of 'expected' failures conditions administrators to ignore logon-failure noise, so a genuine slow spray against a dialog user hides inside it. Abuse/impact scenario: an integration user's password expires; the nightly RFC job fails hundreds of times, the account locks, and the interface stops - while, unnoticed in the same noise, an attacker conducts a low-and-slow credential-guessing campaign against a privileged human account. Because nothing alerts on the spike, both the outage and the attack are found late. Compliance and monitoring impact: the absence of alerting on logon-failure spikes is a weak-monitoring deviation from the SAP Security Baseline and undermines the ability to demonstrate effective access monitoring for SOX. Rated medium because it is frequently benign, but it must be triaged rather than dismissed.
Affected Items (2)
  • MWILSON: 45 failures, 80 successes (ratio: 0.6)
  • SVC_RFC_01: 200 failures, 5000 successes (ratio: 0.0)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review each flagged account in RSAU_READ_LOG (SM20) and the system log (SM21) to determine the failure reason (wrong password, expired, locked). 2. For service/technical accounts, set the user type to SYSTEM or COMMUNICATION in SU01 so dialog logon is impossible, apply a non-expiring credential policy or move to SNC/certificate authentication, and fix stored credentials in the RFC destinations (SM59) and the Secure Store. 3. For human users, contact them, reset the password, and provide guidance. 4. Implement automated alerting on logon-failure spikes via ETD/SIEM correlation rules or a CCMS/RZ20 (Solution Manager) monitor. 5. Keep login/fails_to_user_lock enforced for interactive users while handling service accounts through robust credential management rather than blanket lockout exemptions. 6. Verify the counts drop after remediation using report RSUSR200 and a re-run of the logon review. 7. Rollout caution: do not broadly exempt accounts from lockout to silence the noise, and coordinate credential fixes with interface owners so remediation does not itself cause an outage.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — Logon Monitoring
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Incident response readiness gaps LOG-IR-001 ▶
Security Risk
This finding indicates gaps in incident-response readiness - one or more of runbook/playbook, emergency contact list, escalation matrix, documented forensic-access procedure, log-backup verification, and IR drill/tabletop schedule are missing. When an SAP security incident occurs, the absence of these turns response into an ad hoc scramble at exactly the moment speed matters most. In RISE the situation is compounded by shared responsibility: the customer and SAP each own parts of the response. Without a documented runbook and current SAP RISE/ECS escalation contacts, teams waste hours determining who does what while the attacker persists. Without pre-approved forensic access, investigators cannot pull SAL, system logs, and table-change logs quickly - and in the worst case an untrained admin overwrites the evidence. Without log-backup verification, the one time the logs are needed they are found missing or corrupt. Without drills, the plan fails on first real use. Abuse/impact scenario: ransomware or a fraud event hits production; the team has no SAP incident hotline, no forensic role provisioned, and evidence is overwritten before it is collected, so the GDPR 72-hour breach-notification deadline is missed. Compliance frameworks (NIST SP 800-61, ISO 27035, and SOX incident-handling expectations) all require a tested IR capability, so these gaps are both an operational and an audit exposure. A real incident looks like a delayed, uncoordinated response that amplifies both the breach impact and the regulatory penalty.
Affected Items (3)
  • forensicAccess: Forensic access procedures documented
  • backupVerification: Log backup verification schedule
  • drillSchedule: IR drill/tabletop exercise schedule
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Author an SAP-specific IR runbook covering containment, evidence collection from RSAU_READ_LOG (SM20), SM21, SCU3, ST22, and STAD, account locking via SU01, and RFC/gateway isolation. 2. Maintain an emergency contact list that explicitly includes the SAP RISE/ECS support escalation path plus internal on-call security. 3. Define an escalation matrix mapped to incident severity levels. 4. Pre-provision break-glass forensic access (for example firefighter IDs via SAP GRC Emergency Access Management, with read authorization to the logs) so investigators can act immediately without an approval delay. 5. Schedule and verify log backups/exports (SAL from the database, BTP audit-log exports) and periodically test restoration. 6. Run regular tabletop/IR drills and capture lessons learned to improve the runbook. 7. Verify readiness by executing a tabletop against the runbook and confirming every contact and escalation entry is current. 8. Rollout caution: align the RACI with the SAP RISE contract, and keep the runbook version-controlled and access-restricted. Reference NIST SP 800-61 and ISO 27035.
References
  • NIST SP 800-61 — Incident Handling Guide
MEDIUM P4 · 22 No Security Audit Log event extract supplied — no window could be reviewed LREV-SRC-001 ▶
Security Risk
The upload contains the Security Audit Log filter CONFIGURATION but no event extract, so the retrospective review could only assess whether the log was capturing — not what it captured. The configuration half of this module ran; the pattern half had nothing to read. Without an event export no statement can be made about privileged access outside business hours, failed-logon runs that ended in a success, standard-account use, debug activity, direct table access or changes to the audit configuration itself.
Affected Items (1)
  • security_audit_log.csv: 6 filter configuration row(s), 0 event row(s)
Remediation — Step by Step
Export the Security Audit Log for the period to be reviewed (SM20 / RSAU_READ_LOG, download the result list) and include it in the upload as security_audit_log.csv. Useful columns: date, time, client, user, terminal, transaction code, audit/event class and message text. A 90-day window is a reasonable first review; anything under 30 days cannot show what is normal for the system.
References
  • SAP Note 2191612 — Security Audit Log
  • SAP Security Baseline — Security Audit Log evaluation
  • NIST SP 800-92 — Guide to Computer Security Log Management
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Event class recorded only by a dynamic filter — coverage is lost at restart LREV-FLT-003 ▶
Security Risk
1 event class(es) are recorded only by a dynamic audit filter: transaction_start. Dynamic filters apply until the next system restart and are not reactivated automatically, so after the next restart these classes stop being written while the configuration continues to list them. A retrospective review of a window that spans a restart would then report no events of these classes without anything indicating why.
Affected Items (1)
  • transaction_start: dynamic filter only, no static coverage
Remediation — Step by Step
Move these classes into a static audit profile in SM19 / RSAU_CONFIG so they are activated automatically at system start. Keep dynamic filters for temporary, targeted investigations only.
References
  • SAP Note 2191612 — Security Audit Log (static vs dynamic profiles)
  • SAP Security Baseline — Security Audit Log configuration
MEDIUM P4 · 22 HTTPS endpoints without HSTS (Strict Transport Security) CRYPTO-TLS-003 ▶
Security Risk
HTTPS endpoints are not returning the HTTP Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) response header. HSTS instructs the browser to only ever contact the host over HTTPS and to refuse to fall back to plain HTTP; without it the browser will happily follow an HTTP link or redirect, which opens an SSL-stripping window. The attack is classic sslstrip: an on-path attacker (rogue Wi-Fi, malicious corporate proxy, ARP-spoofing a shared segment) intercepts the victim's first, pre-upgrade request or any http:// redirect to the Fiori Launchpad, terminates it in cleartext to the user while maintaining HTTPS to the server, and transparently relays traffic. Everything the user types or receives is then visible to the attacker - Fiori/WebGUI logon credentials, the MYSAPSSO2 SSO ticket, session cookies and business data - despite the backend genuinely supporting TLS. In a RISE deployment users typically reach Fiori through corporate proxies, VPNs with split tunnelling, or from home networks, all of which give an attacker realistic on-path positions, and the absence of HSTS means there is no browser-enforced backstop. Because this is a downgrade-and-intercept rather than a break of the crypto itself, it works even when the server's ciphers and protocols are perfectly hardened - HSTS is the control that closes the gap. Business impact: credential theft leading to account takeover, session hijack, and exposure of any data in the stripped session; the compromise is silent to the user. Compliance impact: OWASP ASVS and the SAP Security Baseline call for HSTS on web front-ends; its absence is a routine web-assessment finding. This is rated Medium because exploitation requires an on-path position, but it materially amplifies every other TLS weakness.
Affected Items (2)
  • HTTPS_Default (port: 443) — HSTS: not enabled
  • HTTP_ICM (port: 8000) — HSTS: not enabled
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Set the ICM to emit the header by configuring icm/HTTPS/hsts_header = max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains (see SAP KBA 3359291 'Configuring HSTS with Web Dispatcher or ICM'); on some releases the parameter is icm/HTTP/strict_transport_security. 2. Prefer to terminate and set the header at the SAP Web Dispatcher so there is a single, consistent choke point for all backend systems. 3. Ensure the kernel/CommonCryptoLib and ICM patch level supports HTTP response-header handling; if using rewrite rules, follow SAP Note 2042819 (ICM HTTP response header rewriting). 4. Make sure the endpoints only serve HTTPS and that any http:// listener issues a 301 redirect to https:// so the header is honoured on the secured response. 5. Persist the parameter in the instance profile with RZ10 and restart the ICM via SMICM. 6. Verify with 'curl -sI https://host:44300 | grep -i strict-transport-security' - the header with the correct max-age must be present. 7. Set includeSubDomains only after confirming every subdomain is HTTPS-capable, and consider HSTS preload only once full coverage is validated, since preload is hard to reverse. 8. Rollout caution: a one-year max-age is sticky in browsers - roll out in QA first and confirm no internal host is reachable only over HTTP.
References
  • SAP Note 2300507 — HSTS Configuration
MEDIUM P4 · 22 HANA log volume encryption is disabled CRYPTO-HANA-002 ▶
Security Risk
SAP HANA redo log (log volume) encryption is disabled. The redo log captures every committed change to the database - the complete before/after image of inserts, updates and deletes - and log backups are continuously shipped to storage for point-in-time recovery. If the log volumes and log backups are not encrypted, this stream of sensitive transactional data sits on disk in cleartext. Crucially, encrypting the data volume alone is not sufficient: even with CRYPTO-HANA-001 remediated, an attacker who obtains the redo logs or log backups can reconstruct recent transactions - new bank details, payment postings, HR changes, GDPR-relevant record modifications - directly from the log content. Threat scenario in RISE: log backups are typically written frequently to hyperscaler storage; a mis-scoped bucket, a leaked backup file, or filesystem access on the HANA host exposes the log stream, and the attacker replays/parses it to extract the changed records without needing the main data volume. Business impact: partial-to-substantial data breach focused on the most recent (and often most sensitive, actively changing) records, with the same GDPR/SOX/ISO 27001 compliance failures as unencrypted data at rest. Because log data is more granular and change-focused, it can be especially valuable to an attacker profiling recent activity (e.g. treasury or vendor-master changes). A realistic incident: a routine log backup copied for a recovery test is left on an unsecured share and later found to reveal the last several hours of financial postings in plaintext. Rated Medium relative to the full-database data-volume exposure, but it is a necessary companion control - at-rest encryption is only complete when data, log and backup are all covered.
Affected Items (1)
  • Log volume encryption: disabled
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Connect to the HANA database via hdbsql/HANA Cockpit/DBA Cockpit with the appropriate encryption/system privilege. 2. Ensure the encryption root keys in the instance SSFS are backed up before making changes (the same SSFS protects the log root key). 3. Enable redo log encryption with: ALTER SYSTEM LOG ENCRYPTION ON; (AES-256). 4. Confirm backup encryption is also on so log backups are protected: ALTER SYSTEM BACKUP ENCRYPTION ON; and generate fresh log backups afterwards. 5. Verify with: SELECT * FROM M_ENCRYPTION_OVERVIEW WHERE NAME = 'LOG_VOLUME'; the status should show encryption active. 6. Enable data volume and backup encryption together (see CRYPTO-HANA-001) so the at-rest control is complete across data, log and backups. 7. Keep the SSFS/root-key backups in a location separate from the log backups. 8. Rollout caution: only newly written log segments are encrypted going forward, so there is minimal disruption, but validate backup/recovery still works after the change; in RISE raise the enablement with SAP ECS and confirm the resulting M_ENCRYPTION_OVERVIEW state.
References
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Log Encryption
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Key management policy gaps CRYPTO-KEY-001 ▶
Security Risk
The key-management review found one or more governance gaps: no defined key-rotation policy (or manual-only rotation), a rotation interval longer than the configured maximum (default 365 days), and/or no encryption-key backup configured. These gaps concern the cryptographic keys that protect the whole environment - HANA data/log/backup root keys and the SSFS master key, SSO/SAML signing keys, and SNC/SSL certificate key pairs. Without rotation, a key that is exposed or compromised stays valid indefinitely, so a single leak (a copied SSFS, a mishandled backup, a departing administrator) grants an attacker a permanent decryption/impersonation capability and a large window to abuse it. Long rotation intervals extend the same exposure and mean that revoking a suspected-compromised key is a rare, disruptive event rather than routine. The absence of key backup/escrow is an availability catastrophe in waiting: if an encryption root key or the SSFS is lost or corrupted with no backup, the encrypted data volumes, logs and backups become permanently unrecoverable - encryption turns a recoverable outage into irreversible data loss. Abuse scenario: an attacker or insider who obtains a long-lived, never-rotated key decrypts historical backups and current data at will; conversely, an operational error that destroys the only copy of a root key renders the production database unopenable, halting the business. Business impact spans both confidentiality (prolonged compromise) and availability (unrecoverable data), and it fails multiple standards - NIST SP 800-57, ISO 27001 A.10, and PCI-DSS Requirement 3 all mandate defined rotation and secure key storage/backup. A realistic incident: a HANA host is rebuilt, the SSFS/root-key backup was never taken, and the encrypted persistence cannot be brought online - a self-inflicted, irreversible outage. Rated Medium as it is a process/governance weakness, but its worst-case outcomes (permanent data loss, indefinite key compromise) are high-severity.
Affected Items (3)
  • Key rotation policy: not configured or manual-only
  • Key rotation interval: 730d (max: 365d)
  • Encryption key backup: not configured
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Define and document a key-management policy that assigns owners and rotation intervals (target no more than 365 days) for each key type: HANA data/log/backup root keys, the SSFS master key, SSO/SAML signing certificates, and SNC/SSL key pairs. 2. Implement HANA root-key rotation on schedule: ALTER SYSTEM PERSISTENCE ENCRYPTION CREATE NEW ROOT KEY WITHOUT ACTIVATE; back up the new key; then ALTER SYSTEM PERSISTENCE ENCRYPTION ACTIVATE NEW ROOT KEY; repeat for LOG and BACKUP encryption. 3. Configure and test key backup/escrow: back up the instance SSFS and system PKI SSFS every time keys change and before enabling any encryption, and store these backups separately from the data/log backups with strict access control. 4. For certificate keys, schedule renewal via STRUST ahead of expiry (see CRYPTO-CERT-002) and rotate SNC PSE keys periodically. 5. Where an external KMS is in use (SAP Data Custodian / hyperscaler KMS, or SAP BTP Credential Store for BTP-side secrets), enable its automated rotation and centralised audit logging. 6. Automate monitoring/alerting on rotation due-dates and on backup success so lapses are detected. 7. Verify recoverability by performing a test restore of a key backup (and a backup encrypted under a rotated key) in a non-production system. 8. Rollout caution: test every rotation and recovery procedure in non-prod first, keep verified backups at each step, and align the documented process with NIST SP 800-57; in RISE coordinate root-key handling and backups with SAP ECS.
References
  • NIST SP 800-57 — Key Management Recommendations
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Dormant HANA DB users (no logon in 90+ days) HANADB-USER-003 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that active DB users have not successfully connected in the configured threshold (default 90 days) or have never connected. Dormant accounts are effectively unmonitored by their owners, who may have left the organisation, changed roles, or simply forgotten them, yet they remain fully valid attack surface. The danger is that anomalous logons on an account that 'isn't used' produce no baseline deviation that anyone will notice, and the legitimate owner will never report a suspicious lockout or unexpected activity. Attack scenario: an adversary who compromises a dormant credential - from a breach dump, an orphaned service account, or a leaver whose account was never disabled - can operate quietly for extended periods, and dormant privileged accounts are especially damaging because they combine stealth with capability. Dormant accounts also inflate the privilege-review and licensing workload and are a classic audit finding. Business and compliance impact: leaver accounts that remain active are a recurring SOX and ISO 27001 exception and a frequent breach root cause, and unattended access to S/4HANA data is a GDPR exposure. A real incident looks like an ex-employee - or an attacker using their old credentials - logging into HANA six months after departure, exporting data, and going unnoticed for weeks because no dormancy control fired.
Affected Items (2)
  • J_SMITH — last connect 559d ago (2025-02-01)
  • OLD_CONSULTANT — last connect 651d ago (2024-11-01)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify candidates: SELECT USER_NAME, LAST_SUCCESSFUL_CONNECT, USER_DEACTIVATED FROM SYS.USERS WHERE USER_DEACTIVATED='FALSE' ORDER BY LAST_SUCCESSFUL_CONNECT; (a null last-connect means never connected). 2. Cross-check each account against HR leaver lists and the interface/service-account inventory. 3. Deactivate first (reversible): ALTER USER <user> DEACTIVATE USER NOW; and retain the account for a defined grace period (e.g. 30-60 days). 4. After the grace period, if no legitimate need is confirmed, drop it: DROP USER <user> RESTRICT; (resolve owned objects deliberately - use CASCADE only when you are sure no dependent objects are needed). 5. Automate dormancy review with a scheduled report (SAP HANA Cockpit, DBACOCKPIT, or a monitored SQL job) that flags accounts idle beyond the threshold and feeds the joiner-mover-leaver process. 6. Verify: re-run the query; deactivated users show USER_DEACTIVATED = TRUE. 7. Rollout caution: some technical/batch users legitimately connect only monthly or quarterly - confirm true inactivity against interface schedules before disabling, coordinate with interface owners, and validate the impact in non-production where feasible.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Unused users
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Sensitive privileges granted WITH ADMIN OPTION HANADB-PRIV-004 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that sensitive privileges are granted WITH ADMIN OPTION (for system privileges and roles) or WITH GRANT OPTION (for object privileges), which lets the grantee re-grant the privilege to further principals. This creates uncontrolled, self-propagating privilege sprawl: the security team grants a capability to one trusted user, who grants it onward to others outside any review, producing a grant graph that is hard to audit and hard to fully unwind. HANA adds an operational hazard - revoking a privilege the grantee has since re-granted can cascade and unexpectedly strip access from downstream users, or fail, making cleanup risky and error-prone. Attack scenario: a malicious or compromised holder of an admin-option privilege quietly grants a second account the same privilege for persistence, or distributes a sensitive privilege to accomplices; because onward granting is legitimate at the SQL level, it does not trip simple 'who did I grant to' reviews. Business and compliance impact: erosion of least privilege over time, inability to prove access boundaries to auditors, and messy remediation that can itself cause outages. A real incident looks like a 'temporary' admin-option grant seeding a web of re-grants so that, years later, dozens of users hold a sensitive privilege that nobody can explain or safely remove.
Affected Items (2)
  • J_SMITH ← DATA ADMIN (WITH ADMIN/GRANT OPTION)
  • CONTRACTOR1 ← TRACE ADMIN (WITH ADMIN/GRANT OPTION)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Find them: SELECT GRANTEE, GRANTEE_TYPE, PRIVILEGE, OBJECT_NAME, IS_GRANTABLE FROM GRANTED_PRIVILEGES WHERE IS_GRANTABLE='TRUE'; 2. For each, determine whether delegation is genuinely required - in most cases it is not. 3. Before revoking, map downstream re-grants (query GRANTED_PRIVILEGES for the same privilege granted onward by that grantee) so the cascade impact is understood. 4. Re-issue without the option: REVOKE <priv> FROM <grantee>; then GRANT <priv> TO <grantee>; (i.e. grant again without WITH ADMIN/GRANT OPTION). 5. Where delegation truly is required, restrict it to a single governed admin role and log all grant/revoke activity with an audit policy. 6. Verify: re-run the IS_GRANTABLE='TRUE' query - only explicitly approved delegations should remain. 7. Rollout caution: revoking an admin-option grant can cascade to dependent users - plan the revoke order, test the cascade in non-production, and stage under change control with app and interface owners informed. 8. Add WITH ADMIN OPTION review to the recurring access-recertification process.
References
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Granting Privileges
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Audit policies do not cover critical action groups HANADB-AUDIT-004 ▶
Security Risk
The finding is that audit policies are active but do not cover one or more of the highest-value action groups: privilege GRANT/REVOKE, user administration (CREATE/ALTER/DROP USER), system configuration changes, and authentication (CONNECT/VALIDATE USER). These are precisely the events that reveal privilege escalation, backdoor-account creation, security-control tampering, and brute-force or enumeration attempts. If GRANT/REVOKE is unaudited, an attacker can escalate privileges and later clean up with no trace; if USER ADMIN is unaudited, stealth superuser creation is invisible; if configuration change is unaudited, an attacker can disable other controls such as sslenforce or the password policy unseen; if CONNECT is unaudited, brute-force and anomalous-logon detection is impossible. Attack scenario: a knowledgeable adversary deliberately operates in the uncovered category - for example performing the escalation via a path the active policies do not watch. Business and compliance impact: partial blindness that produces incomplete forensic records and weakens breach detection, and a common audit exception even where auditing is otherwise broadly configured. A real incident looks like an investigation that can see data-access events but not the grant that gave the attacker access, because privilege-management actions were outside the active policy set.
Affected Items (3)
  • Uncovered action group: GRANT
  • Uncovered action group: REVOKE
  • Uncovered action group: USER ADMIN
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Determine current coverage: review AUDIT_POLICIES.AUDIT_ACTION_NAME for the active policies (SAP HANA Cockpit -> Security -> Auditing shows the actions per policy). 2. Map the required baseline groups and identify the missing ones: GRANT/REVOKE (privilege and role), CREATE/ALTER/DROP USER and ROLE, SYSTEM CONFIGURATION CHANGE / SET SYSTEM LICENSE, and CONNECT/VALIDATE USER. 3. Extend or add policies for the gaps, for example: CREATE AUDIT POLICY "SEC_USER_ADMIN" AUDITING ALL CREATE USER, DROP USER, ALTER USER, CREATE ROLE, DROP ROLE LEVEL CRITICAL; plus one for SYSTEM CONFIGURATION CHANGE and one AUDITING UNSUCCESSFUL/SUCCESSFUL CONNECT for authentication. 4. Enable each: ALTER AUDIT POLICY "<name>" ENABLE; 5. Keep policies action-scoped to avoid noise while ensuring all four groups are covered. 6. Verify: re-check AUDIT_POLICIES that each critical group now maps to an active policy, then run a representative test action per group and confirm it is captured in the trail. 7. Rollout caution: auditing successful CONNECT is high-volume - at minimum audit unsuccessful connects, plus successful connects for privileged users; validate the volume in non-production and coordinate retention with the SIEM team.
References
  • CIS SAP HANA Benchmark — Audit policy coverage
MEDIUM P4 · 22 HANA cross-database (MDC) access is enabled HANADB-PARAM-005 ▶
Security Risk
global.ini [cross_database_access] enabled = true on the system database. In a multi-tenant (MDC) HANA system, enabling cross-database access allows queries in one tenant database to read objects in another tenant via associated remote users, weakening the isolation boundary that is the main security rationale for tenant separation. If the set of permitted target tenants (targets_for_<source_db_name>) is broad or unmanaged, a compromise or privilege escalation in a low-sensitivity tenant can be pivoted into a high-sensitivity one, and data-residency/segregation assumptions no longer hold. Access is scoped per source tenant via the targets_for_<source_db_name> parameter (one-directional: it lists the databases the named source tenant is allowed to read).
Affected Items (1)
  • [cross_database_access] enabled = true
Remediation — Step by Step
Disable cross-database access unless there is a documented business requirement: [cross_database_access] enabled = false. Where it is required, scope it explicitly with targets_for_<source_db_name> to the minimum set of tenant pairs (e.g. targets_for_DB2 = DB1 to let DB2 read DB1), restrict the associated remote users to least privilege, and review the cross-tenant grants periodically.
References
  • SAP HANA Administration Guide — Cross-Database Access in MDC
  • SAP HANA Security Guide — Tenant Database Isolation
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Global authorization-object disabling is active AUTH-015 ▶
Security Risk
Profile parameter auth/object_disabling_active is set to Y, which enables the global deactivation of individual authorization objects via transaction AUTH_SWITCH_OBJECTS. When an authorization object is globally disabled, the ABAP runtime stops checking it everywhere — every AUTHORITY-CHECK against that object silently succeeds, system-wide, in every program and transaction. This is a powerful maintenance switch that SAP provides for specific, documented situations, but leaving the capability active in production is dangerous because it means a single administrative action can remove an entire authorization control across the whole system without changing a single role. The abuse scenario: an attacker (or a careless administrator) who can reach AUTH_SWITCH_OBJECTS disables a security-relevant object — for example a table-access, RFC, or a custom Z-authorization object protecting sensitive functionality — and thereafter every user passes the check for that object, quietly widening access far beyond what the role design intended. Because roles and profiles look unchanged, this kind of weakening is easy to miss in a normal authorization review; nothing in PFCG reflects it, and SU53/traces show the check 'passing' as if authorized. In an S/4HANA production client this is a Medium-severity control-integrity risk: it undermines the reliability of the authorization concept that SOX/ITGC and GDPR access controls depend on, and a disabled object could mask a breach. A real incident looks like unexplained broad access to a function that role analysis says should be restricted, ultimately traced to a globally-disabled authorization object rather than to any role assignment. The parameter should be off unless a specific, approved object genuinely must be disabled.
Affected Items (1)
  • auth/object_disabling_active = Y
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the current setting: check auth/object_disabling_active in RZ11 (dynamic view) and in the instance/DEFAULT profile via RZ10; note whether it is set in the profile or only dynamically. 2. Review what is actually disabled: run transaction AUTH_SWITCH_OBJECTS and list any authorization objects currently globally switched off; investigate why and re-enable any that are not covered by a documented, approved exception. 3. Set auth/object_disabling_active = N in the instance/DEFAULT profile via RZ10 unless a specific object must remain disabled with sign-off; save and activate the profile. 4. Determine the parameter's dynamic status in RZ11; if it is not dynamically switchable, schedule a coordinated instance restart in a change window for the profile change to take effect. 5. After the SU25/upgrade activities that legitimately use object disabling are complete, ensure the switch is returned to N. 6. Restrict who can reach AUTH_SWITCH_OBJECTS (S_TCODE plus the underlying administration authorization) to a minimal Basis group and put its use under change control. 7. Verify: re-check RZ11 shows N (post-restart if required) and AUTH_SWITCH_OBJECTS shows no unintended objects disabled; confirm a previously-disabled object is checked again via an authorization trace (STAUTHTRACE) / SU53. 8. Rollout caution: an object may have been disabled to work around a genuine issue — re-enabling it can surface authorization failures, so validate in QA first, review SU53/traces for fallout, and coordinate with application owners before enabling in production.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — auth/object_disabling_active
  • SAP Help — Globally deactivating authorization checks
MEDIUM P4 · 22 SSO ticket / session-cookie transport not hardened BASELINE-008 ▶
Security Risk
SAP logon/assertion tickets (the MYSAPSSO2 cookie) and ICF session cookies (SAP_SESSIONID_*) are bearer tokens: possession of the cookie equals an authenticated session, so their transport must be hardened. login/ticket_only_by_https=0 lets the SSO ticket travel over plain HTTP where it can be sniffed on the network. icf/set_HTTPonly_flag_on_cookies not equal to 0 means the HttpOnly attribute is not set on all ICF cookies (the default 3 leaves it off), so client-side JavaScript, for example via an XSS flaw in a Fiori/BSP app, can read the cookie via document.cookie. login/ticket_only_to_host=0 means a ticket is accepted by hosts other than the one that issued it, widening where a stolen ticket can be replayed. Attack scenarios: (a) network sniff, where an attacker on the path captures a MYSAPSSO2 ticket sent over HTTP and replays it to impersonate the user across all SSO-trusted systems until expiry; (b) XSS with no HttpOnly, where crafted script steals SAP_SESSIONID and the attacker rides the session; (c) with ticket_only_to_host=0, a ticket lifted from one system is reused against another, amplifying blast radius. In S/4HANA RISE, Fiori/BTP front-ends rely heavily on HTTP session cookies and SSO tickets, so these weaknesses translate directly into account takeover of business users and admins. Business and compliance impact includes session hijacking, impersonation, unauthorized transactions and data access, and audit/GDPR failures for weak session protection. A real incident shows actions under a victim's identity with no password compromise and no failed-logon trail.
Affected Items (2)
  • login/ticket_only_by_https = 0 (SSO ticket sent over plain HTTP — sniffable)
  • icf/set_HTTPonly_flag_on_cookies = 1 (HttpOnly not set on all ICF cookies)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the three parameters via RSPARAM/RZ11: login/ticket_only_by_https, icf/set_HTTPonly_flag_on_cookies, login/ticket_only_to_host. 2. Set login/ticket_only_by_https = 1 so SSO tickets are sent only over HTTPS (requires the ICM HTTPS/SSL service configured in STRUST and SMICM). 3. Set icf/set_HTTPonly_flag_on_cookies = 0 (HttpOnly active for ALL ICF cookies, the preferred value; default is 3) so scripts cannot read session cookies (SAP KBA 2068872). 4. Set login/ticket_only_to_host = 1 so a ticket is accepted only by the issuing host. 5. Complement with HTTP security session management: activate it via transaction SICF_SESSIONS, ensure the Secure flag is set on cookies (HTTPS-only) and set a sensible login/ticket_expiration_time. 6. These are dynamic parameters (settable in RZ11) but persist them in the profile (RZ10); some cookie behaviour needs an ICM restart (SMICM > Administration > ICM > Restart). 7. Verify by capturing a Fiori/GUI-for-HTML login and confirming MYSAPSSO2/SAP_SESSIONID are sent only over HTTPS and carry the HttpOnly (and Secure) attributes; re-check RSPARAM values. Caution: forcing HTTPS-only requires valid server certificates for every hostname/alias used, so validate the SSL setup in non-prod to avoid locking out Fiori users and coordinate certificate management with the RISE provider.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — SSO ticket / cookie hardening
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Web-tier logging / error disclosure weak (ICM) BASELINE-009 ▶
Security Risk
icm/security_log configures the Internet Communication Manager's security log, the web-tier forensic record of HTTP(S) access, TLS handshakes, denied requests and attack indicators at the ICM/Web Dispatcher layer. If it is empty or set below LEVEL=3 the system lacks the detailed log needed to detect and investigate web attacks (scanning, injection attempts, admin-URL probing) against Fiori/OData/ICF endpoints. is/HTTP/show_detailed_errors=TRUE makes the ICM return verbose error pages (component and stack details, internal paths, server/version data) to remote clients; this information disclosure hands an attacker reconnaissance about the software stack and internal structure and eases targeted exploitation. Attack scenario: an attacker probes the public Fiori/Web Dispatcher endpoint, detailed error pages reveal kernel/version, internal hostnames and code paths, and the attacker fingerprints the system to select known exploits; meanwhile, with the security log off or under-configured, the reconnaissance and exploitation attempts leave little to no web-tier trail, so the SOC cannot detect or reconstruct the attack. In RISE S/4HANA the ICM/Web Dispatcher is the Internet-facing entry point for Fiori and API traffic, so weak logging combined with verbose errors materially raises breach likelihood and lowers detectability. Business and compliance impact includes impaired incident detection, response and forensics, non-compliance with logging requirements (SAP Security Baseline, ISO 27001 A.12.4, PCI-DSS 10), and easier exploitation via leaked internals. A real incident is one discovered late or left un-attributable because the web-tier evidence was never captured.
Affected Items (2)
  • icm/security_log = 'LOGFILE=dev_icm_sec LEVEL=1 MAXSIZEKB=1000' (log level < 3 / not configured)
  • is/HTTP/show_detailed_errors = TRUE (detailed errors leaked to clients)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check both settings via RSPARAM/RZ11: icm/security_log and is/HTTP/show_detailed_errors. 2. Configure icm/security_log to LEVEL=3 with rotation in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10), e.g. LOGFILE=$(DIR_LOGGING)$(DIR_SEP)dev_icm_sec-%y-%m-%d%z,LEVEL=3,MAXFILES=7,MAXSIZEKB=50000,SWITCHTF=day,FORMAT=TABLE (the SAP Security Baseline recommended value). 3. Set is/HTTP/show_detailed_errors = FALSE so production returns generic error pages with no internal detail. 4. Apply the same hardening to any standalone SAP Web Dispatcher fronting the system. 5. These are ICM parameters; activate via an ICM restart (SMICM > Administration > ICM > Restart) or an instance restart. 6. Forward and retain the ICM security log centrally (SIEM), size MAXFILES/retention to policy, and review it alongside the Security Audit Log (SM20/RSAU_READ_LOG). 7. Verify: view active parameters in SMICM (Goto > Parameters), confirm the security-log file is being written under the logging directory, and confirm an intentionally malformed URL now returns a generic error page. Caution: increased logging consumes disk, so size MAXSIZEKB/MAXFILES and monitor the logging filesystem; test error-page behaviour in non-prod so any custom error handling still works.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — ICM security log / error disclosure
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Existing passwords not forced to current policy (login/password_compliance_to_current_policy) BASELINE-010 ▶
Security Risk
login/password_compliance_to_current_policy determines whether users whose stored password no longer meets the CURRENT password policy are forced to change it at their next logon. With value 0, legacy passwords set under an older, weaker policy remain valid indefinitely. Consequently, after the organization tightens policy (for example raising login/min_password_lng or adding complexity via a security policy), existing users keep their short or weak passwords; the stronger policy only applies to newly set passwords. The policy is therefore not enforced for the existing population, which is often the majority and includes long-lived administrator and service accounts. Attack scenario: an attacker performs online or offline guessing, or cracks harvested hashes, against accounts that still carry pre-tightening weak passwords, which are exactly the accounts the new policy was meant to protect; a 6-character legacy admin password survives a move to a 12-character policy and is brute-forced, yielding a valid privileged logon. The weakness is silent because no user is prompted and the posture looks compliant on paper (policy parameters are set) while the effective posture is not. Business and compliance impact includes continued exposure to credential guessing and cracking, privilege escalation via weak admin/service passwords, and audit findings that the password policy is not actually enforced (SOX ITGC, ISO 27001 A.9.4, GDPR access control). A real incident is the takeover of an account that should have had a strong password but was never required to update it.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/password_compliance_to_current_policy = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Check the value via RSPARAM/RZ11 for login/password_compliance_to_current_policy (target value 1). 2. Set login/password_compliance_to_current_policy = 1 in the DEFAULT profile (RZ10) so users with non-compliant passwords are forced to change at next logon; it is dynamic (RZ11) but persist it in the profile. 3. Confirm the surrounding policy is actually strong: review login/min_password_lng, login/min_password_digits, login/min_password_specials, login/min_password_letters and login/password_expiration_time, or the equivalent attributes of a security policy maintained in transaction SECPOL and assigned in SU01, aligned to the SAP Security Baseline. 4. Identify affected users in advance with report RSUSR003 (standard users) and password/last-logon data via SUIM / report RSUSR200 so you can plan communications. 5. Give special attention to technical/service and communication users: a forced change can break interfaces, so proactively set them to compliant passwords via SU01/SU10 and update the consuming SM59 destinations and JCo configurations first. 6. Verify: after activation, confirm a test user with a non-compliant password is prompted to change at logon, and re-check RSPARAM shows value 1. Caution: schedule around a maintenance window and notify users; handle service accounts and their interfaces first so batch jobs and RFC destinations do not fail on a forced password change.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline — password policy enforcement
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Business role bundles more than 30 business catalogs S4AUTHZ-003 ▶
Security Risk
A business role aggregates business catalogs, each granting Fiori apps together with their underlying OData services and authorization defaults. A role that bundles dozens of catalogs (here more than the configured threshold, default 30) is almost certainly over-provisioned: it grants far more app and data access than any single job function requires and it becomes a magnet for segregation-of-duties conflicts, because unrelated duties such as vendor maintenance and payment release end up combined in one role. Broad, catalog-heavy roles make access recertification and SoD analysis impractical, because reviewers cannot reason about what the role actually permits, so risky combinations pass review unnoticed. This is the classic role-bloat anti-pattern. Abuse scenario: a user assigned such a role can quietly reach functions outside their remit; an insider can combine create-and-approve capabilities to commit and conceal fraud, and an attacker compromising the account gains a very wide blast radius. It also cripples incident response, because after a breach it is hard to determine everything the account could touch. Business impact includes failed SoD and least-privilege controls (SOX), scope-creep of PII and financial data access (GDPR), and audit findings for inadequate access governance. Over time the oversized role becomes the path of least resistance that admins keep assigning, compounding the exposure and steadily degrading the whole authorization concept.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_MEGA_ROLE — 32 business catalogs
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List catalogs per flagged role: Maintain Business Roles app > Assigned Business Catalogs (Cloud) or PFCG menu / Fiori catalog assignment and table AGR_TCODES (on-prem). 2. Map each catalog to a concrete job task; identify catalogs no current holder actually uses via usage data (Cloud Display Authorization Trace, or on-prem ST03N app usage / STUSOBTRACE). 3. Split the mega-role into smaller task-based business roles aligned to distinct job functions and drop catalogs that are not required. 4. Run an SoD analysis (SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance, or Access Control ARA rule set) on the redesigned roles to ensure no toxic combinations remain. 5. Adjust the scanner threshold max_business_catalogs only with documented justification; 30 is a conservative design guardrail, not a hard limit. 6. Assign the new granular roles and then withdraw the oversized role. 7. Update role-design documentation and recertification scope to reflect the split roles. 8. Verify: re-run the per-role catalog count and confirm each role is under the agreed threshold, and confirm the SoD report shows no new conflicts. 9. Establish a periodic re-check so catalog counts do not creep back up. 10. Rollout caution: pilot with a small user group because splitting roles can temporarily remove needed apps; keep a rollback role, perform the redesign in Dev/Q, transport through the landscape, and coordinate with business process owners.
References
  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud — Business Role design best practices
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Birthright role collection auto-granted to all federated users S4AUTHZ-008 ▶
Security Risk
On SAP BTP, application authorizations are packaged as role collections, and trust configuration can map a role collection to an IdP group. Mapping a role collection to the 'Default' group (or a wildcard / all-authenticated value) turns it into a BIRTHRIGHT assignment: every user who successfully authenticates through the corporate IdP receives that collection automatically, with no explicit provisioning. If the collection carries only genuinely universal, low-privilege access such as a basic launchpad viewer, this is acceptable; if it carries anything beyond baseline, the entire authenticated population is silently over-provisioned. Birthright grants are easy to overlook during recertification because they are not attached to individual users, so the access is invisible in per-user reviews yet fully effective at runtime. Attack scenario: an attacker who obtains any valid federated identity (a compromised SSO account, or an over-broad IdP that lets many people authenticate) immediately inherits whatever the default-mapped collection grants, potentially reaching applications, APIs, or data that should require explicit entitlement, and without any access request to trip an alert. The insider risk is parallel: any employee can reach the function without ever being formally granted it. Impact includes violation of least privilege and need-to-know, GDPR over-exposure if the collection reaches PII, and an audit finding that access is not individually authorized or recertifiable. A real incident looks like users exercising an app they were never explicitly provisioned for, traced back to a default-group mapping.
Affected Items (2)
  • Z_BASELINE_SELF_SERVICE ← IdP group 'Default' (auto-granted to all federated users)
  • Z_ANALYTICS_VIEWER ← IdP group 'Everyone' (auto-granted to all federated users)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List role-collection-to-group mappings: BTP cockpit > Security > Trust Configuration > select IdP > Role Collection Mappings, or CLI btp list security/role-collection; flag any mapped to Default or a wildcard. 2. For each default-mapped collection, review the roles it contains and decide whether that access is truly universal and low-privilege. 3. If it is not universal, remove the Default-group mapping and instead map the collection to the specific IdP group(s) representing the entitled population. 4. Coordinate with the IdP/IAM team so the required groups exist and are populated (via SCIM or SAML assertion attributes) and legitimate users retain access. 5. Keep only a minimal, deliberately chosen baseline collection as a default assignment, and document it as an accepted birthright. 6. Prefer provisioning through SAP Cloud Identity Services / IAS groups or an IGA tool so assignments are attributable and recertifiable. 7. Verify: authenticate as a test user who is NOT in the target group and confirm the collection is no longer granted. 8. Confirm entitled users still receive the collection through their assigned group. 9. Add the default-mapping review to the periodic BTP access recertification. 10. Rollout caution: removing a default mapping can instantly revoke access for many users, so communicate the change, stage it in a non-prod subaccount, and ensure the replacement group mappings are live before removing the Default mapping to avoid an outage.
References
  • SAP BTP — Role Collections & Trust Configuration (default groups)
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Armed job step user is deleted, locked, expired, or a dialog user JOBCMD-JOB-004 ▶
Security Risk
This armed job step runs under a step user that is absent from the user master (table USR02), locked, past its validity date (USR02-GLTGB), or a dialog user (type A) used for batch. A deleted/absent step user is the sharpest risk: SAP resolves authorizations by user name, so the name is a dangling reference. If an account with that exact BNAME is later re-created - accidentally or maliciously - the new account inherits the job's execution context. An attacker who can create a user with that name (user-provisioning rights) thereby hijacks the job's authorizations. A locked or expired step user usually indicates an abandoned or broken job and signals poor job hygiene and stale ownership. A dialog user (type A) as a batch step user is against best practice - batch should use a dedicated system/background (type B) user. Dialog accounts belong to people who leave, change roles, or get locked, making the job fragile and its privileges person-bound. Attack scenario: a job points at former-employee account 'JSMITH' that was deleted; an admin or attacker with SU01 rights re-creates JSMITH with strong roles. The nightly job now runs with those roles - a quiet privilege path that no one is watching. Business impact: job-hijack potential, failed or duplicated processing, and accountability gaps in S/4HANA batch. Severity is medium because active exploitation usually needs a second condition (re-creation, or the account regaining access). Still, a job pointing at a deleted or dialog account is a latent escalation and reliability defect that should be corrected.
Affected Items (3)
  • JOB_FI_CLOSE — step user DDIC (dialog user used for batch)
  • JOB_MASS_UPD — step user JSMITH (dialog user used for batch)
  • JOB_LEGACY — step user GHOSTUSER (deleted / not in user master (can be re-created to hijack the job))
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify: SM37 / SE16 TBTCP to list step users (AUTHCKNAM), then reconcile against USR02 via SU01/SUIM. 2. Flag names not present in USR02 (deleted), UFLAG showing locked, GLTGB in the past (expired), or USTYP = 'A' (dialog). 3. For each affected job, re-plan it onto a valid, unlocked, least-privilege type B (System) background user (SU01 + PFCG role) via SM36/SM37 step-user change. 4. Never leave a job pointing at a deleted or dialog account; a departed person's dialog ID as step user is both a hygiene and a hijack risk and should be fixed immediately. 5. For locked/expired step users, decide whether the job is still needed; if obsolete, delete it (SM37, or report RSBTCDEL2 for old jobs) rather than reactivating an account to keep it alive. 6. Prevent recurrence: use only technical type B users for batch, and govern who can create users (authorization object S_USER_GRP via PFCG) to limit name-re-creation hijack. 7. Reconcile job step users against USR02 periodically, not just once. 8. Verify: SE16 TBTCP step users all exist in USR02, are unlocked, unexpired, and of type B/S. 9. QA-run the re-planned jobs and confirm success in the SM37 job log. 10. Rollout caution: switching step users changes effective authorizations and can break the job - capture needed authorizations (STAUTHTRACE), test in DEV/QA, and coordinate stale-job deletion with the business owner (SDLUNAME) before removing anything in PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — Background job step user (SM37) / user types (SU01)
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Background job step user differs from scheduler (identity borrowing) JOBCMD-JOB-005 ▶
Security Risk
This job is scheduled by one user (TBTCO/TBTCP field SDLUNAME) but its step runs under a different, more-privileged step user (AUTHCKNAM). A lower-privileged scheduler thereby has code executed with a stronger identity's authorizations. SAP controls this legitimately via authorization object S_BTCH_NAM (field BTCUSERNM): a scheduler may only set a foreign step user they are authorized for. When the scheduler is not an administrator yet the step runs as a powerful technical user, it is a privilege-escalation and accountability gap. Typically this means S_BTCH_NAM is over-granted (e.g., BTCUSERNM = *) or the assignment predates proper controls. Attack scenario: a functional user schedules a job whose step runs as a SAP_ALL technical user - classic identity borrowing. Their own report or command now executes with far greater authority than they hold interactively, bypassing segregation of duties. The audit trail records the powerful step user, not the real scheduler, so activity is mis-attributed. Business impact: subtle privilege escalation and blurred accountability across S/4HANA batch processing. Investigations point at the technical step user and miss the actual actor, delaying incident response. At scale, an over-broad S_BTCH_NAM can produce many such divergent jobs, some running sensitive mass-change reports. Real incident: BTCUSERNM = * let ordinary users schedule jobs running as technical superusers; a review found dozens of divergent jobs, one running a mass data-change report.
Affected Items (3)
  • JOB_FI_CLOSE — scheduled by AGARCIA, runs as DDIC
  • JOB_MASS_UPD — scheduled by AGARCIA, runs as JSMITH
  • JOB_TRANSPORT — scheduled by BJOHNSON, runs as TMSADM
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify: SM37 / SE16 on TBTCO+TBTCP -> list jobs where SDLUNAME (scheduler) differs from AUTHCKNAM (step user), especially where the step user is privileged (SAP*/DDIC/SAP_ALL/standard). 2. For each, confirm the step user reflects the least privilege the job actually needs. 3. If the powerful step user is unnecessary, re-plan the job onto a scoped type B user (SM36/SM37, SU01, PFCG role). 4. Verify the scheduler is legitimately authorized for the step user: review S_BTCH_NAM (field BTCUSERNM) assignments in PFCG and SUIM. 5. Remove BTCUSERNM = '*' and other over-broad grants so schedulers can only use approved technical users. 6. Investigate cases where a non-administrator schedules jobs running as a powerful technical user - check change docs and the Security Audit Log (SM20 / RSAU_READ_LOG). 7. Establish a standard: business jobs run under governed technical users, and only specific admin roles hold broad S_BTCH_NAM. 8. Verify: SE16 shows scheduler/step-user divergence only where justified. 9. Verify: SUIM confirms no wildcard BTCUSERNM outside designated admin roles. 10. Rollout caution: tightening S_BTCH_NAM can stop legitimate schedulers from re-planning their jobs - inventory current usage first, communicate to job owners, and roll the role change through DEV/QA before PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — S_BTCH_NAM / background step user
  • SAP Security Baseline — background processing

Security Risk
1 firefighter ID(s) have log review/delivery turned off, so the controller does not receive the usage log for review — the after-the-fact compensating control is effectively disabled.
Affected Items (1)
  • FF_HR_04 (log review/delivery disabled)
Remediation — Step by Step
Enable log delivery / review workflow for every firefighter ID (GRAC EAM).

Security Risk
3 access request(s) were provisioned without a documented risk analysis. GRC ARM should run ARA risk analysis at request time so SoD conflicts are detected (and mitigated) BEFORE access is granted, not discovered later.
Affected Items (3)

  • req REQ1004: USER_V -> USER_V (risk analysis not done)

Enable mandatory risk analysis in the ARM workflow (ARA-ARM integration).

MEDIUM P4 · 22 Mitigating controls are expired, owner-less or unmonitored GRC-MIT-001 ▶
Security Risk
3 mitigating control(s) are not fit for purpose — missing an owner, missing an assigned monitor, missing a monitoring frequency, expired, or inactive. A mitigating control that no one owns or monitors provides no real compensating assurance for the SoD risks it is claimed to cover, yet it still suppresses those violations from the risk report — masking live exposure.
Affected Items (3)

  • MIT_010: no owner
  • MIT_011: no monitoring frequency, inactive
Remediation — Step by Step
For each control (GRAC Mitigating Controls): assign an owner and an independent monitor, set a monitoring frequency, renew or retire expired controls, and confirm the control activity is actually performed and evidenced.

Security Risk
1 SoD risk(s) have no risk owner. Without an owner accountable for deciding remediation vs mitigation, violations of that risk are never dispositioned.

  • R2R_01

Assign a business risk owner to every SoD risk in the rule set (GRAC).

MEDIUM P4 · 22 SoD rule set appears incomplete / never tailored GRC-RS-003 ▶
Security Risk
Only 5 SoD risk(s) are defined in the rule set. The SAP-delivered Access Control rule set contains 200+ risks across process areas; a rule set this small has likely not been activated/tailored from the delivered content, so most SoD conflicts across P2P/O2C/R2R/H2R/Basis are simply not being detected.
Affected Items (1)
  • 5 risks defined (expected 200+ from delivered content)
Remediation — Step by Step
Import and tailor the SAP-delivered rule set (or a maintained ruleset), covering all in-scope process areas; validate with the business risk owners.

  • SAP GRC Access Control — default rule set import
