MEDIUM P4 · 22 Custom transactions without maintained SU24 authorization proposals RG-SU24-001 ▶
Security Risk
3 custom (Z*/Y*) transaction(s) have no maintained SU24 authorization-default proposal (check indicator U/unmaintained). When such a transaction is added to a PFCG role, the Profile Generator cannot propose the authorization objects it needs, so administrators either add nothing (the role silently under-authorizes) or hand-add broad objects (commonly just S_TCODE, or an over-wide manual authorization). Unmaintained SU24 for custom code is the single biggest root cause of over-authorized and inconsistent custom roles.
Affected Items (3)
  • YHR_REPORT
  • ZFI_CUSTOM1
  • ZMM_TOOL
Remediation — Step by Step
For each custom transaction, maintain SU24 (tcode SU24) so the authorization objects checked by the program are proposed with check indicator 'Check/Maintain'. Run SU25 step 2 after upgrades to reconcile SAP-delivered SU24 changes. Then regenerate the affected roles so the maintained proposals take effect.
References
  • SAP Help — SU24/SU25 authorization default (proposal) maintenance
  • DSAG Prüfleitfaden — Qualität des Berechtigungskonzepts (SU24-Pflege)
  • ISO 27001 A.9.2 — access provisioning based on need
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Roles with no generated authorization profile are assigned to users RG-GEN-001 ▶
Security Risk
1 role(s) have no generated authorization profile (AGR_1016 blank / PFCG 'red' status) yet are assigned to users. A role whose profile was never (re)generated does not actually grant its maintained authorizations — the change 'looks assigned' in AGR_USERS but is not in effect, or the profile is stale versus the current role menu/authorizations. This produces both access that silently does not work and, after edits, authorizations that differ from what was reviewed.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_BC_TRANSPORT (assigned to users)
Remediation — Step by Step
Open each role in PFCG and generate the authorization profile (Authorizations tab -> Generate) so it reaches 'green' status; use mass generation (SUPC / report PFCG_TIME_DEPENDENCY) for many roles. Investigate why profiles were left ungenerated in the transport/change process.
References
  • SAP Help — PFCG profile generation (AGR_1016)
  • DSAG Prüfleitfaden — Rollengenerierung / PFCG-Status
  • SOX ITGC — access changes are complete and effective
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Derived roles have authorizations that drifted from their parent RG-DRV-001 ▶
Security Risk
1 derived role(s) have authorizations that differ from their parent/master role — extra or missing authorization objects, OR different field VALUES on inherited (non-org) fields (e.g. a broadened activity or a hand-added transaction), ignoring org-level field values that are meant to differ. In the master-derived concept a derived role must inherit the parent's authorizations and differ ONLY in organizational field values; a structural difference means someone edited the derived role directly instead of changing the parent and re-deriving. That hides the change from the master-role owner and can silently grant access the master never had.
Affected Items (1)
  • Z_FI_ACCT_1000 (parent Z_FI_ACCT_MASTER): +1 added S_DEVELOP:OBJTYPE
Remediation — Step by Step
Restore the master-derived relationship: make authorization changes in the PARENT role and re-derive/adjust-and-generate the child (PFCG 'Adjust Derived' / mass generation). Remove authorizations added directly to derived roles. Audit how the direct edits bypassed change control.
References
  • SAP Help — master (parent)-derived role concept
  • DSAG Prüfleitfaden — Ableitungskonzept (derived roles)
  • SOX ITGC — authorization changes follow change management
MEDIUM P4 · 22 Financial document number ranges are buffered (completeness gaps) FIN-NR-001 ▶
Security Risk
2 financial number-range object(s) have number-range buffering enabled. Buffering hands out blocks of numbers per application server and discards the unused ones on restart, producing GAPS in the document number sequence. For FI documents that breaks the sequential-completeness assertion auditors rely on to confirm no financial document was deleted or is missing (SOX completeness).
Affected Items (2)
  • RF_BELEG: buffering = X
  • FI_BELEG: buffering = S
Remediation — Step by Step
For financial document number-range objects (SNRO / TNRO, e.g. RF_BELEG), disable buffering (set 'no buffering') so document numbers are assigned gap-free. Weigh the performance trade-off with Basis, but completeness usually governs for FI documents.
References
  • SOX financial-reporting completeness / sequence integrity (PCAOB AS 2201)
  • DSAG Prüfleitfaden — Nummernkreispufferung
  • SAP Note 62077 / SAP Help — number range buffering
LOW P4 · 20 Stale BTP destinations (not modified in 365+ days) BTP-DST-004 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found stale BTP destinations - configurations not modified in over a year. While lower severity, stale destinations accumulate risk quietly. A destination untouched for a year commonly points to a system that has been migrated, decommissioned, or re-addressed, and it frequently carries credentials (stored passwords, client secrets, or trust settings) that predate current password and rotation policies. Such a destination is neither reviewed nor owned, so it escapes access recertification and credential-rotation cycles. The danger materializes in several ways: an old stored credential may still be valid on a live backend, giving unaudited access; a destination re-pointed to a reused hostname/IP could connect an app to an unexpected or attacker-controlled system; and stale trust/certificate settings may permit weak TLS. Stale destinations also distort the connectivity inventory auditors rely on, hiding which apps can still reach which systems. Attack scenario: an attacker who gains binding access enumerates destinations and finds a forgotten one whose long-lived stored credential still works against a production backend, or whose target host has been recycled, and leverages it for access the security team no longer tracks. Business impact is unmanaged access paths, outdated secrets, and a governance/hygiene gap under the SAP Security Baseline and ISO 27001 access-review controls. A real incident surfaces when an old destination's credential is found still authenticating during an investigation or access review.
Affected Items (7)
  • S4H_Backend → https://10.0.1.50/sap/opu/odata — last modified: 2024-11-01 (651d ago)
  • SuccessFactors_API → https://api.successfactors.com/odata/v2 — last modified: 2025-01-15 (576d ago)
  • Ariba_Network → https://openapi.ariba.com — last modified: 2025-02-01 (559d ago)
  • Legacy_ECC_SOAP → http://10.0.2.100/sap/bc/soap — last modified: 2023-05-20 (1182d ago)
  • Bank_API → https://api.bank.com/payments — last modified: 2024-09-10 (703d ago)
  • Test_System_Old → https://10.0.3.10/sap/opu — last modified: 2022-08-15 (1460d ago)
  • Analytics_DWC → https://mycompany.eu10.hcs.cloud.sap — last modified: 2025-02-20 (540d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit, Connectivity > Destinations, identify destinations not modified within your threshold (for example 365 days). 2. For each, confirm with the owning application team and CMDB whether the target system and integration are still in use. 3. Delete destinations that are no longer needed. 4. For destinations still required, refresh credentials/secrets and re-verify the target URL, ProxyType, and TLS trust settings against current policy. 5. Rotate any stored password or client secret that predates the current rotation policy, and migrate Basic Auth to token-based flows (see BTP-DST-001). 6. Confirm TLS validation is enabled (TrustAll=false) and the correct CA is trusted (see BTP-DST-002). 7. Verify each retained destination with 'Check Connection'. 8. Establish a periodic (annual or semi-annual) destination review with owner sign-off. 9. Re-run the scanner to confirm remaining destinations are current and owned. 10. Rollout caution: before deleting, check for low-frequency or seasonal integrations (year-end, statutory reporting) that may legitimately have left a destination unchanged for a year, and archive the configuration for rollback.
References
  • SAP BTP — Destination Lifecycle Management
LOW P4 · 20 BTP services entitled but never provisioned BTP-ENT-001 ▶
Security Risk
The scan found BTP service entitlements that have quota allocated but zero instances provisioned - services the organization is entitled to consume but is not using. While individually low severity, unused entitlements represent dormant, pre-approved capability that can be activated at any time without a fresh procurement or governance checkpoint. Any user with the right role collection (for example subaccount administrator or an entitlement manager) can spin up an instance of an entitled service on demand, immediately expanding the live attack surface - a new database, an object store, a connectivity or integration capability - without triggering the review that a brand-new entitlement request would. This is a governance and shadow-capability risk: the difference between 'what is deployed' and 'what could be deployed instantly' is invisible to controls that only inspect running services. Attack scenario: an insider or an attacker who has compromised an administrative identity provisions an entitled-but-unused service (for example an outbound-capable integration or storage service) to stage data exfiltration or establish persistence, blending in because the entitlement was already sanctioned. Business impact is reduced governance visibility, potential cost sprawl, and a widened latent attack surface; from an audit perspective, an accurate, minimized entitlement footprint is part of cloud-resource governance under ISO 27001 and internal ITGC. A real incident involves an entitled service being quietly activated and misused because nobody was watching allocations that carried no running instances.
Affected Items (8)
  • auditlog/premium — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • credstore/standard — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • malware-scanner/cav — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • cloud-logging/standard — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • alert-notification/standard — entitled: 1, used: 0
  • privatelink/standard — entitled: 2, used: 0
  • application-logs/lite — entitled: 5, used: 0
  • business-rules/basic — entitled: 2, used: 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In the BTP cockpit at the global account/directory level, open Entitlements > Entity Assignments and review allocated quota versus consumed instances per subaccount. 2. Cross-reference with the running Instances and Subscriptions to identify entitlements with quota but zero usage. 3. For services with no current or planned business need, reduce or remove the quota assignment at the directory/global-account level. 4. Retain only entitlements that map to an approved, planned use case with an owner. 5. Implement entitlement governance: a periodic (quarterly) review of allocated vs consumed quota with sign-off. 6. Restrict who can provision instances by tightly controlling the role collections that grant entitlement and instance-management authority. 7. Enable BTP Audit Log and alert on new service-instance creation, especially for outbound/storage/integration services. 8. Verify by re-checking Entity Assignments after adjustment and confirming removed quotas can no longer be provisioned. 9. Rollout caution: confirm with application teams before removing an entitlement, as an upcoming project may depend on it; reducing quota is reversible but removing an in-use entitlement would block provisioning.
References
  • SAP BTP — Entitlement and Quota Management
LOW P4 · 20 Stale webhook registrations with no recent activity INTG-WH-004 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags webhook registrations that have had no activity (no trigger/last-call) for longer than the configured staleness window (default 180 days). A stale webhook is a standing configuration that points at a consumer which may have been decommissioned, migrated, or forgotten; it is credential and endpoint exposure with no offsetting business value. The main risks are dangling-endpoint takeover and unmonitored trust: if the stale destination's domain or infrastructure lapses, an attacker can potentially re-register it and start receiving live events, or the stored signing secret/credential continues to exist unrotated and unwatched. Stale registrations also carry any earlier weaknesses (HTTP, no signature, external domain) indefinitely, and because no one is watching them, abuse is unlikely to be noticed. Attack scenario: a webhook targets partner-old.example.com; the partner lets that domain expire; an attacker registers the lapsed domain and now receives the organization's business events, or uses the still-valid shared secret found in old documentation to forge events. Business impact: latent data-leak and spoofing exposure, plus governance/audit findings on unmanaged integration artifacts. A real incident looks like events being delivered to a domain now owned by a third party, discovered only during a later review. This is rated low because it is a hygiene/lifecycle issue rather than an active exploit, but stale artifacts are a common root cause of larger incidents. Regular cleanup materially shrinks the unmonitored attack surface.
Affected Items (6)
  • SalesOrder_Created → https://integration.company.com/hooks/so-created — last activity: 2025-03-01 (531d ago)
  • Vendor_Updated → http://middleware.company.com/hooks/vendor — last activity: 2025-02-28 (532d ago)
  • Payment_Processed → https://external-bank-api.com/webhooks/payment-notify — last activity: 2025-03-01 (531d ago)
  • Invoice_Approved → https://ariba.procurement.com/callback/invoice — last activity: 2025-02-15 (545d ago)
  • Legacy_ERP_Sync → http://10.0.2.100:8080/callback/erp — last activity: 2024-03-01 (896d ago)
  • Test_Hook_Old → https://test.company.com/hooks/test — last activity: 2023-08-15 (1095d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the flagged stale webhook registrations with their last-activity date and destination. 2. Contact the owning integration/business team to confirm whether each webhook is still required. 3. Delete registrations confirmed obsolete, and revoke/rotate any associated signing secret or credential. 4. For webhooks that are legitimately low-frequency (e.g. annual processes), document the justification and mark them exempt from the staleness rule rather than deleting. 5. Verify that the destination domains of any retained webhooks are still owned and controlled by the intended partner (guard against dangling-domain takeover). 6. Implement a lifecycle policy: periodic (e.g. quarterly) review of webhook registrations with automatic flagging of inactivity. 7. Ensure new registrations record an owner and expected trigger frequency so staleness can be judged reliably. 8. Verify by confirming the deleted registrations no longer appear in the webhook registry and that no interface breaks. 9. Feed registration deletions/changes into the change log/SIEM for auditability. 10. Re-run the check after cleanup to confirm the stale count is reduced. Caution: confirm true inactivity over a sufficiently long window before deleting, and coordinate with owners - a webhook can be dormant simply because its triggering business event is seasonal.
References
  • Integration Governance — Webhook Lifecycle
LOW P4 · 20 CPI data stores with excessive entries INTG-CPI-DS-003 ▶
Security Risk
This finding flags CPI Data Stores that hold more entries than the configured threshold (default 10,000), indicating probable missing cleanup logic and data hoarding. Data stores are meant for transient or short-lived state; when entries accumulate without expiry, the store grows unbounded, which degrades iFlow and tenant performance and, more importantly for security, keeps a large volume of message data resident and exposed far longer than necessary. The security concern is data minimization and blast radius: the more historical message content sits in the store, the larger the loss if the tenant or a management credential is compromised, and the more likely the retention violates data-protection retention limits. Attack scenario: an attacker who gains CPI monitoring/management access finds a bloated data store containing months or years of message payloads and exfiltrates the lot in a single sweep; a store that self-purged would have exposed only a small recent window. Excessive retention of personal data also creates direct GDPR storage-limitation exposure independent of any attacker. Business impact: enlarged breach impact, GDPR retention non-compliance, and performance/operational degradation of integration flows. A real incident looks like a data-store dump yielding a large historical trove of business messages, or a privacy audit finding personal data retained well beyond its lawful period. This is rated low because it is primarily a hygiene/retention issue rather than an active vulnerability, but it directly increases the impact of any other compromise. Bounded retention is a straightforward and effective mitigation.
Affected Items (1)
  • idoc_retry_queue — 15400 entries (max: 10000)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. In Cloud Integration, open Monitor → Manage Stores → Data Stores and review the flagged stores' entry counts and the iFlows that write them. 2. Set an expiration/TTL on the Data Store Write step (Alert/Expiration period) so entries are automatically removed after the business-necessary window. 3. Where entries must be removed explicitly, add a Data Store Delete step after successful processing, or implement a scheduled cleanup iFlow using a Data Store Select/Delete pattern. 4. Reassess whether a data store is even the right mechanism; for large or long-lived data, use a proper database/persistence outside CPI. 5. For stores holding personal data, align retention with the data-protection retention policy and purge anything beyond it. 6. Enable encryption on sensitive stores (see INTG-CPI-DS-001) so the residual data is at least protected at rest. 7. Purge the current backlog of expired/obsolete entries. 8. Verify by re-checking the entry count after cleanup and confirming new entries expire on schedule. 9. Add monitoring/alerting on data-store growth so future hoarding is caught early. 10. Promote configuration changes via transport after non-prod testing. Caution: confirm that in-flight processes do not still need the entries before shortening TTL or deleting - test the cleanup logic in non-prod so you do not remove state that a running interface depends on.
References
  • SAP CPI — Data Store Management
LOW P4 · 20 Fiori apps with zero usage (never launched) FIORI-USAGE-001 ▶
Security Risk
This check identifies Fiori apps present in active catalogs with a launch count of zero: apps provisioned to users but never used. Individually low-risk, unused apps are a meaningful hygiene and attack-surface issue at scale. Every provisioned-but-unused app still carries its catalog tile, its target mapping and, critically, the backend S_SERVICE start authorization and business authorizations bundled into the role that grants it. That means users hold standing access to transactions and OData services they demonstrably do not need, which directly contradicts least privilege and inflates the blast radius of any account compromise: an attacker who takes over such an account inherits not just what the user does but everything the user could do, including dormant sensitive apps nobody is watching. Unused apps also accumulate into SoD conflicts that are hard to spot because no one exercises the combination in daily work, and they bury genuinely needed access in noise during access certifications. In a RISE landscape where SAP delivers thousands of standard apps, ungoverned catalogs drift toward assign-everything, and dormant services that are never monitored are exactly where a slow, low-and-slow data-harvesting attack hides. Business impact: excess-access audit findings, larger breach blast radius, noisier and less trustworthy access reviews, and higher maintenance/licensing overhead. A real incident looks like a compromised account abusing a sensitive app the legitimate user never once opened, so no baseline of normal existed to trigger an alert.
Affected Items (4)
  • F2001: My Profile (catalog: Z_ALL_USERS_CATALOG) — never launched
  • F4020: Approve Leave Requests (catalog: Z_HR_CATALOG) — never launched
  • F5050: Display GL Balances (catalog: SAP_SFIN_BC_GL_ACC_MAINT) — never launched
  • F6060: Custom Legacy Report (catalog: Z_ALL_USERS_CATALOG) — never launched
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Corroborate the zero-usage list with server-side statistics: Gateway usage via transaction /IWFND/STATS, ABAP workload via ST03N, and the Fiori launchpad usage/tracking data where available, over the configured stale window (default 90 days) to avoid removing seasonal apps. 2. For each confirmed-unused app identify the catalog and the roles that grant it via the Launchpad Content Manager (/UI2/FLPCM_CUST) and transaction SUIM. 3. Confirm with the business/role owner that the app is genuinely not required before removal. 4. Remove the tile from the catalog in transaction /UI2/FLPD_CUST, and remove the corresponding S_SERVICE start authorization and any now-orphaned business authorizations from the role in PFCG, then regenerate the profile. 5. Prefer trimming the role/catalog to least privilege over globally deactivating the service, unless the underlying OData service is required nowhere, in which case deactivate it in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE / SICF to also close FIORI-ODATA risk. 6. Feed the result into the periodic access-certification and SoD review so removals are recorded, and clear caches with /UI2/CACHE_DEL afterwards. 7. Verify: confirm the tile is gone for a sample user and that the app no longer appears in the usage catalog; re-run the usage report next cycle to confirm it stays at zero. 8. Rollout caution: usage data can undercount rarely-but-legitimately-used apps and integration-only services, so validate over a full business cycle, stage via transport, and communicate with app owners before removing access in production.
References
  • SAP Fiori — App Usage Analytics
LOW P4 · 20 External OS command not bound to a specific operating system JOBCMD-CMD-005 ▶
Security Risk
Each logical SM69 command should be bound to a concrete target operating system (table SXPGCOSTAB, field OPSYSTEM). This command is defined for 'Any Operating System' (ANYOS) or has an unspecified OS. SAP best practice is to bind each command to the specific OS of the application servers where it is meant to run. An 'any OS' definition is more portable: it can execute against heterogeneous application servers where its behaviour and safety were never validated. In a mixed Linux/Windows landscape the same logical command may resolve to different binaries or paths on different hosts. That ambiguity means a reviewer cannot be sure which executable actually runs where. It widens the blast radius of the higher-severity issues (CMD-001..004) by making abuse portable across servers. It also reduces the precision of change control and auditing for the command catalog. This is the lowest-severity item - a hardening/hygiene gap, not a direct code-execution flaw on its own. Business impact is mainly governance and audit: an unbound catalog is harder to review, reason about, and constrain. Real incident context: after a platform migration, 'any OS' commands kept working in unexpected ways on new hosts, and the ambiguity slowed root-cause analysis during an incident review.
Affected Items (1)
  • ZANYOS (OS: ANYOS)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Inventory: SM69 / SE16 SXPGCOSTAB -> find commands where OPSYSTEM is blank or set to ANYOS / * / ALL. 2. Determine the actual OS of the application servers where each command must run (SM51 lists the instances and their hosts/platform). 3. In SM69, redefine the command for the specific operating system (e.g., Linux, UNIX, or Windows NT) instead of 'Any Operating System'. 4. If it must run on multiple platforms, create one explicit per-OS definition, each with its own correct absolute path. 5. Re-validate the OPCOMMAND path and parameters per OS - they differ between UNIX and Windows (path separators, executable names). 6. Combine this with the CMD-001..004 hardening so each concrete definition is also shell-free, ADDPAR-off, and absolute-pathed. 7. Verify: SE16 SXPGCOSTAB shows a concrete OPSYSTEM for every command. 8. Confirm via SM49 that each command executes only on its intended platform. 9. Document the OS binding in the command catalog's operational records. 10. Rollout caution: binding to an OS can stop a command from running on servers you did not expect - confirm the full app-server list (SM51) and test in DEV/QA before transporting to PRD.
References
  • SAP Help — External OS Commands: operating-system binding (SM69)
LOW P4 · 8 Active accounts that have never logged in USR-007 ▶
Security Risk
This check flags unlocked accounts with no recorded logon (USR02-TRDAT empty). These are pre-staged or orphaned provisioning artifacts, such as bulk-created user shells, aborted onboarding records, or old test IDs, that still carry an initial password and whatever roles were assigned at creation. They are lower severity than an abused live account but remain attractive footholds: initial passwords are often weak, predictable, or set to a shared default across a batch, and because no one has ever used the account, no legitimate owner will notice a takeover. Attack scenario: an attacker who learns the provisioning convention, such as a common initial password or a derivable username scheme, activates a never-used account, changes the initial password, and gains a valid, low-noise identity; if the shell was pre-assigned roles, or worse a broad profile, the attacker inherits them instantly. Never-logged-in privileged IDs are the worst case. Business/compliance impact: unauthorized access, inflated named-user license counts, and access-review findings for accounts that exist without a validated business need. A real incident: a batch of onboarding accounts created with a uniform initial password, one of which is activated weeks later from an external IP and used to browse HR data before anyone notices the shell was ever live.
Affected Items (3)
  • SAPCPIC (created: 20190101)
  • KPATEL (created: 20250101)
  • RMARTINEZ (created: 20250115)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List them with RSUSR200 (select users who have never logged on) or SUIM, filtered to unlocked accounts with no last-logon date, and capture creation date (USR02-ERDAT) and assigned roles. 2. Reconcile with HR/onboarding and the provisioning system to determine which shells are still needed versus abandoned. 3. Lock unneeded accounts immediately in SU01 or in bulk via SU10, and set a validity end date so unused shells expire automatically. 4. Delete or archive shells that have no confirmed business owner after a short grace period. 5. Fix provisioning hygiene by enforcing unique strong initial passwords and a short initial-password validity via login/password_max_idle_initial so unused initial passwords expire quickly, and avoid shared/default initial passwords in bulk creation. 6. Do not pre-assign broad roles or profiles at creation; grant entitlements only on activation through a request workflow (GRC/IPS). 7. Verify by re-running RSUSR200 to confirm never-logged-in unlocked accounts are locked or removed and any remaining shells have an expiry and minimal roles. 8. Add a periodic scheduled RSUSR200 job (SM36) so newly stranded shells are caught each cycle. 9. Caution: some never-used IDs are legitimately pre-staged for an imminent go-live or seasonal hires, so confirm with owners before deleting. 10. Track provisioning-to-first-logon time as a metric so orphaned shells are cleaned up routinely.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark Section 2.5
LOW P4 · 8 Parameter login/disable_multi_gui_login non-compliant PARAM-login/disable_multi_gui_login ▶
Security Risk
login/disable_multi_gui_login controls whether a single user ID may hold multiple simultaneous SAP GUI dialog sessions. When multiple concurrent logons are allowed (value 0), it becomes difficult to detect and prevent credential sharing and stolen-credential reuse: a legitimate user can be actively working while an attacker who has obtained the same credentials logs on in parallel, and both sessions appear valid. This undermines accountability and non-repudiation, complicates SoD enforcement (one physical person effectively multiplying their presence), and can mask an intruder's activity behind an active legitimate session. It also has licensing implications, but the security concern is the loss of a one-user-one-session invariant that helps surface anomalous concurrent access. In S/4HANA landscapes where a compromised dialog credential is the typical entry point, disallowing concurrent GUI sessions raises the chance that a parallel malicious logon is noticed or blocked. Attack scenario: an attacker phishes a controller's credentials and logs on to post fraudulent journal entries while the controller is simultaneously logged on for normal work, with nothing preventing the second session. Business impact: harder incident detection, weakened accountability, potential fraud under a shared identity. Compliance impact: relates to CIS SAP 1.2.6 and general access-accountability expectations. This is a lower-severity, defence-in-depth control rather than a critical exposure, and a legitimate exception list is often required for administrators.
Affected Items (1)
  • login/disable_multi_gui_login = 0
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Review the current value in RZ11 for login/disable_multi_gui_login. 2. In RZ10 edit the DEFAULT profile and set login/disable_multi_gui_login = 1 to prevent multiple concurrent GUI sessions per user. 3. Where specific accounts genuinely need multiple sessions (certain admins or technical monitors), list them in login/multi_login_users as a controlled, documented exception rather than disabling the whole control. 4. Save and activate the DEFAULT profile; the login/* parameters are dynamically switchable but persist them in the profile. 5. Verify the active value with RSPARAM and per-instance via RZ11, and confirm the exception list contents. 6. Use SM04/AL08 to review current active sessions and identify accounts routinely holding concurrent logons before enforcing, to avoid disrupting legitimate workflows. 7. Communicate to users that concurrent GUI sessions will be blocked and provide the exception process. 8. Combine with Security Audit Log monitoring so any concurrent-logon exceptions are visible. 9. Pilot in DEV/QA and coordinate with teams that use shared or multi-session workflows. 10. Re-run the scanner to confirm compliance.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark 1.2.6
LOW P4 · 8 Expired role assignments still present in user master IAM-EXP-002 ▶
Security Risk
This flags role assignments whose validity end-date has already passed but which are still physically present in the user master (AGR_USERS). SAP does enforce validity dates at runtime, so an expired assignment does not by itself grant access — which is why the severity is low — but leaving expired rows in place still matters. It pollutes the access baseline: SoD analysis, access reviews and audits become noisy and error-prone because the reported assignment set does not reflect effective access, and reviewers may waste effort on or be confused by stale entries. It can also mask reactivation risk — an administrator re-opening the validity window (or a mass job doing so) could silently restore access that everyone assumed was gone. The practical impact is data-quality and control-hygiene: accumulated expired assignments bloat AGR_USERS, complicate reporting, and reduce confidence that the access model is clean. A real incident is less a breach and more an audit friction point — reviewers cannot reconcile 'who has what' against the raw table, and an expired-but-present privileged role gets accidentally reactivated during a role-copy or mass-change operation.
Affected Items (6)
  • AGARCIA → Z_MM_BUYER (expired: 20260601, 74d ago)
  • AGARCIA → Z_MM_GR_POSTER (expired: 20260601, 74d ago)
  • DLEE → Z_SD_ORDER_MGMT (expired: 20251231, 226d ago)
  • TNGUYEN → Z_HR_PAYROLL (expired: 20241231, 591d ago)
  • KPATEL → Z_MM_BUYER_TEMP (expired: 20250401, 500d ago)
  • RMARTINEZ → Z_FI_POSTING (expired: 20260115, 211d ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Confirm the population from AGR_USERS (SE16N: TO_DAT earlier than today) and separate genuinely expired assignments from those with future or open validity. 2. Run report PRGN_COMPRESS_TIMES (SA38/SE38) with the option to delete expired assignments; it compresses and removes past-dated role/user links in AGR_USERS. 3. Run it in the correct system — on the CUA central system if Central User Administration is in use — and review its log of changes. 4. Schedule PRGN_COMPRESS_TIMES as a periodic background job (SM36) to keep the assignment table clean going forward. 5. After cleanup, run PFUD (user master comparison) so profiles are consistent. 6. Verify by re-extracting AGR_USERS and confirming expired rows are gone and no active access was affected. 7. Rollout caution: first run in simulation/QA and review the log, because compression can also merge overlapping validity intervals — confirm no still-valid assignment is inadvertently removed, and back up AGR_USERS before the first production run.
References
  • SAP Note 1763498 — AGR_USERS Cleanup
LOW P4 · 8 Custom roles without descriptions IAM-ROLE-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags custom (Z/Y) roles that have no description text. On its own a missing description is low severity, but it is a meaningful governance and maintainability weakness at scale. A role whose purpose is not documented cannot be effectively reviewed, recertified or safely modified: an access reviewer cannot judge whether the role is appropriate for a user if they cannot tell what it does, and a security administrator maintaining it risks adding or removing authorizations blindly. Undocumented roles tend to become 'mystery grants' that reviewers rubber-stamp because challenging them is too hard, which is exactly how inappropriate or over-broad access survives recertification. The scenario is slow decay rather than a direct attack: over years, undocumented custom roles proliferate, accumulate authorizations through copy-and-tweak maintenance, and nobody can confidently clean them up because their intent is lost — so privilege creep and SoD risk grow under a veil of poor documentation. Impact is degraded auditability and higher long-term risk of over-provisioning, and auditors do cite role documentation as part of access-governance quality. A real incident is an access review where dozens of Z-roles are approved without scrutiny because no one can explain them, later found to contain excessive or conflicting authorizations.
Affected Items (5)
  • Z_BC_TRANSPORT
  • Z_API_GW_FULL
  • Z_LEGACY_ROLE_01
  • Z_DECOM_2023
  • YTEST_ROLE
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract custom roles lacking descriptions from AGR_TEXTS / AGR_DEFINE (SE16N) or via SUIM to produce the work list. 2. In PFCG, open each custom role and add a meaningful description on the role definition, covering business process, intended user group and the approval/change reference. 3. Establish a role-documentation standard and enforce it in your role-build/change procedure so no new custom role is transported without a description. 4. Where GRC Business Role Management is used, capture the business rationale and owner alongside the technical role. 5. Prioritize privileged and financially significant roles first. 6. Verify by re-extracting AGR_TEXTS and confirming the custom-role description gap is closed for the prioritized set. 7. Rollout caution: description changes are low-risk but still travel by transport in a governed landscape — make them in DEV and transport through QA to PRD rather than editing directly in production, and align text with any existing naming/role-catalog conventions.
References
  • SAP Security Best Practices — Role Documentation
LOW P4 · 8 Custom roles with no menu/transaction assignments IAM-ROLE-003 ▶
Security Risk
This flags custom (Z/Y) roles whose menu/transaction count is zero — roles that contain no transactions. Empty roles are typically leftover artifacts: remnants of a role-redesign project, half-built roles that were never completed, or roles whose content was stripped but the shell was never deleted. On their own, empty roles grant little or nothing, so severity is low, but they degrade the cleanliness and trustworthiness of the role catalog. They inflate the number of roles that must be reviewed and maintained, confuse access reviewers and administrators, and occasionally mask risk — an 'empty' role may still carry authorization-tab objects even with no menu, or may later be re-populated and assigned without fresh review, quietly reintroducing access. The scenario is mostly hygiene and audit-noise: over time, dozens of empty Z-roles clutter the catalog, some remain assigned to users (implying assignments that convey no function and should be removed), and the sheer clutter makes it harder to reason about the access model. Impact is reduced maintainability and review efficiency, and a minor audit observation about catalog hygiene. A real incident is an access review bogged down by empty and near-empty roles, or an empty role being reused as a template and unexpectedly given content that bypasses the normal build/approval path.
Affected Items (5)
  • Z_RFC_FULL
  • Z_INT_ARIBA
  • Z_API_GW_FULL
  • Z_LEGACY_ROLE_01
  • Z_DECOM_2023
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Identify empty custom roles (menu/transaction count zero) via SUIM or by inspecting AGR_1251/AGR_DEFINE for roles with no menu entries. 2. For each, confirm in PFCG that the role truly has no menu and check the Authorizations tab in case objects exist without menu transactions. 3. Verify no users are assigned (AGR_USERS via SE16N); if users are assigned to a genuinely empty role, remove those pointless assignments (SU10). 4. Delete confirmed-empty, unused roles in PFCG following your change/transport process. 5. Add a step to your role-redesign/decommission procedure so retired roles are deleted, not just emptied. 6. Verify by re-extracting the catalog and confirming the empty roles are gone and no assignments were left dangling. 7. Rollout caution: ensure a role is truly obsolete before deletion (some 'empty' roles are deliberate org-level or value-role containers, or are referenced by composite roles); make changes in DEV and transport through QA, and keep the transport as a rollback point.
References
  • SAP Note 1763498
LOW P4 · 8 Active users in default/unassigned user groups IAM-USRGRP-001 ▶
Security Risk
This flags active (unlocked) users who sit in the default or an unassigned user group (blank, 000, DEFAULT or SUPER) in the CLASS field of USR02. The user group ('User Group for Authorization Check') is more than a label: it is an administrative-segmentation control enforced through authorization object S_USER_GRP, which governs who may maintain which users. When users are left in a default/blank group, that control layer is unusable for them — any administrator with broad S_USER_GRP can maintain them, and it becomes impossible to delegate or restrict user administration by segment (e.g. letting a regional admin manage only their region's users, or ring-fencing highly privileged accounts). Concentrating users in a catch-all group therefore weakens both least-privilege delegation and the protection of sensitive accounts. The scenario: because sensitive or privileged accounts are not segregated into a protected user group, a helpdesk-level administrator whose S_USER_GRP is not tightly scoped can reset passwords or modify high-value accounts (including admin IDs) they should not be able to touch, enabling privilege escalation or account takeover. Impact is weakened administrative segregation and a CIS SAP benchmark gap. A real incident looks like a lower-tier administrator resetting a privileged account's password because no user-group boundary existed to stop them, then using it to escalate.
Affected Items (4)
  • SAP* (group: 000)
  • DDIC (group: 000)
  • SAPCPIC (group: 000)
  • TMSADM (group: 000)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract users with blank/default user groups from USR02 (CLASS field, via SE16N or SUIM RSUSR002 by user group) and prioritize privileged accounts. 2. Define a meaningful user-group scheme (by region, function, or sensitivity — e.g. a protected group for admin/technical IDs) in transaction SUGR. 3. Assign users to the appropriate group via SU01 (Logon Data tab, 'User Group for Authorization Check') or mass via SU10. 4. Scope administrators' S_USER_GRP authorization to only the groups they should manage, so user administration is properly segmented and privileged accounts are protected. 5. Ensure highly privileged/technical accounts sit in a restricted group only senior admins can maintain. 6. Verify by re-extracting USR02 and confirming active users carry meaningful groups and that a test lower-tier admin can no longer maintain a protected account. 7. Rollout caution: changing user groups affects who can administer whom — coordinate with all user-administration teams, test the S_USER_GRP scoping in QA, and stage changes so you do not accidentally lock every admin out of a group of users.
References
  • CIS SAP Benchmark — User Group Management
LOW P4 · 8 Custom code that nothing reaches is still installed CODE-INV-002 ▶
Security Risk
6 of 15 custom object(s) have positive evidence that nothing reaches them: the inventory says nothing references them AND records no execution inside the last 365 days. Dead code is still installed code — it remains compiled and remains executable by anyone able to name it (SA38, an RFC-enabled function module, a job step), so whatever it contains stays on the attack surface. Removing it removes that content permanently, which is a stronger and cheaper outcome than hardening it in place. Reported at LOW rather than INFO because this is an actionable reduction of attack surface with a named object list, not a statistic; it is no higher than LOW because nothing is known to be wrong inside these objects and nothing currently calls them.
Affected Items (6)
  • Z_LEGACY_MIGRATION (PROG)
  • Z_MM_PO_UPLOAD (PROG)
  • Z_OBSOLETE_IDOC (PROG)
  • Z_OLD_REPORT_2019 (PROG)
  • Z_TEMP_FIX_2021 (PROG)
  • Z_TEST_PROGRAM_01 (PROG)
Remediation — Step by Step
Run this as a decommissioning campaign, not as individual tickets. Confirm disuse over a full business cycle first — year-end, statutory and disaster-recovery code can be genuinely dormant for months and still be needed — using ABAP Call Monitor (SCMON) usage data and the SAP custom-code migration/decommissioning tooling. Then delete the confirmed objects through the normal transport path so the removal is auditable and reversible.
References
  • SAP Security Baseline
  • SAP — Custom Code Lifecycle Management
  • SAP — ABAP Call Monitor (SCMON) usage data
LOW P4 · 8 Stale SAP modifications (5+ years old) CODE-MOD-003 ▶
Security Risk
SAP standard modifications more than five years old remain in place. Very old modifications are a maintenance and upgrade liability: the original developer and business rationale are usually gone, the modification predates numerous SAP corrections and Support Packages, and it may now conflict with, or silently re-open issues fixed by, current SAP code. Although lower severity, aged modifications accumulate into an unmanaged risk surface. The security-relevant danger is drift: a five-plus-year-old modification may have been made against an old version of a standard program that has since received security fixes. If the modification overrides or is reapplied over patched code, it can reintroduce a defect that SAP already remediated, or hold the object at an outdated, less-secure logic level. Because it is old and unreviewed, no one is watching for this interaction. Abuse/failure scenario: an SP or upgrade adjustment (SPAU) reapplies a stale modification over freshly patched standard code, reverting a security fix; because the modification is ancient and unexamined, the regression ships to production and remains until independently rediscovered. Business impact: upgrade friction and cost, and a latent chance of security regression or defect reintroduction. It is primarily a technical-debt and hygiene issue with a governance dimension: the organization cannot demonstrate that all deviations from standard are current and justified. A real incident is a post-upgrade regression traced to a long-forgotten modification that should have been retired years earlier.
Affected Items (3)
  • SAPLSU01 (type: PROG, by: LWANG) — modified: 20210315 (5 years ago)
  • SAPMHTTP (type: PROG, by: FORMER_DEV) — modified: 20190601 (7 years ago)
  • SAPLSTMS (type: PROG, by: ADMIN) — modified: 20200301 (6 years ago)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. List the stale modifications via the Modification Browser (transaction SE95) and confirm the age and current relevance of each. 2. For each, determine whether the original requirement still exists; contact the owning functional/development team for confirmation. 3. Retire modifications that are no longer needed by resetting the object to SAP standard (via SE95/SPAU). 4. For still-needed modifications, re-implement using a supported extension (BAdI/enhancement framework) where possible, then revert the core modification. 5. Re-validate any retained modification against the current standard code so it aligns with the latest SAP corrections and does not override a security fix. 6. Ensure all retained modifications are registered and documented so SPAU handles them correctly at the next upgrade. 7. Fold this review into the S/4HANA upgrade / custom-code adaptation project so stale items are actively decisioned rather than carried forward. 8. Verify by re-running SE95 and confirming the stale count is reduced and remaining items are documented and current. 9. Regression-test any reverted/replaced logic in QA before transporting DEV->QA->PRD. 10. Maintain a modification register and re-review ages periodically so modifications do not silently become stale again.
References
  • SAP Upgrade Guide — Modification Handling
LOW P4 · 8 Custom code objects without designated owner CODE-DEAD-002 ▶
Security Risk
Custom code objects have no designated owner (empty owner/responsible/created-by). Ownerless code is unmanaged code: when no team or individual is accountable for an object, it is not maintained, not patched, not reviewed for security, and not properly included in assessments or upgrade planning. It falls into a governance blind spot where problems accumulate unaddressed. The security relevance is that unowned objects are the ones most likely to retain latent vulnerabilities - missing authority checks, injection, hardcoded secrets, dangerous statements - because there is no one to triage or remediate findings against them. During a security assessment or S/4HANA migration, ownerless code cannot be validated (no one can confirm whether it is still needed, what it does, or whether it is safe), so it is often left in place by default, perpetuating risk. Abuse/failure scenario: an ATC/CVA scan flags a serious finding in an unowned object; because no owner exists, the finding is never assigned, never fixed, and eventually aged out or ignored - and the vulnerable object stays live and callable indefinitely. Attackers benefit from exactly this remediation gap. Business impact: weakened custom-code governance, slower and less reliable security remediation, and audit findings on change/ownership controls. While lower severity on its own, ownerlessness is a force-multiplier for every other custom-code risk. A real incident is a vulnerability that persisted only because the object it lived in had no owner to drive the fix.
Affected Items (6)
  • Z_FI_POSTING_BAPI (FUGR)
  • Z_OLD_REPORT_2019 (PROG)
  • Z_TEST_PROGRAM_01 (PROG)
  • Z_UTILS_COMMON (PROG)
  • Z_DATA_EXPORT (PROG)
  • Z_OBSOLETE_IDOC (PROG)
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Extract the list of ownerless objects and reconcile against the custom-code inventory and the SAP Custom Code Migration / ATC metadata. 2. Determine responsibility from available signals: created-by user, package/development-class assignment, transport history (who last changed it), and functional area. 3. Assign a named owning team (and ideally an individual/product owner) to every custom object; record ownership in the package/application metadata and in the code inventory register. 4. Where no owner can be found and the object is confirmed unused (via SCMON, see CODE-DEAD-001), route it for decommissioning rather than leaving it ownerless. 5. Establish a custom-code governance standard that no object may be transported without a designated owner, and enforce it as part of the transport/ATC release checklist. 6. Feed ownership into ATC/CVA so future security findings are automatically routed to the responsible team for remediation. 7. Include ownership review in the S/4HANA custom-code adaptation project so every retained object has an accountable owner. 8. Verify by re-running the inventory/ownership report and confirming the ownerless count is driven to zero (assigned or decommissioned). 9. Communicate assigned ownership to the development teams so they accept maintenance and remediation responsibility. 10. Periodically re-audit ownership (e.g., after reorganizations or offboarding) so objects do not become orphaned again.
References
  • SAP — Custom Code Governance
LOW P4 · 8 Security logs without archiving configured LOG-RET-002 ▶
Security Risk
This finding indicates one or more security log types have an online retention period but no archiving configured, so once retention expires the data is deleted permanently with no long-term copy anywhere. While day-to-day monitoring may be satisfied by online retention, several obligations require multi-year availability that online storage will not provide. Examples include SOX-adjacent financial record expectations, industry regulations, and litigation legal holds that can span several years. Without an archive, a legal hold or a long-running investigation simply cannot be satisfied - the evidence no longer exists. Online-only logs are also more exposed to tampering by a privileged administrator and to loss under storage pressure, whereas archives can be written to immutable/WORM media. Abuse and impact scenario: litigation triggers a legal hold requiring three-year-old access and change logs; only one year is available online and nothing is archived, creating spoliation risk and the possibility of an adverse-inference ruling. From a fraud-investigation angle, the absence of an immutable archive also means a determined insider who tampers with or reorganises online logs can destroy the only copy. Although rated lower severity because online logs may still serve near-term detection, the long-tail compliance and evidentiary exposure is real and typically surfaces at the worst possible moment - during an audit or a lawsuit.
Affected Items (3)
  • Security Audit Log (SM20): archiving not configured
  • System Log (SM21): archiving not configured
  • ICM Access Log: archiving not configured
Remediation — Step by Step
1. Configure archiving for each security log type instead of allowing outright deletion at retention expiry. 2. For the Security Audit Log, use RSAU_ADMIN reorganisation together with a SARA archive process for long-term storage. 3. For change documents, archive via the SARA archive object CHANGEDOCU; for table change logs, archive the DBTABLOG data. 4. Define an archive retention period aligned to compliance (for example seven years where financial-record rules or legal hold apply). 5. Store archives on immutable/WORM or otherwise access-restricted storage, and encrypt them. 6. For BTP, export retrieved audit logs to immutable object storage for the required horizon. 7. Verify the control by performing a test retrieval of an archived record (read SAL from archive, or view archived table changes via SCU3) to confirm the archive is usable and indexed. 8. Rollout caution: index archives for retrievability, and balance long retention against GDPR data-minimisation obligations. Reference SAP archiving (SARA) documentation and the applicable retention policy.
References
  • SAP — Log Archiving Configuration
INFO P4 · 14 SAP note check ran against a curated subset, not the full patch history HOTNEWS-COVERAGE ▶
Security Risk
This check compared the applied notes against 11 curated entries (10 HotNews, 1 High), the newest released 2025-04. It is NOT the full SAP Security Patch Day history, and a clean result here means none of those 11 is missing — not that the estate is fully patched. Notes released after 2025-04, and lower-priority notes at any date, were not assessed.
Affected Items (1)
  • catalogue of 11 notes, curated through 2025-04
Remediation — Step by Step
Confirm patch status against SAP Support Portal / Maintenance Planner for the periods this catalogue does not cover, and treat this check as a floor rather than a clearance.
References
  • SAP Security Patch Day
  • SAP Note 2871952 - Security Patch Day process
INFO P4 · 0 Further security parameters not found in export PARAM-MISSING-OTHER ▶
Security Risk
This finding lists CRITICAL/HIGH baseline parameters that were entirely absent from the export. Missing does not mean safe: when a parameter is not set in any profile the system silently uses the kernel default, and for many security parameters that default is weak or off. Concretely, if login/no_automatic_user_sapstar, rsau/enable, gw/sec_info or gw/reg_info are absent, the system may be exposed to the SAP* hard-coded backdoor, may have no security audit trail, and may have an unrestricted RFC gateway that permits remote registration and start of external programs - each of which is independently exploitable. The danger is compounded because operators frequently assume 'we didn't change it, so it's fine', when in fact the SAP-delivered default is the insecure state. In a RISE/ECS context these are precisely the application-layer controls the customer still owns, so leaving them at default is a customer-side gap that SAP's infrastructure controls do not cover. Attack scenario: an adversary who reaches the gateway port (3300/33NN) of a system with no reg_info/sec_info can register a malicious RFC server or start OS-level programs, achieving remote code execution as the <sid>adm user; separately, if no_automatic_user_sapstar is unset on an older release, deleting the SAP* master record re-activates SAP* with the default password PASS. Business impact spans full system compromise, undetectable fraud (no audit log), and audit findings for missing ITGC. A real incident would look like unexplained external program starts in SMGW logs, or an SAP* logon from an unexpected terminal, with no Security Audit Log to reconstruct events.

  • abap/ext_debugging_possible (Development Controls)

  • dbs/dba/ccms_security_level (Security Parameters)

Remediation — Step by Step
1. Take the affected-items list from this finding as the work list of parameters to explicitly set. 2. In RZ10 open the DEFAULT profile (system-wide) or the relevant instance profile in extended maintenance. 3. For each missing parameter, add it with the secure target value: login/no_automatic_user_sapstar=1, rsau/enable=1 (or configure via RSAU_CONFIG on 7.50+), gw/sec_info and gw/reg_info pointing to hardened ACL files, gw/reg_no_conn_info per SAP Note 1444282, and the password/lockout minimums from the other findings. 4. Confirm each parameter's exact meaning and allowed values first in RZ11 (it shows official documentation and whether the parameter is dynamically switchable). 5. Save and activate the profile; schedule the required instance restart during a maintenance window for static parameters (RZ11 flags which are dynamic). 6. For gateway ACL parameters, after placing the files reload them via SMGW -> Goto -> Expert Functions -> Reread (no restart needed). 7. Verify with report RSPARAM after restart that every previously-missing parameter now shows an explicit, compliant value rather than 'default'. 8. Roll out in DEV/QA first and coordinate with interface owners, because gateway and RFC hardening can break registered external programs if ACLs are wrong. 9. In RISE/ECS raise a change request to the SAP operations team for any parameter you cannot maintain directly. 10. Re-export parameters and re-run the scanner to confirm PARAM-MISSING is cleared.
INFO P4 · 0 Transaction-level SoD deferred to permission-level analysis IAM-SOD-DEFERRED ▶
Security Risk
Transaction-level Segregation of Duties analysis did not run here because the AGR_1251 authorization export (role_auth_values) is available and the Access Risk Analysis module performs the same analysis at permission level — matching on authorization object, field and activity rather than transaction code alone. That is strictly more precise and does not raise the display-only false positives this coarser check produces. SoD results for this run are the ARA-* findings.
Affected Items (1)
  • Advanced IAM SoD rules (IAM-SOD-*)
Remediation — Step by Step
No action. This records why one module is quiet so that an empty IAM-SOD-* result is not read as an absence of SoD conflicts. To run the coarser transaction-level check anyway, exclude the 'ara' module or omit the role_auth_values export.

INFO P4 · 0 Trust user admission could not be assessed from this export IAM-FEDCOV-002 ▶
Security Risk
2 trust configurations in this subaccount can authenticate users interactively and carry no attribute stating which users of their identity provider they admit — under any of the attribute names this check reads (userRestriction, allowedUsers, allowedUserDomains, allowedDomains). The question IAM-FED-002 exists to answer was therefore not answered for them. This is a gap in the evidence and not a verdict: a trust in this state may be scoped to a single named group, or may admit every contractor, B2B guest and service identity the provider will authenticate, and this scan cannot tell which. It is stated explicitly because the alternative — a federation section with no admission finding in it — reads as 'admission was checked and is fine', which is the one thing it does not mean.
Affected Items (2)
  • Trust: sap.default — no user-admission attribute in the export
  • Trust: corp-aad-tenant — no user-admission attribute in the export
Remediation — Step by Step
Two steps, and the second one matters whether or not the first works. First, re-export the trust configurations as the full objects the platform returns rather than a summarised subset (docs/EXPORT_GUIDE.md, btp_trust) and re-run the scan; the attribute names this check reads are listed in this finding's details, so if your export names the restriction differently that difference is a gap in this scanner and can be reported as one. Second — because no export shape we have seen carries it — verify the control directly with the identity-provider owner: confirm that the application or assertion issued to this subaccount is scoped to a named group or directory branch rather than to every user the provider will authenticate; in IAS, that is the conditional authentication rules on the corresponding application. Record that verification with this scan so the gap is closed by evidence rather than by silence.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — Trust Configuration
  • SAP Security Baseline — Identity Federation
INFO P4 · 0 Identity federation certificate expiry could not be assessed from this export IAM-FEDCOV-003 ▶
Security Risk
Of the 2 trust configurations this scan could name in this export, 2 carry no certificate-expiry attribute at all, under any of the attribute names this check reads (certificateExpiryDate, certificateValidTo, signingCertificateExpiry, certificate_expiry, certificateExpiry). The expiry of the certificate that signs each federation listed below is therefore unknown to this scan. That is a gap in the evidence and not a verdict — the certificates may have years left, or may already have lapsed. It is stated because a certificate lapse takes single sign-on down for every user of the trust at once, the standing workaround is to re-enable the default or local identity provider under outage pressure, and a report that is silent about expiry is read as a report that checked it.
Affected Items (2)
  • Trust: sap.default — no certificate-expiry attribute in the export
  • Trust: corp-aad-tenant — no certificate-expiry attribute in the export
Remediation — Step by Step
Re-export the trust configurations as the full objects the platform returns rather than a summarised subset (docs/EXPORT_GUIDE.md, btp_trust) and re-run the scan; this finding's details list the attribute names the check reads and the values it could not parse, so an export that names the expiry differently can be reported as a gap in this scanner. Meanwhile, do not wait for the scan to tell you: ask the identity-provider owner for the validity end of each trust's signing certificate and put those dates in the change calendar. Renewal needs the identity-provider owner and the subaccount owner together, so it is scheduled work — a certificate discovered on the day it lapses cannot be renewed on that day.
References
  • SAP BTP Security Guide — Trust Configuration
  • SAP Security Baseline — Identity Federation

INFO P4 · 0 Custom-code estate inventory CODE-INV-001 ▶
Security Risk
The custom-code inventory lists 15 object(s) across 3 object type(s). Of these, 9 have positive evidence that something reaches them, 6 have positive evidence that nothing does, and 0 carry no evidence either way. This is a measurement, not a defect: it is the denominator every other custom-code number in this report is a fraction of, and it is the custom-application register that platform hardening starts from — under RISE the entire custom estate is the customer's responsibility, and nobody else is counting it.
Affected Items (3)
  • PROG — 12 object(s)
  • FUGR — 2 object(s)
  • CLAS — 1 object(s)
Remediation — Step by Step
Nothing to fix. Publish this inventory as part of the system documentation and re-take it each release, so growth in the custom estate is a number somebody owns rather than something discovered during an upgrade. Objects counted here are the population the ATC / code-scanning checks in this report should be covering.

INFO P4 · 0 Custom code with no recent recorded execution CODE-INV-003 ▶
Security Risk
15 of 15 custom object(s) have no execution recorded within the last 365 days; 6 of them carry no usable execution date at all. Dormancy is NOT unreachability: 9 of these are still referenced by other objects and are therefore reachable — code that can run and simply is not running. The horizon is the same one this report's reachability verdicts use, so this count and the priority given to a code finding about the same object cannot disagree. Treat the number as scoping information for a custom-code review: it is where the review should start, not a list of defects.

Remediation — Step by Step
Read this against how usage data was collected. If ABAP Call Monitor (SCMON) collection was switched on recently, or the export was taken over a short window, 'dormant' here means 'not observed' rather than 'not used' — widen the collection window before acting. Where dormancy is confirmed over a full business cycle, fold the objects into the custom-code decommissioning backlog.
